under normal physiological conditions (Arraiano et al., 2010; Chung et al., 2010; Viegas and Arraiano, 2008). Nonetheless, both enzymes are required for the two-step sequential maturation reaction of the 16S rRNA 5′ end (Arraiano et al., 2010). 

RNase Y is a single-strand specific endoribonuclease present in B. subtilis, which prefers $5 ^ { \prime }$ monophosphorylated RNA substrates (Shahbabian et al., 2009). The absence of the RNase Y gene (rny) results in the accumulation of several mRNAs, including several transcriptional regulators of stress responses and biofilm formation (Lehnik-Habrink et al., 2011). In this bacterium, RNase Y was shown to interact with both RNase J1 and RNase III, thereby controlling the amount of total mRNAs (Durand et al., 2012a). Furthermore, as already mentioned, RNase Y interacts with RNase J1 in a degradosome-like complex (Commichau et al., 2009). RNase Y orthologs, despite being identified in 40% of the eubacteria, are not present in either archaea or eukaryotic organisms, except in Drosophila willistoni (Arraiano et al., 2010). 

RNase III was the first dsRNA-specific endoribonuclease to be discovered (Robertson et al., 1968). Since then, it has been shown that RNase III is widely distributed among other organisms, being the prototype of the RNase III family (Arraiano et al., 2010). Like the other members of its family, RNase III is a hydrolytic enzyme capable of degrading dsRNAs yielding both a 5′ monophosphate end and a 2 nt overhang in the 3′ hydroxyl terminus (Meng and Nicholson, 2008). In E. coli, RNase III is encoded by the rnc gene and plays an essential role not only in rRNA and tRNA maturation but also in mRNA decay (Arraiano et al., 2010). Even though RNase III is not essential in this bacterium, rnc mutant cells grow slower when compared to the wild-type strains. This RNase is involved in the formation of the 16S and 23S rRNAs by processing the 30S rRNA precursor (Arraiano et al., 2010). In similar fashion to the eukaryotic RNase III orthologs, Dicer and Drosha, the E. coli RNase III is also involved in translational silencing. However, whereas Dicer and Drosha have a role in micro-RNA (miRNA) maturation, RNase III is involved in the degradation of small RNA (sRNA)– mRNA complexes (Denli et al., 2004; Meng and Nicholson, 2008). RNase III also acts as a stress modulator controlling the steady-state level of genes involved in cellular adaptation to stress (Arraiano et al., 2010). In B. subtilis, this RNase was shown to be essential (Durand et al., 2012b). 

In E. coli, there are three main exoribonucleases involved in RNA decay: PNPase, RNase R, and RNase II. All these enzymes degrade RNA processively and nonspecifically from the 3′ end. The action of these enzymes is often stimulated by the addition of poly(A) tails to the 3′ end of the RNA molecules. 

PNPase belongs to the PDX family of exoribonucleases. This RNase is encoded by the pnp gene and has processive, sequenceindependent, phosphorolytic activity, being capable of synthesizing and degrading ssRNA, depending on the conditions (Arraiano et al., 2010). The phosphorolytic activity exerted by PNPase requires a 3′ overhang of 7–9 nt of RNA, frequently stalling in the presence of structured RNAs (Carpousis et al., 

2008). Nonetheless, folded RNAs, such as sRNAs, can also be targeted by PNPase if a 3 polyadenylated tail is present. PNPase can associate with other enzymes in the degradosome, which is capable of degrading highly structured RNAs (Arraiano et al., 2010). PNPase is known to be implicated in the posttranscriptional regulation of several sRNAs, having a preponderant role in their degradation (Andrade and Arraiano, 2008; De Lay and Gottesman, 2011), with the steady-state levels of several sRNAs being increased in pnp mutants (Saramago et al., 2014a). Moreover, E. coli PNPase is a cold shock protein (CSP), essential at low temperatures (Awano et al., 2008). 

The E. coli RNB family of enzymes is present in all domains of life and includes RNase II, RNase R, and the eukaryotic Rrp44/Dis3, Dis3L1, and Dis3L2 proteins (Lathem, 2014). These proteins have a cold shock domain (CSD) at the N-terminal region and a C-terminal S1 domain, both involved in RNA binding. They also have a central RNB domain responsible for the catalytic activity (Lathem, 2014). RNase II is encoded by the rnb gene, which can be transcribed from two promoters, P1 and P2, and terminates in a Rho-independent terminator 10 nucleotides downstream of the rnb stop codon (Arraiano et al., 2010). This enzyme hydrolyses RNA in the $3 ^ { \prime } { - } 5 ^ { \prime }$ direction in a processive way. In E. coli, RNase II is the major hydrolytic enzyme and participates in the terminal stages of mRNA degradation. However, it is not capable of cleaving secondary structures and halts when the transcript is double-stranded. Moreover, RNase II is not essential in this bacterium unless PNPase is also missing (Arraiano et al., 2010). RNase R is encoded by the rnr gene and was shown to be involved in several cellular processes. This RNase is able to unwind and degrade RNA secondary structures, a critical process at low temperatures (Barria ´ et al., 2013). RNase R takes part in the degradation of mRNAs, and plays an important role in the removal of mRNAs with stable stem loops, such as repetitive extragenic palindromic (REP) elements (Cheng and Deutscher, 2005). This RNase has an important role in RNA quality control, namely in the degradation of defective tRNAs. Together with PNPase, RNase R also eliminates aberrant fragments of the 16S and 23S rRNAs (Arraiano et al., 2010). RNase R is considered a stress response enzyme, with its levels being increased in several stresses, such as cold shock, stationary phase, and heat shock (Cairrao˜ et al., 2003; Chen and Deutscher, 2005). 

Besides the individual action of RNases, cells contain complexes that are important in RNA processing and/or degradation. The degradosome is a large multiprotein complex in which the components contribute to the efficient degradation of mRNA. 

In E. coli, the degradosome is formed by two RNases, PNPase and RNase E; the adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-dependent RhlB helicase; and the glycolytic enzyme enolase (Arraiano et al., 2010). RNase E provides the organizing scaffold for the degradosome. The C-terminal half of RNase E has four segments (A, B, C, and D) with different roles in the degradosome assembly. The segment A localizes the complex to the inner cytoplasmatic membrane, whereas a 69-residue conserved segment downstream of segment B is the binding site of the RhlB helicase. Segment C is the binding site of the enzyme enolase, and segment D interacts with PNPase (Arraiano et al., 2010). RhlB helicase assists in the function of both RNase E and PNPase by unwinding extensively structured RNAs (Carpousis, 2007). The role of the glycolytic enzyme enolase in the degradosome is still unclear (Arraiano et al., 2010). 

The degradosome composition changes depending on the microorganism and/or growth condition. In E. coli, upon a temperature drop, RNase E can interact, simultaneously or not, with both the RhlB and DeaD helicases (Barria ´ et al., 2013). In Pseudomonas syringae, RNase E interacts with another helicase, RhlE, and with the exoribonuclease RNase R, instead of PNPase (Arraiano et al., 2010). Moreover, in Helicobacter pylori, a minimal degradosome complex consisting of RNase J and rhpA, an RNA helicase was described (Redko et al., 2013). Another degradosome-like complex was suggested to exist in B. subtilis, composed of RNase J1 (which interacts with RNase J2), PNPase, RNase Y, the helicase CshA, and the glycolytic enzymes enolase and phosphofructokinase (Commichau et al., 2009). 

## 2.13.2 Adaptation to temperature changes

Bacteria have to constantly adapt to changes in the environment, such as temperature fluctuations (either heat or cold shock). A proper response enables the cell to counteract these unfavorable changes, mostly by the selective production of proteins, depending on the temperature. 

## 2.13.2.1 Heat shock

The heat shock response in bacteria is triggered by a temperature upshift, usually from $3 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } \ \mathrm { t o } \ 4 2 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . It is characterized by the rapid induction of heat shock proteins (HSPs), up to 15-fold, followed by an adaptation period where the production rate of this group of proteins decreases until a new steady-state level is reached (Bukau, 1993; see Section 14). In E. coli, this response is under the control of the alternative sigma factor, RpoH $( \sigma ^ { 3 2 } )$ (Yura et al., 1993). In other microorganisms, the same group of proteins is induced, but the regulatory mechanisms are not identical (Rasouly and Ron, 2009). An upshift in the temperature leads to a transient increase in $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ transcription as well as to a stabilization of the $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ protein level, which is normally unstable. $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ directs the transcription from the heat shock promoter, leading to an increase of HSPs (Morita et al., 1999). This group of proteins is mainly composed of chaperones such as DnaK, DnaJ, GrpE, ClpB, HtpG, IbpA, IbpB, GroEL, and GroES, but it also includes proteases like Lon, ClpAP, ClpXP, HslUV, and FtsH (Wick and Egli, 2004; see Chapters 4.3, 13.4, 14.1, 14.2, 14.3). FtsH plays the major role in the heat shock adaptation since it is the protease responsible for the degradation of $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ (Herman et al., 1995). The exact role of RNases during an increase in temperature is not clearly understood. However, there are a few reports relating an eventual connection of RNases with heat stress (Figure 2.13.1). 

RNase E has been shown to co-precipitate with GroEL, a chaperone that is heat shock induced (Sohlberg et al., 1993). GroEL is required for the proper folding of many proteins and interacts functionally with an RNase E–like activity. When subjected to heat shock conditions, in the groEL mutant cells the amount of 9S RNA was increased when compared with the control cells (Sohlberg et al., 1993). 

RNase E and RNase III were shown to be involved in the degradation of the heat shock protein dnaK. When compared to the wild-type strain of E. coli, there was an increase of 2.3- fold in the RNase E mutant cells and 1.3-fold in the RNase III mutant cells (Stead et al., 2011), suggesting that these RNases play an important role in the degradation of this mRNA. 

RNase R is an RNase that is induced in several stress conditions and was shown to be induced 2-fold upon shifting to $4 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in E. coli strains (Chen and Deutscher, 2005). 

In other bacteria, such as B. subtilis, it has been shown that upon heat shock, the sRNA bsrG is rapidly degraded (Jahn et al., 2012). This sRNA is part of the toxin–antitoxin system, bsrG– SR4. The bsrG RNA encodes an acid toxin, whereas SR4 is an antisense RNA that acts as the antitoxin (Jahn et al., 2012). Both bsrG RNA and SR4 are degraded by RNase Y and RNase R, and PNPase processes three antisense SR4 precursors to the mature RNA form (Jahn et al., 2012). 

In Thermus thermophilus, a Gram-negative bacterium, the PNPase homolog (Tth PNPase) was shown to have phosphorolytic activity at the optimal temperature of $6 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . In fact, this enzyme is able to completely degrade RNAs with very stable intramolecular secondary structures (Falaleeva et al., 2008). 

## 2.13.2.2 Cold shock

In bacteria, the cold shock response is triggered by an abrupt drop of temperature, usually from its optimum growth temperature to a lower temperature (around $1 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ . Upon temperature downshift, there is a stabilization of the nucleic acids’ secondary structures. This phenomenon ultimately results in a reduced efficiency of RNA transcription, translation, and degradation (Barria´ et al., 2013; see Chapters 15.1, 15.5, 15.6, 15.8). To counteract these changes, the cell begins an adaptation process termed the acclimation phase. During the acclimation phase, there is a transient arrest of cell growth for 3 to 6 hours in which the production of most proteins stops. As an exception, there is an increase of a specific group of proteins that are induced in this stress condition, the CSPs (Polissi et al., 2003). After this stage, the cells become adapted to the cold, the CSP’s protein production is reduced, and the bulk of protein synthesis restarts (Barria´ et al., 2013). 

The majority of the CSPs are involved in RNA metabolism, including the proteins from the Csp family and the ribonucleases RNase R and PNPase. The Csp family of proteins acts mainly as nucleic acid chaperones, preventing secondary structure formation and, as a result, enabling RNase cleavage (Barria´ et al., 2013; see Section 14). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/b90a586075149d5266355c07ede587fcd25462361b4e991ddb7816efbd3cac9f.jpg)



Figure 2.13.1 Interaction network between different stresses and the RNases that modulate stress adaptation responses. PNPase, RNase R, and RNase II are exoribonucleases, whereas RNase Y, RNase J1/J2, RNase III, RNase E, and RNase G are endoribonucleases. These ribonucleases affect the bacterial responses to heat and cold shock; the adaptation to the stationary phase, biofilms, and interaction with other cells; the survival of bacteria despite osmotic, oxidative, and acidic stresses; as well as the control of toxin–antitoxin and metal resistance systems. An outward arrow indicates the participation of the respective RNase in a given stress response.


Upon temperature downshift, RNase R increases its level about 10-fold (Andrade et al., 2009; Cairrao˜ et al., 2003). Its main role in the cold relies on the ability to degrade secondary structures. In fact, due to its ability to unwind secondary structures, the E. coli RNase R is the only exoribonuclease capable of processively digesting dsRNA without the assistance of a helicase. This capacity was shown to be dependent on RNase R CSDs (Awano et al., 2010) and enables this RNase to suppress a DeaD– CsdA deletion phenotype in the cold (Phadtare, 2012). In P. syringae and Pseudomonas putida, RNase R was shown to be essential for growth at low temperatures (Purusharth et al., 2007; Reva et al., 2006). Moreover, in P. syringae, RNase R substitutes the PNPase in the degradosome, with rnr mutant cells displaying an accumulation of unprocessed 16S and 5S rRNA (Purusharth et al., 2007). 

PNPase increases its level about 2-fold during cold shock and is extremely important for E. coli during cold survival (Awano et al., 2008; Zangrossi et al., 2000). At the end of the acclimation phase, this RNase is required to repress the production of the Csps family of proteins by promoting the degradation of the csp mRNA. In fact, at low temperatures, cells lacking pnp maintain a high level of Csps proteins, even after 24 hours (Yamanaka and Inouye, 2001). PNPase selective degradation is required for the transition from the cold shock acclimation phase to the cell growth resumption stage (Barria´ et al., 2013; Yamanaka and Inouye, 2001). Moreover, it has been shown that the catalytic domains of PNPase are essential at low temperatures and that pnp deletion inhibits cell growth in cold conditions (Awano et al., 2008). In strains lacking pnp, it was investigated whether in cold conditions its function could be complemented by other 

RNases. In fact, it was shown that its function could be complemented by RNase II, but not by RNase R (Awano et al., 2008). 

CspE, a member of the csp family of E. coli, is a poly(A)- binding protein, and when CspE binds to the poly-A tails it prevents their cleavage by PNPase and also inhibits internal cleavage by RNase E (Barria ´ et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2001). Moreover, it was shown that cspE mRNA had a 4-fold increase in the RNase E mutant cells and a 2.2-fold increase in the RNase III mutant cells, when compared to the wild-type strain (Stead et al., 2011) (see Chapter 15.4). 

RNase E was also shown to be associated with another cold shock protein, DeaD. This protein is a DEAD-box helicase that probably helps to degrade structured RNAs (Barria ´ et al., 2013). Furthermore, under cold conditions, this helicase is incorporated into the degradosome (Prud’homme-Genereux et al., 2004). The degradosome helicase, RhlB, is still detected, which suggests that both helicases associate with RNase E in the cold (Khemici et al., 2004) or that cold shock cells have a heterogeneous population of degradosomes (Prud’homme-Genereux et al., 2004). 

## 2.13.3 Stationary phase

In their natural habitat, bacteria stay mostly in the stationary phase due to nutrient limitation (Kolter et al., 1993). The longterm survival of bacteria depends, therefore, upon the establishment of defense systems against various stresses. It is expected that the cells stop the transcription of most of their genes as a defense mechanism, but some genes need to be upregulated (Navarro Llorens et al., 2010). Most of these upregulated genes are stress related and will confer resistance to the harsh conditions subsequent to the stationary phase. It is well known that bacteria undergo physical and morphological changes when entering the stationary phase (Hengge-Aronis, 1999; Ishihama, 1997). The extensive transcriptomic rearrangement necessary for the cells’ adaptation requires not only a transcriptional adjustment but also modulation of the RNA stability. RNases are essential for controlling RNA degradation and, therefore, play a crucial role in the cellular adaptation to the stationary phase. 

A global study involving all the RNases of T. thermophilus suggested that the endoribonucleases might have a more relevant role in the exponential phase, whereas the exoribonucleases, namely RNase R and PNPase, act mainly during the stationary phase (Ohyama et al., 2014). In E. coli, RNase R has also been shown to significantly affect gene expression in the stationary phase (Andrade et al., 2006). RNase R is a stress-induced exoribonuclease, and its activity is 10-fold higher in the stationary phase than in the exponential phase (Andrade et al., 2006; Chen and Deutscher, 2005). However, the higher levels of RNase R activity are not due to an increase in its transcription, but rather to a stabilization of the protein itself (Chen and Deutscher, 2010; Liang and Deutscher, 2012; Liang et al., 2011). This stabilization in the stationary phase depends on the acetylating enzyme Pka, which in turn is regulated under stress conditions (Liang and Deutscher, 2012; Liang et al., 2011). As for PNPase, its role in the stationary phase has been mainly linked to the degradation of sRNAs (Andrade and Arraiano, 2008; Andrade et al., 2012). It is noteworthy that the vast majority of the known sRNAs are upregulated in stress conditions, including the stationary phase. Moreover, sRNAs are able to control multiple targets, which is therefore a very efficient way for the cell to rapidly adjust its transcriptome (Andrade et al., 2013). Consequently, the role of PNPase in the stationary phase is of great importance because the degradation of sRNAs can greatly affect the expression levels of several different mRNAs. Namely, the sRNA ssrS (6S) is a transcript that is essential for adaptation to the stationary phase. The 6S RNA binds to both $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ (rpoD, the σ subunit involved in the transcription of most genes during exponential growth) and RNA polymerase, thereby suppressing the $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ -dependent transcription during the stationary phase (Wassarman and Storz, 2000). Although no study has yet determined the degradation pathway for this sRNA, it has been already shown that ssrS is processed by the endoribonucleases RNase E and RNase G (Kim and Lee, 2004). 

One of the most important upregulated transcripts in the stationary phase is the sigma factor rpoS (σs ), with the protein levels being 30% higher in the stationary phase than in the exponential phase (Jishage and Ishihama, 1995). RpoS interacts with RNA polymerase and controls the expression of about 10% of the E. coli genome (Battesti et al., 2011). RNase E and RNase III were shown to be involved in the degradation of the rpoS mRNA (Basineni et al., 2009; Freire et al., 2006; McCullen et al., 2010). 

The RNases are, therefore, important modulators of the stationary phase (Figure 2.13.1), affecting the expression of several genes essential for the bacterial adaptation to this growth condition. 

## 2.13.4 Biofilms

Under certain conditions, bacteria can aggregate into communities known as biofilms. This multicellular lifestyle is accompanied by the production of an extracellular matrix, which promotes intercellular adhesion and provides protection to the bacteria (Flemming and Wingender, 2010; see Section 22). However, biofilms are a cause of many medical and technological problems and can lead to persistent infections (Costerton et al., 1999). Although biofilms can be an advantage for bacteria, they are also a source of stress (see Chapters 22.4, 22.5, 22.8). Due to cellular superposition, the bacteria present in a biofilm need to adapt to several stressful conditions, such as nutrient starvation, oxygen limitation, and accumulation of waste products that can cause an increase in the pH of the surrounding environment (Serra and Hengge, 2014). It is, therefore, not surprising that many of the stationary-phase and stress-induced genes are also triggered in a biofilm environment (Schembri et al., 2003). One such genes is the stress response master regulator rpoS, which, as mentioned, is degraded by both RNase E and RNase III (Basineni et al., 2009; Freire et al., 2006; McCullen et al., 2010). Moreover, like in the stationary phase, there are several sRNAs that are upregulated in biofilms (Mika and Hengge, 2013, 2014). Most of these sRNAs were shown to be degraded by PNPase, RNase E, and RNase III (Saramago et al., 2014a). 

The RNases greatly affect biofilm formation. In E. coli, deletion mutants for RNase II and RNase R formed more biofilms than the wild type, whereas a PNPase deletion mutant did not form any biofilm, thus suggesting that PNPase might be essential for biofilm formation in E. coli (Pobre and Arraiano, 2015). In Salmonella Typhimurium RNase II, PNPase, RNase E, and RNase III also significantly affected biofilm formation (Saramago et al., 2014b), while in B. subtilis the sole overexpression of RNase Y was sufficient to induce its formation (Lehnik-Habrink et al., 2011). The role of the RNases in the biofilm formation might be even more important if we consider the fact that bacterial biofilms are associated with resistance to antibiotics (McCarthy et al., 2015). In fact, several RNases have been already described to affect the susceptibility of bacteria against ribosome-targeting antibiotics (Saramago et al., 2014b; Song et al., 2014). 

## 2.13.5 Interaction with other cells

The interaction of bacterial pathogens with their host cells can be considered a stressful condition because the bacteria will need to adapt to the new environment and even evade the defenses of the host cells. During the host cell invasion process, bacteria will express several specific genes that will allow their survival. The role of the RNases in the regulation of these virulence genes has been studied. PNPase’s role in the establishment of virulence in several pathogens has been well described (Matos et al., 2012; Rosenzweig and Chopra, 2013). In Salmonella enterica, PNPase activity decreases the expression of genes belonging to pathogenicity islands (Clements et al., 2002), while in Dichelobacter nodosus, PNPase acts as a virulence repressor in benign strains (Palanisamy et al., 2009). In Yersinia spp., PNPase modulates the type three secretion system (TTSS), and the pnp deletion mutant is less virulent than the wild type (Rosenzweig et al., 2005, 2007). In Campylobacter jejuni, a PNPase mutant showed decreased motility (Haddad et al., 2009) and a reduced ability to adhere and invade host cells (Haddad et al., 2012). Also, in Streptococcus pyogenes, PNPase affects the decay of sagA and sda, which code for important virulence factors (Barnett et al., 2007). Interestingly, these two virulence factors are also affected by the RNases J1 and J2 in S. pyogenes (Bugrysheva and Scott, 2010). Another RNase with a well-established role in virulence is RNase R (Matos et al., 2012, 2014). In Shigella flexneri, RNase R was shown to be important for the expression of several invasion factors (Tobe et al., 1992). Moreover, in Legionella pneumophila and Mycoplasma genitalium, RNase R is the only hydrolytic exoribonuclease present, and it is essential for both growth and competence (Charpentier et al., 2008; Hutchison et al., 1999). In Aeromonas hydrophila, the absence of RNase R leads to a reduction in motility and virulence (Erova et al., 2008). In Streptococcus pneumoniae, there is a unique homolog of the RNase II family of enzymes that was shown to be an RNase R–like protein (Domingues et al., 2009). RNase R was also shown to be important for the first steps of infection of C. jejuni in eukaryotic cells (Haddad et al., 2014). RNase Y also plays a significant role in the mRNA processing of virulence genes in S. pyogenes (Chen et al., 2013; Kang et al., 2010), and in Staphylococcus aureus this RNase is involved in the activation of several virulence genes (Marincola et al., 2012). RNase E and RNase III affect Salmonella enterica motility and proliferation inside the host cells (Viegas et al., 2013). Moreover, RNase III also regulates virulence genes’ expression in S. aureus (Huntzinger et al., 2005; Lioliou et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2011). 

All these studies demonstrate how important RNases are to pathogenic bacteria and how they influence their ability to invade and survive inside the host cells. 

## 2.13.6 Osmotic stress

In bacteria, internal osmolality control mechanisms generate cell turgor, which is usually perceived as the driving force for both cellular expansion and division (Csonka, 1989). Generally, in order to sustain this outward force, the intracellular osmotic pressure must be greater than the one found in the extracellular environment. In the case of hyperosmotic shock, this condition is maintained by accumulating osmoprotectants such as glycine betaine and glutamate (Csonka, 1989; Gowrishankar and Manna, 1996; see Chapters 11.1 to 11.4). 

In the majority of the Enterobacteriaeceae family, the proU operon encodes an ABC transport system that specializes in the uptake of the osmoprotectants glycine betaine and proline betaine (Gowrishankar and Manna, 1996; Kavalchuk et al., 2012). For numerous years, the underlying mechanisms responsible for the regulation of this operon were not fully understood. Recent work on this subject in E. coli has demonstrated that, under low-osmolality conditions, the enzyme RNase III processes the proU mRNA, effectively removing it from the cellular RNA pool (Kavalchuk et al., 2012). Furthermore, under similar settings, RNase III has also been implicated in the degradation of the hyperosmolality-induced bdm, betT, and proP mRNAs (Lim and Lee, 2015; Sim et al., 2010, 2014). It was likewise demonstrated that hyperosmotic stress thwarts RNase III activity, a phenomenon that ultimately results in an increased cellular level of PNPase (Sim et al., 2010). This RNase III absence of activity at high-osmolality conditions has caused some authors to speculate about the existence of an unidentified, high-osmolality-induced RNase III inhibitor (Sim et al., 2010). 

Collectively, these new studies on osmoregulatory systems demonstrate that RNase III, under low-osmolality stress conditions, may act as a central posttranscriptional regulatory hub, efficiently adapting the cell’s response to rapidly changing osmotic environments. 

## 2.13.7 Oxidative stress

When exposed to oxidative stress, E. coli exhibited a decrease in growth and protein synthesis, altogether with an increase in protein degradation (Davies and Lin, 1988; see Section 10). 

The adaptive response to oxidative stress in bacteria is coordinated by two major transcriptional regulators, OxyR and SoxRS (Lushchak, 2011). OxyR responds to hydrogen peroxide induction, and SoxRS responds to superoxide anion induction. The products from the genes regulated by OxyR and SoxRS are implicated in the prevention of oxidative damage. 

PNPase was suggested to be indispensable in E. coli strains under oxidative stress. This RNase binds to RNA treated with hydrogen peroxide $\left( \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \right)$ with higher affinity than untreated RNA. In fact, in the presence of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ , cells lacking the pnp gene had a reduction in their growth and accumulated oxidatively damaged RNA. Cellular viability was restored when complemented with a plasmid containing the pnp gene. The PNPase role in the oxidative stress was shown to be in a degradosomeindependent fashion, because RNase E mutant cells lacking the PNPase-binding site did not lose cell viability under this stress (Wu et al., 2009). 

## 2.13.8 Acidic stress

The existence of acid resistance mechanisms enables the survival and proliferation of bacteria in low-pH environments. This phenomenon is of particular importance in enteric pathogens, such as Shigella spp. and Listeria monocytogenes, since any invading species must first endure, and survive, a gastric pH of 2 before reaching the less acidic intestinal habitat. The necessity for a swift and effective acid adaptation is, therefore, paramount (Cotter et al., 2001; Cotter and Hill, 2003; Foster, 2004; Gordeb and Small, 1993; see Section 16). 

The most prominent acid response mechanism in several bacteria species is the glutamate decarboxylase system (GAD), whose modus operandi is based on the export of protons via incorporation in glutamate acid (Castanie-Cornet et al., 1999; Cotter and Hill, 2003; Karatzas et al., 2012). This system’s regulatory network is complex, being targeted by several layers of posttranscriptional control (Chen et al., 2015). Among these, particular interest goes into the influence of the RNasemediated RNA-processing pathway on the translation rate of several GADs’ RNAs. For example, in E. coli, RNase E and RNase III have been individually implicated in the maturation and processing of both the sRNA gadY and its target, the gadX–gadW transcript (Opdyke et al., 2004, 2011; Takada et al., 2007). Moreover, it was recently demonstrated in Streptococcus mutans that the RNases J1 and J2 severely affect cell survival in pH 5 conditions (Chen et al., 2015). Taken altogether, these reports hint to the existence of an as-yet-poorly understood RNasemediated posttranscriptional control network in the acid response system. 

## 2.13.9 Toxin–antitoxin

Toxin–antitoxin (TA) systems are associated with a plethora of distinct conditions, ranging from plasmid maintenance to stress responses. Typically, these systems encode both a stable toxin and an unstable, antagonist antitoxin, which can be either a protein or an antisense RNA (Blower et al., 2011; Jester et al., 2012; see Chapter 2.7 and Section 6). 

The enzyme RNase III seems to be essential for B. subtilis. This peculiarity has prompted Durand and coworkers to investigate the possible role of this enzyme in the TA systems, particularly the txpA–RatA and yonT–as-yonT systems (Durand et al., 2012b). In this case, the formation of RNA duplexes between txpA–RatA and yonT–as-yonT triggers rapid RNase III–mediated degradation and, consequently, protects B. subtilis from lysis, because the toxin mRNAs txpA and yonT will be degraded (Durand et al., 2012b; Fozo et al., 2010; Silvaggi et al., 2005). 

The constantly increasing number of characterized antisense RNAs may, in the near future, expose the enzyme RNase III as a fulcrum in the regulation of not only several TA systems (Blomberg et al., 1990; Jahn et al., 2012) but numerous stressrelated mechanisms as well. 

## 2.13.10 Metal resistance

Metals are ubiquitous to the metabolic processes of life. In low concentrations, they play a crucial role in several biochemical functions. At higher concentrations, however, their presence can have detrimental effects (Nies, 1999). In order to prevent this scenario and maintain an optimal intracellular level of metals, a tightly controlled metal homeostasis system is needed (see Chapter 2.12 and Section 20). 

The corA gene product is considered to be the dominant $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ influx system in bacteria. Additionally, corA mediates the influx of both $\mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { N i } ^ { 2 + }$ (Smith and Maguire, 1995). In E. coli, studies of the functional role of RNase III in the corA mRNA processing have revealed that this enzyme controls the mRNA degradation in a rate-limiting reaction (Lim et al., 2012). The authors further demonstrate that RNase III upregulation results in corA downregulation and, consequently, in increased resistance to both cobalt and nickel stress (Lim et al., 2012). Nonetheless, despite the enzyme’s involvement in corA processing, RNase III levels were not altered in cobalt and nickel stress conditions. These observations hint to the existence of another corA regulatory pathway, perhaps regulated by the exoribonuclease PNPase, whose mRNA levels are increased in cobalt stress conditions (Lim et al., 2012). 

## 2.13.11 Concluding remarks

In this chapter, we have portrayed the impact that RNases can have on several bacterial stress adaptations (Figure 2.13.1). Due to new, diverse studies on the subject, it is now becoming increasingly clear that RNases play a predominant role in the posttranscriptional regulation of several distinct stress-activated networks.

Several stresses can originate from preexisting ones. The modulation of RNase activity may not only allow the cell to swiftly respond to changing environments, but also indirectly anticipate the regulatory requirements of a change in genetic expression. For example, the downregulation of RNase III activity results in the upregulation of PNPase levels. This phenomenon has revealed another layer of intricate interconnection between several stress pathways. Nonetheless, further work on this field is required to provide a more detailed RNase–stress interaction model.

## 2.14.1 Introduction

Since the 1930s–1940s “modern synthesis,” when the ideas of Mendel and Darwin were fused to understand evolution, the mutations that drive evolution were presumed to occur randomly in time, constantly and gradually, and also randomly in genomic space (Mayr, 1982). Stochastic mutagenesis was an economical assumption given that biologists had yet to learn the molecular basis of genes as DNA (Avery et al., 1944; Hershey and Chase, 1952), DNA structure (Watson and Crick, 1953), and how it replicates (Meselson and Stahl, 1958), let alone how mutations in genes might form. 

Experiments of Joshua and Esther Lederberg supported the hypothesis that mutations were not specifically induced to fit a given environment (Lederberg and Lederberg, 1952). They showed that Escherichia coli colonies replica-plated onto medium with streptomycin included resistant mutants, arguing that resistance mutations arose before antibiotic exposure. Thus, at least some mutations both arose apparently without bias toward those that would be useful, and were not induced by the antibiotic. 

The idea of mutagenesis as a stochastic process, not tuned to environmental input, was further supported by the Luria and Delbruck fluctuation test, in which mutations in proliferating ¨ cultures arose randomly with a precise relationship to cell generations (Luria and Delbruck, 1943). They found that distribu-¨ tions of E. coli phage-resistant-mutant colonies among multiple independent cultures not previously exposed to the phage followed a Poisson distribution as projected on the generations of the dividing cells in those cultures. Their data argued for mutagenesis as a probabilistic, stochastic, and generation-dependent phenomenon, rather than an environmentally inducible process. These early mutagenesis workers appear to have been comforted by the congruence of their results with the modern-synthesis assumption of random mutagenesis. 

In this chapter, we review a fundamentally different paradigm for “spontaneous” mutagenesis. In both the Lederbergs’ and the Luria and Delbruck experiments, lethal selections for mutants¨ were used. By contrast, under nonlethal growth-limiting conditions, cells are stressed and activate stress responses. Over the past 20 years, our laboratories and others’ have described multiple molecular mechanisms of mutagenesis upregulated by stress responses in bacterial, yeast, and human cancer cells. Among these mechanisms, there is more than one mechanism of stressresponse-promoted mutagenic repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). Stress-response-induced switches to mutagenic break repair (MBR) are found in E. coli and human cancer cells, induced by a wide variety of stressors, and dependent on various stress responses. 

MBR and its nonrandomness will be our focus. MBR is upregulated by stress responses, causing mutations when cells are poorly adapted to their environments. MBR is also nonrandom in genomic space, occurring preferentially in clusters near sites of DNA breakage. The localized clustering of mutations could promote concerted evolution (multiple mutations) within genes, a significant problem in evolution of protein function. Also, the occurrence of mutations near DSB sites opens the possibility that cells could bias mutations to particular genomic regions in response to different environments by controlling (biasing or directing) the locations of spontaneous DNA breakage. The temporal and spatial regulation or restriction of mutagenesis changes our understanding of evolution, including evolution that drives cancer development, infectious disease, and aging, and suggests possible novel anti-evolvability therapies (Rosenberg and Queitsch, 2014; see Chapters 9.1 to 9.4). 

## 2.14.2 Double-strand-break repair in E. coli

Nearly all DSB repair in E. coli occurs via RecBCD-mediated homologous recombination (HR) (reviewed in Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008; Kuzminov, 2011). RecBCD is a DSB endspecific helicase and nuclease that erodes DSB ends, creates single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), and then loads the RecA strandexchange protein onto the ssDNA (Figure 2.14.1a–c). The specificity of RecBCD for DSBs is absolute both in solution and in living cells. Thus, cellular events that require RecBCD, as DSB repair does, can be inferred to require a DSB(s) and/or its repair for some aspect of the process. 

E. coli does not possess Ku, a conserved protein used for nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ), but many other bacteria do (Bowater and Doherty, 2006). Ku-carrying bacteria use NHEJ alternatively with, and in addition to, HR-DSB repair. 

The RecBCD role of end resection and RecA loading, though performed by other proteins in other organisms, is universal in all organisms. RecA and its orthologs throughout the tree of life perform strand exchange to bring the damaged ssDNA in contact with complementary DNA sequences for repair, usually using a sister chromosome. When a strand-exchange intermediate or D-loop is formed (e.g., Figure 2.14.1c), repair synthesis (dashed lines in Figure 2.14.1c,d) can occur using the intact, complementary duplex DNA as a template to replace lost or eroded DNA sequences. The structure with exchanged strands must be resolved or separated back to two discrete DNA molecules or regions, a job often done by the RuvABC protein machine, a helicase endonuclease complex (West, 1997) (between steps d and e–f in Figure 2.14.1), followed by nick sealing via DNA ligase.

Figure 2.14.1 The general stress response throws a switch to mutagenic double-strand break (DSB) repair by (somehow) licensing use of alternative error-prone DNA pols in repair: the HR-MBR and MH-MBR mechanisms. Black and blue lines, single strands of DNA; parallel lines, base pairing; dotted lines, newly synthesized DNA; DSB, double-strand break; red X’s, DNA polymerase errors that become mutations; thick blue arrows in (g), duplicated double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) segments; HR-MBR, homologous-recombinational mutagenic break repair; MH-MBR, microhomologous mutagenic break repair. Three steps in HR-MBR (see text): (1) Formation and repair by HR of a DSB (a–f). RecBCD resects DSB ends and loads RecA strand-exchange protein. The RecA-coated ssDNA invades dsDNA and establishes base pairing with complementary DNA (e.g., a sister chromosome), allowing repair replication that uses DNA Pol III in unstressed cells (Motamedi et al., 1999). (2) Induction of the SOS DNA-damage response transcriptionally upregulates error-prone DNA Pol IV/DinB 10-fold, and allows production of error-prone Pol V, as well as increasing Pol II levels. (3) Separate induction of the RpoS general stress response licenses use of DNA pols other than Pol III in DSB repair, by as-yet-unknown means. Use of Pol IV promotes nearly all HR-MBR, forming base substitutions and indels. Use of Pols V and II allows some base substitutions and indels, respectively. Use of Pol I underlies switching of 3′ -ssDNA ends to a microhomologous ssDNA region, creating genome rearrangements such as copy-number variations (amplification shown in (g)): MH-MBR. Figure 2.14.2 shows a detailed model for MH-MBR by microhomology-mediated break-induced replication (MMBIR).


Both RecA and RecBCD function in HR-DSB repair, and also in activation of the SOS DNA damage response, which turns on when cells accumulate persistent ssDNA (Sassanfar and Roberts, 1990). RecA is required for any SOS response and RecBCD for SOS activation only in response to DSB-inducing treatments (McPartland et al., 1980; Pennington and Rosenberg, 2007). RuvA, RuvB, and RuvC proteins of the RuvABC protein machine play no role in activation of the SOS response, and so are specific indicators of processes using HR and cleavage of four-way DNA junctions. 

Most HR-DSB repair in E. coli requires the major replicative DNA polymerase, Pol III (Motamedi et al., 1999). The repair is via a break-induced-replication (BIR) process that includes conservative segregation of new DNA strands in the repaired region (Motamedi et al., 1999), similar to that described later in yeast (Saini et al., 2013). A minor Pol III–independent HR pathway repairs DSBs producing “break–join” recombinant DNA molecules, which lack apparent new DNA synthesis (Motamedi et al., 1999). Pol III is a high-fidelity (low-error-rate) DNA polymerase that is also highly processive (McHenry, 2011). In unstressed cells, repair of DSBs via the major Pol III–dependent pathway is relatively nonmutagenic; but DSB repair becomes mutagenic using alternative, error-prone DNA polymerases during stresses that activate the general or starvation stress response controlled by RpoS (σS) (Ponder et al., 2005; Shee et al., 2011). 

## 2.14.3 Two E. coli MBR mechanisms

In stressed cells, depending on the RpoS general or starvation stress response, repair of DSBs becomes mutagenic via either of two different mechanisms. A homologous-recombinationbased MBR mechanism (HR-MBR), which generates base substitutions and indels, results from DNA polymerase errors made by error-prone DNA polymerases during the DNA synthesis in HR repair of the DSB. An alternative mutagenic microhomologous repair mechanism (MH-MBR) produces gene amplifications and other gross chromosomal rearrangements (Hastings et al., 2000, 2004, 2009b), most probably via microhomologymediated BIR (MMBIR) (Hastings et al., 2009a), discussed later in this chapter. 

## 2.14.3.1 The E. coli HR-MBR mechanism

Three events must occur simultaneously for the HR-MBR mechanism to ensue (Figure 2.14.1a–f) (Ponder et al., 2005; Shee et al., 2011): (1) a DSB and its repair by HR; (2) activation of the SOS DNA damage response, which transcriptionally upregulates the error-prone DNA polymerase (Pol) IV or DinB 10-fold; and (3) activation of the RpoS general or starvation stress response, which allows Pol IV and other low-fidelity DNA polymerases into the DSB-repair replisome, at the expense of high-fidelity Pol III, by an as-yet-unknown mechanism (Figure 2.14.1). 

## Step 1 of HR-MBR: a DSB (and repair by HR)

Spontaneous DSBs occur about once per hundred cell divisions in proliferating E. coli cultures (Pennington and Rosenberg, 2007; Shee et al., 2013). They are precisely correlated with cell divisions (Shee et al., 2013), and probably most result from DNA replication mishaps (Merrikh et al., 2012). Multiple molecular mechanisms are likely to form spontaneous DSBs, but only some of them are known (Kuzminov, 1995; Merrikh et al., 2012). 

## Single-strand nicks and fork collapse

In starvation-stressed and other stressed cells in which replication initiations are limited, there are likely to be other major routes to formation of spontaneous DSBs and/or alternative ways to begin the DNA replication that generates DSBs. MBR was discovered (Harris et al., 1994; Rosenberg et al., 1994) via an E. coli assay using a lac frameshift-mutation-reporter gene in an F′ conjugative plasmid over days of starvation (Cairns and Foster, 1991). The starvation-provoked mutagenesis is RecBC dependent, and so it is DSB dependent (Harris et al., 1994). In that assay, F’-encoded TraI ssDNA endonuclease, which creates an ssDNA nick at the F′ oriT, is required for the RecB-dependent (RecA-, Ruv- RpoS, SOS-, and DinB-dependent) mutagenesis (i.e., for HR-MBR) (Ponder et al., 2005); but TraI is more than substituted by a DSB delivered to the F′ by I-SceI site-specific double-strand endonuclease (Ponder et al., 2005). I-SceI cuts substituted for TraI and increased mutation an additional 70- fold (Ponder et al., 2005). The ssDNA nick can readily become a DSB end when hit by a replication fork (Kuzminov, 1995) (called fork collapse; Figure 2.14.2e,f). Importantly, both in this study (Ponder et al., 2005) and in a study of I-SceI-induced HR-MBR in chromosomes of plasmid-free cells (Shee et al., 2011), I-SceI does not substitute for RpoS, SOS, DinB, RecABC, and Ruv, indicating that all of those proteins function in HR-MBR downstream of generation of the DSB that provokes mutation upon its repair (see Figure 2.14.1). The data indicate that TraImade nicks become DSBs via fork collapse (Ponder et al., 2005). TraI-independent source(s) provoke spontaneous chromosomal DSBs (observed; Pennington and Rosenberg, 2007; Shee et al., 2013), leading to spontaneous HR-MBR (Shee et al., 2011). 

## Transcriptional R-loops promote DNA breakage

One source of forks that collapse in starving cells appears to be RNA–DNA hybrids resulting from transcription (R-loops) (Wimberly et al., 2013), (Figure 2.14.2). The data supporting this conclusion are the following: 

First, overproduction of RNase H1, which degrades RNA from RNA–DNA hybrids, reduces RpoS-, SOS-, DinB-, DSB-, and HR-protein-dependent lac reversion in starved cells. Therefore, RNA–DNA hybrids are needed for the HR-MBR. (Also, knockout of RNaseH1 increased HR-DSB-dependent mutagenesis.) Second, many experiments showed that the RNA results from transcription, including that Mfd, which moves stalled RNA polymerase helping to form R-loops (Figure 2.14.2b,c), is required for about half the HR-MBR at lac. Third, providing I-SceI substituted for (negated effects of) both RNaseH1 and Mfd, indicating that the R-loops act before DSB formation in MBR, and are not needed if DSBs are made by I-SceI. The R-loop-promoted DSBs were additionally visualized as foci of a fluorescent DSB-specific binding protein (Wimberly et al. (2013), as described by Shee et al. (2013)). A compelling model for why both TraI and R-loops are needed simultaneously for DSBs to form is that R-loops, which can initiate replication forks (Kogoma, 1997), do so in starving cells (Figure 2.14.2d); and those forks then collapse at a ssDNA nick to form DSBs (Figure 2.14.2e,f). In the F’, TraI makes most of the ssDNA nicks that lead to DSBs (Ponder et al., 2005; Wimberly et al., 2013).

## RpoE membrane stress response promotes DNA breakage

Perhaps surprisingly, the membrane–protein stress response is required in addition to TraI and R-loops for formation of the DSBs that drive MBR in the F’-plasmid-based assay (Gibson et al., 2010). A screen for mutants defective in MBR-lac reversion identified a transposon insertion between the -10 and -35 regions of the promoter of rpoE, which encodes $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ (Gibson et al., 2010). $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ is an alternative sigma factor, transcriptional activator, and subunit of RNA polymerase that activates the membrane stress response (De Las Penas et al., 1997). $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ directly and indirectly activates transcription of a regulon of at least 200 genes in response to misfolded protein accumulation between the inner and outer membranes (Dartigalongue et al., 2001; Kabir et al., 2005; Rhodius et al., 2006). 

$\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ is an essential protein (De Las Penas et al., 1997) that is required for viability for a role other than its role in stress response activation (Gibson et al., 2010). We showed that the MBR-abolishing transposon insertion in the rpoE promoter is a separation-of-function mutation that ablates stress response activation without perturbing the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ essential function (Gibson et al., 2010). Therefore, the RpoE response itself is required for MBR, at least in the $\mathrm { F ^ { \prime } }$ plasmid. Like R-loops and ssDNA nicks, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ is more than substituted by I-SceI-produced DSBs (Gibson et al., 2010). Therefore, the RpoE response promotes MBR at some stage of generation of the DSBs that underlie $\mathrm { F ^ { \prime } }$ lac reversion (Gibson et al., 2010). One possibility, not drawn specifically in Figure 2.14.2a, could be that perhaps transcription from a $\ : \mathfrak { o } ^ { \mathrm { E _ { \circ } } } \ :$ dependent promoter in the $\mathrm { F ^ { \prime } }$ may generate the R-loops that lead to DSBs there (the transcription in Figure 2.14.2a). Many other models for how the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ response promotes DNA breakage are possible. 

## Spontaneous DSBs and HR-MBR in the chromosome underlie spontaneous mutagenesis during starvation

Spontaneous DSBs also occur in chromosomes of plasmid-free E. coli (Pennington and Rosenberg, 2007; Shee et al., 2013), and are repaired during starvation stress via HR-MBR (Shee et al., 2011). Using assays for either of two drug-resistance mutations that report on base substitutions and -1 base pair (bp) deletions, in cells with no I-SceI or other engineered endonuclease, half the spontaneous mutagenesis was DSB-dependent (RecBCdependent) and via HR-MBR. The cells were starved (without drugs present), rescued from starvation, and then selected for mutants. A highly significant half of the spontaneous base substitution and indel mutagenesis was dependent on RuvC and RecABC (HR-DSB repair), RpoS, SOS, and DinB, indicating the HR-MBR pathway. The RecBC dependence indicates DSB dependence. The origins of the spontaneous chromosomal DSBs that permit spontaneous HR-MBR remain to be investigated. Importantly, HR-MBR contributes a sizable fraction of spontaneous mutagenesis. Given the decades-old difficulty of understanding any fraction of spontaneous mutagenesis in E. coli (Drake, 1993), assigning half to the HR-MBR pathway is an important advance. The data show that HR-MBR is a pathway that E. coli cells usually use (Shee et al., 2011). 

## Step 2 of HR-MBR: SOS response upregulation of error-prone DNA polymerases

HR-MBR (Figure 2.14.1a–f), but not the microhomologous gene amplification pathway (Figure 2.14.1g), requires activation of the SOS DNA-damage response (McKenzie et al., 2000, 2001). The SOS response is activated by persistent ssDNA, which signals DNA-damage (see Section 9). The SOS response turns on in about 25% of cells with a repairable DSB (Pennington and Rosenberg, 2007). Thus, this Step 2 occurs with Step 1 – doublestrand breakage. 

The SOS response transcriptionally upregulates ∼40 unlinked genes (the SOS genes) during DNA damage, many of which promote DNA repair and DNA damage survival (Simmons et al., 2008). In cells with persistent ssDNA, the DNA damage signal, the SOS genes are induced via destruction of their transcriptional repressor, LexA. LexA binds a 20-bp consensus sequence (TACTGTATATATATACAGTA) upstream of the SOS genes, preventing or decreasing their transcription. When ssDNA accumulates, RecA binds the ssDNA, forming RecA nucleoprotein filaments. The RecA nucleoprotein complex acts as a co-protease that binds LexA and facilitates its autoproteolytic cleavage, causing transcriptional upregulation of the SOS genes (Simmons et al., 2008). When DNA damage is repaired or removed, LexA cellular levels rise and the SOS genes are again repressed. 

Several SOS genes are required for all or some of HR-MBR: RecA (Cairns and Foster, 1991; Harris et al., 1994), RecBC (Harris et al., 1994), RuvA and RuvB (Foster et al., 1996; Harris et al., 1996), and DinB/Pol IV (McKenzie et al., 2001), all of which are required for all or most HR-MBR), as well as DNA Pol II, which accounts for about 15% of frameshift reversions by MBR (Frisch et al., 2010); DNA Pol V, which is required for some base substitutions (Petrosino et al., 2009) and some indels generated by HR-MBR (Shee et al., 2011); and SulA, which blocks septation, allowing completion of replication and DNA repair by HR in cells with DNA damage. SulA promotes some of HR-MBR (McKenzie et al., 2000), possibly by allowing sister chromosomes to remain in the same cell for repair, or for allele swapping between chromosomes carrying SOS-induced mutations (Bos et al., 2015), or both. DNA Pols IV, V, and II are low-fidelity DNA polymerases, which allow synthesis across base damage that cannot be traversed by the replicative DNA Pol III (Nohmi, 2006). Though not required for repairing DSBs, Pols IV, II, and V participate in DSB repair and make it mutagenic, but only if the RpoS response is also activated (Ponder et al., 2005; Shee et al., 2011) (Step 3 of Figure 2.14.1, and discussed further below). 

The SOS response role in HR-MBR is its 10-fold transcriptional upregulation of DinB (Galhardo et al., 2009); but SOS must also promote some HR-MBR by allowing production of Pol V (inferred) as follows. In a frameshift-reversion assay for starvation-induced HR-MBR, a catalysis-defective dinB allele reduces indels by 85% (McKenzie et al., 2001) or more (Ponder et al., 2005). The remaining 15% requires DNA Pol II (Frisch et al., 2010). An “SOS-off ” uncleavable mutant form of LexA, which prevents SOS gene induction, strongly inhibits HR-MBR (Cairns and Foster, 1991; McKenzie et al., 2000, 2001). This demonstrated the need for SOS upregulation of one or more SOS genes for HR-MBR. We mutated the dinB gene’s LexA binding site to create an operator-constitutive allele, dinB(oc ), that produces 10-fold higher levels of DinB, as seen during an SOS response, constitutively (Galhardo et al., 2009). The dinB(oc ) mutation completely reverses the mutagenesis defect in SOS-off LexA-uncleavable mutant cells, implying that only DinB, and no other SOS-upregulated protein, need be present at SOS-induced levels for HR-MBR to occur (Galhardo et al., 2009). However, DNA Pol V is not required for the frameshift reversion of that particular mutation-reporter gene (lac) (McKenzie et al., 2000), whereas Pol V is required for some HR-MBR indel mutagenesis in a tet frameshift reversion assay (Shee et al., 2011) and all or most of the base substitutions that result from HR-MBR in a gene-inactivation mutagenesis assay (Petrosino et al., 2009). Because Pol V is believed not to be synthesized at all in the absence of an SOS response (Simmons et al., 2008), we infer that the SOS response also promotes HR-MBR via its production of Pol V. 

## Step 3 of HR-MBR: RpoS throws the switch to mutagenic break repair by allowing error-prone DNA pols to participate

Although cells may have a DSB, may repair it via HR, and may induce their SOS response, causing vast upregulation of errorprone DNA Pol IV (DinB), and production of Pol V and Pol II, the repair of DSBs is relatively nonmutagenic unless the general or starvation stress response is also induced (Ponder et al., 2005; Shee et al., 2011). This is observed for repair of I-SceI-created 

DSBs in an $\mathrm { F ^ { \prime } }$ plasmid (Ponder et al., 2005) or in the chromosome of plasmid-free cells (Shee et al., 2011), with RpoS induced either via an RpoS-inducing stressor or by artificial upregulation of RpoS in unstressed cells. 

## General stress response

The RpoS (general or starvation) stress response is activated by many different stressors, including starvation, transition to the stationary phase, and acid, osmotic, oxidative, temperature, and antibiotic stresses (Battesti et al., 2011; Gutierrez et al., 2013; Hengge-Aronis et al., 1993; Lee et al., 1995). Presumably, all of these would switch DSB repair to mutagenic HR-MBR and MH-MBR modes, allowing the use of alternative DNA polymerases. Stressors shown to trigger RpoS and mutagenesis include starvation (Al Mamun et al., 2012), bile (Hernandez et al., 2012; Prieto et al., 2006), and antibiotics (Gutierrez et al., 2013). For ampicillin, the mutagenesis induced depends on RpoS and DinB/Pol IV, but not apparently on DSBs (Gutierrez et al., 2013). The RpoS response is activated by production of the σS (also known as $\sigma ^ { 3 8 } )$ transcriptional activator (sigma factor), encoded by rpoS, which works with RNA polymerase to directly and indirectly regulate the transcription and expression of over 500 genes (Ito et al., 2008). $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { S } }$ (RpoS) protein levels are low (often undetectable) during exponential growth of unstressed cells, are upregulated in the late exponential phase, and remain high through the stationary phase and during other stresses (Lange and Hengge-Aronis, 1991). The multiple different mechanisms of downregulation of RpoS, and thus the general stress response, in unstressed growing cells are summarized in Figure 2.14.3. 

## Switch to mutagenic break repair

The general stress response somehow licenses the use of the error-prone DNA pols in HR-DSB repair, throwing the switch to mutagenic DSB repair under conditions that induce the RpoS response, as shown by the following results: 

First, site-specific DSBs made by a chromosomal regulatable I-SceI endonuclease (Gumbiner-Russo et al., 2001) are repaired well by HR in chromosomes of plasmid-free cells (Shee et al., 2011) or in an $\mathrm { F ^ { \prime } }$ plasmid (Ponder et al., 2005), both in unstressed growing cells and during starvation stress. The repair itself (survival of I-SceI cleavage), with or without stress, is independent of RpoS or DinB. The repair by HR presumably uses a sister chromosome as its repair partner, which is present even in starved stationary-phase cells. About 40% of starved cells carry a sister (Akerlund et al., 1995). Although less frequent $( \leq 1 0 ^ { - 3 }$ of cells), repair using a spontaneous duplicated chromosomal segment is also possible (see Rosenberg et al., 2012). 

Second, as cells enter starvation, there is a time-of-starvationdependent increase in mutagenesis of chromosomal (Al Mamun et al., 2012; Shee et al., 2011, 2012) or plasmid-based (Ponder et al., 2005) mutation-reporter genes near the cutsite. I-SceI cutting causes a 50-fold increase of mutagenesis of a 2-kb-distant chromosomal indel-mutation-reporter gene (Shee et al., 2011, 2012) or base-substitution-reporter gene (Al Mamun et al., 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/717956dc5ad53d79ebdb1c298b2a6c0391fefb987adc585836ddcd597d480cea.jpg)



Figure 2.14.3 Multiple layers of downregulation of the RpoS response in unstressed cells. RpoS is downregulated in unstressed cells at the transcriptional, translational, and posttranslational levels (Battesti et al., 2011). A long upstream untranslated region in the rpoS messenger RNA (mRNA) prevents translation by forming a stem–loop structure. This translation block can be relieved by binding any of three small RNAs (sRNAs) that all require the RNA chaperone, Hfq, to function: RprA, ArcZ, and DsrA (Brown and Elliott, 1996). Thus, like RpoS, Hfq is required for MBR (Al Mamun et al., 2012). RpoS is also downregulated in unstressed cells posttranslationally by the RssB protein, which binds RpoS protein and targets it for degradation by the ClpXP protease. Deletion of RssB increases RpoS levels (Klauck et al., 2001; Muffler et al., 1996) and MBR (Al Mamun et al., 2012). RpoS is additionally downregulated by the ArcBA two-component regulatory system via three separate mechanisms (Mika and Hengge, 2005). ArcA (the response regulator) binds and represses the rpoS promoter, while ArcB (the histidine kinase) phosphorylates and thus activates RssB, leading to RpoS degradation by the ClpXP protease (Mika and Hengge, 2005). ArcBA also repress the sRNA ArcZ, which promotes rpoS mRNA translation. Thus, ArcBA reduce RpoS protein levels transcriptionally, translationally, and posttranslationally.


2012), and a 70-fold increase in frameshift reversion of 4–11 kb distant reporters in an $\mathrm { F ^ { \prime } }$ plasmid (Ponder et al., 2005). This mutagenesis depends on the presence of the cutsite and production of I-SceI (i.e., it is DSB-dependent). The I-SceI/DSBdependent mutagenesis requires functional RpoS and SOS stress responses, Pol IV, and the HR-DSB repair proteins (RecA, RecBC, and Ruv) (Al Mamun et al., 2012; Ponder et al., 2005; Shee et al., 2011), and partially requires Pol V (Al Mamun et al., 2012; Shee et al., 2011), in some mutation-reporter genes. Indel mutagenesis in a different reporter gene required Pol IV (85%; McKenzie et al., 2001) or Pol II (15%; Frisch et al., 2010) but not Pol V (McKenzie et al., 2000). 

## Stress not needed; RpoS response sufficient

Importantly, artificial activation of the RpoS response independent of stress is sufficient to allow MBR. Unstressed proliferating cells given chromosomal (Shee et al., 2011) or plasmid-targeted (Ponder et al., 2005) I-SceI cuts repair them without associated mutagenesis, measurable above uncut levels. But if a small amount of RpoS is artificially produced, the repair becomes mutagenic, with the mutagenesis dependent on Pol IV, RpoS, and the DSB (Ponder et al., 2005; Shee et al., 2011). RpoS has multiple layers of downregulation in unstressed cells (reviewed in Figure 2.14.3). 

In these experiments, only one of the many layers was removed, either by medium-copy expression (Ponder et al., 2005) or by deletion of the gene encoding RssB, which targets RpoS for proteolytic degradation (Shee et al., 2011). These studies show that cells do not need stress, but merely activation of the RpoS general stress response, for DSB repair to switch from high-fidelity to mutagenic, using alternative DNA polymerases. 

## In solution

The role of Pol IV in repair synthesis and error production at a D-loop DNA substrate (illustrated in Figure 2.14.1e,f) has been demonstrated in solution with purified proteins (Pomerantz et al., 2013). These data strongly support the model shown in Figure 2.14.1. 

## Molecular mechanism

How RpoS licenses the use of DNA polymerases other than replicative Pol III in DSB repair replisomes remains mysterious. RpoS upregulates Pol IV by about two-fold (Layton and Foster, 2003). Whether this small increase in Pol IV levels is sufficient to license Pol IV, and allow all of the other DNA pols (V, II, and I discussed here for MH-MBR) to participate in HR-DSB repair, is unknown. The mechanism by which RpoS licenses use of alternative DNA polymerases in DSB repair, at the expense of Pol III (Figure 2.14.1c,d), remains one of the most important outstanding questions in the molecular mechanisms of MBR, for both HR-MBR and MH-MBR. 

Mutations generated by E. coli HR-MBR. The mutations generated by HR-MBR are mostly base substitutions with -1 bp deletions also prevalent. For example, in a forward-mutation assay for loss-of-function mutations in the ampD gene in starved cells, the mutations are mostly G-to-T transversions, then -1 bp deletions, followed by A-to-T and G-to-A substitutions (Petrosino et al., 2009). These form by HR-MBR as seen by their dependence on RecBCD (DSBs), RecA and Ruv (HR), RpoS, SOS, and DinB. For years, MBR was studied only in frameshift reversion assays, in which -1 bp deletions in small mononucleotide repeats dominated (Foster, 1997; Foster et al., 1994; Ponder et al., 2005; Rosenberg et al., 1994; Shee et al., 2011, 2012). -1 bp deletions in mononucleotide repeats are characteristic of DNA polymerase errors made by Pol IV, though Pol IV makes more base substitutions (Kim et al., 1997; Nohmi, 2006; Tang et al., 2000). In MBR, the ampD mutations (Petrosino et al., 2009), and those in various other assays (Al Mamun et al., 2012; Shee et al., 2011), show that base substitutions dominate RpoS-response-induced HR-MBR. 

## MBR creates mutation hotspots near DSBs

Strong local hotspots from DSB resection and repair. HR-MBR causes strong local mutation hotspots and clusters near DSBs (Figure 2.14.4). In a study of MBR in chromosomes of plasmid-free cells, we moved a tet indel mutation-reporter gene to varying distances from various I-SceI cutsites and assayed mutagenesis during starvation (Shee et al., 2012). The tetA gene reverts by a +1 bp frameshift in a run of four G’s (Foster, 1997), conferring resistance to the antibiotic tetracycline when it does. At multiple chromosomal locations, DSBs provoke strong local MBR hotspots – 50–90-fold above background (uncut) levels. The hotspots are strongest in the first few kilobase pairs (kb)

Figure 2.14.4 Mutation hotspots at DSBs in E. coli: two mechanisms and a possible evolution catalyst. Summary of results of Shee et al. (2012). Strong (50–90-fold) local mutation hotspots occur within a ∼100 kb zone surrounding I-SceI-generated DSBs, and they are dependent on RecD, a RecBCD subunit required for DSB resection activity but not for RecA loading and repair of DSBs. The RecD dependence implies that the strong local hotspots are caused by exonucleolytic resection and error-prone synthesis at the DSBs. Because HR-MBR mutations occur in clusters (Bull et al., 2000), localized clustering could facilitate concerted evolution within genes and linked gene groups – a major problem in evolution of new protein functions. DSB-induced clusters also help explain mutation storms seen in cancer genomes (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2012). Because weak (∼threefold) long-distance mutation hotspots extend as far as 1 Mb away from DSB sites and are RecD-independent, we suggested that they are caused by mutagenic break-induced replication (BIR) (Shee et al., 2012). Both the local and long-distance hotspots require error-prone Pol IV/DinB and so result from DNA polymerase errors. We suggested that the weak long-distance hotspots result from only one of the two ends of the I-SceI-made DSB engaging the sister DNA molecule and priming BIR (Shee et al., 2012).


of the cutsite, and decline logarithmically to about 60 kb away on either side. Hotspotting near a DSB is independent of the position of the DSB in the genome, and the orientation of the mutation-reporter gene; the mutations follow the DSBs. These strong local hotspots disappear in recD null-mutant cells, which are DSB repair proficient but exonuclease defective. RecBC lacking its RecD subunit is a functional helicase and RecA loader that performs repair (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008; Kuzminov, 2011), but does not make long degradation tracts at DSBs. The data imply that strong local hotspots are caused by the exonucleolytic resection of the DSB and fill-in synthesis. 

Mutation clustering. HR-MBR mutations occur in clusters (Bull et al., 2000). HR-MBR-generated lac revertants showed ${ \sim } 1 0 ^ { 3 }$ times more mutagenesis of a neighboring gene (∼10 kb away) than predicted if each gene’s mutations formed independently. The occurrence of multiple mutations (Bull et al., 2000) in ∼100 kb hotspots (Shee et al., 2012) mimics the mutation storms observed in the same year in cancer genomes (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Roberts et al., 2012). The E. coli work reviewed here, and subsequent work in yeast (Sakofsky et al., 2014), show that DSB repair produces DSB-localized clusters as in cancer mutation storms, providing a plausible mechanism. Human cells have the additional mutagenic activity of APOBEC cytidine deaminases, which cause C-to-U changes in ssDNA, such as the ssDNA that occurs at repairing DSBs (Burns et al., 2013a, b; Roberts et al., 2012). The C-to-U changes become C-to-T mutations upon replication. 

Weak long-distance hotspots independent of resection. In addition to the strong local hotspots, a weak roughly threefold increase in HR-MBR mutations is seen 0.5–1 Mb away from I-SceI-made DSB sites (Shee et al., 2012). The weak, long-distance hotspots are Pol IV–DinB-dependent but independent of RecD, and thus the RecBCD resection activity. Whereas the strong local hotspots are understandable as the zones of resection and resynthesis primed by each of the two DSB ends created by I-SceI, we suggested that weak long-distance hotspots could result from HR-mediated BIR, when only one of the two ends primes replication using the complementary sister chromosome (Shee et al., 2012). Such one-ended replication should in principle be able to continue indefinitely in the E. coli chromosome, to the replication terminus (Motamedi et al., 1999). The fact that the longdistance mutation zones end 0.5–1 Mb away from the cutsite suggests either that BIR is not perfectly processive in E. coli or that the BIR fork becomes nonmutagenic after some distance. This may be analogous to BIR forks in yeast, which become less prone to template jumping after a distance (Smith et al., 2007). We can imagine several possible reasons why the fork could convert to a nonmutagenic one. Perhaps resolution of the Holliday junction trailing such a BIR replication fork occurs, which would convert it into a standard fork. A standard fork might be less susceptible to the low-fidelity DNA polymerases. Standard forks also have semiconservative segregation of new strands (Meselson and Stahl, 1958), unlike BIR forks at which the new strands segregate conservatively (Motamedi et al., 1999; Saini et al., 2013). Standard forks are thus subject to mismatch repair using the old strand to direct correction of DNA polymerase errors, as noted by yeast workers (Saini et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2008). Many other models are possible. 

## MH-MBR and microhomology-mediated break-induced replication

In starvation-stressed cells, microhomologous MBR also occurs, also promoted by the general stress response, as described here. lac “revertant” colonies with gene amplifications of the weakly functional lac gene appear during starvation stress, with later kinetics than indel revertants (Hastings et al., 2000), also depending on RpoS (Lombardo et al., 2004) but not on the SOS response or DinB/Pol IV (McKenzie et al., 2001). They form by a separate pathway and mechanism from HR-MBR (Hastings et al., 2004). The amplifications result from DSBs as follows: (1) the amplifications require the R-loops, ssDNA nicks (Wimberly et al., 2013), and RpoE response (Gibson et al., 2010) that promote DSBs in the F′ (Step 1, above), unless I-SceI cuts are given. Amplifications (2) require RecBCD (DSBs) (Slack et al., 2006), (3) are promoted by I-SceI-induced DSBs (Ponder et al., 2005), and (4) are blocked by production of a phage DSB-endbinding protein that blocks DSB repair (Wimberly et al., 2013). The amplified DNA is present in the original replicon as tandem repeats (Hastings et al., 2000), with the novel DNA join-points between the repeated segments having tiny regions of microhomology at which the joins occurred: from a few to fewer than 20 bp, far fewer than is needed for HR (Slack et al., 2006). Amplification requires DNA polymerase I and 3′ ssDNA ends, the latter shown by reduction of amplifications in cells that overproduce the 3′ ssDNA exonuclease, ExoI (Slack et al., 2006). We proposed that the stress-induced genome rearrangements form by a long-distance template-switch mechanism when replication forks stall. In the long-distance template-switch model, the 3′ primer terminus jumps to and pairs with a distant stretch of ssDNA, then primes synthesis there, forming rearrangements, including copy-number variations (CNVs) (Slack et al., 2006). We suggested that this long-distance template-switch model or mechanism generated human CNVs (Slack et al., 2006). The long-distance template-switch model was renamed FoSTES the next year in a human CNV paper (Lee et al., 2007). Longdistance template switching or FoSTES is now superseded by the microhomology-mediated break-induced replication (MMBIR) model, in which the demonstrated role of DSBs is taken into account (Hastings et al., 2009a). In MMBIR, BIR occurs when the 3′ ssDNA end at a DSB alights on ssDNA with microhomology elsewhere, to create rearrangements (Hastings et al., 2009a). This is illustrated and described in Figure 2.14.2g–j. MMBIR is now a leading model for mechanisms of genome rearrangements in humans and many other organisms (Liu et al., 2012). 

HR-MBR network. A screen for transposon-insertion mutants defective in MBR identified 93 genes that promote 

MBR (most by promoting HR-MBR), shown in three HRspecific MBR assays (Al Mamun et al., 2012). This work identified many of the previously known dozen or so proteins required for HR-MBR, and 76 new ones, the vast majority of which are not traditional DNA-repair, -replication, -maintenance, or mutagenesis proteins. These genes form a coherent network by various criteria. As reviewed in Chapter 9.3, we showed that more than half the genes in this network promote MBR by sensing stresses and transducing the stress signals that ultimately activate three stress-response regulators and responses: RpoS (general or starvation-stress response), RpoE (membrane stress response), and SOS DNA damage response (Al Mamun et al., 2012). Chapter 9.3 reviews the functional systems-biological analyses that allowed deconvolution of the functions of an unusually large fraction of this network (more than half), and the conclusions. A major conclusion is that sensing stress is the most important allocation of E. coli genes to MBR. Because the stress-response regulators are nonredundant hubs in the network, they are also attractive candidates for potential novel anti-evolvability therapies to block mutagenesis that lets pathogens resist drugs and our immune systems and lets cancers evolve (Al Mamun et al., 2012; Rosenberg and Queitsch, 2014).

Elsewhere, we and others have reviewed the mechanisms by which the hypoxic stress response switches DSB repair from high-fidelity HR to genome-destabilizing nonhomologous and microhomologous pathways in human cancer cells (Bindra et al., 2007; Rosenberg et al., 2012). In human cancer cells, two different hypoxic stress responses also downregulate mismatch repair, the major error correction system conserved from bacteria to humans, causing increased indel and base substitution mutagenesis (Bindra et al., 2007). Regulation of mutagenesis by stress responses, including mutagenesis associated with DSB repair, appears across the tree of life. We wonder whether the mutagenic break repair observed in yeast (Malkova and Haber, 2012; Rattray and Strathern, 2003; Strathern et al., 1995) might also be a stress-response-activated switch. Mutagenesis dependent on the Msn general stress response occurs in yeast (Shor et al., 2013). Whether activation of any stress response is required for MBR in yeast is not known.
