# Sigma factor competition in Escherichia coli: kinetic and thermodynamic perspectives

Kuldeepkumar Ramnaresh Gupta and Dipankar Chatterji 

Molecular Biophysics Unit, Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore, India 

## 2.15.1 Introduction

In eubacteria, a multi-subunit enzyme called RNA polymerase (RNAP) carries out transcription. The RNAP holoenzyme is composed of a core subunit (E) and a dissociable interchangeable sigma subunit (σ). The core RNAP is composed of α2ββ’ω subunits and is able to bind DNA nonspecifically, but it attains specificity only when a sigma factor binds to it (Feklistov et al., 2014; Gross et al., 1992). This holoenzyme, known as holo RNAP or Eσ, can recognize DNA specifically and carry out transcription from specific classes of promoters. All bacteria have at least one essential sigma factor responsible for the expression of genes related to housekeeping functions, and most have at least one alternative sigma factor (Gruber and Gross, 2003). Bacteria are constantly subjected to fluctuating environments; in order to adapt and survive, they need to modulate gene expression accordingly. The number of sigma factors used to modulate and synchronize transcription to changing cellular requirements differs very extensively among bacterial species, and is generally indicative of their lifestyle. For example, soil-inhabitant Streptomyces coelicolor, which faces multiple nutritional or physicochemical stresses, encodes more than 60 sigma factors (Gruber and Gross, 2003). In contrast, Escherichia coli, a gut commensal, encodes seven sigma factors (Gruber and Gross, 2003; Osterberg et al., 2011). In E. coli, the housekeeping sigma factor $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ , encoded by the rpoD gene, is essential and responsible for the expression of growth-related and housekeeping genes (Hengge-Aronis, 1993; Loewen and Hengge-Aronis, 1994); and the six alternative sigma factors are $\sigma ^ { 5 4 } , \sigma ^ { 3 8 } , \sigma ^ { 3 2 } , \sigma ^ { 2 4 } , \sigma ^ { 2 8 }$ , and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F e c I } }$ . The alternative sigma factor $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ is involved in the expression of genes regulated by the availability of nitrogen (Merrick, 1993). The general stress response sigma factor $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ is involved in the expression of stationary-phase and stress-related genes (Tanaka et al., 1993). The heat shock sigma factor $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ binds to core RNAP in increased concentration as the demand increases for products of the heat shock genes (Gross et al., 1992; see 

Chapter 13.1). Expression of flagellar and chemotaxis genes is governed by $\sigma ^ { 2 8 }$ (Helmann, 1991; see Chapter 22.1). Alternative sigma factors $\sigma ^ { 2 4 }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F e c I } }$ are involved in the expression of genes related to cell envelope stress and transport of ferric citrate or iron, respectively (Erickson and Gross, 1989; Pressler et al., 1988; Raina et al., 1995; Rouviere` et al., 1995; see Sections 18 and 19). Thus, it can be seen that different sigma factors bind to the same core RNAP to express different sets of genes. 

Except for $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ , the rest of the alternative sigma factors belong to the $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ family of proteins. Members of this family have a modular structure consisting of up to four regions (Osterberg et al., 2011). The housekeeping $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ is the canonical member of this family. It is composed of four domains (viz., σ1, σ2, σ3, and σ4), which have been further divided into subregions. For example, regions 2.1 and 2.3 make contact with the β and $\beta ^ { \prime }$ subunit of RNAP (Osterberg et al., 2011). Similarly, regions 2.4 and 4.2 recognize the -10 and -35 promoter elements (Gopal et al., 1994; Gopal and Chatterji, 1997; Osterberg et al., Reddy et al., 1997). 

Even though alternative sigma factors have structures that are similar to that of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ , they recognize different promoter classes and thus transcribe a different set of genes. The key feature of this kind of gene regulation is the replacement of one type of sigma factor by another. Hence, the determination of various biophysical parameters that dictate the sigma substitution becomes necessary. 

Within bacterial cells, the amount of core RNAP molecule is limiting, which varies seldomly under various physiological conditions (Grigorova et al., 2006; Piper et al., 2009). Hence, the alternative sigma factors compete for the limited pool of core RNAP (Maeda et al., 2000). Does the replacement of one sigma subunit by another boil down to their affinity for the core RNAP, or are there additional factors governing this competition? In this chapter, we will review the kinetic and thermodynamic data that are available for sigma factor competition in E. coli and put it in perspective with regard to other factors that govern the sigma factor competition in vivo. 

## 2.15.2 Thermodynamic and kinetic perspective on ??-factor competition

The binding constants for $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } , \ \sigma ^ { 3 8 } , \ \sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ , and other alternative sigma factors for the core RNAP have been determined using various biophysical methods such as gel filtration chromatography, the Langmuir–Blodgett (LB) technique, and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) (Ganguly and Chatterji, 2012; Maeda et al., 2000). The most recent values of binding constants of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } , \sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ , and $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ for the core RNAP have been determined using the LB and SPR techniques at varying temperatures and ionic strengths (Ganguly and Chatterji, 2012). The LB technique involves the use of a special trough to generate a monolayer of an amphipathic molecule at the air–water interface (Blodgett, 1935; Langmuir, 1917). The presence of an amphipathic molecule reduces the surface tension (or surface pressure) of water present in the trough. The reduction in the surface pressure is measured using an electrobalance known as Wilhemy’s plate. The molecules spread on the air–water interface can be compressed using a barrier in the trough that is used to change the molecular density or area per molecule. The surface pressure is plotted against the molecular area to give the pressure area (PA) isotherm. Ganguly and Chatterji immobilized hexahistidine-tagged core RNAP with the help of amphipathic molecule nickel–arachidate. A saturation binding experiment with core RNAP was carried out by injecting increasing concentrations of σ-factors into the immobilized layer of core RNAP. The PA isotherms were used to derive the fractional saturation plot for E–σ interaction (Figure 2.15.1). The binding constants of various sigma factors for core RNAP were calculated from the factional saturation plots.

The temperature sensitivity of $\operatorname { E } { - } \sigma$ interaction over the temperature range of $2 0 { - } 4 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ was also determined using the LB technique (Table 2.15.2). 

It is apparent that the affinity of sigma factors for the core RNAP decreases with the concomitant increase in the temperature, and the sensitivity of this interaction varies as $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } > \sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ $> \sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ . The qualitative indication of the temperature susceptibility of the core RNAP and sigma factor interaction is shown in Figure 2.15.1. It is evident from Figure 2.15.1a that at $2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } C ,$ the $\mathrm { E } { - } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ interaction is weak, but with the increasing concentration of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ , it grows stronger. At higher temperatures of $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and $4 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ the interactions become more uniform. This implies that the fluctuations in the estimated macroscopic dissociation constant values and the enthalpy of formation derived from them are more at lower temperature. For the alternative sigma factors $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ , the binding to the core RNAP is uniform over the temperature ranges of $2 0 { - } 4 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Figure 2.15.1b,c). It is evident that interaction of $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ with the core RNAP is virtually unaffected by the variations in the temperature (Figure 2.15.1c). It can be seen clearly that while the temperature rises from 20 to $4 0 \ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ there is a reversal in order of the relative binding affinities of sigma factors for the core RNAP, with cross over taking place at $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ (Figure 2.15.2). 

Hence, the order of affinity between sigma factors and the core RNAP seems to be $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } > \dot { \sigma ^ { 3 2 } } > \sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ at $2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in 10 mM NaCl; but this order is reversed to $\sigma ^ { 3 8 } > \sigma ^ { 3 2 } > \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ at $4 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . When E. coli is growing at the favorable temperature (i.e., is in a “feasting” or exponential-growth phase), most of the core RNAP is bound to $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ (Nystrom, 2004). But when the ambient temperature increases, it is sensed as stress by the bacterium. To counter this situation, stress-related genes must be transcribed; consequently, $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ is replaced by $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ or $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ . This may account for the superior temperature sensitivity displayed by $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ (heat shock sigma factor) compared with $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ (general stress response sigma factor).

Effects of temperature and osmolarity on the $\operatorname { E } { - } \sigma$ interaction were also determined using the SPR technique. The SPR technique is one of the most reliable techniques to measure the binding interaction. It measures changes in the refractive index in terms of response units when two or more molecules interact (Daghestani and Day, 2010). The changes in the response units are used to derive binding-on and bindingoff rates of the interacting partners. The ratio of off rate to on rate gives the value of equilibrium dissociation constants. The effect of increasing temperature on E–σ interaction over the temperature range of $2 0 { - } 4 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ was studied using SPR (Table 2.15.3). 

It is clear that when all other variables are kept constant, the strength of binding to the core RNAP among sigma factors and changes in binding seen with the variation in temperature correlated well with the values obtained from the LB studies.

Comparison of panels a and b of Figure 2.15.3 shows the effect of salt is more noticeable at lower temperature on $\mathtt { E } \mathrm { - } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ interaction. In the same way, Figure 2.15.3c,d reveals that increased ionic strength has negligible effect on the core RNA E– $- \sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ interaction. Likewise, Figure 2.15.3e,f shows that at lower temperature, a small variation is observed in the interaction of E– $- \sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ , but changes in temperature do not affect this variation significantly. Thus, both LB and SPR data show that $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ has the strongest affinity for E compared with $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ . A comparison of KD values listed in Table 2.15.1 reveals that $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ has 12-fold and approximately ninefold higher affinity for the core RNAP than those of $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ , respectively. Taken together, comparative binding affinity of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } , \sigma ^ { \bar { 3 } 2 }$ , and $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ for the core RNAP is as follows:

$$

\sigma^ {3 8} > \sigma^ {3 2} > \sigma^ {7 0} \text {   at   } 4 0 ^ {\circ} \text { C }
$$

The equilibrium dissociation constants of all seven sigma factors of E. coli for core RNAP were determined using gel filtration chromatography (Table 2.15.4) (Maeda et al., 2000). Based on the binding constants listed in Table 2.15.4, the relative order of binding affinity to the core RNAP among the seven sigma factors is as follows: $\dot { \sigma } ^ { 7 0 } > \sigma ^ { 5 4 } > \sigma ^ { 2 8 } > \sigma ^ { 3 2 } > \sigma ^ { 1 8 } > \sigma ^ { 2 4 } > \sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ . It can be seen that both $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ have lesser affinity for the core RNAP compared to σ70. The affinity of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ for core RNAP is 16-fold and approximately fivefold higher than those of $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ , respectively. 

A comparison of binding affinities of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } , \sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ , and $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ for the core RNAP at $2 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ reveals that, irrespective of the method used to determine the binding constants, the relative order remains the same (Table 2.15.5). Thus, gel filtration data support the LB and the SPR data. 

## 2.15.3 A molecular thermodynamic outlook on E–?? interaction

Interaction of a sigma factor with the core enzyme results in a single adduct called a holoenzyme. Such phenomena usually result in the increase of the configurational entropy of the system. However, the values given in Table 2.15.1 indicate that, when sigma factors bind to the core RNAP, the entropy change is negative. We can account for this by assuming large conformational changes in both the core RNAP and sigma factor. The $\mathtt { E } \mathrm { - } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ interaction involves binding of a small 70 kD protein to a large core RNAP, in which the structure of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ gets distorted so that conserved regions 2.1 and 2.3 can make contacts with both β (150) and $\beta ^ { \prime }$ (155 kDa) subunits of RNAP (Vassylyev et al., 2002). The energy for these large-scale conformational changes comes from the energy freed in the electrostatic interactions between charged protein lobes (Vassylyev et al., 2002). Therefore, the observed enthalpy for the E–σ interaction would be the surplus energy released after making allowance for conformational changes on the sigma factor. If the released enthalpy is smaller, the sigma factor would have to be distorted more to interact with RNAP, and hence the magnitude of negative entropy would be more. The entropy and enthalpy values share inverse correlation. These values can be used to estimate binding affinity of σ-factor for the core RNAP (Ganguly and Chatterji, 2012). Though $\sigma ^ { 3 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ belong to the $\sigma ^ { \hat { 7 } 0 }$ family of sigma factors, they exhibit divergence at the level of amino acid sequence from the conserved sequence of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ (Mittenhuber, 2002). This implies that the binding of alternative sigma factors to the core RNAP would not be as optimal as in the case of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ . To compensate for this, alternative sigma factors may go through more structural distortions in order to bind core RNAP. This explains the release of lesser free energy of interaction and small enthalpy values when alternative sigma factors interact with the core RNAP (Ganguly and Chatterji, 2012). 

## 2.15.4 Factors affecting ??-factor concentration in vivo

Equilibrium dissociation constants determined using various biophysical techniques provide only a partial picture of sigma factor competition. How can replacement of high-affinity $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ by low-affinity $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ or $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ be explained within the cells? It turns out that there are factors such as alarmone ppGpp (see Section 7) and antisigma factors that regulate sigma factor competition in vivo (Osterberg, 2011; Sharma and Chatterji, 2010). It is increasingly becoming evident that bacterial alarmone is the master regulator not only of transcription but also of σ-factor competition in vivo (Jishage et al., 2002). This view is rooted in data showing that (i) in the presence of ppGpp, alternative sigma factors compete far better against $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ in both in vitro and in vivo transcription assays (Jishage et al., 2002; Laurie et al., 2003); (ii) in cells lacking ppGpp, the fraction of $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ bound to the core RNAP is reduced in the stationary phase (Jishage et al., 2002); (iii) specific mutations in rpoD (gene encoding $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } )$ , which reduces the affinity of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ for the core RNAP, alleviate the ppGpp requirement of genes transcribed by the alternative sigma factor (Jishage et al., 2002; Laurie et al., 2003); (iv) the fraction of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ bound to the core RNAP in vivo is reduced by (p)ppGpp (Jishage et al., 2002); and (v) underproduction of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ or overproduction of the anti- ${ \boldsymbol { \cdot } } { \boldsymbol { \sigma } } ^ { 7 0 }$ factor Rsd circumvents the requirement of ppGpp for the promoters dependent on ppGpp (Jishage et al., 2002; Laurie et al., 2003; Mitchell et al., 2007; Piper et al., 2009).

It has been found that E. coli mutants lacking ppGpp have phenotypes similar to those of rpoS mutants that lack $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ (Gentry et al., 1993; Lange et al., 1995). It is also well-known that there is sluggish expression of heat shock genes in the absence, or with very low levels, of ppGpp (Kvint et al., 2000). The alarmone ppGpp destabilizes the open promoter complex of the stringently controlled promoters like rrn promoters (Barker et al., 2001; Zhou and Jin, 1998). Upon entry into a stationary phase, core RNAP may fall off such promoters, which consequently increase the core RNAP concentration in the cytosol. This increased availability of the core RNAP may favor association with alternative sigma factors (Barker et al., 2001; Nystrom, 2004; Zhou and Jin, 1998) 



Helmann JD. 1991. Alternative sigma factors and the regulation of flagellar gene expression. Molecular Microbiology 5: 2875– 2882. 



Anti-σ70 factor Rsd (a regulator of sigma D) forms a 1:1 complex with $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ and sequesters free $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ (Ilag et al., 2004; Westblade et al., 2004). It also has been shown to remove $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ actively from $\mathtt { E } \mathrm { - } \sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ complexes in vitro. The levels of Rsd increase during the stationary phase, and it sequesters approximately 25% of $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ (Piper et al., 2009). Hence, Rsd helps alternative sigma factors to access core RNAP. An E. coli protein Crl binds t $) \sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ and favors its association with core RNAP (Gaal et al., 2006; Typas et al., 2007). 



Hengge-Aronis R. 1993. Survival of hunger and stress: the role of rpoS in early stationary phase gene regulation in E. coli. Cell 72(2): 165– 168. 



Thus, alarmone ppGpp and proteins like Rsd and Crl help low-affinity alternative sigma factors compete against highaffinity $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ for the limited pool of core RNAP. There could be novel mechanisms that help alternative sigma factors to compete against housekeeping σ70, but they await discovery.

# Iron homeostasis and iron–sulfur cluster assembly in Escherichia coli

Huangen Ding 

Department of Biological Sciences, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, Louisiana, USA 

## 2.16.1 Introduction

In the reducing iron-rich, sulfide-rich environment that predominated on Earth about two billion years ago (Wachtersh¨ auser, 1992), iron–sulfur clusters are believed¨ to have spontaneously assembled in primitive macromolecules (e.g., early proteins or their precursors) with properly positioned ligands (Meyer, 2008). Throughout evolution, iron–sulfur clusters have become integral parts of diverse physiological processes, including photosynthesis; nitrogen fixation; sugar metabolism; biosynthesis of heme, biotin, lipoic acid, and amino acids; protein synthesis; RNA modification; DNA replication and repair; and regulation of gene expression (Beinert et al., 1997; Johnson et al., 2005; Lill, 2009; Meyer, 2008; Rouault, 2012). On the other hand, oxygen produced by early photosynthetic organisms has severely limited iron and sulfide availability for iron–sulfur cluster assembly, and thus forced organisms to adapt a group of dedicated proteins for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis. This chapter will focus on how intracellular iron may be recruited for iron–sulfur cluster assembly under aerobic conditions and how other transition metals such as copper may disrupt iron delivery and block iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis in Escherichia coli cells. 

## 2.16.2 Iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis in E. coli

In E. coli, there are two major gene clusters, iscR–iscSUA– hscBA–fdx (Zheng et al., 1998) and sufABCDSE (Lee et al., 2004; Outten et al., 2004; Takahashi and Tokumoto, 2002), that are responsible for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis (Figure 2.16.1). 

The housekeeping iron–sulfur cluster assembly proteins encoded by iscSUA–hscBA–fdx are highly conserved from bacteria to humans (Lill, 2009; Rouault, 2012). However, the inducible iron–sulfur cluster assembly proteins encoded by sufABCDSE (Lee et al., 2004; Outten et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 2001) are present only in some bacteria and in plastids in plants (Van Hoewyk et al., 2007; Xu and Moller, 2008). Among the iron–sulfur cluster assembly proteins shown in Figure 2.16.1, IscR is a global regulator for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis (Schwartz et al., 2001; see Chapter 19.3). When IscR binds a [2Fe-2S] cluster, IscR is a repressor to repress the expression of gene cluster isc (Fleischhacker et al., 2012). When the accessible iron and sulfide are limited in cells, IscR loses its [2Fe-2S] cluster, and apo-IscR de-represses the expression of gene cluster isc and activates the expression of gene cluster suf (Yeo et al., 2006) to promote iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis in E. coli cells. IscS and SufS are pyridoxal 5′ -phosphate-dependent cysteine desulfurases (Cupp-Vickery et al., 2003; Flint, 1996). Whereas IscS is a major cysteine desulfurase for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis (Schwartz et al., 2000), SufS has a low catalytic activity that can be fully activated upon binding with the SufE and SufBCD complex (Loiseau et al., 2003; Outten et al., 2003; Ye et al., 2006). IscU is a scaffold protein that hosts transient iron–sulfur clusters (Agar et al., 2000; Kato et al., 2002; Kurihara et al., 2003; Mansy et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2001, 2005; Urbina et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2002) and transfers the assembled clusters to target proteins (Raulfs et al., 2008; Unciuleac et al., 2007). IscS and IscU form a protein complex that facilitates the transfer of sulfur from IscS to IscU (Marinoni et al., 2012; Nuth and Cowan, 2009). Two heat shock cognate proteins, HscB and HscA, specifically interact with IscU (Silberg et al., 2004; Tapley and Vickery, 2004) and promote the transfer of the assembled clusters from IscU to apoproteins in an adensine triphosphate (ATP)-dependent reaction (Alderson et al., 2014; Bonomi et al., 2008; Chandramouli and Johnson, 2006). Ferredoxin (Fdx) contains a stable [2Fe-2S] cluster (Ta and Vickery, 1992) and may provide electrons for iron–sulfur cluster assembly (Chandramouli et al., 2007; Shi et al., 2012). The SufBCD complex has also been proposed as a scaffold complex for the SufS-mediated iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis (Chahal et al., 2009; Wollers et al., 2010). In addition, other proteins such as specific glutaredoxins may be involved in storing and transporting iron–sulfur clusters from scaffold proteins to target proteins (Li et al., 2012; Mapolelo et al., 2013; Shakamuri et al., 2012).

Figure 2.16.1 Two gene clusters for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis in E. coli. The isc gene cluster consists of iscR, iscS, iscU, iscA, hscB, hscA, and fdx. The suf gene cluster consists of sufA, sufB, sufC, sufD, sufS, and sufE.


It is now evident that sulfur in iron–sulfur clusters is primarily provided by cysteine desulfurases IscS and SufS. However, the iron donor(s) for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis remain(s) largely elusive. Frataxin, a mitochondrial protein that has been linked to the neurodegenerative disease Friedreich’s ataxia (Campuzano et al., 1996), has been previously characterized as an iron chaperone for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis (Layer et al., 2006; Yoon and Cowan, 2003). Frataxin is highly conserved from bacteria to humans (Babcock et al., 1997). However, frataxin and its homologs have a weak iron-binding activity (Ding et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2010; Stemmler et al., 2010) with an iron-binding constant of 4 to 55 μM (Bou-Abdallah et al., 2004; Kondapalli et al., 2008; Yoon and Cowan, 2003). Such a weak iron-binding activity would preclude frataxin from binding any significant amount of iron in cells under physiological conditions (Ding et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2010). Moreover, deletion of frataxin or its homologs has very little or no effect on iron– sulfur proteins in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Duby et al., 2002), Salmonella enterica (Vivas et al., 2006), and E. coli (Li et al., 1999). Only in iron-rich media, deletion of a frataxin homolog has a mild effect on iron–sulfur proteins in E. coli cells (Roche et al., 2015). In fact, the frataxin-deficient yeast cells can be rescued by expressing either mitochondrial ferritin (Campanella et al., 2004) or the vacuolar iron transporter CCC1 (Chen and Kaplan, 2000). Thus, it is likely that frataxin acts as a gatekeeper to regulate iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis by activating cysteine desulfurase (Bridwell-Rabb et al., 2014; Pandey et al., 2013) or directing sulfur flux from cysteine desulfurase (Adinolfi et al., 2009; Prischi et al., 2010; Tsai and Barondeau, 2010; Yan et al., 2013). 

## 2.16.3 IscA has a unique iron-binding activity among the iron–sulfur cluster assembly proteins in Escherichia coli

Among the iron–sulfur cluster assembly proteins encoded by iscR–iscSUA–hscBA–fdx in E. coli (Zheng et al., 1998), IscA has a unique and strong iron-binding activity with a stoichiometry of one iron per IscA dimer in vitro (Ding et al., 2004; Landry et al., 2013) (Figure 2.16.2). 

The iron association constant of E. coli IscA is about 1.0 × $1 0 ^ { 1 9 } \mathrm { { M } ^ { - 1 } }$ in the presence of the thioredoxin–thioredoxin reductase system in vitro (Ding and Clark, 2004; Ding et al., 2005; Landry et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2006). Similar iron-binding activity has been reported for the IscA homologs from Azotobacter vinelandii (Mapolelo et al., 2012), S. cerevisiae (Muhlenhoff et al., 2011), and humans (Lu et al., 2010), suggesting that the iron-binding activity of IscA is highly conserved among organisms.

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/b42e4f01010c00918a3aedbc0f5558a858f8c2a49cc8e59cdbb07170e7c4d273.jpg)


The in vivo iron-binding activity of IscA is also analyzed by expressing recombinant IscA in E. coli cells grown in M9 minimal medium supplement with increasing concentration of exogenous iron (from 0 to 1.0 μM). As shown in Figure 2.16.3, the iron binding in IscA is gradually increased as the iron concentration in M9 minimal medium increases. Thus, IscA has a high iron-binding activity in vitro and in vivo. 

Importantly, IscA fails to bind iron in E. coli cells (Figure 2.16.4a) or in vitro (Figure 2.16.4b) under anaerobic conditions. Only under aerobic conditions is IscA able to bind iron, suggesting that iron binding in IscA may require oxygen, and that IscA may have a strong binding affinity for ferric iron rather than ferrous iron. 

Despite the robust iron-binding activity of IscA under aerobic conditions, the iron center in IscA can be readily mobilized by L-cysteine (Ding et al., 2005; Landry et al., 2013). Figure 2.16.5 shows the electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectra of IscA. The iron-bound IscA has an EPR signal at g = 5.9 and 4.0, which represents an unusual mononuclear ferric iron center of $S = 3 / 2$ (Landry et al., 2013). When the iron-bound IscA is incubated with L-cysteine, the ferric iron in IscA is readily released to form the L-cysteine–ferric iron complex with an EPR signal at $g = 4 . 0$ . The apparent L-cysteine–ferric iron complex is subsequently reduced to ferrous iron by L-cysteine, and becomes available for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis (Ding et al., 2004; Landry et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2006). 

To further explore the role of IscA, the iron-bound IscA is compared with “free” iron as the iron source for iron–sulfur cluster assembly in vitro. Under anaerobic conditions, ferrous iron and the iron-bound IscA are almost equal in providing iron for iron–sulfur cluster assembly in IscU (Figure 2.16.6a and 2.16.6b). However, under aerobic conditions, no iron–sulfur clusters are assembled in IscU when ferrous iron is used as the iron source without IscA (Figure 2.16.6b). 

It is likely that ferrous iron in the reaction solution is oxidized to ferric hydroxide by oxygen without IscA. On the other hand, the iron-bound IscA is not affected by oxygen and can efficiently provide iron for iron–sulfur cluster assembly under aerobic conditions (Landry et al., 2013; Lu et al., 2008; Tan et al., 2009). The results further suggest that IscA may act as an iron chaperone for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis under aerobic conditions.

## 2.16.4 IscA and its paralog SufA are essential for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis in Escherichia coli

For E. coli cells, deletion of IscA has only a mild effect on cell growth. However, deletion of IscA and its paralog SufA results in a null-growth phenotype in M9 minimal medium under aerobic conditions (Lu et al., 2008; Mettert et al., 2008; Vinella et al., 2009) (Figure 2.16.7). 

Similar to that observed in E. coli cells (Figure 2.16.7), depletion of IscA in Azotobacter vinelandii also results in a nullgrowth phenotype in modified Burks minimal medium under elevated oxygen conditions (Johnson et al., 2006). In S. cerevisiae, depletion of IscA homologs (Isa1 and Isa2) leads to dependency on the amino acids lysine and glutamate for cell growth under aerobic conditions (Jensen and Culotta, 2000; Kaut et al., 2000). In Schizosaccharomyces pombe, deletion of IscA homologs is lethal (Kim et al., 2010). In cultured HeLa cells, depletion of the IscA homolog (hIscA1) also decreases the enzyme activity of iron–sulfur proteins in mitochondrion and cytosol under aerobic conditions (Song et al., 2009). Thus, IscA and its homologs are essential for cell growth under aerobic conditions. Nevertheless, the E. coli cells with deletion of IscA and SufA can grow in M9 minimal medium under anaerobic conditions (Figure 2.16.7), suggesting that IscA and SufA are dispensable under anaerobic conditions. 

The function of IscA and SufA has been explored further by expressing a recombinant endonuclease III [4Fe-4S] cluster in the E. coli mutant cells carrying deletions of IscA and SufA. Figure 2.16.8 shows that E. coli cells with deletion of IscA and SufA fail to assemble iron–sulfur clusters in endonuclease III under aerobic growth conditions (Tan et al., 2009). However, the iron– sulfur clusters are assembled in endonuclease III in the E. coli cells with deletion of IscA and SufA under anaerobic growth conditions. 

Similar results are also observed when other iron–sulfur proteins, including aconitase B (Varghese et al., 2003), phosphogluconate dehydratase (Jang and Imlay, 2007), and dihydroxyacid dehydratase, are expressed in the E. coli IscA/SufA-deleted mutant cells (data not shown). Evidently, IscA and SufA are essential for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis in E. coli cells under aerobic conditions, but not under anaerobic conditions. Perhaps, under anaerobic conditions, intracellular ferrous iron is adequate for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis. Under aerobic conditions, however, ferrous iron is severely limited, and IscA and its paralog SufA are required to recruit intracellular iron and facilitate iron delivery for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis. 

## 2.16.5 IscA also has a strong copper-binding activity

Although copper is an essential element for all living cells, excess copper is highly toxic (Karlsson et al., 2008; Rodriguez-Montelongo et al., 1993). It was proposed that excess copper may mediate production of reactive oxygen species via the Fenton reaction to create cellular oxidative damage (Karlsson et al., 2008; Rodriguez-Montelongo et al., 1993; see Chapter 2.12). However, recent studies have argued that copper does not promote oxidative damage in E. coli cells under aerobic or anaerobic conditions (Macomber et al., 2007). Instead, copper may disrupt the labile [4Fe-4S] clusters of dehydratases and block multiple cellular metabolic pathways (Fung et al., 2013; Macomber and Imlay, 2009). 

Since IscA has a flexible iron-binding site with three conserved cysteine residues (Bilder et al., 2004; Cupp-Vickery et al., 2004; Morimoto et al., 2006), it is possible that IscA may bind other transition metals such as copper in the same metal-binding sites. Indeed, among the iron–sulfur cluster assembly proteins encoded by the gene cluster iscSUA–hscBA–fdx, IscA has a unique and strong copper-binding activity (Figure 2.16.9). The EPR measurements showed that IscA binds $\mathrm { C u ^ { + 1 } }$ , which can be oxidized to $\mathrm { C u } ^ { + 2 }$ by nitric acid (2.5% (V/V)) (Figure 2.16.9).

The strong copper-binding activity of E. coli IscA is further confirmed by the in vitro titration experiments (Figure 2.16.10). 

If both iron and copper bind to the same metal-binding sites in IscA, copper may compete with iron for the metal-binding sites in the protein. Figure 2.16.11 shows that when twofold excess of copper is present, the iron binding in IscA is severely blocked, indicating that copper can indeed compete for the iron-binding sites in IscA. 

## 2.16.6 Copper binding in IscA inhibits iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis in Escherichia coli

Like E. coli IscA, E. coli SufA has a similar copper-binding activity under the same experimental conditions (data not shown). If copper competes with iron for the metal-binding sites in IscA and SufA, copper would inhibit the IscA–SufA-mediated iron– sulfur cluster biogenesis in cells. To test this idea, we express recombinant iron–sulfur proteins in the E. coli cells grown in lysogeny broth (LB) medium supplemented with or without copper. 

E. coli dihydroxyacid dehydratase (IlvD) requires an intact [4Fe-4S] cluster for its catalytic activity (Flint et al., 1993). The enzyme activity of IlvD has previously been used to assess the [4Fe-4S] cluster assembly in E. coli cells (Ren et al., 2008). In the experiments, recombinant IlvD is expressed in the E. coli cells grown in LB medium. Adding copper to LB medium before the recombinant IlvD is expressed in E. coli cells decreases the total IlvD enzyme activity by 90% (Figure 2.16.12a). However, the enzyme activity of IlvD in the cells can be largely restored by reconstituting with iron–sulfur clusters, suggesting that copper in LB medium blocks the iron–sulfur cluster assembly in IlvD without affecting the protein synthesis (Tan et al., 2014).

## 2.16.7 Excess copper emulates the phenotype of IscA deletion in Escherichia coli

The proteins encoded by gene cluster iscSUA–hscBA–fdx represent the housekeeping machinery for iron–sulfur cluster assembly (Zheng et al., 1998). If IscA is a target of copper toxicity in E. coli cells, addition of excess copper could emulate the phenotype of the E. coli cells with deletion of IscA. To test this idea, the gene encoding IscA is deleted in E. coli cells, and a recombinant endonuclease III [4Fe-4S] cluster is expressed in wild-type and IscA-deleted mutant cells grown in LB medium supplemented with or without copper. Endonuclease III is then purified from the E. coli cells and subjected to ultraviolet (UV)-visible absorption measurements. Figure 2.16.13 shows that deletion of IscA or addition of copper severely blocks the iron–sulfur cluster assembly in recombinant endonuclease III in wild-type E. coli cells. However, copper has no additional inhibitory effect on the iron– sulfur clusters in endonuclease III in the IscA-deleted E. coli cells, suggesting that IscA is one of the primary targets of copper toxicity in E. coli cells (see Chapter 2.12).

Figure 2.16.14 A proposed model for the function of IscA in iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis. Under anaerobic conditions, intracellular iron is adequate for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis, and IscA is dispensable. Under aerobic conditions, IscA recruits intracellular iron and delivers iron for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis. When excess copper is present, copper competes for the metal-binding sites in IscA and blocks the IscA-mediated iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis in cells.

Vinella D, Brochier-Armanet C, Loiseau L, Talla E, Barras F. 2009. Ironsulfur (Fe/S) protein biogenesis: phylogenomic and genetic studies of A-type carriers. PLoS Genetics 5(5): e1000497. 



Epsilonproteobacteria, Spirochaetes, Fusobacteria, Thermotogae, and most of PVC (Planctomycetales–Verrucomicrobia– Chlamydiae) do not have IscA homologs. Interestingly, many of the bacteria that do not have IscA homologs either are anaerobic organisms or live at the extremes of pH, temperature, and salinity (Iwasaki, 2010). In archaea, most of the sequenced organisms do not have IscA homologs either. In eukaryotes, almost all organisms contain at least one copy of IscA, with the exception of two groups: amitochondria entamoeba and microsporidia, which do not have IscA homologs (Vinella et al., 2009). Amitochondria entamoeba are the only anaerobic eukaryotic organisms, whereas microsporidia are the smallest eukaryotic sporeforming organisms living in extreme environments. On the other hand, other key iron–sulfur cluster assembly proteins such as cysteine desulfurase and scaffold proteins are present in both aerobic and anaerobic organisms. Thus, IscA and its homologs may have been adapted in aerobic organisms for iron–sulfur cluster assembly under aerobic conditions. The observations that IscA has a strong iron-binding activity (Figure 2.16.2) and is essential for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis are consistent with the idea that IscA may act as an iron chaperone for iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis under aerobic conditions (Figure 2.16.14). The competition of iron and copper for the metal-binding sites in IscA also suggests that IscA is a primary target of copper toxicity and that intracellular copper may modulate iron–sulfur cluster biogenesis via binding to IscA in cells.

# Mechanisms underlying the antimicrobial capacity of metals

Joe A. Lemire and Raymond J. Turner 

Biofilm Research Group, University of Calgary, Calgary, Alberta, Canada 

## 2.17.1 Introduction

Metals participate in chemistries that cannot be replicated solely by organic molecules in biological systems, making them essential micronutrients for microorganisms (Lemire et al., 2013). Properties including a high charge-to-size ratio, electrophilicity, and the ability – of select metals – to undergo reduction– oxidation reactions make them essential players in cellular biochemistry (Lemire et al., 2013). Specific metal ions are required for maintaining the structure of DNA, cell membranes, and proteins, and are key to the function of many enzymes (Andreini et al., 2004; Waldron et al., 2009). Still, essential metals are toxic to the microbial cell when present in excess. Additionally, select non-essential metals, including Silver (Ag), mercury (Hg), and tellurium (Te), impart toxicity to microorganisms at remarkably low concentrations (Harrison et al., 2004; Lemire et al., 2013; Nies, 1999). Because metals exhibit such potent activity against microorganisms, they have found utility throughout history as agents to prevent spoilage and combat infection (Lemire et al., 2013, and references within). More recently, the antimicrobial potential of certain metals – Ag, Copper (Cu), and Gallium (Ga) – is being explored as coatings for wound care as well as intravital products (Kollef et al., 2008; Lemire et al., 2013; Malin et al., 2013), surfaces in the clinic (Grass et al., 2011), and anti-biofilm agents (Britigan and Singh, 2006; Kaneko et al., 2007). Additionally, recent findings have demonstrated the capacity for Ag to revitalize and enhance the efficacy of antibiotics against some antibiotic-resistant Gram-negative bacteria (Morones-Ramirez et al., 2013). This finding is ever important to medical microbiologists because we are experiencing an era where a dwindling pipeline of new antibiotics is coinciding with an increase in antibiotic-resistant infections. 

It turns out that the mechanism of toxicity for metal ions is related to their chemical and physical properties. Essentially, metal ions interact with discrete targets within the microbial cell (Lemire et al., 2013). Cellular targets including enzymes, membranes, and DNA are vulnerable to disruption by metal ions. Thus, microbial cells have evolved physiological mechanisms to adapt to and resist metal intoxication (Figure 2.17.1). 

Indeed, the mechanisms of metal resistance have been well defined (see Chapter 2.12 and Section 20). Unfortunately, much less is understood about the particular ways that metals poison microbial cells. This arises mainly because of the diverse biochemistries encountered amongst different microorganisms. However, if we aim to design a generation of metal-based antimicrobial products, an understanding of metal toxicity is necessary. Moreover, as metal contamination increases in the environment, an insight into the mechanisms of how metals exert their toxic effect on bacterial cells will be necessary to develop new bioremediation strategies and understand how metal pollution might alter microbial ecology (see Sections 19 and 20). 

In this chapter, we will explore what is currently known about the antimicrobial activity of metals. Furthermore, we will examine aspects of metal biochemistry and toxicology to reveal mechanisms of how metals can injure and kill microbial cells. Although many mechanisms have not been fully described, we will also discuss proposed mechanisms of metal toxicity in hopes of priming future research efforts that will explore the antimicrobial activity of metals. Likely, the first step of metal intoxication is intracellular accumulation of the metal – with the exception of starving the bacterial cell by competing with the uptake of an essential metal. However, a discussion of how metals enter the microbial cell is outside the scope of this chapter. For a comprehensive list of current, established metal transport mechanisms, refer to Lemire et al. (2013) and the references within. Instead, here we will categorize the mechanisms by which metals impose their antimicrobial activities. It is important to note, firstly, that mechanisms of metal toxicity may not be exclusive, and likely cell death or growth inhibition is the result of the orchestration of multiple mechanisms (see Section 20). Secondly, the speciation of the metal (what chemical form the metal is in) often results in a different toxicological profile (Lemire et al., 2013).

Figure 2.17.1 Microbial resistance and adaptation to metal stress. The genetic and biochemical determinants that allow microorganisms to resist and adapt to metal stress have been well characterized. It is important to note that resistance mechanisms are not universal, and usually multiple methods are employed to resist metal intoxication. (a) Reduced uptake: Bacteria have evolved regulatory mechanisms that modulate the activity of metal transporters in the membrane, providing a way to control toxic metal influx (Ma et al., 2009; Outten and O’Halloran, 2001). (b) Efflux: Microorganisms possess a range of genes that encode for transporters that can efflux toxic metals out of the cell (Nies, 1999, 2003; Silver and Phung, 1996). (c) Sequestration: Certain microbes have the capability to produce extracellular polymers or siderophores in response to metal exposure. These extracellular polymers have functional groups that have the capacity to bind or precipitate metal ions. In addition to binding metals in the extracellular environment, bacteria have also been observed precipitating metals at their cell membranes and within the periplasm – although the biochemical mechanism of the latter process has not been fully described. Additionally, microorganisms can employ cytoplasmic proteins to sequester and store metals (Braud et al., 2009; Carrondo, 2003; Chaturvedi et al., 2012; Dimkpa et al., 2008; Hannauer et al., 2012; Harrison et al., 2007; Johnston et al., 2013; Langley and Beveridge, 1999; Silver and Phung, 1996; Zannoni et al., 2008). (d) Chemical modification: Most metals can be modified through redox and covalent reactions within the bacterial cell. This process alters their chemical reactivity and converts the metal ions to less toxic species or lowers their bioaccessibility (Silver and Phung, 1996). (e) Alternative pathways: Some bacterial cells have the capacity to use alternative metabolic pathways to circumvent pathways that are challenged by metal stress. Often, the alternative proteins have catalytic cores that are unaffected by the toxic metal (Lemire et al., 2010). (f) Repair: Some cellular molecules have functional groups that are vulnerable to oxidation by reacting with metals or reactive oxygen species (ROS). These oxidation-prone proteins can be repaired by chaperones, enzymes, and antioxidants (Harrison et al., 2009). IM, inner membrane; M, metal with a charge of n; OM, outer membrane; S, sulphur.


## 2.17.2 Reactive oxygen species production and antioxidant depletion

One commonly reported observation when microbial cells are exposed to toxic levels of metal ions is the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (see Section 10). Even essential metals such as Fe(II) and Cu(II) can induce a state of oxidative stress and subsequent DNA damage within the bacterial cell, which may explain the tight regulatory mechanisms governing their homeostasis (see Section 19) (Imlay et al., 1988; Macomber et al., 2007; Nunoshiba et al., 1999; Touati et al., 1995; Warnes et al., 2012; Warnes and Keevil, 2011). Even non-essential metals including Cr(VI), As(III), and Te(IV) have been observed to poison microbial cells by generating ROS (Harrison et al., 2009; Itoh et al., 1995; Parvatiyar et al., 

2005; Perez et al., 2007; Sumner et al., 2005). Often, metal detoxification efforts can result in the production of ROS. For example, Escherichia coli, as well as many Pseudomonas and Bacillus species, can enzymatically reduce Cr(VI) to Cr(III) (Ackerley et al., 2006). However, the one-electron reduction of Cr(VI) to Cr(V) – a highly reactive species of Cr – can undergo redox cycling to generate ROS (Ackerley et al., 2006; Cervantes et al., 2001). Likewise, the reduction of tellurite (Te(IV)) to elemental tellurium, by reductases, leads to the generation of superoxide $( \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } { \cdot } ^ { - } )$ (Chasteen et al., 2009). Undeniably, ROS generation is a major mechanism of metal toxicity in microbial cells. When bacterial and Saccharomyces cerevisiae mutants are deficient in ROS-scavenging enzymes (superoxide dismutase, glutathione reductase, and catalase) and cellular antioxidants, they become more sensitive to $\operatorname { C r } ,$ 

As, Te, Fe, and Cu (Geslin et al., 2001; Itoh et al., 1995; Parvatiyar et al., 2005; Sumner et al., 2005; Touati et al., 1995). Additionally, other studies have reported that bacteria and yeast exposed to Cu(II), Cr(VI), As(III), or Te(IV) upregulate genes involved in ROS defence including superoxide dismutase, heat shock proteins, and catalase (Jin et al., 2008; Parvatiyar et al., 2005; Perez et al., 2007; Teitzel et al., 2006). Thus, the toxicity of certain metals would, at least in part, be due to oxidative stress – a process that can induce protein, membrane, and DNA damage (see Section 10). In fact, some limited studies have demonstrated that certain metals including Al(III), Ga(III), and Cr(VI) lead to an increase in oxidized proteins and lipids in select microbial species (Mailloux et al., 2007; Sumner et al., 2005). However, directly measuring ROS production under metal toxicity poses a challenge to researchers due to the short half-life of many oxidative species. Metal-catalysed oxidation is a natural, orchestrated, and essential cellular process that usually does not harm the cell. Aerobic respiration readily generates partially reduced species of molecular oxygen, including $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } { \cdot } ^ { - }$ , that can react with Fe via Fenton chemistry to auto-oxidize (Stohs and Bagchi, 1995; Valko et al., 2005). Fenton chemistry is essentially a process whereby Fe intensifies oxygen toxicity by catalysing singlet electron transfer from a $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ donor molecule. Often, free radical chain reactions involving metals may be propagated by $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ itself. Moreover, the redox cycling of metals during Fenton reactions can consume cellular antioxidants. Hence, redox-sensing transcription factors often regulate ROS detoxification machinery as well as modify metal ion homeostasis (Faulkner and Helmann, 2011). 

## 2.17.2.1 Oxidative stress

The chemistry underlying how metals can induce ROS production can be summarized into three proposed mechanisms (Figure 2.17.2; see Section 10): 

1 Redox-active metals (metals that can gain or lose electrons and participate in reduction or oxidation reactions) – such as Fe, Cu, Cr, Co, V, and Ni – can participate in Fenton chemistry in vitro (Stohs and Bagchi, 1995; Valko et al., 2005). With the exception of Cu (Macomber et al., 2007), establishing whether or not other redox-active metals participate in Fenton chemistry in vivo is complicated to assess due to many factors that affect chemistry including pH, the presence of coordinating ligands, and the variability of cellular reduction potential. 

2 Select metals have the capacity to disrupt donor ligands responsible for coordinating Fe. One of the primary targets for metals (Al, Cu, Ag, Cd, Zn, Te, and Hg) is the solventaccessible [4Fe-4S] iron–sulphur cluster of proteins (Calderon et al., 2009; Macomber and Imlay, 2009; Macomber et al., 2007; Middaugh et al., 2005; Xu and Imlay, 2012). In E. coli, under normal conditions, intracellular iron concentrations are approximately 0.1 mM (Outten and O’Halloran, 2001). The concentration of labile Fe is strictly regulated within the microbial cell through storage and coordination, leaving approximately 20 μM that can participate in Fenton chemistry to produce ROS (Keyer and Imlay, 1996). Thus, destruction of iron–sulphur clusters by metals can result in the release of free Fe into the cytoplasm, where it can induce ROS production (see Chapter 19.3). Of particular interest is the potential for ROS-disturbed [4Fe-4S] iron–sulphur clusters to participate in the induction of genes involved in anaerobiosis. In E. coli, [4Fe-4S] iron–sulphur clusters can oxidize to [3Fe-4S] clusters, followed by a non-redox reaction to yield a [2Fe-2S] cluster, which causes a conformational change in fumarate– nitrate reductase allowing it to bind to DNA and act as a transcription factor for genes involved in metabolism and oxygen sensing – a process that is also initiated by ROS (Crack et al., 2004). Previous observations, where Ag, Hg, and Ga led to the generation of ROS (Park et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2012), are likely due to the capacity of these redox-inactive metals to interfere with Fe homeostasis and release Fe from iron–sulphur clusters into the cytoplasm. Additionally, the cells may need to subsequently upregulate ROS detoxification enzymes to avoid a toxic effect from these aforementioned metals (Gordon et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2011; Stojiljkovic et al., 1999).

Figure 2.17.2 Mechanisms underlying metal-mediated ROS production in microbial cells (see Section 10). A frequently observed hallmark of metal toxicity is an increase in oxidative stress. Metals can induce ROS production by (a) undergoing Fenton chemistry in the cell, which can produce ROS through singlet electron exchange with $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ or other oxidative molecules such as $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ or depleting antioxidants (Stohs and Bagchi, 1995; Valko et al., 2005). (b) Some metals have the capacity to interfere with the homeostasis of Fe (see Chapter 19.1). Once the labile Fe pool is disrupted, free Fe in the cell can catalyse ROS production via the Fenton reaction (Park et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2012). (c) Reduced thiols constitute one of the largest reservoirs of antioxidants in the bacterial cell. Thiophilic metals such as Ag(I), Cd(II), Co(II), Zn(II), Cr(VI), As(III), and Te(IV) have the capacity to oxidize thiols such as glutathione, leading to the depletion of these crucial cellular moieties (Fauchon et al., 2002; Harrison et al., 2009; Helbig et al., 2008a, 2008b; Liau et al., 1997). M, metal with a charge of n; S, sulphur.


3 Metal ions can induce oxidative stress in the bacterial cell through the depletion of antioxidants. Numerous in vitro studies have demonstrated that thiol-mediated reduction of Fe(III), Cu(II), Cr(VI), As(III), and Te(IV) can generate ROS through a sulphur radical intermediary. Some metals, for example Cr(VI), react with thiols to produce more toxic species – Cr(III), Cr(IV), and Cr(V) – that are redox active and undergo Fenton chemistry to produce ROS (Valko et al., 2005). This phenomenon, however, has never been experimentally established in bacterial cells. Likewise, the capacity of S radicals to generate ROS has never been demonstrated in vivo. 

## 2.17.2.2 Thiol depletion

Cellular thiols are a major reservoir of antioxidants, and they are necessary for discrete biochemical reactions. Soft as well as borderline Lewis acid metals, in addition to some metal oxyanions, form energetically favourable covalent bonds with reduced thiols (a soft Lewis base) (Lemire et al., 2013). The resulting chemistry leads to metal ions binding to protein sulphydryl groups and the depletion of thiol-based antioxidants such as glutathione (Fauchon et al., 2002; Harrison et al., 2009; Helbig et al., 2008a, 2008b; Liau et al., 1997). Experimentally, when E. coli is exposed to toxic doses of Ag(I), Cd(II), Zn(II), Cr(VI), As(III), and Te(IV), there is a resultant depletion of cellular thiol pools (Harrison et al., 2009). It is not surprising, then, that enzymes involved in reducing oxidized thiols and maintaining glutathione homeostasis are essential determinants of E. coli’s capacity to tolerate thiophilic metals such as Cu (Harrison et al., 2009; Helbig et al., 2008a, 2008b). 

## 2.17.3 Metal disruption of cellular functions

Two commonly used terms in metal toxicology are the oligodynamic effects of metals (the ability of metals to bind to multiple cellular ligands) and molecular or ionic mimicry (the capacity of non-essential metals to interfere with the homeostasis of essential metals). In both cases, toxic doses of metals can lead to the disruption of cellular functioning by impairing membrane function, interfering with nutrient homeostasis, inducing genotoxicity, and disabling enzymes (Figure 2.17.3). 

## 2.17.3.1 Membrane disruption

The membrane of bacterial cells contains polymers (lipids, sugar, and proteins) that are dense with electronegative charges that serve as binding sites for metal cations (Zhang and Rock, 2008). One of the proposed, but not experimentally demonstrated in vivo, mechanisms of Al(III) toxicity is by coordinating with phosphate heads on phospholipids (MacKinnon et al., 2004; Zambenedetti et al., 1994); see Chapter 20.2. Because of the ability of the cell membrane to coordinate metal ions, it has been the hypothesized site of toxicity for many metals including Ag(I) and Cu(II) (Lemire et al., 2013). Experimental analysis using electron microscopy has revealed that the cytoplasmic membrane of E. coli and Staphylococcus aureus is disturbed by toxic doses of Ag and Al (Feng et al., 2000; Jung et al., 2008; Li et al., 2010; Yaganza et al., 2004; Yamanaka et al., 2005). However, the mechanistic details of how these metals are eliciting their deleterious effects remain unclear. Other investigations into metal toxicity have demonstrated that metals, particularly Ag, Ga, and Al, can disrupt the bacterial electron transport chain (Bragg and Rainnie, 1974; Chenier et al., 2008; Gordon et al., 2010; Mailloux et al., 2007). A mechanistic example of how this works was shown in Vibrio harveyi exposed to toxic doses of Ag(I). NADH–quinone–oxidoreductase (NQR) is an essential component of the respiratory chain for generating a redox-driven transmembrane Na+ and chemiosmotic proton gradient in some bacteria (Fadeeva et al., 2011). In V. harveyi, Ag(I) inhibits the activity of NQR, a process that is reversed by introducing site-specific mutations in the proteins (Fadeeva et al., 2011). It has also been proposed that Ag(I) dissipates the chemiosmotic potential of the membrane, through NQR-independent mechanisms, by causing proton leakage across the membrane (Dibrov et al., 2002). 

Lipid peroxidation is another reported and proposed mechanism of metal toxicity to bacterial cells. To date, the majority of evidence for lipid peroxidation has been collected using eukaryotic systems. Moreover, eukaryotic cells are rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids (Janero, 1990; Valko et al., 2005), whereas most bacterial membranes contain monounsaturated fatty acids (Zhang and Rock, 2008). In bacteria and yeast, Cu (II), Al(III), Ga(III), and Cd(II) exposure has been linked to an increase in lipid peroxidation (Grass et al., 2011; Hong et al., 2012; Howlett and Avery, 1997; Mailloux et al., 2007). When genetic mutations are introduced to encourage a cell to produce more unsaturated fatty acids, or cells are supplemented with polyunsaturated fats, lipid peroxidation increases under toxic metal exposure (Hong et al., 2012; Howlett and Avery, 1997). However, it is important to note that these results were obtained using the thiobarbituric acid-reactive substance (TBARS) assay on cell extracts. Unfortunately, the TBARS assay does not monitor the by-products of lipid peroxidation directly, which can often be more toxic and is also prone to false positives from several oxidized cellular molecules (Janero, 1990). Thus, results obtained with the TBARS assay should be interpreted with caution, and lipid peroxidation as a mechanism of metal toxicity warrants further investigation. 

## 2.17.3.2 Interference with nutrient homeostasis

Metals can often inhibit the growth of microorganisms by interfering with the homeostasis of other essential nutrients. In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Ga interferes with Fe homeostasis by inhibiting Fe(III) uptake in a concentration-dependent manner. The mechanistic determinant of this competitive uptake in P. aeruginosa is the ability of Ga(III) to repress the Fe-responsive transcriptional regulator PvdS, which subsequently inhibits the expression of genes involved in Fe(III) uptake (Kaneko et al., 2007). Thus, the partial mechanism of Ga(III) toxicity is the capacity to dysregulate the expression of genes involved in Fe homeostasis. However, in P. aeruginosa, substituting Fe(III) for Ga(III) did not reverse the toxic effects in a concentrationdependent manner (Kaneko et al., 2007), whereas in Pseudomonas fluorescens Fe substitution did partially relieve the Ga toxicity phenotype (Al-Aoukaty et al., 1992) – prompting further investigation into the effects of Ga on Fe homeostasis. Another good experimental example of metals interfering with nutrient homeostasis is the capacity of Cr(VI) to induce sulphate starvation in S. cerevisiae. Chromate has a similar affinity for

Meanwhile, Cu(II) and Cd(II) have been demonstrated to disrupt the membrane by inducing lipid peroxidation (Grass et al., 2011; Hong et al., 2012; Howlett and Avery, 1997). (b) Interference with nutrient homeostasis: Ga(III) has been demonstrated to repress the Fe-responsive transcriptional regulator PvdS, which subsequently inhibits the expression of genes involved in Fe (III) uptake (Kaneko et al., 2007). (c) Genotoxicity: Toxic doses of Fe have been observed to induce double-stranded DNA breaks (Lemire et al., 2013; Linley et al., 2012). (d) Protein dysfunction: (i) Select metals can oxidize cysteine residues within catalytic sites in proteins (e.g., peptide deformylase), causing release of the bound metal (Anjem and Imlay, 2012). (ii) Many metals have a demonstrated capacity to disrupt Fe–S clusters either directly or indirectly (via production of ROS), causing loss of protein activity (Calderon et al., 2009; Macomber and Imlay, 2009; Xu and Imlay, 2012). Toxic metals can participate in ionic mimicry of essential metals to replace (iii) catalytic metals or (iv) structural metals, rendering a decrease in protein activity. For example, (iii) Pb(II) can replace Zn(II) in the active site of δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD); and (iv) Ni(II) can replace Zn(II) in fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase (FbaA) (Macomber et al., 2011).

Subsequently, the sulphur-sparing response is induced (Fauchon et al., 2002; Pereira et al., 2008). Supplementing the cells with other sources of sulphur can reverse the sulphur starvation phenotype, suggesting direct nutrient competition. However, growth inhibition and the sulphur-sparing response are induced at chromate concentrations that are 20- fold lower than the sulphate concentration, suggesting that other mechanisms also contribute to chromate-mediated sulphur starvation (Pereira et al., 2008). 

## 2.17.3.3 Genotoxicity

It has been well established that Fe-mediated Fenton chemistry can induce lethal DNA damage to E. coli (Lemire et al., 2013; Linley et al., 2012). Hence, metals that interfere with Fe homeostasis and release free Fe into the cytoplasm can induce DNA damage in bacterial cells, such as mutations that disrupt Fe homeostasis, increase the amount of Fenton-active Fe in the cell, accelerate DNA damage, and result in cell death (Keyer and Imlay, 1996; Touati et al., 1995). This effect can be reversed if cells are treated with permeable Fe chelators prior to treatment with $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (Imlay et al., 1988). Though the link between Fe toxicity and DNA damage has been well established, the same cannot be said for many other metals. When genotoxicity testing is performed using the Ames test and other similar assays, poisonous doses of Mn(II), Cr(VI), Co(II), Cd(II), Mo(IV), Sb(III), and As(III) are mutagenic to bacterial cells (Asakura et al., 2009; Nishioka, 1975; Wong, 1988). But toxic concentrations of Ni(II), Cu(II), Te(IV), Pb(II), Ag(I), and Al(III) do not result in increased mutation rates (Asakura et al., 2009; Nishioka, 1975; Wong, 1988). In fact, recent observations suggest that Cu can protect E. coli from $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ -mediated DNA damage even though this metal is redox active and has the capacity to generate ROS (Macomber et al., 2007). It is important to note that this capacity of Cu to protect E. coli from ROS production appears to be biochemically restricted to the oxidative environment of the periplasm, suggesting that it is isolated from the DNA in the cytosol (Macomber et al., 2007). Further, even though Cr(VI) is accepted as one of the most mutagenic metals (Asakura et al., 2009; Nishioka, 1975; Wong, 1988), S. cerevisiae strains that lack DNA repair mechanisms are no more susceptible to Cr(VI) toxicity (Sumner et al., 2005). Though many in vitro studies do demonstrate that many metals do promote genotoxicity, more investigation is required to demonstrate that it is a bona fide mechanism of toxicity for metals in vivo. 

## 2.17.3.4 Protein dysfunction

Hypothetically, proteins would seem a likely target for metal intoxication due to their reservoir of a variety of ligands – reduced thiols, carboxylate groups, and amines. However, little work has been performed experimentally to demonstrate this mechanism of toxicity in the bacterial cell. Moreover, studies in E. coli suggest that at most a few amino acid residues are susceptible to metal-catalysed oxidation and that those residues are in proximity to metal-binding sites (Requena et al., 2003; Stadtman and Levine, 2003; Stadtman et al., 2003). Oxidative protein damage arises when metals catalyse oxidation of amino acid side chains (histidine, arginine, lysine, and proline are exceptionally vulnerable) resulting in carbonyl derivative production – a marker to monitor oxidative protein damage (Stadtman and Levine, 2003). Metals may therefore cause a loss of catalytic activity of proteins and induce protein degradation by oxidizing amino acid side chains (Stadtman et al., 2003). An example of this mechanism is observed with toxic doses of Cr(VI), which causes an ROS-independent rapid increase in S. cerevisiae protein carbonyl levels. Of the oxidized proteins, those found in the cytosolic fraction – especially glycolytic enzymes – were affected the greatest by Cr(VI) and represent a major source of Cr(VI) toxicity (Sumner et al., 2005). In P. fluorescens, toxic levels of both Al(III) and Ga(III) result in an increase in oxidized proteins, which might partially explain their toxicity (Mailloux et al., 2007). 

Many mononuclear metalloenzymes are dependent on divalent cations such as Zn(II), Cu(II), Mn(II), Fe(II), and Co(II) for their structure and/or function. Some of these enzymes have been demonstrated to be sensitive to ROS – for example, E. coli peptide deformylase (PDF), threonine dehydrogenase (Tdh), and cytosine deaminase (Anjem and Imlay, 2012). PDF and Tdh coordinate an Fe(II) atom via a cysteine residue that can be readily oxidized to sulphinic [RSO(OH)] or sulphonic $[ \mathrm { R } \mathrm { S } ( { = } \mathrm { O } ) _ { 2 } { - }$ OH], resulting in loss of enzyme function (Anjem and Imlay, 2012). In an effort to counteract this effect, E. coli exposed to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ stress will increase Mn(II) uptake. Mn(II) can displace Fe(II) in the $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ -sensitive metalloenzymes. Since Mn(II) is not sensitive to ROS in vivo, it is hypothesized that this alteration in metallation protects these enzymes from destruction from ROS (Anjem and Imlay, 2012; Anjem et al., 2009; see Section 10). 

Several studies have demonstrated that bacterial Fe–S dehydratases are especially sensitive to site-specific inactivation by toxic metals (Calderon et al., 2009; Macomber and Imlay, 2009; Xu and Imlay, 2012). Because these dehydratases are essential for producing branched-chain amino acids, the loss of these enzymes leads to growth arrest under metal toxicity. Similarly, this growth arrest phenotype is encountered under toxic doses of ROS, which have been demonstrated to destroy solventaccessible [4Fe-4S] iron–sulphur clusters in the same enzymes that are involved in branched-chain amino acid biosynthesis (dihydroxy-acid dehydratase and isopropylmalate isomerase (IPMI)) (Macomber and Imlay, 2009). In addition, Cu toxicity has also been demonstrated with the inactivation of IPMI and decreased activities of fumarase A and 6-phosphoglucanate dehydratase – another two enzymes dependent on Fe–S clusters for catalysis (Macomber and Imlay, 2009; see Chapter 19.3). Similarly, in P. fluorescens, Al(III) has been demonstrated to lead to the decreased activity of a variety of Fe–S cluster dependent enzymes including aconitase, fumarase A, and succinate dehydrogenase (Chenier et al., 2008; Mailloux et al., 2007; Middaugh et al., 2005). Experimentally, it has been demonstrated that the mechanism by which metals destroy [4Fe-4S] iron–sulphur clusters is oxygen independent – which is not the case for ROS (see Section 10). Under anaerobic conditions, Cu(I) toxicity converts [4Fe-4S] clusters to [3Fe-4S] clusters in vitro (Macomber and Imlay, 2009). This implies that Cu(I) can poison E. coli under anoxic conditions. 

Ag(I), Hg(II), Cd(II), Zn(II), Co(II), Ni(II), and Pb(II) have been experimentally demonstrated to damage Fe–S-containing dehydratases in vitro, independent of ROS, and inhibit these enzymes in vivo at concentrations that cause bacteriostasis (Xu and Imlay, 2012). Because the activity of the Fe–S dehydratases can be repaired by enzymes that restore Fe–S clusters (cysteine desulphurase or SufA), it is apparent that the mechanism of toxicity of metals is destruction of Fe–S clusters and not the proteins that contain them (Macomber and Imlay, 2009; Xu and 

Imlay, 2012). In E. coli, Te(IV) has also been shown to abolish Fe–S-containing enzymes, such as fumarase A and aconitase B. However, this only happens under aerobic conditions, suggesting that unlike the divalent cations, metal oxyanions disrupt Fe– S clusters in an ROS-dependent manner (Calderon et al., 2009). 

Metals also possess the capacity to participate in other sitespecific inhibition of enzymes by a process called ionic mimicry. An example of ionic mimicry is the displacement of Zn(II) from the active site of δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD) by Pb(II), resulting in inhibition of the enzyme’s activity and in cell death (Erskine et al., 1997; Lemire et al., 2013). Likewise, when S. cerevisiae is treated with Ag(I), the Ag can replace Cu(I) in the Cu-binding site in Cu–Zn superoxide dismutase, leading to a loss of enzyme activity (Ciriolo et al., 1994). Metals can also substitute into non-catalytic metal-binding sites in enzymes, and inhibit enzyme activity. For example, Ni(II) can replace Zn(II) at the non-catalytic Zn site of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase (FbaA) in E. coli, leading to a loss of activity of this critical glycolytic enzyme (Macomber et al., 2011).

Studying the mechanisms underlying the antimicrobial capacity of metals is pertinent to both medical and environmental microbiologists to design new metal-based antimicrobials and understand how inorganic environmental contamination will affect microbial ecology as well as bioremediation efforts, respectively.

## 2.17.4.1 Metal-based antimicrobials

Of primary concern when considering the use of metals for antimicrobials is the toxicity to human cells. Currently, research is lacking on the toxicological profile of many metals. Certainly, the toxicity of certain metals to mammalian cells has been well documented – for example, Pb, Hg, As, and Cd (Jarup, 2003). ¨ Meanwhile, the widespread use of Cu and Ag as antimicrobials and antifungals is occurring unabated and without much oversight (Lemire et al., 2013), particularly in the agricultural industry. That being said, the toxicological profile of Ag is still being investigated (Braydich-Stolle et al., 2005; Hollinger, 1996; Kim et al., 2010). Limiting the use of metals to surfaces, textiles, and medical devices can circumvent the risk to human health. Aside from Ag and Cu, Ga is making headway as a promising therapeutic agent against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria in vitro and in animal models (Lemire et al., 2013). Currently, Ga is also used as a chemotherapeutic agent (Collery et al., 2002); however, concerns remain over how this affects Fe homeostasis. A recent study has also demonstrated that Ag can enhance and revitalize antibiotics in Gramnegative and antibiotic-resistant bacterial strains, respectively (Morones-Ramirez et al., 2013). With a global increase in antibiotic resistance and a dwindling pipeline of new antibiotics, metals are returning to the forefront as antimicrobials.

A current concern with increased anthropogenic use and mobilization of metals is the effect this may have on microbial diversity. Recent estimates suggest that metal pollution can eliminate 99.9% of microbial diversity normally found in untouched soils (Gans et al., 2005). Thus, the mass release of metals into the environment from medical, agricultural, and industrial sources can devastate rare bacterial taxa. Hence, understanding the mechanisms by which metals may poison microbial cells is important for maintaining the ecology of microorganisms in soils, vegetation, and waterways as well. From a bioremediation standpoint, inorganic pollutants including metals co-contaminate the majority of polluted sites that are contaminated by organic pollutants; thus, a mechanistic understanding of how metals will toxify these microorganisms is also pertinent for bioremediation to be successful.
