# Acyl-homoserine lactone-based quorum sensing in members of the marine bacterial Roseobacter clade: complex cell-to-cell communication controls multiple physiologies

Alison Buchan1, April Mitchell1, W. Nathan Cude1, and Shawn Campagna2 

1Department of Microbiology, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Tennessee, USA 

2Department of Chemistry, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Tennessee, USA 

## 2.18.1 Introduction

Bacteria have evolved a variety of genetic mechanisms for behavior modulation in response to environment signals. One of these mechanisms, frequently referred to as quorum sensing (QS), is dependent upon the concentration of bacterially produced, diffusible chemical cues. Bacteria capable of producing these signal molecules release them into the local environment where they can be sensed by bacteria of the same or different species, resulting in regulation of gene expression in a manner that depends upon signal concentration and potentially other environmental cues (see Chapter 21.1). Through the use of these signaling systems, bacterial communities can communicate, cooperate, and/or compete with one another. It is hypothesized that QS allows these bacterial consortia to behave as pseudo-multicellular organisms. Phylogenetically diverse bacteria use QS systems to coordinate gene expression (e.g., Case et al., 2008; Fuqua et al., 2001). QS networks have been implicated in bacterial behaviors, including biolumescence, host colonization, biofilm formation, coordinated motility (swarming), and virulence (Fuqua et al., 2001; see Section 21). 

Several classes of small molecule signals are known to mediate intraspecies signaling in bacteria. These signals often upregulate their own production and have been termed autoinducers (Fuqua et al., 2001; Schaefer et al., 1996; Shiner et al., 2005). The major class of intraspecies signal in Proteobacteria is the N-acylhomoserine lactones (AHLs) (Case et al., 2008). Canonical AHL-QS systems produce and respond to AHLs via two proteins, LuxI and LuxR, respectively (see Chapter 21.3). The genes encoding these proteins are most often located adjacent to one another on the bacterial chromosome (Fuqua et al., 

2001). LuxI family proteins synthesize AHLs via cyclization of S-adenosyl methionine, forming a lactone ring to which an acylated carbon chain, derived from fatty acid biosynthesis, is conjugated (Schaefer et al., 1996). Acyl chain length and saturation, combined with the presence or absence of oxidation at the third carbon, by either a hydroxyl or carbonyl group, allow for species or group specificity (Fuqua et al., 2001; Schaefer et al., 1996). LuxR proteins represent a large family of proteins, all of which are response regulators (Fuqua et al., 1996). Those LuxR proteins that function in QS systems mediate gene expression required for communal behavior in response to intracellular concentrations of their cognate AHLs (Fuqua and Winans, 1994; Fuqua et al., 1996). Activated LuxR proteins (i.e., LuxRs bound to their cognate AHLs) typically upregulate luxI transcription, which enhances the rate of AHL synthesis. Activated LuxR proteins also modulate expression of other genes, including those involved in secondary metabolite production, motility, biofilm formation, and other functions (Case et al., 2008; Fuqua et al., 1996, 2001; see Chapter 21.3). 

The Roseobacter clade of marine Alphaproteobacteria is one of the most abundant and biogeochemically active groups of marine bacteria (Buchan et al., 2005). As such, it has been the focus of numerous studies detailing various physiological aspects of group members. Indeed, several recent studies have begun to examine the contribution of QS to the physiology of cultivated representatives. These studies were reviewed and presented alongside a genomic analysis of 43 publicly available Roseobacter genomes by Cude and Buchan (2013). In this chapter, we provide an updated review of the current state of knowledge regarding QS in Roseobacters as well as an updated analysis of the currently available Roseobacter genomes. 

## 2.18.2 The Roseobacter lineage

Members of the Roseobacter clade fall within the Rhodobacteraceae family of the Alphaproteobacteria class and are well represented across diverse marine habitats, from coastal to open oceans and from sea ice to sea floor. The lineage encompasses a large, phylogenetically diverse group of bacteria. At present, the clade contains well over 50 described genera and thousands of uncharacterized isolates and clone sequences (Buchan et al., 2014). It has been proposed that the clade can be parsed into five deeply branching subclades based on a phylogenetic analysis of 70 concatenated conserved single-copy genes (Newton et al., 2010). The first described members of the group were Roseobacter litoralis and Roseobacter denitrificans, both pink-pigmented bacteriochlorophyll-a producers (Shiba, 1991). Subsequent cultivation of clade members, however, revealed that many strains are neither pink nor bacteriochlorophyll-a producers. With very few exceptions, the Roseobacter clade is exclusively marine or hypersaline (Buchan et al., 2014). High natural abundances of Roseobacters were first demonstrated in the coastal waters of the southeastern United States in the late 1990s using culture-independent approaches (Gonzalez and Moran, ´ 1997). Subsequent studies based on culture collections, 16S rRNA gene clone libraries, and single-cell analyses reveal that Roseobacters are found in almost all marine environments sampled (Buchan et al., 2005). Molecular-based approaches targeting 16S rRNA genes demonstrate that the Roseobacter clade is one of the major marine bacterial groups, typically comprising upward of 20% of coastal and 15% of mixed-layer ocean bacterioplankton communities (Buchan et al., 2005). Members have been found to be free-living or particle-associated, or in commensal relationships with marine phytoplankton, invertebrates, and vertebrates (reviewed in Buchan et al., 2005). Furthermore, representatives of this clade stand out as among the most readily cultivated of the major marine lineages (Giovannoni and Rappe, ´ 2000). These isolated representatives are serving as the foundation for an improved understanding of marine bacterial ecology and physiology. Many of these studies are facilitated by the wealth of genome data that are available for both cultured and uncultured representatives. 

Genome sequences of cultivated Roseobacter strains reveal relatively large genomes (∼4.5 Mb) with gene content that suggests versatility may be driving this cosmopolitan group’s ecological success (Moran et al., 2007). Evidence from environmental, microbiological, genomic, and metagenomic studies points to the involvement of members of the Roseobacter lineage in several key biogeochemical processes, including mineralization of plant-derived compounds and transformations of reduced inorganic and organic sulfur compounds (Buchan et al., 2005; Gonzalez and Moran, 1997). Another trait char-´ acteristic of Roseobacter clade strains is the production of secondary metabolites, including AHLs (Cude and Buchan, 2013). 

## 2.18.3 The role of quorum sensing in Roseobacter biology

The first evidence of QS in Roseobacters demonstrated AHL production in representative strains isolated from marine snow using an Agrobacterium tumefaciens bioreporter strain (Gram et al., 2002). Subsequent studies have provided evidence that QS is involved in the colonization of both living organisms and nonliving surfaces in marine environments and have shown the involvement of QS in a variety of physiologies, from secondary metabolite production to cellular morphology (Berger et al., 2011; Dang and Lovell, 2002; Wang et al., 2014; Zan et al., 2012). To date, only a few representative Roseobacters have been the primary focus of experimental studies of QS in the clade, and key findings from these studies will be reviewed here. 

AHLs characterized from Roseobacter isolates possess some of the longest acyl side chains recognized, with lengths ranging from $\mathrm { C } _ { 4 }$ to $\mathrm { C } _ { 1 8 }$ and possessing differing degrees of saturation and oxidation (reviewed in Cude and Buchan, 2013). Relatively common among Alphaproteobacteria, long-chain AHLs are hydrophobic in nature, often causing them to partition in cell membranes where they may not be as readily available as signals (Schaefer et al., 2002). QS signal efflux pumps have been identified in other Proteobacteria, but similar mechanisms have yet to be identified in Alphaproteobacteria. Thus, the biological implications of membrane “sequestering” of QS molecules are not yet fully appreciated. In addition, it has been noted that long-chain AHLs are more stable than their shorter chain counterparts in alkaline environments, such as the world’s oceans. Thus, it has been recently suggested that the slight alkalinity of seawater may be a driving force in shaping the AHL repertoire of Roseobacters (Zan et al., 2014). As discussed in Section 2.18.4, it is fairly common for individual Roseobacter genomes to possess multiple copies of luxRI, or orphan luxI, homologs. This likely contributes to the variety of AHL structures that have been characterized from individual strains. 

Culture-based studies indicate that Roseobacters are the primary symbiont producers of AHLs in marine sponges (Taylor et al., 2004), and Ruegeria sp. KLH11 has been established as a model for sponge-associated Roseobacters (Zan et al., 2015). KLH11 contains two sets of luxRI homologs, designated ssaRI (RKLH11 1559 and RKLH11 2275) and ssbRI (RKLH11 1933 and RKLH11 260). This strain also possesses an orphan, or solo, luxI, designated sscI, in its genome. Orphan luxI genes lack a corresponding luxR homolog in adjacent regions of the chromosome. SsaI, SsbI, and SscI predominantly produce long-chain saturated and unsaturated AHLs ranging in size from $\mathrm { C } _ { 1 2 }$ to $\mathrm { C } _ { 1 6 } .$ SsaI produces 3O-AHL variants, whereas SsbI and SscI produce 3OH-AHLs (Zan et al., 2012). The binding affinity of signaling molecules to LuxR homologs is influenced by modifications at the third carbon, and this may allow KLH11 to finely tune its metabolism to cellular density and AHL diversity (Koch et al., 2005). KLH11 mutants deficient in QS display decreased transcription of genes encoding flagella biosynthesis machinery, resulting in motility deficiencies. Recent work has shown that the cckA–chpT–ctrA regulatory circuit, which controls motility in KLH11, is involved in a complex regulatory network involving ssaRI, ssbRI, and sscI (Zan et al., 2014). 

Similar to Ruegeria sp. KLH11, the algal symbiont Dinoroseobacter shibae DFL12 is another representative of the Roseobacter clade reported to have two luxR-like cassettes as well as an luxI orphan, designated luxRI1, luxRI2, and luxI3, respectively (Wagner-Dobler et al., 2010). luxRI1 and luxRI2 are located on the chromosome, while luxI3 is plasmid encoded. Deletion of luxI1 abolishes production of AHLs by the strain, and the luxRI1 system has been shown to regulate expression of luxI2 and luxI3. Furthermore, a role for luxI1 in the regulation of the cckA–chpT–ctrA regulatory circuit, which mediates cell cycle in this strain and influences cellular morphology, has been demonstrated (Patzelt et al., 2013). D. shibae populations show variation in cell morphology that is hypothesized to contribute to fitness in changing environments (Veening et al., 2008). 

Integration of QS and the cckA–chpT–ctrA regulatory circuit in Roseobacters is an emerging area of research. While the specific mechanistic details of the interactions have yet to be elucidated, it has been shown in D. shibae that not only is the cckA–chpT–ctrA regulatory circuit impaired in QS mutants but also AHL production is impaired in a ctrA mutant (Wang et al., 2014). Thus, the regulatory network of these two systems is clearly connected, in at least some Roseobacters. The extent to which this integration of networks is present among the larger collection of Roseobacters has been probed bioinformatically. CtrA, which functions as a master regulator in many Alphaproteobacteria, has a conserved binding site that can be recognized by genome analysis (Wang et al., 2014). Wang et al. (2014) found CtrA binding sites within the luxRI cassettes of five of the 10 Roseobacter genomes analyzed. Octadecabacter antarcticus 307 possesses CtrA binding sites in both of its luxRI cassettes. R. denitrificans, R. litoralis, Ruegeria pomeroyi, and D. shibae are all predicted to have a single CtrA binding site within one luxRI cassette found within these strains. Thus, there is strong indication that the integration of these networks is common among, but not absolutely conserved in, Roseobacters. 

Integration of QS and other regulatory networks appears to be a common trait of Roseobacters. In Phaeobacter sp. strain Y4I, QS appears to be part of a multilayered control system in the regulation of secondary metabolite production. This strain possesses two luxRI cassettes, phaRI and pgaRI, and the production of the redox reactive compound indigoidine involves both of these systems (Cude et al., 2012). It has recently been shown that the strain produces two dominant AHLs, the novel monounsaturated N-(3-hydroxydodecenoyl)-HSL $\left( 3 \mathrm { O H C } _ { 1 2 : 1 } - \right.$ HSL) and the relatively common C8-HSL (Cude et al., 2015), which are synthesized by the PhaI and PgaI proteins, respectively. However, the QS system is only part of the hierarchal regulatory network dictating production of this antimicrobial. Surface-attached growth, principally as a biofilm, is also a primary requirement for indigoidine production. Mutants in either of the two luxRI systems in the strain show deficiencies in indigoidine production and have alterations in other physiologies, including motility and biofilm formation (Cude et al., 2015). Indigoidine production has been shown to be important in the competitive fitness of Y4I against Vibrio fischeri during surface-attached growth (Cude et al., 2012). Interestingly, C8- HSL, one of the AHLs produced by Y4I, is commonly produced by a number of different Proteobacteria, including V. fischeri, as a signaling molecule (Fuqua et al., 2001). Given the prevalence of this signal among bacteria, it could be hypothesized that Y4I may use C8-HSL to ascertain information concerning not only its only population status but also that of various potentially competitive populations (Cude et al., 2015). 

Tropodithietic acid (TDA) is another antimicrobial produced by several different Roseobacters, typically those within the Phaeobacter and Ruegeria genera, and there is some evidence that its production is mediated by QS. Phaeobacter inhibens (formerly P. gallaeciesis) 2.10 produces TDA in response to AHLs while colonizing the marine alga Ulva australis. TDA is predicted to protect the alga from bacterial, fungal, and larval pathogens (Rao et al., 2007). In P. inhibens (formerly P. gallaeciesis) DSM17395, which has also been shown to colonize U. australis, the TDA biosynthetic operon is upregulated in response to the endogenously produced N-3-hydroxydecanoylhomoserine lactone $\mathrm { ( 3 O H C _ { 1 0 } . }$ -HSL), which is synthesized by PgaI (Berger et al., 2011). Interestingly, in a ΔpgaI strain of DSM17395, addition of exogenous TDA is sufficient to upregulate the TDA biosynthetic operon. This finding indicates that regulation of TDA biosynthesis may involve multiple signals in some strains. The dual role of TDA as both an autoinducer and an antimicrobial has also been shown in Ruegeria sp. TM1040, which lacks AHL-based QS (Geng and Belas, 2010). These findings show that Roseobacters can also use novel molecules in addition to AHLs to potentially transmit cellular information. Indeed, novel nonfatty acyl-HSLs have been found in at least one Roseobacter, Ruegeria pomeroyi DSS-3. This strain is capable of producing p-coumaroyl-homoserine lactone (pC-HSL) when grown in the presence of the lignin decomposition product p-coumaric acid. However, the protein responsible for pC-HSL production is unknown (Schaefer et al., 2008). This capability has also been recently suggested for Ruegeria sp. KLH11 (Zan et al., 2015). A surprising result from one study is that a KLH11 mutant disrupted for all three luxI-type genes (ssaI, ssbI, and sscI) retains the ability to produce a molecule with properties similar to those of pC-HSL when provided with exogenous p-coumaric acid. This suggests that a non-LuxI homolog in KLH11 is responsible for the synthesis of the bioactive molecule (Zan et al., 2015). 

## 2.18.4 QS gene homology and organization in Roseobacters

An analysis of the QS systems in 43 publicly available Roseobacter genomes was provided in Cude and Buchan (2013). Since that analysis, the number of publicly available Roseobacter genomes has nearly doubled. Here, an updated analysis of the luxRI homologs present in 78 Roseobacter genomes, representing at least 18 genera, is presented that builds from the principle findings of the prior review. As LuxR homologs are known to bind a variety of ligands, including non-AHL molecules from eukaryotes, it is often difficult to assess their contribution to AHLbased QS by sequence analysis alone. Thus, the gene products of luxR genes that are not immediately adjacent to luxI genes on the chromosomes of examined genomes were excluded from this analysis. Of the 78 genomes analyzed, 82% (64 genomes) possessed at least one luxRI gene cassette, and nearly 28% (18) of these genomes possess two luxRI cassettes. The genome of one strain, Phaeobacter caeruleus (GCA 000473325), possesses four luxRI cassettes. However, three of these luxRI cassettes are immediately adjacent to prophage-like genes, including transposases, suggestive of a recent acquisition and/or questionable stability. 

In Cude and Buchan (2013), the relatedness of AHL-based QS systems among sequenced Roseobacters was examined by performing a phylogenetic reconstruction of the LuxI and their neighboring LuxR-like sequences. This initial analysis indicated that there are at least four LuxR-like (designated Rα, Rβ, Rγ, and Rδ) and four LuxI-like (designated Iα, Iβ, Iγ, and Iδ) groups that cluster based on sequence similarity and are present in Roseobacter genomes. Here, we expand the prior analysis to include an additional 26 LuxR and 37 LuxI protein sequences derived from the expanded collection of Roseobacter genomes. The majority of the additional LuxR (62%) and LuxI (73%) proteins clustered into one of the existing previously defined protein groups (Figures 2.18.1 and 2.18.2). For those genomes possessing multiple LuxRI encoding genes, it is somewhat rare for LuxRI orthologs to be found in the same protein group. Indeed, among the Roseobacter LuxI proteins analyzed, there is only one instance in which two LuxI proteins from a single strain, Ruegeria lacuscaerulensis ITI-1157, fall into the same group (Iβ). The genes encoding these two proteins share 76.3% identity at the DNA level and 87% identity at the protein level. However, one of these genes (SL1157 1706) lacks a cognate luxR and is located <1 kb from a putative transposase. The close proximity of a transposase raises the possibility that this gene is a relatively recent acquisition to this region of the chromosome. 

In addition to a sequence-based analysis of the LuxR and LuxI proteins, Cude and Buchan (2013) provide a summary of the genetic orientation and putative functions of the luxRI genes and those genes in their immediate vicinity. Such an analysis provides another basis for classification of QS systems in Roseobacters. We previously identified 27 gene topologies among the original 38 genomes analyzed. With this expanded collection of 78 genomes, several additional, novel orientations were recognized. However, the most conserved gene topologies remain the A and B groups identified by Cude and Buchan (2013) (Figure 2.18.3). Thirty-two different Roseobacter genomes contain at least one of these orientations. Genomes containing luxRI genes in the A configuration have highly similar LuxI and LuxR sequences (>63 and >70% similarity, respectively), and the seven strains possessing this configuration fall into two defined genera (Ruegeria and Roseovarius). All but one strain, Ruegeria sp. TM1035, also possess an additional luxRI pair elsewhere on the genome. All of the LuxI and LuxR sequences for strains with A topology fall into the Iα and Rα groups (Figures 2.18.1 and 2.18.2). However, not all proteins that fall within the Lux-Rα–Iα clusters necessarily demonstrate the A topology. All genomes with the A topology contain a trigger factor (TF) encoding gene immediately downstream from luxRI (Figure 2.18.3). While the function of the TF gene has not been studied in Roseobacters to date, TFs have been shown to be important in folding and secreting proteins in Vibrio cholera (Ludham et al., 2004). 

The B topology is present in 24 of the 64 Roseobacter genomes containing QS systems, making it the most common luxRI gene orientation among this collection of strains. The genomes possessing this gene topology represent at least nine different genera and include representatives from all five Roseobacter subclades defined by Newton et al. (2010). There are five different variations of this topology (B–B4; Figure 2.18.3), yet the LuxI and LuxR protein sequences are highly similar (>73%) among the strains that demonstrate this topology. All of these proteins cluster within the Iβ and Rβ groups (Figure 2.18.1). The core genetic features of the B topology are the presence of a crotonyl– coenzyme A (CoA) reductase preceding the luxRI cassette and an adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-dependent helicase following the cassette (Figure 2.18.3). Crotonyl-CoA reductase interconverts unsaturated crotonyl-CoA to saturated butyryl-CoA, a precursor of fatty acid biosynthesis (Wallace et al., 1995). ATPdependent helicases have been shown to be involved in DNA repair, protein degradation, or genetic regulation in a variety of bacteria (Snider et al., 2008). Whether either of these genes is co-regulated with the luxRI cassette is not clear at this time. The B1 subgroup has the greatest number of strains at 14. In this genetic configuration, a short-chain dehydrogenase is located immediately downstream of the ATP-dependent helicase. Shortchain dehydrogenases modify carbon chains of many substrates (Joernvall et al., 1995). We hypothesize that the protein encoded by this gene functions to modify AHL biosynthesis substrates before or after AHL production (Cude and Buchan, 2013; Joernvall et al., 1995). 

The D topology is found in seven strains, all of which fall into Subclade 4 of the Roseobacters. The LuxI and LuxR proteins for these strains are >52 and >64% similar, respectively, and fall into the Iγ and Rδ groups. There are three different variations of this topology (D–D2; Figure 2.18.3), but all share two genes, flanking the luxRI cassette, in common. fliG is upstream of luxI, and an adenylosuccinate lyase is downstream. FliG has been best characterized in Escherichia coli, where it serves as the flagellar motor switch that controls the spin direction of flagella (Roman et al., 1993). As reviewed in this chapter, correlations between

QS and motility have been reported for some Roseobacters previously, but not for any of the strains possessing the D topology. Adenylosuccinate lysase is important in de novo purine biosynthesis and in controlling intracellular adenosine monophosphate (AMP) and fumarate concentrations (Tsai et al., 2007). The close physical proximity of this gene to the luxRI cassette indicates that purine biosynthesis may be in some way mediated by QS.

## 2.18.5 Solo luxI genes

Nearly one-third (21) of the 64 luxRI-containing Roseobacter genomes also possess a solo luxI gene, which is a luxI homolog that lacks a cognate luxR homolog in the immediate vicinity. Furthermore, 12 genomes, representing seven genera, of the 78 genomes analyzed possess a solo luxI and no luxRI cassette. The presence of solo luxI genes is most common among members of the Sulfitobacter, Ruegeria, and Phaeobacter genera. There are three conserved gene topologies for these luxI-containing strains, designated H, I, and J, and all LuxI proteins within strains with these topologies are found in the Iδ group. However, many strains possess unique topologies that are not shared among other sequenced Roseobacters, and LuxI proteins can be principally found in the Iδ group (Figure 2.18.1). The J topology is the most common orientation for solo luxI genes, and it is found in 12 strains. All H, I, and J topologies possess a putative histidine kinase (HK) upstream of the solo luxI, indicating that these LuxI proteins may be part of a two-component phospho-relay system (Figure 2.18.3). Vibrio harveyi contains a hybrid two-component HK, designated LuxN, that has been shown to activate gene circuits that lead to coordinated behaviors, including bioluminescence, in response to AHLs (Laub and Goulian, 2007). The HKs found adjacent to the solo luxI genes in Roseobacters share modest identity with the V. harveyi LuxN (<26%), and it is unclear if the V. harveyi LuxN system is a valuable comparative model for Roseobacter solo LuxIs. Indeed, detailed studies of solo LuxI proteins from any bacteria are rare, and this is an area ripe for study (Cude and Buchan, 2013). Additional detailed characterization of bacteria possessing solo luxI genes will undoubtedly lead to a better understanding of the biological roles of these enzymes in Roseobacters, as well as other proteobacterial lineages. 

## 2.18.6 Conclusions and future directions

AHL-based quorum-sensing systems are prevalent in cultured Roseobacter representatives. Furthermore, the inventory of chemical signals produced by Roseobacters is anticipated to be large and result in complex chemical signaling pathways in lineage members. Some of these pathways may be involved in interspecies interactions that influence biogeochemical cycles. For instance, uncharacterized Roseobacters have been shown to be epibionts of Trichodesmium. AHL-based interactions between Trichodesmium and select epibionts have been shown to stimulate phosphorus acquisition in this marine cyanobacterium (Hmelo et al., 2012; Van Mooy et al., 2012). However, a definitive role for Roseobacters in this symbiosis has not yet been defined. Similarly, it has been suggested, but not yet demonstrated, that QS plays a role in the switch from mutualistic to antagonistic behavior in Phaeobacter gallaeciensis against the bloom-forming marine phytoplankton species Emiliana huxleyi (Seyedsayamdost et al., 2011). Finally, Roseobacters are critical mediators of the decomposition of vascular plant material in coastal oceans, which is an essential process within the global carbon cycle. In these systems, Roseobacters colonize plant material and mediate the transformation of plant-derived aromatic compounds. Only recently has the role of QS in the colonization of plant material and subsequent production of antimicrobials to prevent colonization by competitors begun to be explored (Cude et al., 2015). Indeed, the nature of Roseobacter “conversations” is anticipated to be essential in the varied relationships these bacteria have with marine primary producers and undoubtedly influences the marine food web as well as the Earth’s climate.

# Native and synthetic gene regulation to nitrogen limitation stress

Jorg Schumacher ¨ 

Department of Life Sciences, Imperial College London, London, UK 

## 2.19.1 Introduction

Organisms require large amounts of nitrogen for the synthesis of nucleic acids, proteins, and other nitrogen-containing compounds such as putrescine, spermidine, glucosamines, and cell wall components (reviewed in Reitzer, 2003). In bacteria, about one nitrogen atom is assimilated for every four carbon atoms, based on its elemental composition (BNID 101800). Almost all organisms derive nitrogen from inorganic (mainly ammonium, nitrates, and nitrites) or organic matter, and only a few specialised bacteria (diazotrophs) are capable to reduce (fix) the abundant but inert atmospheric di-nitrogen into ammonium (reviewed in Dixon and Kahn, 2004). Bacterial regulation of nitrogen assimilation and nitrogen fixation is generally dependent on the alternative σ54 RNA polymerase. The enterobacteriaceae Escherichia coli and the closely related Klebsiella pneumoniae are, respectively, the model organisms for the regulation of nitrogen assimilation and nitrogen fixation, the topic of this chapter. 

The major N assimilation enzyme is glutamine synthetase (GS) (Figure 2.19.1). GS catalyses ammonium amination of glutamate into glutamine, which serves as the N source for biomass production and is the main signal for cellular N sufficiency. Glutamate is formed either through ammonium amination of the Krebs cycle intermediate α-ketoglutarate by glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH), or through amination of α-ketoglutarate from glutamine by glutamate-oxoglutarate amidotransferase (GOGAT) (reviewed in van Heeswijk et al., 2013). α-ketoglutarate is the second major signal of N regulation, and the ratio of glutamine to α-ketoglutarate is referred to as the N status (Kamberov et al., 1994b). Glutamine levels are sensed by the bifunctional uridylyl transferase–uridylyl removase (UT/UR), posttranslationally modifying the two largely identical signalling proteins, PII and its homologue GlnK, which have some redundant functionalities (Jiang and Ninfa, 1999). When glutamine is limiting, UTase–UR covalently binds UMP to PII and GlnK at the conserved T-loop, altering their interactions with target proteins. The regulatory functions described for PII are shared with GlnK, as a glnB (PII) deletion shows a nearly indistinguishable nitrogen adaptation phenotype as the wild type, while a double glnB–glnK mutant is severely growth impaired. Unlike glnB, glnk expression (glnK–amtB operon) is nitrogen regulatory protein C (NtrC) regulated, and GlnK regulates the high-affinity ammonium transporter AmtB (Atkinson et al., 2002a). PII (glnB) and GlnK (glnK) regulate nitrogen assimilation both at the enzymatic level and at the transcriptional level. PII-UMP stimulates the bifunctional adenylyl transferase–adenylyl removase (AT/AR) to de-adenylylate GS, while the non-modified PII stimulates the adenylyl transferase function. This arrangement ensures that under N-limiting conditions, the active non-adenylylated form of GS predominates over the inactive GS-AMP (adenosine monophosphate) (Okano et al., 2010). Conversely, GS becomes inactivated under N-rich conditions, and it has been proposed for Salmonella typhimurium that the deactivation of GS enhances fitness after nitrogen upshift (Kustu et al., 1984). PII directly binds α-ketoglutarate, inhibiting its stimulatory effect on AT, thus integrating both major signals of the cellular N status (Jiang and Ninfa, 2009). PII regulates N assimilation at the transcriptional level by binding the two-component histidine kinase NtrB (nitrogen regulatory protein B), inhibiting its autophosphorylation and/or phospho-transfer function to the response regulator NtrC (glnG), the nitrogen regulator protein (Pioszak and Ninfa, 2004) (see also chapter 3). 

NtrC is a bacterial enhancer binding protein (bEBP) that specifically activates the major alternative $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ RNA polymerase, rpoN (reviewed in Schumacher et al., 2006). bEBPs are commonly associated with adaptation to stress and pathogenicity (Buck et al., 2006; Jovanovic et al., 2011). Common to all bEBPs is the catalytic AAA+ domain, which directly contacts the $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ RNA polymerase and couples adenosine triphosphate (ATP) hydrolysis to the restructuring of the closed promoter complex 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/dd6a448d2d4dc412952e5897125b884bc03b870cb5b36341352ca90b0427045c.jpg)



Figure 2.19.1 Nitrogen regulation scheme for Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae (see text).


into a transcriptionally competent open conformation (Rappas et al., 2005). Well-studied bEBP representatives are the phage shock protein F (PspF) (Schumacher et al., 2004), the zinc responsive activator (ZraR) (Sallai and Tucker, 2005), the nitrogen fixation activator (NifA) (Martinez-Argudo et al., 2004), and several homologues of NtrC (Chen et al., 2007). The Cterminal HTH domain of bEBPs bind to upstream activator sequences (enhancers), and transcriptional regulation depends on the DNA looping between the enhancer-bound bEBP and the promoter at which the $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ RNA polymerase is bound (reviewed in Rappas et al., 2006). Most bEBPs comprise an N-terminal regulatory domain that controls its activity in response to specific signals, in the case of NtrC the phosphorylation of the response regulator receiver domain. In most cases studied, regulation of bEBPs relies on the assembly of inactive dimers into active hexameric ring structures of the AAA+ domains, which are required for efficient ATP hydrolysis and the restructuring of the $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ RNA polymerase (Schumacher et al., 2008). The structural relationship between the regulatory and/or the HTH domains towards the AAA+ domains plays an important role in this regulation and may differ between bEBPs (Batchelor et al., 2008). For instance, in NtrC the regulatory domain is required for its overall activity (Rombel et al., 1998), while deletions of the regulatory GAF domain of NifA result in a constitutively active protein (Berger et al., 1994). 

Under N limitation, phosphorylated NtrC activates 15 operons, comprising 45 genes involved in N metabolism, N transport, and N regulation in E. coli (Zimmer et al., 2000). The glnALG operon (coding for GS, NtrB, and NtrC) plays a central role in coordinating the multitude of adaptations to N availability as it encodes the major enzyme of nitrogen assimilation and its various complex promoters provide both positive and negative autofeedback loops that are NtrB and NtrC dependent (Ueno-Nishio et al., 1984). 

In K. pneumoniae, NtrC additionally activates the expression of the nifLA operon, where NifL negatively regulates NifA, the $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ enhancer binding protein that regulates nif genes required for nitrogen fixation (nif regulon, 7 operons, and 18 genes). A further regulatory link between N assimilation (ntr regulon) and N fixation (nif regulon) in K. pneumoniae is provided via GlnK, which affects the association and thus regulation between NifL and NifA (Dixon and Kahn, 2004). 

## 2.19.2 Materials and methods

Experimental setup, bacterial strains, and constructs: Strain NCM3722 was used as wild-type K-12 E. coli (Soupene et al., 2003). Strain NCM3722ΔglnG was constructed by transduction using the P1vir bacteriophage as described (Miller, 1992), with JW3839 from the Keio collection serving as donor strain and NCM3722 as recipient strain (Baba et al., 2006). Chimeric bEBPs constructs: Initial chimeric constructs of bEBPs were designed and tested as described (Wang et al., 2013a). Briefly, a library of coding sequences of the zraR receiver and AAA+ domains were combined with coding sequences of the NtrC HTH domain, comprising variable domain boundaries, linker sequences, and lengths. Constructs were tested in a double blue-white colony screen with replica plates in NCM3722ΔglnG to activate transcription from the glnA–lacZ promoter under zincinducing (0.5 mM $\mathrm { Z n C l } _ { 2 } )$ and non-inducing conditions. Blue and white colonies under these two conditions were picked, and constructs analysed. Selected constructs were tested for activation of the glnK promoter using pglnK13 as reporter (Atkinson et al., 2002b), kindly provided by Alexander Ninfa. Transcription activities were determined by the β- galactosidase assay (Miller, 1992). 

Culturing conditions and sampling: Cells for quantitative (or real-time) polymerase chain reaction $( \mathrm { q P C R } )$ , proteomic, and metabolomic analyses were taken from the same batch cultures, and experiments repeated at least twice. Cultures were grown in Gutnick medium (33.8 mM ${ \mathrm { K H } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { P O } } _ { 4 } ,$ , 77.5 mM $\mathrm { K } _ { 2 } \mathrm { H P O } _ { 4 } , 5 . 7 4$ mM $\mathrm { K } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } , 0 . 4 1$ mM $\mathrm { { \cal M g S O } _ { 4 } ) , }$ supplemented with Ho-LE trace elements (Atlas, 2010), 0.4% glucose, and containing 10 mM $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } C l }$ (ammonium rich) or 3 mM $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } C l }$ (ammonium starved) or 5 mM freshly prepared glutamine. Samples from cultures grown in 10 mM $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } C l }$ or 5 mM glutamine were taken at mid log phase $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } \sim 0 . 5 )$ . For N-starved conditions, samples were taken 10 min after growth stopped due to ammonium running out. Ammonium concentrations were determined using the Aquaquant ammonium quantification kit (no. 114428; Merck Millipore). 

Quantitative PCR: Cell samples were RNA stabilised with Qiagen RNA protect reagent. The Invitrogen RNA Purification Kit was used to extract total RNA, stored $\mathrm { a t } - 8 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ The High Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (Applied Biosystems) was used to produce complementary DNA (cDNA) from 100 ng RNA with custom-designed primers (TaqMan gene expression assays, Invitrogen). qPCR was performed on an Applied Biosystems 7500 Fast RealTime PCR machine, with 16s RNA as internal control, showing the same expression levels across the conditions tested. The relative expression ratios were calculated using the delta–delta method (PerkinElmer). 

Multiple reaction monitoring proteomics with protein standard absolute quantification (PSAQ): Sample preparation: Samples were prepared using minimal handling and involved no enrichment step to increase reproducibility. 10 ml samples were extracted during logarithmic growth between $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.4 and 0.6, or 10 min after growth arrest when grown in 3 mM $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } C l } .$ . Cells were harvested by 20 min centrifugation at 5000×g at $4 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . For cell disruption and protein extraction, pellets were re-suspended in 1 ml 1× Gutnick medium, 7 M urea, 1 mM TCEP. Re-suspended pellets were disrupted on ice by sonication for a discontinuous 7.5 min using a VWR7000 sonicator with 40% pulse. Extracted urea-soluble proteins were recovered in the supernatant fraction following centrifugation at 15000 × g for 45 min at $4 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . We found that 7 M urea greatly increased disruption and solubilisation efficiencies, and prolonged sonication improved reproducibility. 

Protein standard preparation: Protein standards for PSAQ were doubly labelled at arginine and lysine $( ^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N } _ { 2 } , { } ^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C } _ { 6 } , { } ^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N } _ { 4 } -$ $\mathrm { A r g }$ and $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C } _ { 6 } , ^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N } _ { 2 } \mathrm { - L y s } ;$ Sigma-Aldrich) residues in vivo. NCM3722 cells were transformed with AG1 (pCA24N, - gfp: NtrC (JW3839), GS (JW3841), IlvE (JW5606), IDH (JW1122), and FNR (JW1328)) plasmids from the Aska(−) collection (Kitagawa et al., 2005) and standard proteins of interest overexpressed as N-terminal His tag fusions. Overnight cultures were grown in Gutnick minimal medium with 0.4% glucose and 10 mM $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } C l , }$ at ${ 3 7 } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ comprising labelled arginine and lysine and 18 unlabelled amino acids at 1 mM concentrations. Overnight cultures were diluted 50-fold for 100 ml day cultures grown in the same medium. When cultures reached an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ of 0.5, isopropyl-β-Dthiogalactopyranosid (IPTG) was added to a final 1 mM, and cultures grown for a further 4 h. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at $4 \ ^ { \circ } C ,$ 4000 rpm, for 20 min, and pellets were stored $\mathrm { a t } - 2 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . Cell pellets were resuspended in 10 ml 1× Gutnick medium with 7 M urea, and cells disrupted by sonication for a discontinuous 7.5 min using a VWR7000 sonicator with 40% pulse, followed by centrifugation at 15000×g, 45 min, at $4 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ Histidine-tagged proteins were purified from the urea-soluble fraction by nickel affinity chromatography on an Akta fast protein liq- ¨ uid chromatography (FPLC) system (General Electric). The soluble fractions were loaded onto 1 ml HisTrap HP columns (General Electric), the columns were washed extensively with binding buffer (20 mM sodium phosphate, 0.5M NaCl, pH 7.4, 7 M urea), and column-bound proteins were eluted during a 20 ml imidazole gradient (from 0 to 200 mM) at 1 ml/min flow rate in an otherwise identical buffer as the binding buffer. Fractions containing the desired proteins, as judged by SDS-PAGE, were pooled and dialysed against 1× Gutnick, 7 M urea, 50% glycerol, 1 mM TCEP (Tris(2- carboxyethyl)phosphine), for storage at $- 8 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to prevent oxidation. Protein standard purities for $\mathrm { N t r } { \mathrm { C } }$ and GS were 89% and 92% pure, respectively, and isotopic labelling was 100% and 97%, respectively. Trypsin digestion: 25 μl of extracted protein samples were mixed with 10 μl internal standard mix. Before addition of trypsin, 250 μl $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } H C O _ { 3 } }$ and TCEP were added to give final concentrations of 50 mM and 1 mM, respectively, and to lower the urea concentration to below 1 M, compatible with trypsin activity. 20 μg lyophilised modified trypsin (Promega) was re-suspended in 50 μl trypsin resuspension buffer (50 mM acetic acid). 10 μl of re-suspended trypsin was added to each sample following incubation at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 4 h and at room temperature overnight. Digestions were stopped by adding formic acid to a final concentration of 1 mM. Across 18 biological samples, total protein extraction in 7 M urea was 92.91% (standard error (SE) 0.58%), and average trypsin digestion efficiency was 89.25% (SE 1.95%). 

Mass spectrometry (MS) of peptides: Trypsin-digested samples were analysed on an Applied Biosystems QTrap MS coupled to an Agilent 1100 LC (liquid chromatography) stack. The Agilent stack consisted of a binary pump, a capillary pump, a well plate autosampler, and a column oven with an integrated six-port valve. The system was configured to load samples (50 ml) onto a trap column (Agilent Zorbax SB 5 mm × 0.3 mm × 35 mm) using the binary pump; the trap column was washed and then switched into the capillary flow; and peptides were separated on a capillary column (an Agilent SB 5 μm 0.5 mm × 150 mm column). The LC was interfaced to the MS with a Turbo Ion Spray Source. The loading or washing solvent was $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ containing 0.2% COOH, 0.02% TFA at a flow rate of 150 μl/min, and the resolving solvent was a gradient system of 0% B to 40% B over 45 min at a flow rate of 10 μl/min ((A) 94.9% $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } ,$ 5% CH3CN, 0.1% COOH; and (B) 94.9% CH3CN, 5% H O, 0.1% COOH). The column oven was heated to 40 ${ } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ;$ the valve was switched to direct the flow from the trap into the resolving column after a 5 min wash. Typically, the MS parameters were set to curtain gas 10 psi, GS1 20 psi, GS2 20 psi, interface heater on, TEM $1 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ DP 65, and CE (collision energy) was set according to either empirically determined values or those estimated by MIDAS software (Applied Biosystems). The MS was used in “Trap” mode to acquire enhanced product ion (EPI) scans for peptide sequencing and “Triple Quadruple” mode for multiple reaction monitoring (MRM). Data analysis was performed using Analyst software (AB SCIEX). 

Metabolomics: Samples for extraction and endo-metabolome analysis were prepared by rapid filtration, using a protocol adopted from Bolten et al. (2007) and described in Behrends et al. (2012) with minor changes. Briefly, 10 mL of cell suspension was harvested by vacuum filtration (filter: polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), 0.45 Lm pore size, 47 mm; stand: magnetic filter funnel, Pall Corp.), and washed with 5 mL of 1.2× Gutnick medium. Filters were transferred to a precooled $\left( - 4 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } \right)$ 50 ml reaction tube containing 10 ml methanol– acetonitrile–H O (2:2:1, v/v/v) and frozen in liquid nitrogen. The procedure took less than 40 s. Harvested cells were lysed through two freeze–thaw cycles and sonication, and cell extracts centrifuged. Pellets were dried in a vacuum concentrator and re-suspended in 1 ml methanol–acetonitrile– $\cdot \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ (2:2:1, v/v/v). Eighty percent of the re-suspended sample was routinely used for nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and 10% was used for LC/MS. For NMR measurements of the endo-metabolome, the samples were dried in a vacuum concentrator, re-suspended in NMR buffer (90% D2O, 1 mM DSS, 5 mM NaN ), and transferred to a 5 mm NMR tube. For LC/MS analysis, samples were dried in a vacuum concentrator, re-suspended in 50 μl methanol–acetonitrile– $\boldsymbol { \cdot } \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ (2:2:1, $\mathbf { v } / \mathbf { v } / \mathbf { v } )$ , and mixed with 25 μl 15 μM $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C } _ { 5 } , ^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { N } _ { 2 }$ -glutamine in the same solvent for quantification. For analysis of the exometabolome, samples were obtained by centrifuging 500 μl of culture (16000 g, 1 min, room temperature). Of the supernatant, 480 μl was then mixed with 120 μl NMR buffer (5 mM 2,2-dimethyl-2-silapentane-d6-5-sulfonic acid (DSS), 25 mM NaN in 100% $\mathrm { D } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } )$ ). 

Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy: Spectra were acquired on a Bruker Avance DRX600 NMR spectrometer (Bruker BioSpin), with a magnetic field strength of 14.1 T and resulting in a 1 H resonance frequency of 600 MHz, equipped with a 5 mm inverse probe following an approach described in Bolten et al. (2007). One-dimensional spectra of extracts were routinely acquired with 768 transients with eight dummy scans using a standard NOESYPR1d water suppression pulse sequence, and supernatants were acquired with 64 scans. After acquisition, spectra were Fourier transformed and phased in iNMR (Nucleomatica). The fullresolution data were exported as ASCII and imported into MATLAB (Mathworks) using an in-house code for further analysis. Peaks were assigned using spectral information from previous studies (Behrends et al., 2012) and the BioMagResBank online database (Beckonert et al., 2007). 

Liquid chromatography mass spectrometry: LC/MS was performed using a method adapted from Spagou et al. (2011). Briefly, the samples were chromatographed on an Acquity UPLC system with an Acquity UPLC BEH HILIC (1.7 μm, 2.1×100 mm) column (Waters Corp.) at $4 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ Separation of glutamine from glutamate and α-ketoglutarate was achieved with gradient elution of (A) $9 0 { - } 1 0 \% \mathrm { A C N - H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ and (B) $5 0 { - } 5 0 \% \mathrm { A C N - H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 3 }$ , both containing 0.1% (v/v) formic acid and 10 mM ammonium acetate, at a flow rate of 0.4 mL/min. Starting conditions were 99.0% A and 1% B for 1.0 min, changing linearly to 100% B over the next 11 min, after which the solvent composition returned to starting conditions over 0.1 min, followed by re-equilibration for 3.9 min prior to the next injection. Spectra were acquired in negative mode on a Waters Xevo TQ-S tandem quadrupole mass spectrometer. Monitored parent-to-fragment ion transitions were 147→84 for glutamine, 148→84 for glutamate, and 154→89 for $^ { 1 3 } \mathrm { C } _ { 5 } , ^ { 1 5 } \mathrm { \bar { N } } _ { 2 }$ -glutamine. The cone voltage and collision energy were set to 25 V and 15 V, respectively. Data were exported as Common Data Format (CDF) files and integrated in MATLAB using an in-house code based on Behrends et al. (2009). 

## 2.19.3 Results and discussion

## 2.19.3.1 The glutamine paradox

Glutamine is the major intracellular metabolite signalling nitrogen sufficiency, so it seems somewhat paradoxical that when E. coli and K. pneumoniae are grown on glutamine as a sole nitrogen source, growth is slow and NtrC-dependent genes are strongly de-repressed. Indeed, many if not most studies on nitrogen regulation used growth on glutamine as a nitrogen-“limiting” condition (e.g., Atkinson and Ninfa, 1998; Atkinson et al., 2002b; Sasse-Dwight and Gralla, 1988; Shiau et al., 1992; van Heeswijk et al., 2009). It was long assumed that glutamine import via the high-affinity glutamine transporter (glnHPQ) was too slow to support fast growth and explaining the apparently nitrogen-starved transcriptional phenotype (Bender and Magasanik, 1977). We grew wild type E. coli NCM3722 and NCM3722ΔglnG in ammonium-rich (10 mM $\mathrm { { N H } _ { 4 } C l ) }$ , glutamine-rich (5 mM glutamine), and ammoniumpoor (3 mM $\mathrm { N H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { C l } )$ defined minimal Gutnick medium, with the latter running out of ammonium and stopping to grow during the mid-exponential phase $\mathrm { ( O D } _ { 6 0 0 } 0 . 5 \mathrm { - } 0 . 6 )$ ), at which point cultures where starved and samples harvested for transciptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic analyses. NCM3722 is the strain nearest to the initially sequenced but lost wild-type E. coli K-12 (Soupene et al., 2003) and increasingly used in systems biology studies, allowing comparisons (Brown et al., 2014; Yan, 2007). Table 2.19.1 shows the growth rates for NCM3722 and NCM3722ΔglnG under N-rich, glutamine, and N-poor conditions (prior to running out), consistent with growth rates previously reported (Kashket and Brodie, 1962). NCM3722ΔglnG grew slower under all conditions and is most strongly affected when grown on glutamine and under N-poor conditions. These observations would be consistent with a glnG deletion resulting in diminished expression of both high-affinity transporters for ammonium (amtB) and glutamine (glnHPQ). 

Using NMR and LC-MS metabolite analysis, we measured the intracellular concentrations of the N assimilation pathway: α- ketoglutarate, glutamate, and glutamine (Figure 2.19.2). Surprisingly, we found that when grown with glutamine, the intracellular concentration of glutamine was much higher in NCM3722 than when grown on the preferred ammonium as the sole N source. Therefore, the slow growth on glutamine cannot be readily rationalised by slow glutamine import, as initially proposed (Bender and Magasanik, 1977). 

In NCM3722ΔglnG, glutamine levels when grown on glutamine were lower than those of the wild type, which can be rationalised by diminished glnHPQ expression, but they were higher when compared to the glutamine levels when grown on ammonium. Thus, the strong growth defect of NCM3722ΔglnG under glutamine growth cannot be explained by low intracellular glutamine concentrations alone. Glutamate, the substrate of GS for glutamine production but also the product of glutamine via the GOGAT pathways, was at comparable levels across all samples so that slow growth was not due to low glutamate levels. It has been reported that maintaining high glutamate concentrations is important for growth and required to maintain the $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ pool, where GOGAT plays a key role (Yan, 2007). The second striking observation from the metabolite analysis is the high concentrations of α-ketoglutarate in cells grown with glutamine compared with ammonium-rich conditions. Two non-exclusive hypotheses may explain the high α-ketoglutarate concentrations: (i) the lack of ammonium in the $\mathrm { N H } _ { 4 } .$ -starved conditions prevents N assimilation, thus impeding the drainage of α-ketoglutarate into glutamate and glutamine; and (ii) in the case of growth on glutamine, there is a reverse net metabolic flow from glutamine to α-ketoglutarate, via glutamate, catalysed by GOGAT and GDH. It is noteworthy that the GDH-catalysed reaction from glutamate to α-ketoglutarate, as its name implies, is reversible. The prediction from hypothesis ii would be that under glutamine growth, ammonium would accumulate in the culture medium near neutral pH, as ammonia can freely diffuse the membrane under such conditions (Kim et al., 2012). However, this could not be validated experimentally using the Aquaquant ammonium assay, because glutamine interferes with such assays (not shown).

In summary, growth on glutamine is not nitrogen limited, and other factors need to account for the poor growth on this nitrogen source. If nitrogen is not limited when grown on glutamine, why are NtrC-dependent genes highly de-repressed under glutamine growth? 

## 2.19.3.2 Transcription activity from glnAp1, glnAp2, glnLp, and glnKp promoters

The glnALG operon (coding for GS, NtrB, and NtrC) tops the transcription regulatory hierarchy of the ntr regulon. When nitrogen becomes limiting, first glnALG is activated, leading to increased concentrations of NtrB and NtrC, followed by the activation of other genes of the ntr regulon by phosphorylated Ntrc (NtrC-P). Because the glnA promoter is co-regulated by the cyclic AMP (cAMP)-bound catabolite repressor protein (Crp), it is possible that the high intracellular α-ketoglutarate concentrations under glutamine growth could result in carbon metabolism imbalances, causing increased glnALG expression and thus increasing transcription of other NtrC-dependent genes. For instance, it has been shown that α-ketoglutarate directly downregulates glucose uptake (Doucette et al., 2011) and that NtrC exists in equilibrium between active and inactive conformations, independent of phosphorylation (Volkman et al., 2001). Therefore, high expression levels of glnG that are independent from the glutamine concentrations could account for increased expression of NtrC-dependent genes downstream of the glnALG operon. 

The architecture of the strong glnA promoter is complex (Figure 2.19.3), comprising promoters glnAp1 and glnAp2. glnAp1 is a $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ -dependent promoter that is activated by Crp– cAMP under conditions of non-PTS (phosphor-transferase system) sugars and is repressed by NtrC-P (Doucette et al., 2011), an arrangement that enables glnALG transcription under poor carbon source conditions (e.g., glycerol) and nitrogen-replete conditions (Tian et al., 2001). The glnAp2 promoter is activated by NtrC-P under N-poor conditions, but also comprises several governor sites that repress transcription from glnAp1, so that NtrC acts as both a positive and negative regulator, although the physiological role of this architecture is not clear (Atkinson et al., 2002c). A recent CHiP-seq study mapped the chromosomal NtrC binding sites, fully consistent with NtrC binding to glnAp1 and glnAp2 under ammoniumrich and -poor conditions, respectively (Brown et al., 2014). The glnALG operon further contains the $\sigma ^ { 7 0 } .$ -dependent glnL promoter; however, its role has not been extensively studied. 

The transcript levels of four promoters under N-rich, glutamine, and N-poor conditions were determined in NCM3722 and NCM3722ΔglnG using qPCR. Three different primer pairs (probes 1–3) were chosen within the glnALG operon (Figure 2.19.3) to quantitatively investigate composite transcript levels from glnAp1, glnAp2, and glnLp. Furthermore, the transcript levels were determined for glnK, thought to be exclusively NtrC dependent (Atkinson et al., 2002b). Figure 2.19.4 shows qPCR results relative to 16S messenger RNA (mRNA) from three biological replicates for the four transcripts. The glnAp1 promoter is nearly inactive under all conditions in NCM3722. Some low-level activity from glnAp1 in NCM3722ΔglnG is in agreement with the repressor activity of NtrC at this Crp–cAMP-dependent promoter. It may be noteworthy that in NCM3722ΔglnG under N-rich conditions, where α-ketoglutarate concentrations are lowest, glnAp1 is most active. However, it remains to be established if α-ketoglutarate would indirectly, via the PTS system, act on cAMP levels to account for this observation. Under all conditions, transcription activity from the glnAp2 promoter was much stronger than that from glnAp1 (<1%), indicating that the strong de-repression of NtrC-dependent genes under glutamine growth is not due to Crp–cAMP-dependent activation from glnAp1 resulting in higher glnLG repression and causing further downstream activation events.

Figure 2.19.3 Complex transcription regulation of the glnALG operon. Operon architecture of glnALG, comprising three promoters and several NtrC-dependent positive and negative feedback loops (see text). Probes used for quantitative PCR are shown in green (see figure 2.19.4).


In order to exclude the possibility that the poorly understood glnL promoter would be strongly activated under glutamine growth by a not-yet-understood mechanism that would result in glnG expression and cascading transcription activation downstream, we measured transcript levels using Probe 3. Transcript levels with Probe 3 show a similar pattern as those with Probe 2, albeit being more than one order of magnitude lower. These results indicate that NtrC-dependent transcription under glutamine growth is not a result of high transcription activity from the glnL promoter. The lower level of glnG and presumably glnL, when compared to glnA, is probably due to the negative autoregulation of NtrC at the glnL promoter to which it can bind and or because of a predicted rho-independent terminator preceding $g l n L p$ (Ueno-Nishio et al., 1984). A comparison of the ratio of transcript levels derived from Probes 2 and $~ 3 ~ ( g l n G - g l n A )$ may suggest that repression of $g l n L p$ is NtrC-P dependent, because it inversely correlates with the activation activity of NtrC-P at the gln $A p 2$ promoter. However, it remained unclear why NtrC-dependent transcription is relatively strong under glutamine growth.

Transcription from the $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ -dependent $g l n A p { 2 }$ is strongest under N-starved conditions and weakest under N-rich conditions. The intermediate levels when grown with glutamine may be surprising, given that the intracellular concentrations are very high (Figure 2.19.2), but are consistent with numerous observations when growth on glutamine was considered N limiting. 

## 2.19.3.3 Specific activator and repressor activities of NtrC

The above results indicated that NtrC activates the glnA (and glnK) promoter under glutamine growth, albeit at a lower rate than under N-starved conditions. NtrB specifically phosphorylates NtrC under N-limiting conditions but also dephosphorylates NtrC when in complex with non-uridylated PII in a regulated phosphatase reaction (Atkinson et al., 1994). The degree of NtrC phosphorylation depends on the level of glutamine that determines the uridylylation state of PII and also on ATP, adeonosine diphosphate (ADP), and α-ketoglutarate, which are allosteric effectors modifying PII’s ability to regulate NtrB activities, at least in vitro (Jiang and Ninfa, 2009). Phosphorylation of the receiver domain of NtrC shifts the equilibrium from inactive to active NtrC conformational states (Volkman et al., 2001). Therefore, transcription control by NtrC depends on both NtrC abundance and conformation. Under glutamine growth, NtrC was significantly more active than under N-rich conditions, implying that NtrC should be in its active, phosphorylated state, despite high glutamine concentrations. In principle, a high copy number of non-phosphorylated NtrC could explain the activation of NtrC-dependent genes. 

Advances in selective or multiple reaction-monitoring MS (SRM and MRM, respectively) allow targeted gel-free (Schumacher et al., 2014) protein quantification from complex biological samples with increasing sensitivity and specificity (Elschenbroich and Kislinger, 2011). MRM-MS together with PSAQ were used to quantify NtrC and GS (Picotti and 

Aebersold, 2012). Table 2.19.2 shows the intracellular concentrations of NtrC and GS expressed as average copy per cell, based on a cell volume of 1 fl and $1 . 1 1 \times 1 0 ^ { 9 }$ ce $1 1 s / \mathrm { m l / O D } _ { 6 0 0 }$ (1000 molecules per cell corresponding to a concentration of 1.61 mM) (Kubitschek and Friske, 1986). 

GS is most abundant under glutamine growth and least abundant in high ammonium, in line with previous transcription reporter studies (Table 2.19.2). NtrC was less abundant than GS, supporting the transcription data (Figure 2.19.4). In ΔglnG, NtrC was absent and GS levels were drastically reduced, confirming the dominant and direct role that NtrC plays in regulating glnA and itself. For growth in N-rich and glutamine, glnA and glnG transcript levels correlate well with GS and NtrC protein levels. However, NtrC and GS levels in starved cells are lower than those seen for cells grown in glutamine, despite higher glnA and glnG transcripts levels, indicating a higher specific NtrC transcription activity under N-starved conditions compared to glutamine growth. However, we could not directly determine the phosphorylation state of NtrC by MRM-MS, probably because NtrC-P is labile (Kamberov et al., 1994a). 

## 2.19.3.4 Specific activities of NtrC at different promoters

The availability of both transcript and NtrC protein levels allowed evaluating specific activities of NtrC at different promoters in vivo. Given the relatively long protein halflife compared to the short half-life of bacterial mRNA (minutes), it is reasonable to assume that the ratio of transcripts to that of the transcription activator should faithfully reflect its activity at the point of sampling, both as an activator and as a repressor. We thus expressed transcript–NtrC as NtrCspecific transcription activity (mRNA-[NtrC]:NtrCA), whereas the inverse relationship was expressed as repression activity ([NtrC]/mRNA:NtrCR) at the various promoters. Recall that $\mathrm { { N t r C ^ { A } } }$ depends on adopting an active higher oligomeric state, while $\mathrm { N t r C ^ { R } }$ may not (De Carlo et $a l .$ , 2006; Yan and Kustu, 1999). Transcription from the simpler glnK promoter depends exclusively on the activation of NtrC through phosphorylation, and therefore transcription levels from glnKp in relation to NtrC levels report on $\mathrm { { N t r C ^ { A } } }$ (Atkinson et al., 2002b). $\mathrm { { N t r C ^ { A } } }$ is lowest in N-rich conditions, as expected (Figure 2.19.5). 

Surprisingly, $\mathrm { { N t r C ^ { A } } }$ was markedly higher in N-starved conditions than in glutamine conditions, suggesting that only a subpopulation of NtrC was active in the latter conditions (Figure 2.19.5). This finding is consistent with the high intracellular glutamine levels that would result in PII-mediated repression of NtrC phosphorylation. Nonetheless, NtrCA under glutamine growth was higher than $\mathrm { { N t r C ^ { A } } }$ in N-rich conditions, despite a 5.6-fold higher glutamine concentration. At the same time, α- ketoglutarate concentrations under glutamine growth were 3.5 times higher when compared to ammonium-rich conditions, providing a feasible rationale for the intermediate $\mathrm { { N t r C ^ { A } } }$ activity at the glnA and glnK promoters: under glutamine growth, i.e. high α-ketoglutarate can partly override glutamine signalling through direct binding to PII (Figure 2.19.1). The high abundances of GS and NtrC under glutamine growth is likely due to accumulation that outpaces their dilution during growth of these proteins during pseudo-steady-state growth with intermediate transcription from the glnAp2 promoter.

Taken together, these findings indicate that when E. coli is grown with glutamine as its sole nitrogen source, NtrCdependent genes are not activated because of the hitherto assumed slow glutamine uptake which would signal N deficiency, but, rather, because high intracellular glutamine results in nitrogen assimilation reverse flow to increase α-ketoglutarate levels, acting as a metabolic signal of nitrogen regulation via PII and possibly GlnK. This interpretation would explain a previously reported inconsistency between the expected glutamine, glutamate, and α-ketoglutarate levels and NtrC-dependent transcription. Thomas Goss and colleagues pointed out that when E. coli is deleted for the structural genes for GOGAT (gltBD), the glutamine concentrations should be high (since it cannot be depleted rapidly) and could not account for the lack of NtrC-dependent activities and for slow growth (Goss et al., 2001). When grown on glutamine as the sole N source, NtrCdependent activities were highly upregulated (Histidase and GS) in wild-type E. coli as expected, but not in gltD mutants. A high glutamine concentration in a gltD mutant could not produce glutamate from glutamine and therefore not reverse the N assimilation flux to α-ketoglutarate, resulting in de-repressed NtrC. Furthermore, growth of the same GOGAT-deficient strains on glutamate as the sole N source also resulted in highly activated NtrC-dependent activities (Goss et al., 2001). Neither phenotype (Ntr−) could be explained by glutamine starvation inducing the NtrB–NtrC system, but they are fully consistent with high α-ketoglutarate concentrations de-repressing NtrC in vivo. Because GOGAT and GDH are NtrC independent, the expectation would be that the α-ketoglutarate concentrations would also be elevated under glutamine growth in ΔglnG, consistent with our measurements (Figure 2.19.5). 

It remains unclear why growth on glutamine is slow, as cells are limited neither in nitrogen nor in carbon sources, as the glutamine and α-ketoglutarate concentrations indicate. One possibility is that the nitrogen regulatory system has not adequately evolved to adapt to growth on glutamine as a sole nitrogen source; such conditions might be rarely encountered during E. coli’s lifespan. Therefore, expression of NtrC-dependent genes under glutamine growth may be a laboratory artefact; nonetheless, it is a useful one since it highlighted the regulatory role of α-ketoglutarate as a signalling molecule for the nitrogen status. This role is most likely to play an important role under physiological conditions to coordinate between nitrogen and carbon metabolism, albeit probably in a more nuanced fashion than under somewhat extreme laboratory conditions. Slow growth on glutamine can be rationalised by assuming that, under glutamine growth, NtrC would activate the entire ntr regulon with adverse effects on growth. Recently, Brown and colleagues have shown that under N starvation (conditions identical to the ones described in this chapter), NtrC also regulates and activates transcription of relA, the major gene required for the stringent response (Brown et al., 2014) (see also chapter 7). However, further studies are required to substantiate this hypothesis. 

## 2.19.3.5 Synthetic biology approaches to N regulation

This chapter may have illustrated how systems biology approaches can complement more conventional approaches to study adaptation processes involved in N regulation. It is reassuring that, even though the widely held assumption about nitrogen-limiting conditions during glutamine growth has not been confirmed (conditions used in many, if not most, genetic studies), the interpretations drawn from them remain largely valid. 

The importance of bacterial nitrogen regulation has been a matter of long-standing interest in biotechnology, and, with the emergence of synthetic biology, novel strategies to control nitrogen regulation have emerged. The coordination between the nitrogen and carbon metabolism is of particular interest for the central metabolism and biomass production. It is relevant for biotechnology processes that use bacterial cell factories for the production of carbon- and nitrogen-rich compounds. For instance, nitrogen-poor conditions can force carbon into metabolic pathways, inducing the production of organic solvents (Monot and Engasser, 1983), biofuels (Rismani-Yazdi et al., 2012), hydrogen gas (Kumazawa and Mitsui, 1981), or polyesters (Kessler et al., 2001). Of specific interest to biotechnology is, further, the regulation of nitrogen fixation in diazotrophic bacteria, with the aim to enhance biological nitrogen fixation to enhance crop yields. At the time of this writing and against the backdrop of global food (in-)security, there is renewed impetus to study and manipulate nitrogen regulation using synthetic biology approaches. 

Synthetic biology may be viewed as a conceptual advance in which design principles from engineering (abstraction, modularity, and standards) are applied to biology to achieve a desired function, often to meet a biotechnological objective. In doing so, synthetic biology shifts the perspective on biology from the more descriptive to the design of biological systems, with the successes and failures of such designs in turn testing and enriching our knowledge and manipulative capabilities of such systems and their component parts. Perhaps the main challenge of synthetic biology is the complexity of cellular networks in which any synthetic design is embedded; synthetic systems must to a certain degree be uncoupled from the native system, yet rely on and affect the cell’s physiology. 

Genes involved in nitrogen assimilation and nitrogen fixation are organised in complex regulons (ntr and nif) that, in most bacteria, are regulated by the bEBPs NtrC and NifA, respectively, to control transcription by the σ54 RNA polymerase. Strategies to gain transcription control of ntr and nif genes currently focus on designing sets of synthetic gene control elements (Wang X et al., 2013) and/or nif regulon reorganisations (Temme et al., 2012), or the engineering of synthetic bEBPs (Wang B et al., 2013). These examples may illustrate the potential and challenges of synthetic biology approaches to control bacterial nitrogen management for biotechnology purposes. 

In a systematic strategy, Temme and colleagues have refactored the nitrogen fixation genes from Klebsiella oxytoca to achieve orthogonal transcription control of nitrogen fixation genes (Temme et al., 2012). They used a bottom-up strategy to simplify the complexity of gene regulation of the nif regulon: removing the native regulation by nilL–nifA, predicted non-coding sequences, and non-essential genes within the nif regulon. Furthermore, codons were randomised, nif operons reorganised, and their T7 promoters introduced for each transcription unit. The refactored gene clusters were connected to a controller in which the expression of the T7 RNA polymerase was inducibly controlled. The synthetic system comprised 89 parts (promoters, ribosomal binding sites, genes, terminators, etc.), and their individual activities were characterised. The overall performance of the refactored gene cluster for the functioning of the nitrogenase was maximally 26% when compared to the wild type (Temme et al., 2012). It was not the objective of this study to necessarily engineer a synthetic gene circuit that outperforms the wild-type nif regulon; rather, it illustrates the potential to also use synthetic biology to challenge natural gene circuits. For instance, it allows evaluation of the importance of regulatory interactions within the nif subsystem and the wider cellular physiology, such as feedback loops and temporal control of gene expression and co-regulation with other (nitrogenindependent) regulatory networks at complex promoters, which were removed in the synthetic system. 

In order to identify and overcome functional barriers in the context of nitrogen fixation, Wang and co-workers adopted a strategy in which the transcriptional control of the genes required for nitrogen fixation in K. pneumoniae were placed under synthetic operator control and transferred to E. coli (Wang X et al., 2013). Six nif operons were constructed so that their expression was dependent on T7 RNA polymerase promoters by the E. coli heterologous, constitutively expressed T7. Transcription control was engineered by placing lacO operator sequences downstream of the T7 promoters, so that transcription was blocked in the presence of the LacI repressor binding to lacO. The system could then be readily induced by addition of IPTG, releasing LacI from operator sites. The inducible transcription units were introduced into E. coli, and nitrogenase activity was measured under increasing IPTG concentrations. This synthetic system was compared with a system where the native Klebsiella regulon was transferred to E. coli (i.e., a system where the control of nif operons remained σ54 (rpoN) and nifLA dependent). Only at an optimal IPTG concentration did the synthetic transcription control reach nearly 100% of the E. coli heterologous but Klebsiella native system. Results indicated near orthogonal control of the T7 regulated nif genes, largely independent of regulation by the NtrB–NtrC and NifL–NifA regulators. However, nitrogenase activity was sensitive to IPTG levels, indicating the importance of the stoichiometric expression of nif operons for functionality, and possibly explaining the lower nitrogenase activities observed in the Temme et al. (2012) study in which DNA transcription control elements differed between operons. 

An alternative strategy to synthetically gain transcription control of genes involved in nitrogen assimilation and fixation can be adopted through the engineering of protein chimeric master transcription regulators of the ntr and nif regulons (Wang B et al., 2013). A few examples of rewiring signalling pathways to gain orthogolous transcription control through novel protein domain–domain interactions have been described (Levskaya et al., 2005, 2009; Skerker et al., 2008). The modularity of bEBPs was exploited to engineer chimeric proteins in which the regulatory and AAA+ domains of ZraR were functionally combined with the HTH domain of NtrC, so that NtrC-dependent genes could be controlled using the ZraR-specific inducer Zn2+. Figure 2.19.6 shows transcription activity of such a chimera to activate the glnK promoter under N-rich and N-poor conditions.
