## One-, two-, and three-component regulatory systems and stress responses

## C H A P T E R 3.1

# Two-component systems that control the expression of aromatic hydrocarbon degradation pathways

Tino Krell 

Department of Environmental Protection, Estacion Experimental del Zaid ´ ´ın, Consejo Superior de Investigaciones Cient´ıficas, Granada, Spain 

## 3.1.1 Introduction

Two-component systems (TCSs) are a major bacterial signal transduction mechanism and regulate virtually all types of cellular processes (Galperin, 2005; Krell et al., 2010; Mascher et al., 2006). The basic units of a TCS are a histidine sensor kinase and a response regulator. There is an important diversity in the architecture of both proteins, which has led to the differentiation between prototype and more complex, hybrid TCSs. The prototype sensor kinase is composed of a periplasmic sensor domain and a cytosolic autokinase module harbouring a dimerization– histidine phosphotransfer domain as well as a catalytic domain (Figure 3.1.1). 

Signal binding to the sensor domain alters the activity of the autokinase module which in turn modulates the transphosphorylation activity towards its cognate response regulator. Most of the response regulator output domains possess a helix-turnhelix containing a DNA-binding domain, and the corresponding TCSs are involved in the regulation of gene expression. Other output domains have enzymatic activities or are able to bind to other proteins or RNA (Galperin, 2010; see Chapters 3.2 to 3.5). 

A significant number of bacteria are able to degrade aromatic hydrocarbons into Krebs cycle intermediates, which permits them to use these toxic compounds as growth substrates. In the field of biodegradation, the metabolization of toluene has become a model system, and at least eight different toluene degradation pathways have so far been reported (Parales et al., 2008). Pathway expression is under tight transcriptional control, but the mechanisms of regulation differ significantly (Parales et al., 2008). Whereas some degradation routes are regulated by one-component transcriptional regulators, like XylS or XylR, other toluene degradation pathways are under the control of TCSs. It is currently not well understood why some pathways are regulated by one-component systems, whereas others are by TCSs. Examples of TCS-based regulatory mechanisms are the control of the toluene dioxygenase pathway in Pseudomonas putida by the TodS–TodT TCS (Lau et al., 1997), the regulation of the anaerobic toluene degradation pathway in Thauera aromatica by the TutC–TutB TCS (Coschigano and Young, 1997), and the regulation of the toluene-4- monooxygenase pathway in Pseudomonas mendocina RK1 by the TmoS–TmoT system (Ramos-Gonzalez et al., 2002). 

The inspection of the predicted molecular architecture of the sensor kinases of these TCSs showed that they are distinct from prototype systems. As illustrated in Figure 3.1.1 for TodS, major differences to prototype systems include the absence of transmembrane regions, a very large size (almost 1000 amino acids), and a complex domain arrangement. These sensor kinases contain a central response regulator receiver domain flanked on each side by a fragment containing a PAS sensor domain and an autokinase module. Interestingly, systems with such topology not only have been observed for toluene degradation pathways but also have been found to be involved in styrene degradation, and the corresponding system has been termed StyS–StyR (Leoni et al., 2005; Velasco et al., 1998). The complexity of the molecular architecture of the sensor kinases and its divergence from the prototype system have motivated significant research efforts, which we would like to review in this chapter. From this family of TCS, three members – the TodS–TodT, StyS–StyR, and TmoS–TmoT systems – have been characterized to different degrees, and the data available are summarized in the remainder of this chapter. 

## 3.1.2 The TodS–TodT system

P. putida F1 contains the tod operon that encodes genes for the degradation of benzene, toluene, and ethylbenzene via the toluene dioxygenase pathway (Zylstra and Gibson, 1989; Zylstra et al., 1988). Lau et al. provided first evidence that the two genes located next to the tod operon form a TCS that is involved in the regulation of the tod operon expression; the system was named TodS–TodT, and mutation of each of the genes resulted in the incapacity of the strain to grow on toluene (Lau et al., 1997). The authors showed that purified, un-phoshorylated TodT binds to the $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ promoter that controls tod operon expression. Evidence that TodT activity is modulated by phosphorylation was obtained by mutating the aspartate residue 56, predicted to be the phosphoryl group accepting residue. No pathway activity was observed in a strain containing the TodTD56N mutation (Lau et al., 1997). In addition, expression from $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ was found to be dependent on the integration host factor (IHF), and the promoter was shown to contain an IHF-binding sequence (Lacal et al., 2006). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/026ee07a9cbda8f1e5ff23d5791a83b659552c0d588f07385d54ec1624663115.jpg)



Figure 3.1.1 Schematic view of a prototype two-component system, the TodS–TodT system and the minimal version Min-TodS–TodT. PAS, Per-Arnt-Sim type sensor domain; DHp, dimerization–histidine phosphotransfer domain; Ca, catalytic domain; RRR, response regulator receiver domain; DNA-b, DNA-binding domain; P, phosphoryl group. The phosphoryl group–accepting residues and the phosphor-relay of the TodS–TodT system are indicated as established by Busch et al. (2009). The Min-TodS–TodT system was reported in Silva-Jimenez et al. (2012a).


## 3.1.2.1 TodS is a complex multidomain sensor kinase

Whereas TodT appeared to be a prototype response regulator composed of a receiver and DNA-binding domain, the authors noticed that TodS is a very atypical sensor kinase (Lau et al., 1997). As mentioned in this chapter, TodS is unusually large and complex (Figure 3.1.1). The prediction that the N-terminal fragment of TodS represents a basic leucine zipper motif (Lau et al., 1997) could not be confirmed by subsequent studies showing that this fragment corresponds to a PAS-type sensor domain (PAS1) (Busch et al., 2007). In addition to the PAS1 sensor domain, TodS has a second PAS2 domain that, as Lau et al. 

(1997) noted, shares some sequence similarities with the oxygensensing PAS domain of the FixL sensor kinase. 

Since sensor kinases recognize signal molecules and modulate gene expression accordingly, Lacal and co-workers addressed the question of which signals modulate TodS–TodT activity and consequently the tod operon expression (Lacal et al., 2006). Using a $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X } { - } l a c Z$ fusion, the authors demonstrated that pathway induction is induced to different degrees by the three pathway substrates, toluene, benzene, and ethylbenzene, but in addition by a variety of differentially substituted monoaromatic compounds (Lacal et al., 2006). Toluene was the compound that was most efficient in inducing $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ promoter activity. 

Contrary to most sensor kinases, TodS was predicted to be free of transmembrane regions, which permitted the purification of the recombinantly produced TodS from the soluble fraction of E. coli lysates (Lacal et al., 2006). Purified TodS and TodT offered the possibility to cast light into the mechanism of action of this unusual system. Isothermal titration calorimetry (Krell, 2008) studies showed that toluene binds to purified TodS with sub-micromolar affinity (Lacal et al., 2006). Autophosphorylation assays demonstrated that toluene stimulated the autokinase activity of TodS and, consequently, the transphosphorylation to TodT (Lacal et al., 2006). Since TodS contains two PAS domains, it was likely that toluene binds to one of them. To assess this question, recombinant TodS fragments corresponding to the N-terminal and C-terminal halves of TodS were titrated with toluene. Binding was only observed for the N-terminal half, suggesting that toluene binds to the PAS1 domain (Lacal et al., 2006), a finding that was later consolidated by microcalorimetric titrations of full-length TodS containing site-directed mutations in amino acids of the PAS1 signal-binding cavity (Busch et al., 2007). 

However, when the microcalorimetric titrations of TodS were extended to other compounds, an unexpected observation was made: Some aromatic compounds that did not stimulate $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ expression in vivo bound tightly to purified TodS (Busch et al., 2007). Representative examples are the three xylene isomers, of which only the meta and para forms induced gene expression, whereas the ortho isomer did not stimulate transcription. However, all three isomers bound to purified TodS with submicromolar affinities in vitro (Busch et al., 2007). This enigma was resolved by TodS autophosphorylation assays that demonstrated that some compounds that bind to TodS do not stimulate but even reduce gene expression (Busch et al., 2007). The compounds that bind but do not stimulate autokinase activity were termed antagonists, whereas those that bound and stimulated expression are referred to as agonists. We were able to show that agonists and antagonists compete in vitro for the same binding site at PAS1 of TodS (Busch et al., 2007). This competition was also reflected in vivo, as illustrated by Figure 3.1.2. 

Figure 3.1.2 shows beta galactosidase measurements of $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ expression in the presence of the agonist toluene and the three antagonists o-xylene, o-chlorotoluene, and 1,2,3- trimethyltoluene. Although all four compounds bind with high affinity to purified TodS (Busch et al., 2007), only toluene induced gene expression. However, when these experiments are repeated with 1:1 and 1:5 mixtures of toluene with each of the three antagonists, a significant reduction of gene expression is observed as compared to that seen with toluene. This indicates that $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ expression is controlled by the concerted actions of agonists and antagonists. The biotechnological relevance of this finding is that crude oil is a mixture of agonists and antagonists, which is a fact that needs to be considered when designing efficient strategies for crude oil bioremediation. 

Another intriguing question concerned the fact that TodS contains two autokinase modules and an internal receiver domain (Figure 3.1.1). The analysis of a series of site-directed mutants and TodS fragments permitted researchers to establish that TodS operates by a phosphorelay mechanism, as indicated in Figure 3.1.1 (Busch et al., 2009). Toluene was shown to exclusively stimulate the autokinase activity of the N-terminal autokinase module. Phosphoryl groups are then transferred to the internal receiver domain and subsequently to the C-terminal autokinase module. It was also shown that TodT phosphorylation occurs exclusively from the C-terminal kinase module of TodS (Busch et al., 2009). We have also constructed a minimal version of TodS, termed Min-TodS, corresponding to a fusion of the PAS1 domain with the C-terminal autokinase module (Figure 3.1.1), and resembling prototype sensor kinases in its domain arrangement (Silva-Jimenez et al., 2012a). Min-TodS was found to form a TCS with TodT. However, in contrast to TodS–TodT, the Min-TodS–TodT system showed significant activity in the absence of toluene and a reduced magnitude of response in the presence of different agonists. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/bd2aec94747b7cbd03d6791e676cd058e737ad7117539144de40575a7a061a2e.jpg)



Figure 3.1.2 The concerted action of agonists and antagonists mediates $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ expression by the TodS–TodT system. The left-hand side of this graph shows beta-galactosidase measurements of $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ expression in the presence of the agonist toluene and the antagonists ortho-xylyne, ortho-chlorotoluene, and 1,2,3-trimethylbenzene (1,2,3-TMB). All four compounds were found to bind with high affinities to purified TodS. The right-hand side of this graph shows beta-galactosidase measurements in the presence of 1:1 and 1:5 mixtures of toluene with each of the three antagonists. This is a modified version of the figure reproduced with permission from Busch et al. (2007).


One- and two-component transcriptional regulator systems are central to bacterial transcriptional regulation (see Section 3). In contrast to one-component systems, TCSs represent a genetic and metabolic burden to the cell since two instead of one protein is to be synthesized, and in addition TCSs require adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to function. It has been proposed that the capacity of prototype sensor kinases (Figure 3.1.1), containing an extracytoplasmic sensor domain, to respond to extracytoplasmic signals is a major advantage that compensates the burden. This hence raises the question on the advantage of cytosolic TCSs, like TodS–TodT, over one-component-systembased mechanisms. Some data suggest that the capacity of cytosolic sensor kinases to respond to multiple signals may be a feature that justifies their existence (Krell et al., 2009). 

We have addressed this question using the TodS–TodT system. Since a number of other complex sensor kinases respond to changes in the redox state by recognizing different quinone signals (Bock and Gross, 2002; Georgellis et al., 2001), we have conducted autokinase assays of TodS in the presence of different oxidative agents (Silva-Jimenez et al., 2014). We were able to show that menadione reduced the autokinase activity in vitro and gene expression from $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ in vivo. Site-directed mutagenesis experiments indicated that this reduction is due to a covalent modification of TodS cysteine 320 (Figure 3.1.1), which is the only conserved one of the 15 cysteine residues of TodS. Since the exposure of P. putida to toluene was shown to induce oxidative stress (Dominguez-Cuevas et al., 2006), the menadione-induced reduction of TodS activity was proposed to be an internal feedback mechanism (Silva-Jimenez et al., 2014). 

## 3.1.2.2 TodT binds to a complex promoter

The availability of purified TodT also made it possible to study in detail its interaction with the $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ promoter. DNAseI footprinting assays showed that there are three TodT-binding sites at $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ (Lacal et al., 2008a). Two of them are pseudo-palindromes (box 1 and box 2), whereas the box 3 binding site is a half-palindrome. Unphosphorylated TodT is monomeric in solution and binds with high affinity to the different operator sites. Its phosphorylation half-life was very low and thus did not permit researchers to elucidate in detail the effect of protein phosphorylation on DNA binding. Initial data, however, suggested that phosphorylation does not alter affinity in a significant manner, and protein phosphorylation was proposed to facilitate the recruitment of the RNA polymerase. TodT binds with positive cooperativity to its target promoter (Lacal et al., 2008a). 

A microcalorimetric study using different promoter fragments allowed researchers to distinguish two different levels of positive cooperativity (Lacal et al., 2008b). The first level consists of the cooperative binding of two TodT monomers to the pseudo-palindromes, whereas the second level consists of cooperative effects between the individual TodT boxes. Data are consistent with a model in which TodT binding occurs in a sequential manner, starting at box 1 at lower concentrations and proceeding to boxes 2 and 3 as protein concentration increases (Figure 3.1.3). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/52566fee16f11c8f381f3274259642f6d67ea1d3f8a2dee456e0f6a8167a0b0c.jpg)



Figure 3.1.3 Model of TodT binding to the $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ promoter. This model has been established based on the data reported in Lacal et al. (2008a, 2008b).


A similar model has been established for the OmpR promoter of E. coli (Yoshida et al., 2006). Target DNA in the presence of low and high concentrations of TodT has been analysed by atomic force microscopy (Lacal et al., 2008b). At low TodT concentrations, only slight DNA bending was observed upon protein binding, whereas at high TodT concentrations a DNA hairpin bend was introduced in between boxes 2 and 3. We hypothesize that protein binding at box 3, which occurs at high concentrations, induces this bend. The expression of the todS–todT genes is under the control of the $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d S }$ promoter (Busch et al., 2010). We have shown that this promoter is under catabolite control, and promoter activity in the presence of glucose was significantly reduced (Busch et al., 2010). 

In summary, the transcriptional activity from $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ depends thus, firstly, on the TodS–TodT concentration (catabolite control); secondly, on the presence of agonists and antagonists; and, thirdly, on the reducing agent menadione. 

## 3.1.3 The StyS–StyR system

Different strains of Pseudomonas are able to degrade styrene (Marconi et al., 1996; Panke et al., 1998; Velasco et al., 1998). Two genes similar to those of todS and todT were found to be associated with the genes of the upper styrene degradation pathway, which converts styrene into phenylacetic acid. These regulatory genes were found to be essential for the metabolization of styrene by the upper pathway, and their gene products were termed StyS and StyR (O’Leary et al., 2001; Santos et al., 2002; Velasco et al., 1998). Both proteins share some 40% sequence identity with TodS and TodT and have the same domain arrangement. 

A recent study has investigated molecular mechanisms of StyS activation (O’Leary et al., 2014). The authors provide data that suggest the existence of two different activation mechanisms. A first mechanism, analogous to that of TodS, resides in the binding of styrene to the PAS sensor domain. A second activation mode appears to be linked to a transmembrane protein StyE involved in styrene transport. It was shown that co-expression of StyE with StyS, containing an altered PAS sensor domain, caused an activation of the sensor kinase by an alternative mechanism. 

However, studies of the StyS–StyR TCS enhanced particularly the knowledge on the response regulator. It was shown that small-molecular-weight phosphoryl group donors like acetylphosphate phosphorylate StyR, which in turn induced protein dimerization and enhanced its binding to the DNA operator (Leoni et al., 2003). Three pseudo-palindromic StyRbinding sequences were identified in the cognate $\mathrm { P } _ { s t y A }$ promoter. StyR was found to bind with different affinities to these three sites, and a model was proposed in which StyR acts as either activator or repressor depending on the operator site it binds to (Leoni et al., 2005). As in the case of $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X } ,$ the $\mathrm { P } _ { s t y A }$ promoter is subject to catabolite repression, and its activity depends on IHF (Rampioni et al., 2008). However, the corresponding molecular mechanisms appear to differ for the TodS–TodT and StyS–StyR systems. For the latter system, a model was proposed (Rampioni et al., 2008) in which, when grown on styrene only, phosphorylated StyR binds to the high-affinity site Sty2 in $\mathrm { P } _ { s t y A }$ and IHF to a site overlapping with site Sty1. Under catabolite repression conditions (growth on styrene plus glucose), StyR was proposed to bind to the Sty2 site and in addition to Sty1 replacing bound IHF. Protein bound at both sites was proposed to interact, introducing a DNA loop hampering the access of the RNA polymerase. 

The structure of unphosphorylated StyR has been solved at 2.2 A (Figure 3.1.4) and presents several interesting features˚ (Milani et al., 2005). StyR is composed of an N-terminal receiver domain and a C-terminal DNA-binding domain. In contrast to other response regulators, both domains are not in contact with each other and are well separated by an unusually long linker helix rich in Gln residues, termed Q-linker, which was also observed for other response regulators. The authors of this structure have deposited in the protein data bank a monomeric structure, which is consistent with biochemical studies showing that StyR, in analogy to TodT, is monomeric in the unphosphorylated state (Leoni et al., 2003). In other response regulators, the helix analogous to helix 4 (Figure 3.1.4) is involved in interdimer contacts. Since this helix is unusually short and reduced to a single turn, the authors suggest that this feature may be responsible for StyR being monomeric in solution. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/552e1850b5de8a9edf92407885573de3895ab9cc2f337a4e1962abe1f9cb3b7d.jpg)



Figure 3.1.4 The three-dimensional structure of the StyR response regulator. The structure was reported by Milani et al. (2005) (pdb ID 1YIO). Helix 4, with which equivalents in other response regulator structures mediate dimer contact, is annotated.


As mentioned in this chapter, the upper styrene degradation pathway gives rise to phenylacetic acid, and its conversion into Krebs cycle intermediates is accomplished by the lower pathway of which the paaF-encoded phenylacetyl–coenzyme A ligase is the initial enzyme. Interestingly, Pseudomonas sp. strain Y2 has three paaF genes. It was shown that StyS–StyR, apart from regulating the expression of the upper pathway, regulates the expression of the paaF3 gene of the lower pathway (del Peso-Santos et al., 2008). The authors conclude that this dual function of the StyS–StyR system enables a coordinated expression of the upper and lower pathways. 

## 3.1.4 The TmoS–TmoT system

The study of the TodS sensor kinase has resulted in two unexpected features: the fact that its activity is modulated by a wide range of aromatic hydrocarbons, including those that are not pathway substrates, and the existence of antagonists that reduce TodS activity. An important question was to elucidate whether such behaviour is restricted to TodS or whether it is more like a property of the family of TodS-like proteins. To address this issue, we have studied the TmoS–TmoT system of P. mendocina RK1, which controls the expression of the toluene-4- monooxygenase pathway (Parales et al., 2008). The two components of this system share more than 80% sequence identity with the TodS–TodT TCS. Isothermal titration calorimetry titrations of TmoS, conducted under the same conditions as for analogous studies of TodS (Busch et al., 2007; Lacal et al., 2006), showed that the protein recognized a wide range of aromatic hydrocarbons with affinities that were in most cases higher than those observed for TodS (Silva-Jimenez et al., 2012b). From the ligands studied, toluene was found to bind most tightly, and the corresponding $K _ { \mathrm { D } }$ of approximately 150 nM is amongst the highest ever observed affinities of signal molecules for a bacterial sensor protein. In vitro autophosphorylation experiments demonstrated that TmoS activity is also controlled by agonists and antagonists (Silva-Jimenez et al., 2012b). Interestingly, TodS agonists were also TmoS agonists, and TodS antagonists also behaved as TmoS antagonists. We have also conducted in vivo gene expression studies to assess the effect of different effectors on the activity of $\mathrm { P } _ { t m o X }$ . 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/5e3e05c157b057032bac4ab58d44bb6ffed9b9e68d799d1d496cf2e74735b425.jpg)



Figure 3.1.5 Expression from promoters $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ and $\mathrm { P } _ { t m o X }$ . Shown is a plot of beta-galactosidase activity of $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ (y-axis) against the corresponding value of $\mathrm { P } _ { t m o X }$ (x-axis) for different compounds. Expression in the absence of any added compound was found to be 2±1 and 15±4 MU, respectively, for $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ and $\mathrm { P } _ { t m o X } .$ . Shown in this graph are the compounds for which an activity of at least twice the basal rate is observed for both promoters. Figure was reproduced with permission from Silva-Jimenez et al. (2012b).


Apart from very minor discrepancies, the effectors that did not activate $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ were also unable to increase $\mathrm { P } _ { t m o X }$ activity. Interestingly, all effectors that increased $\mathrm { P } _ { t o d X }$ activity also stimulated $\mathrm { P } _ { t m o X }$ activity. Figure 3.1.5 shows a plot of the two corresponding sets of beta-galactosidase activities. These data show that there is a linear correlation of the magnitudes of gene expression induced by the same compound in the two systems. 

Data also indicate that toluene is, in both systems, the most efficient inducer. These data demonstrate that the wide effector range and the existence of agonists and antagonists is not specific to TodS but also a feature of homologous systems. 

## 3.1.4.1 The family of TodS–TodT-like systems

Sequence analyses showed that TCSs with a domain architecture comparable to that of TodS (Figure 3.1.1) may be all involved in the regulation of hydrocarbon degradation pathways. Apart from the three systems discussed here, other family members include the TutC–TutB system that controls the anaerobic toluene degradation pathway in Thauera aromatica (Coschigano and Young, 1997), as well as a number of uncharacterized homologues from other hydrocarbon degrading bacteria like Dechloromonas aromatica (Salinero et al., 2009) or Methylibium petroleiphilum (Kane et al., 2007). Many questions still remain to be answered on this family of TCS. One of these is to understand why sensor kinases with this particular domain arrangement appear to regulate the degradation of hydrocarbon degradation pathways.

## 3.2.1 Introduction: complex populations of actinobacteria in soil and other habitats; the relevance of Streptomyces in soil

Bacteria are extremely diverse and are able to live in a great variety of habitats on our planet, particularly in soil, in water (rivers, lakes, and oceans), and on the surface or internal tissues (endophytic bacteria) of many living beings, including plants and animals. In each habitat, bacteria are subjected to changes in their nutrient availability and environmental conditions. These changes are particularly drastic in the soil because of the important differences existing in soil composition between different areas of a geographical region, and as the result of the influence of temperature, humidity (water content), soil pH, metals, phosphate content, salts, and many other environmental conditions. In this chapter, we will focus our attention on the soil-dwelling actinobacteria (also named actinomycetes) and particularly on members of the genus Streptomyces and related actinobacteria. These Gram-positive bacteria produce many bioactive secondary metabolites (Bibb, 2005; Mart´ın et al., 2000), including antibacterial and antifungal antibiotics, antitumor agents, immunosuppressants, pigments, and so on. 

The genetic information for the biosynthesis of antibiotics and other secondary metabolites occupies a significant part of the large genomes (7 to 11 Mb) of Streptomyces (Barreiro et al., 2012; Bentley et al., 2002; Medema et al., 2010). Together with the biosynthetic genes, this genetic information includes multiple regulatory genes (Bibb, 2005; Mart´ın and Liras, 2012) that control the expression of the biosynthetic genes and the formation of precursors of secondary metabolites from common intermediates of primary metabolism (Mart´ın and Liras, 1989). Studies of the biosynthesis and molecular genetics of secondary metabolites are facilitated by the fact that many biosynthetic and some regulatory genes are clustered in the genomes of Streptomyces and related actinobacteria. There are several clusters for different secondary metabolites, such as 29 clusters in the genome of Streptomyces coelicolor (Bentley et al., 2002), 37 in Streptomyces avermitilis (Omura et al., 2001), and 48 in Streptomyces clavuligerus (Medema et al., 2010). 

These gene clusters often include membrane transporter genes that are involved in detoxification by secreting the antibiotic molecules to avoid suicide (Cundliffe and Demain, 2010; Mart´ın et al., 2005), or perhaps serve as importers of extracellular signal molecules that are used as communication signals in either interspecies or intraspecies (quorum-sensing) contexts (Davies, 2007; Mart´ın and Liras, 2010). Some of these clusters may be located on large plasmids, for example on the 1.8 Mb dispensable plasmid pSCL4 of S. clavuligerus (Alvarez-´ Alvarez´ et al., 2014; Medema et al., 2010) or the SCP1 plasmid of S. coelicolor (Chater and Bruton, 1985). Each secondary metabolite gene cluster may extend for 10 to over 100 kb and is usually expressed as a few polycistronic transcripts that correspond to sets of adjacent genes (Santamarta et al., 2011). For optimal expression of a gene cluster, evolution has implemented coordination mechanisms mediated by different regulatory genes (discussed further in this chapter). 

## 3.2.2 Global and cluster-situated (pathway-specific) regulators

Some of the regulators affect expression of hundreds of genes and are traditionally designated as global regulators. Others are designated as wide-domain regulators because of the multiple effects and interactions that occur between their gene products and the genes encoding the biosynthetic pathways and their products (Table 3.2.1). 

On the other hand, pathway-specific regulators are located in a given gene cluster (or, in a few cases, outside of the regulated cluster) and control primarily the expression of genes in the cluster where they are situated. However, increasing evidence suggests that some of these genes control distant clusters or genes outside the cluster in which they are located. For this reason, the name cluster-situated regulator (CSR) has been proposed instead of pathway-specific genes (Liu et al., 2013), and the CSR designation will be used in this chapter hereafter.

In a simplified signal transduction cascade, global regulators in response to changes in nutritional or environmental factors bind to the promoters of CSR genes, which in turn control the expression of the biosynthetic, resistance, and secretion genes in the respective clusters (Mart´ın and Liras, 2012). The CSRs include several classes of pathway-specific regulators belonging to different protein families. One of these classes comprises the SARP (Streptomyces antibiotic regulatory proteins) typified by the actII–orf4 gene of S. coelicolor (Arias et al., 1999) and the ccaR of S. clavuligerus (Perez-Llarena´ et al., 1997; Santamarta et al., 2011). However, the term SARP is confusing because it has been used to include not only the classical small proteins, like ActII–orf4 or CcaR, but also other, large regulators such as AfsR (Liu et al., 2013), which are wide-domain regulators (discussed further in this chapter). In this chapter, we focus our attention on the global and wide-domain regulators and particularly in the interactions between them. 

## 3.2.3 Integration of stress signals: the AfsR–AfsS system

Nutritional and environmental stress signals are integrated at different levels, producing a “metabolism homeostasis” response that allows the cells to adapt to drastic changes in nutritional and/or environmental conditions. One of the known signal integration systems in Streptomyces is mediated by AfsR and the small protein AfsS (63 amino acids; also known in some Streptomyces species as AfsR2). AfsR is a prototype of the large antibiotic regulators (993 amino acids). This protein consists of a typical SARP DNA-binding domain in its N-terminal region, an adenosinetriphosphatase (ATPase) region in the center, and a tetratricopeptide repeat in its C-terminal region that appears to be involved in protein–protein interaction (Horinouchi, 2003; Umeyama et al., 2002). 

AfsR is not a real global regulator since it appears to have a limited number of targets in the Streptomyces genome. Actually, the only well-characterized target of AfsR is the gene encoding the small protein AfsS that in S. coelicolor and Streptomyces lividans is linked to AfsR (but not in some other Streptomyces species). The fate of the small protein AfsS is not known, but it appears to interact with RNA polymerase, triggering directly or indirectly up to 117 genes in S. coelicolor (Lian et al., 2008). Most of these genes respond to nutrient stress responses and include antibiotic biosynthesis genes, regulators, and sigma factors. 

AfsR acts as a positive regulator of actinorhodin and undecylprodigiosin biosynthesis in both S. coelicolor and S. lividans (Horinouchi et al., 1990). AfsR-like regulators have been also reported to stimulate the production of other structurally unrelated secondary metabolites such as avermectin, doxorubicin, flaviolin, herboxidiene, pikromycin, polyoxin, pradimicin, pristinamycin, and pyochelin in different Streptomyces species (Jha et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2000; Li et al., 2010; Maharjan et al., 2008, 2010; Parajuli et al., 2005; Paudel et al., 2011; Seipke et al., 2011). Curiously, whereas in many Streptomyces species AfsR is involved in secondary metabolism regulation, in Streptomyces griseus this protein is only conditionally needed for morphological differentiation, and not directly involved in streptomycin production (Umeyama et al., 1999). 

The AfsS–AfsK system appears to serve as an integrator of signals responding to different nutritional stress signals and to abnormal S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) levels in the cell (discussed in Section 3.2.4 and Subsection 3.2.4.1). 

## 3.2.4 Cross-talk between PhoP and AfsR

Inorganic phosphate (Pi) limitation triggers the biosynthesis of many secondary metabolites in several Streptomyces species (Mart´ın, 2004). The Pi starvation response in this genus is mediated by PhoP, an OmpR-like transcriptional regulator (Mart´ın et al., 2012a; Sola-Landa et al., 2003) that binds to specific promoter sequences called PHO boxes (Sola-Landa et al., 2005, 2008). The absence of PHO boxes in the genes encoding the antibiotic biosynthetic enzymes or in most of the CSR genes suggests that the mechanism of PhoP control involves connections with other regulators (Santos-Beneit et al., 2009). Actually, PhoP has been shown to interact at least with two global regulators, such as AfsR (Santos-Beneit et al., 2009) and GlnR (Rodr´ıguez-Garc´ıa et al., 2009; see below), interfering with secondary metabolism regulation and nitrogen utilization, respectively. In recent years, the detailed characterization of the Pi starvation response in S. coelicolor has revealed a vast regulatory network involving multiple connections between different global regulators and several other genes affecting many metabolic reactions (Allenby et al., 2012; Mart´ın et al., 2012b). 

## 3.2.4.1 Involvement of PhoP in the AfsR–AfsS system

The complete signal transduction system of AfsR includes additional components, such as AfsK and AfsS. Upon sensing particular signals, such as the accumulation of SAM, AfsR is phosphorylated on serine and threonine residues by the serine–threonine kinase AfsK (Jin et al., 2011; Matsumoto et al., 1994). At least two additional serine–threonine kinases (AfsL and PkaG) are able to phosphorylate AfsR (Sawai et al., 2004), which suggests that AfsR integrates multiple signals. Phosphorylated AfsR binds to the −35 region of the afsS promoter and activates its transcription (Lee et al., 2002; Tanaka et al., 2007). Floriano and Bibb (1996) found that the stimulatory effect of AfsR on antibiotic production was exerted through the activation of the CSR genes actII–ORF4 and redD, most probably with the intermediation of AfsS (Vogtli¨ et al., 1994). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/f21928c9c0c0265d601d4f68eea1fa9ad212be44b3b44f80d4296f7bd68daf85.jpg)



Figure 3.2.1 Sequence logo of the AfsR-binding site obtained from the alignment of 40 different 11 nt sequences corresponding to the afsS promoter region of 20 different Streptomyces species (Santos-Beneit et al., 2011). Obtained from http:/weblogo.berkeley.edu/logo.cgi


However, AfsR is not the only protein that binds to afsS; PhoP also does. Using an electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) with a labeled afsS DNA fragment, Santos-Beneit and coworkers (2009) showed that keeping a constant AfsR concentration while increasing that of the PhoP protein prevented the formation of the AfsR–DNA complex and resulted in the formation of the PhoP–DNA complex. In addition, these authors performed deoxyribonuclease (DNase) I footprinting assays and showed that PhoP and AfsR protected the same region in the afsS promoter, including a highly conserved 11-nucleotide direct repeat (Figure 3.2.1) (Lee et al., 2002; Santos-Beneit et al., 2009). In conclusion, these experiments demonstrated that AfsR and PhoP compete for binding to the afsS promoter region, providing for the first time a new insight in the regulatory interactions between these global regulators. The binding of PhoP to the afsS promoter has been confirmed using the ChIP (chromatin immunoprecipitation) technique (Allenby et al., 2012). 

The role of PhoP in the regulation of afsS was initially thought to be negative because of its competitive binding with the AfsR activator and on the basis of the afsS overexpression displayed by a phoP-null mutant (Santos-Beneit et al., 2009). Following further experimentation, the complex control exerted on the afsS gene by these two global regulators was elucidated (Santos-Beneit et al., 2011). It was shown that both proteins behave as competitive activators of afsS, with each of these regulators being able to activate the transcription of the afsS gene when acting separately, but acting as competitive proteins when present together (Santos-Beneit et al., 2011). These authors also demonstrated the weight of each nucleotide of the afsS operator for the binding of either AfsR or PhoP. In this manner, it was realized that different mutant operator sequences were able to bind one, both, or none of the two proteins. The highest promoter activities were observed with the promoters that bound only one of the two proteins (AfsR or PhoP). Among them, the highest activity was obtained with the promoter that only binds AfsR. 

The alignment of the afsS operator (i.e., two 11 nt direct repeats) from 20 different streptomycetes shows a very high conserved 8 nt sequence (i.e., CGTTC/TATC; Figure 3.2.1). Actually, nucleotides at positions 2 (G), 3 (T), 4 (T), and 6 (A) were fully conserved. Interestingly, position 5 showed either a C or a T with an exact 50% frequency (i.e., always a C in one repeat and a T in the other). Santos-Beneit and coworkers (2011) determined by mutagenesis, EMSA, and promoter activity analyses that the cytosine at the fifth position prompts the binding of PhoP, while thymine promotes binding of AfsR. According to this finding, these authors engineered two artificial promoters named superPhoP and superAfsR (i.e., a promoter containing a perfect CGTTCA or CGTTTA direct repeat, respectively). Both promoters were more active than the wild type when introduced in S. coelicolor as determined by afsS-mediated antibiotic production. 

From an evolutionary point of view, the dual regulation of afsS by AfsR and PhoP would allow streptomycetes to integrate different signals (e.g., Pi starvation and SAM accumulation) in order to fine-tune secondary metabolism. 

## 3.2.4.2 Mechanism of AfsR action on phosphate and nitrogen regulations

AfsR is able to bind not only its adjacent gene (afsS) but also a key phosphate transporter gene (pstS) and other regulatory genes (phoRP and glnR) (Santos-Beneit et al., 2009, 2012). The main binding features of AfsR in these new targets are the following: 

1 AfsR protects two separate sequences in the pstS promoter. The higher affinity site overlaps partially with the −35 element and the PhoP-binding site. Since pstS transcription is totally dependent on PhoP activation, AfsR prevents the binding of PhoP. The low-affinity site is located more than 40 nt upstream compared to the first one. Distal binding sites often act as repressor elements, where the binding of the protein induces a loop in the DNA (Browning and Busby, 2004). Therefore, it is possible that this secondary site reinforces pstS repression at higher AfsR concentrations. The negative effect of AfsR on the expression of pstS was confirmed by promoter activity studies using an S. coelicolor afsR-null mutant strain (Santos-Beneit et al., 2009). It should be noted that regulation of pstS is quite complex; besides AfsR and PhoP, the protein AfsQ1 is also involved in its control (Wang et al., 2013). This global regulator is able to bind and regulate the pstS gene, pointing to an important cross-talk of these three global regulators in phosphate transport (discussed further here). 

2 The AfsR binding site in phoRP overlaps with the transcription start point of this operon, probably acting as a repressor by blocking the advance of the RNA polymerase (Santos-Beneit et al., 2009). However, contrary to the case of pstS, the effect of AfsR on phoRP expression has not yet been studied. 

3 The AfsR-binding site in glnR overlaps completely with the previously characterized PhoP-binding site (Rodr´ıguez-Garc´ıa et al., 2009), which in turn overlaps with one of the three transcriptional start sites of the glnR gene (Wray and Fisher, 1993). The effect of AfsR over glnR is dependent on the presence of PhoP, as was shown by luciferase studies (as reporter enzyme) with S. coelicolor wild type and the ΔphoP, ΔafsR, and ΔphoP–ΔafsR mutant strains (Santos-Beneit et al., 2012). 

In summary, both AfsR and PhoP proteins seem to compete for binding in three (afsS, pstS, and glnR) of the four operators described here. Interestingly, the fully required second direct repeat existing in the afsS promoter (i.e., CGTTTA) is not found in any of the other targets. The exception is the SCO6372 gene encoding a small protein of unknown function, a new AfsR target with two very conserved repeats in its promoter region (GCGTTCAGGCCGCGTTCAGGCT) which also binds PhoP (Santos-Beneit, unpublished). Note that the second repeat in SCO6372 also lacks the “superAfsR” requirement of three consecutive thymines. Surprisingly, the alignment of the six AfsR binding sequences known till now (those of afsS, phoRP, glnR, SCO6372, and the two found in the pstS promoter) reveals conservation of only the seven-nucleotide sequence GCGTTCA. However, this sequence is present 1523 times in the S. coelicolor genome. Therefore, additional features of the AfsR recognition sequences must exist that allow discrimination of the correct operators; clarification of the sequence pattern recognized by AfsR will require detection of additional operators as well as more directed mutagenesis studies. 

## 3.2.5 Cross-talk of PhoP and AtrA: effect on N-acetylglucosamine transport

The global regulator PhoP binds to the promoter of atrA, encoding a regulator that belongs to the TetR family (Table 3.2.1) (Allenby et al., 2012). In S. coelicolor, AtrA binds to the actII–orf4 promoter and controls actinorhodin production, but mutants altered in the atrA gene are not affected by the expression of RedZ and CdaR cluster-situated regulators of the undecylprodigiosin and CDA (calcium-dependent antibiotic) pathways. In S. griseus, AtrA binds to the promoter of the strR regulatory gene that controls expression of adjacent genes in the streptomycin gene cluster (Uguru et al., 2005). AtrA also binds to and activates the nagE2 gene of S. coelicolor that encodes the N-acetylglucosamine transporter and, therefore, the genes regulated by intracellular N-acetylglucosamine (further discussed here). In addition, nagE2 is repressed by the DasR regulator (Rigali et al., 2008; van Wezel and McDowall, 2011) establishing a cross-talk of PhoP, AtrA, and DasR mediated by nagE2 and the intracellular N-acetylglucosamine levels. 

## 3.2.6 Cross-talk between PhoP and GlnR

GlnR is the main regulator involved in the response to changes in nitrogen availability, in S. coelicolor and other Streptomyces species (e.g., Streptomyces venezuelae) (Pullan et al., 2011) controlling the expression of genes at the transcriptional level (Reuther and Wohlleben, 2007; Wray and Fisher, 1993). Under nitrogen limitation conditions, GlnR activates the transcription of the glutamine synthetases glnA and glnII; the amtB–glnK– glnD operon, involved in ammonium transport and metabolism (Reuther and Wohlleben, 2007; see also Chapter 2.19); and other genes related to nitrogen assimilation, secondary metabolism, amino acid biosynthesis, and, interestingly in the context of cross-talk of regulators, carbon metabolism (Pullan et al., 2011; Tiffert et al., 2008, 2011; Wang and Zhao, 2009). In the case of genes for nitrate–nitrite assimilation, this activation is mediated through NnaR, which might act as a GlnR co-activator for nirB expression (Amin et al., 2012). GlnRII is a second regulator similar to GlnR that also binds to the promoters of glnA, glnII, and amtB genes (Fink et al., 2002), although its role in nitrogen regulation is not yet clear (Reuther and Wohlleben, 2007). 

PhoP and GlnR are related proteins belonging to the OmpR family of response regulators (Hutchings et al., 2004; Mart´ın et al., 2012a). PhoP is the response regulator of the well-defined PhoR–PhoP two-component system, whereas GlnR is classified as an orphan response regulator; it contains the domains defining a response regulator but is not linked to a cognate sensor kinase (Fink et al., 2002; Hutchings et al., 2004; Wray et al., 1991). Recently, it has been shown that GlnR of actinomycetes is atypical with respect to its unphosphorylated conserved Asp residue. This amino acid is involved in critical charge interactions, essential for maintaining the biologically active homodimer conformation (Lin et al., 2014). 

The expression of several genes involved in nitrogen metabolism is increased in a S. coelicolor ΔphoP mutant after a phosphate downshift (Rodr´ıguez-Garc´ıa et al., 2007). The control of PhoP over these genes is exerted in two ways. On one hand, there is a binding of PhoP to the promoter of the glnR gene (Allenby et al., 2012; Rodr´ıguez-Garc´ıa et al., 2009), responsible for the activation of nitrogen metabolism genes (Reuther and Wohlleben, 2007). On the other hand, PhoP binds directly to the promoters of at least six other genes related to nitrogen metabolism: glnA, glnII, the amtB–glnK–glnD operon, ureA, SCO0255, and SCO1863 (Rodr´ıguez-Garc´ıa et al., 2009; Sola-Landa et al., 2013). The interaction of PhoP with GlnR varies depending on the relative position of the sequences recognized by each of these proteins. In the glnA promoter, there is a direct competition between PhoP and GlnR because both regulators recognize overlapping sequences (Sola-Landa et al., 2013). In the amtB promoter, the PhoP and GlnR binding sequences are not totally overlapping, although they are very close and the binding of PhoP can alter the correct binding of GlnR (Sola-Landa et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2012). Interestingly, PhoP binds to the promoter of glnR but not to that of glnRII, suggesting a second nitrogen regulatory cascade independent of PhoP mediated by GlnRII (Rodr´ıguez-Garc´ıa et al., 2009). The interaction between phosphate and nitrogen metabolism regulation is not symmetric since purified GlnR does not bind to promoters of the pho regulon (Sola-Landa et al., 2013), although it cannot be excluded that in vivo modification of GlnR by ligands or by interaction with other proteins may allow binding of GlnR to PhoP-regulated promoters.

## 3.2.7 Cross-talk of AfsQ1 and GlnR

Another type of control over nitrogen metabolism genes is exerted by the AfsQ1–AfsQ2 two-component system. The afsQ1/Q2 system from S. coelicolor was initially identified by its ability to stimulate actinorhodin, undecylprodigiosin, and Afactor production when afsQ1 was introduced in S. lividans (Ishizuka et al., 1992). However, the disruption of the response regulator encoding the afsQ1 gene or the sensor kinase encoding the afsQ2 gene in S. coelicolor does not alter the secondary metabolism or morphogenesis under the experimental conditions tested (Ishizuka et al., 1992). More recently, the effect of afsQ1/Q2 over the secondary metabolism has been known to occur in S. coelicolor in minimal medium supplemented with L-glutamate as the sole nitrogen source (Shu et al., 2009). Using this medium, these authors have shown that the expression of glnA, glnII, amtB, and ureA genes is increased in a ΔafsQ1/Q2 mutant (Wang et al., 2013). EMSA analyses with AfsQ1 showed that this protein is able to bind to the promoters of these four genes, in addition to those of gdhA, nirB, and nasA, but not to glnR or glnRII promoters (Wang et al., 2013). It is noteworthy that PhoP is also able to bind to five of the seven promoters recognized by AfsQ1 (Rodr´ıguez-Garc´ıa et al., 2009; Sola-Landa et al., 2013). The repressor role of AfsQ1 over nitrogen metabolism genes is exerted by a direct competition with GlnR for the binding to the promoters, at least for glnA and nirB, where sequences recognized by GlnR and AfsQ1 are overlapping (Wang et al., 2013). Interestingly, in the glnA promoter, the sequences recognized by AfsQ1 and PhoP are also overlapping (Wang et al., 2013), as well as those recognized by PhoP and GlnR (Figure 3.2.2) (Sola-Landa et al., 2013), meaning that a very complex cross-talk mechanism is involved in glnA regulation. 

PhoP, GlnR, GlnRII, and AfsQ1 are not the unique regulators involved in the expression of glnA; ArgR is also involved. Thus, this protein is needed for optimal glnA expression; glnA is downregulated in a ΔargR mutant (Perez-Redondo´ et al., 2012; and discussed further in this chapter). 

## 3.2.7.1 Complex interactions of AfsQ1 with other regulators on the control of pstS

AfsQ1 is involved also in the complex regulation of pstS. The pstS gene codes for the phosphate-binding protein belonging to the high-affinity phosphate-specific transport system (pst) and is a major member of the pho regulon (Rodr´ıguez-Garc´ıa et al., 2007; Sola-Landa et al., 2005). Expression of the pstS gene shows the highest activation after phosphate starvation (Allenby et al., 2012; Rodr´ıguez-Garc´ıa et al., 2007), and it has been shown that pstS expression decreases in a ΔafsQ1/Q2 mutant (Wang et al., 2013). On the other hand, AfsR negatively controls the expression of pstS both directly (competing with PhoP for binding) and indirectly (controlling the expression of phoP) (as discussed). In addition, a repeated sequence upstream of the PHO boxes in the pstS promoter might be recognized by an as-yetunknown repressor because its deletion in S. lividans increases pstS expression (Esteban et al., 2008). Probably there are additional regulators involved in the regulation of pstS because pstS is also controlled by the carbon source. PstS is highly accumulated in the supernatant of liquid cultures when the bacteria are grown in the presence of different sugars such as fructose, mannose, or galactose under phosphate limitation conditions (D´ıaz et al., 2005; Esteban et al., 2008). This sugar control could be related to the glycosylation of PstS by the enzymes Ppm1 and Pmt, although it is not clear how this glycosylation affects the PstS activity (Wehmeier et al., 2009). 

All these control mechanisms over key genes of primary metabolism (such as glnA or pstS) enable the cell to adapt rapidly to changing environmental conditions. 

## 3.2.8 The DasR1–DmdR1 connection: interaction of N-acetylglucosamine utilization and iron metabolism

An important wide-domain regulator is DasR, a member of the GntR family (Rigali et al. 2008). DasR is primarily involved in the metabolism of chitin and its degradation product N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc). The GlcNAc molecule is a favored carbon and nitrogen source for S. coelicolor. Its intracellular catabolism requires the combined actions of the N-acetylglucosamine-6-phosphate deacetylase, encoded by nagA, and the glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminase– isomerase, encoded by nagB. GlcNAc acts as a signaling molecule in the DasR-mediated nutrient-sensing system, activating development and antibiotic production under poor growth conditions. Using nagA, nagB, and nagK mutants, it was shown that the nag genes are part of the DasR regulon in S. coelicolor, which explains their transcriptional induction by GlcNAc. In S. coelicolor, GlcNAc is internalized as GlcNAc-6-P via the phosphoenolpyruvate-dependent sugar phosphortransferase system (PTS). GlcNAc is an important signaling molecule for S. coelicolor and promotes differentiation and antibiotic production (Colson et al., 2008; Rigali et al. 2008; van Wezel and McDowall, 2011). Under starvation conditions, a complete signaling pathway was proposed, from GlcNAc uptake to the onset of antibiotic production, whereby the pleiotropic regulator DasR controls the genes for GlcNAc transport and metabolism and for antibiotic synthesis (Rigali et al., 2006, 2008). Glucosamine-6-phosphate is a key molecule in this signaling cascade and acts as an allosteric effector preventing the DNA-binding ability of DasR. It is unclear if the DasR mechanism is conserved in all other Streptomyces species. 

Initially, Rigali and coworkers identified a DasR-binding sequence -ACTGGTCTAGACCAGT- in the promoter of several genes, including genes involved in chitin degradation and N-acetylglucosamine utilization (Nothaft et al., 2010; Rigali et al., 2006, 2008). Later, in a bioinformatic search of possible genes regulated by DasR in the genome of S. coelicolor, a putative DasR-binding sequence was found in the promoter of the dmdR1 gene that encodes the iron divalent metal-dependent regulator that controls biosynthesis of desferriosamines and other siderophores (Flores et al., 2005; Flores and Mart´ın, 2004; Tunca et al., 2009). The involvement of DasR and the Nacetylglucosamine-6-P in the control of dmdR1 gene expression was confirmed by EMSA studies using purified His-tagged DasR protein and also by RNA studies (real-time polymerase chain reaction; RT-PCR) (Craig et al., 2012). DasR control of iron regulatory genes is specific for dmdR1 but does not affect expression of the paralogous dmdR2 iron regulator that serves as an alternative repressor of the siderophore biosynthetic genes in S. coelicolor (Flores et al., 2005). This is another example of a functionally equivalent regulatory gene that responds to different signals. 

Interestingly, the DasR regulation of dmdR1 reported in S. coelicolor has also been observed in S. lividans (Craig et al., 2012) and seems to be conserved in several other Streptomyces species, suggesting the presence of DasR-binding sequences in the promoter of dmdR1 genes in other species. 

The regulation by N-acetylglucosamine (a product derived from fungal chitin degradation in soil) of DasR-mediated regulation of siderophore biosynthesis in soil-dwelling Streptomyces suggests that the DasR–DmdR1 connection may respond to a competition for nutrients in the soil between fungi and Streptomyces (Craig et al., 2012). 

## 3.2.9 ArgR controls several regulatory genes, sigma factors, and genes related to nitrogen metabolism

In enterobacteria, the ArgR repressor is a rather specific regulatory protein that controls expression of the arginine biosynthesis genes. Type I ArgR proteins bind specific, palindromic sequences of 18 nt separated by 2 nt (ARG boxes) and use L-arginine as co-repressor (Grandori et al., 1995; Rodr´ıguez-Garc´ıa et al., 1997). Similar observations have been made in Lactococcus and other diverse bacteria (Caldara et al., 2006; Larsen et al., 2008). 

In Streptomyces species, ArgR is of type II. It binds specific ARG boxes, but does not require L-arginine as co-repressor. Transcriptomic studies of S. coelicolor and a mutant deleted in argR show that the type II ArgR acts mostly as a repressor protein but occasionally activates the expression of target genes and is a wider domain regulator than previously proposed. About 1500 genes are affected directly or indirectly, either activated or repressed, in the mutant lacking ArgR. Some of them are expected genes, such as those for arginine or pyrimidine biosynthesis, but others are genes for nitrogen metabolism, such as those for ammonium transport or nitrate utilization; clusters for secondary metabolites, such as actinorhodin or undecyprodigiosin; and multiple genes for membrane proteins, secreted proteins, differentiation, or sporulation, which are important processes in Streptomyces (Perez-Redondo´ et al., 2012). ARG boxes are present in many of these genes, and they have been identified by bioinformatic analysis and validated in several cases by EMSA; several other genes do not contain ARG boxes for ArgR binding. Therefore, the action of ArgR on the control of gene expression might be direct, through binding to the ARG box, or indirect by acting on the expression of other regulatory genes. As such, ArgR binds the ARG boxes that are present upstream of pyrA and pyrB (for pyrimidine biosynthesis) but also acts on the pyrimidine general regulator, pyrR. The transcription of 78 genes encoding transcriptional regulators of different families and members of two-component systems shows significant differences between the wild-type strain and the argR defective mutant at some point along fermentation in MG (maltose–glutamate) medium, using a very strict Benjamini–Hochberg p value $( p > 0 . 0 0 5 )$ . The effect of the lack of ArgR on expression of some genes is very strong and continuous along the fermentation, as in the case of SCO2865 (more than 16-fold increase), which encodes a DNA-binding protein of unknown function; but in other cases, the effect is smaller or occurs at specific periods during the fermentation, suggesting that it may have specific roles in temporal physiological and morphological differentiation. Some of the regulators affected by the lack of ArgR are the stiI, coding for a protease inhibitor, which is underexpressed; afsS, controlling antibiotics biosynthesis (see above); rstP; or the putative integral membrane regulator encoded by SCO3583. 

The genes encoding the sigma factors HrdC, SigK, SigM, and SigG are also strongly overexpressed (twofold to eightfold) in the ΔargR mutant, and a clear ARG box is present upstream of sigM. Similarly, the antagonist of an antisigma factor, encoded by SCO4027, is strongly overexpressed in the ΔargR mutant.

As indicated in this chapter, since the 2000s an increasing number of reports have confirmed that there are several examples of global regulator cross-talk in actinomycetes, particularly in species of soil-dwelling Streptomyces. One of the most interesting examples of cross-talk is between PhoP and GlnR when the cultures are limited either in phosphate or in an easily assimilable nitrogen source such as ammonium ions or (in other cases) glutamate. The nutritional stress caused by limitation of an essential nutrient triggers a response that drives the cell to enter a differentiation process resulting in spore formation and in the production of secondary metabolites that serve as antagonists to other competitors (e.g., other bacteria or filamentous fungi) or as intraspecies communication (e.g., quorum-sensing) signals.

The consequence of the known cross-talk mechanisms is to preserve a metabolic equilibrium by adjusting the central metabolism to the challenge produced by starvation of an essential nutrient. These cross-talk phenomena act as a “safety net” that prevents irreversible metabolic damage that will result in cell death.
