## 3.3.1 Two-component signaling

Signal transduction systems are pathways that connect environmental signals to adaptive responses in all living organisms. Two-component-signal signaling is the predominant mechanism for stimulus response in bacteria (Laub and Goulian, 2007; Stock et al., 2000). A typical two-component signaling pathway (Figure 3.3.1) consists of two protein components: a stimulusresponsive autophosphorylating histidine kinase and a response regulator protein. The complexity of two-component systems is variable, however. The number of two-component signaling pathways in organisms is also variable; bacterial genomes are known to encode from as few as 10 to as many as 200 twocomponent signaling systems. 

In a typical histidine kinase, an extracellular sensory domain or a short extracellular loop is responsible for detecting an external stimulus in the environment of the organism (Mascher et al., 2006). Signal detection results in a change in the autophosphorylation state of a conserved histidine residue within an intracellular kinase domain. Histidine kinases function as dimers; during autophosphorylation, each monomer trans-phosphorylates its partner (Figure 3.3.1). 

Response regulators are typically multidomain proteins consisting of a receiver domain and a C-terminal effector domain. Response regulators are activated when the phosphoryl group on the histidine residue of a kinase is transferred to a conserved aspartic acid residue within the receiver domain of the response regulator, a process catalyzed by the latter. Generally, phosphorylation stabilizes a conformation capable of promoting activity of the effector domain, thereby eliciting a downstream response to the initial stimulus (Figure 3.3.1). The duration of the response is often regulated through autophosphatase activity of the response regulator or through phosphatase activity of the kinase toward its cognate response regulator (Georgellis et al., 1998; Thomas et al., 2008; Zapf et al., 1998). 

This simple, rapid, and reversible form of signaling is widespread in bacteria (see Section 3) and is involved in diverse processes such as chemotaxis, light perception, osmoregulation, and quorum sensing. Many two-component systems deviate from the simple system (two proteins, one phosphoryl transfer step) described here, however (Cock and Whitworth, 2007; Mascher et al., 2006). For example, multiprotein, multistep phosphorelay events between signal detection and cellular response are common. In some systems, the sensor domain of a histidine kinase is replaced by an accessory protein, which directly detects the stimulus and conveys it to the kinase via a protein–protein interaction. These modified two-component signaling systems are sometimes referred to as threecomponent signaling systems. In hybrid histidine kinase signaling, the histidine kinase has a receiver domain in addition to sensory and kinase domains. Thus, a His-to-Asp phosphotransfer takes place within the hybrid kinase, and then a histidinecontaining phosphotransfer protein (Hpt) is required to relay the signaling phosphate from the histidine kinase to the appropriate response regulator in two additional phosphotransfer steps. 

## 3.3.2 NO and bacteria

Two-component signaling systems respond to a wide variety of environmental stimuli. NO has been well studied as a eukaryotic signaling molecule and recently has been implicated in bacterial signaling as well. Selected in 1992 as Science’s Molecule of the Year (Culotta and Koshland, 1992), NO is extremely important in eukaryotic biology. In mammals, NO is produced from the conversion of L-arginine to L-citrulline by NO synthase enzymes (Alderton et al., 2001). As a diffusible, diatomic gas molecule, NO is ideal for intercellular signaling (Denninger and Marletta, 1999; Ignarro, 1991; Ignarro et al., 1987; Murad, 1994). It is able to act either in the same cell or in adjacent cells, where it binds to protein receptors to regulate essential physiological processes such as blood flow, platelet aggregation, myocardial function, tissue formation, and angiogenesis, to name a few. Put another way, impaired NO signaling in eukaryotes can result in ailments ranging from cardiovascular disease and diabetes to cancer. 


Figure 3.3.1 A typical two-component signaling pathway consists of a sensor-histidine kinase that alters its autokinase activity upon detection of an external stimulus. The kinase also participates in phosphorelay with the receiver domain of a response regulator protein, whose effector domain elicits a downstream response as a function of its phosphorylation state.


![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/11da5562e77b64e45f5b32d56604f33f5da7d856a1639532fc55477092e268ba.jpg)


Every signaling molecule requires a receptor that will detect the chemical signal in a selective and sensitive manner. In eukaryotes, the chief NO receptor is the enzyme soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC), which binds NO at a heme cofactor to activate the enzymatic conversion of guanosine triphosphate (GTP) to the second messenger signaling molecule cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) (Derbyshire and Marletta, 2012). cGMP has an array of downstream targets resulting in the regulation of calcium channels and protein phosphorylation cascades, ultimately regulating the physiological processes mentioned here. 

In recent years, NO signaling in bacteria has emerged as a widespread phenomenon (see Chapter 17.3) and fascinating area of study. NO is toxic to bacteria at high concentrations and is, in fact, one line of defense that NO-producing eukaryotes have against bacterial infection. As such, an increasing number of reports are uncovering novel NO-response and detoxification mechanisms in bacteria (Bogdan, 2001; MacMicking et al., 1997; Poole, 2005; Spiro, 2007). In addition, there are several studies of bacteria that respond to low, nontoxic concentrations of NO to activate pathways with functions related to bacterial group behaviors such as biofilm formation, pathogenicity, quorum sensing, and symbiosis (Barraud et al., 2015; McDougald et al., 2012). For example, NO is implicated in establishing symbiosis between Euprymna scolopes and Vibrio fischeri (Davidson et al., 2004). In Nitrosomonas europaea (Schmidt et al., 2004) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Barraud et al., 2006, 2009), nanomolar concentrations of NO cause biofilm dispersal. NO is also linked to anti-biofilm properties in model systems (Carpenter and Schoenfisch, 2012). 

## 3.3.3 H-NOX, a bacterial NO sensor

Just as in eukaryotes, NO signaling in bacteria requires a receptor. A number of NO-responsive regulatory proteins have been identified and characterized (Spiro, 2007). Using bioinformatics, a family of NO-responsive hemoproteins, proteins that are highly homologous to the NO-binding heme domain from sGC (soluble guanylate cyclase), was discovered more than 10 years ago (Iyer et al., 2003). This family of proteins is called H-NOX, for heme-nitric oxide/oxygen binding protein. 

Since the initial identification of bacterial H-NOX proteins, many have been identified and characterized biochemically as well as physiologically (Arora and Boon, 2012; Boon et al., 2005, 2006; Boon and Marletta, 2005a,b; Carlson et al., 2010; Henares et al., 2012; Karow et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2007; Pellicena et al., 2004; Plate and Marletta, 2012; Price et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2010a). All of the H-NOX domains characterized to date, as predicted from similarity to sGC, are histidine-ligated protoporphyrin IX heme proteins that form 5- coordinate, high-spin complexes in the unligated ferrous state [Fe(II)]. The ferrous proteins all form 6-coordinate, low-spin carbon monoxide complexes [Fe(II)–CO], with a weak Fe–CO bond and strong C–O bond. The H-NOX domains from aerobic bacteria all share ligand-binding properties with sGC; they bind NO as a 5-coordinate complex [Fe(II)–NO], but do not bind molecular oxygen, even under 1 atm of pure molecular oxygen. The H-NOX domains from obligate anaerobes characterized so far, however, have ligand-binding properties similar to the globins, forming 6-coordinate NO complexes and stable ferrous-oxy complexes $[ \mathrm { F e ( I I ) - O } _ { 2 } ]$ . 

Bacterial hnoX genes are encoded in a variety of genetic arrangements (Figure 3.3.2). The first characterized H-NOX protein is encoded by Thermanaerobacter tencongensis as a gene fusion with a methyl-accepting chemotaxis protein (Karow et al., 2004; Pellicena et al., 2004). Typically, however, H-NOX proteins are encoded as stand-alone polypeptides and are found in putative operons with predicted signaling proteins such as two-component histidine kinases and diguanylate cyclases or cyclic-di-GMP phosphodiesterases (Iyer et al., 2003). Interestingly, these H-NOX-associated signaling proteins have no predicted sensing domains of their own, so H-NOX is expected to serve as a NO sensor regulating downstream enzymatic activities of these associated enzymes. 

## 3.3.4 Cyclic-di-GMP signaling

Since the 2000s, it has become apparent that a wide variety of bacteria use cyclic-di-GMP (aka cyclic diguanylate; 3′ ,5′ -cyclic diguanylic acid; and c-di-GMP) as a second-messenger signaling molecule (Hengge, 2009; Jenal and Malone, 2006; Romling et al., 2005). As the intracellular concentration of cyclic-di-GMP goes up, a higher percentage of bacteria enter biofilm or persistence modes; as the intracellular concentration of cyclicdi-GMP drops, bacteria become motile or more virulent. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/eba402d363a61e166aa06a2f84c3ab988deb0cd45bd988e4d8d2af808fde586a.jpg)



Figure 3.3.2 Genetic arrangements of H-NOX. The hnoX gene is found in a variety of genetic arrangements in bacteria. The most common arrangement is for hnoX to be upstream of a gene coding for a two-component histidine kinase. It is also found in the same putative operon as diguanylate cyclase–phosphodiesterase enzymes and quorum-sensing histidine kinases. In obligate anaerobes, hnoX is found as a gene fusion with a methyl-accepting chemotaxis protein. Listed alongside each operon arrangement are examples of bacterial species in which that arrangement can be found.


Although this is a relatively new area of inquiry, the emerging theme is that the total concentration of intracellular cyclicdi-GMP is tightly regulated by a variety of enzymes that both synthesize and degrade cyclic-di-GMP. Diguanylate cyclases, which are identified by a GGDEF motif (a 5-amino-acid conserved sequence), synthesize cyclic-di-GMP from two equivalents of GTP (Ryjenkov et al., 2005). Cyclic-di-GMP phosphodiesterases hydrolyze cyclic-di-GMP to the linear molecule pGpG, which is not thought to serve a signaling function. These enzymes are identified by a conserved EAL (Schmidt et al., 2005) or HD-GYP amino acid motif (Dow et al., 2006). The details of cyclic-di-GMP regulation in bacteria are under investigation, but current evidence indicates that cyclic-di-GMP synthase and phosphodiesterase activities are controlled by environmental sensing and signal transduction. 

## 3.3.5 Early-indication NO–H-NOX-regulated two-component signaling

As mentioned, although some H-NOX proteins are co-cistronic with cyclic-di-GMP processing enzymes or methyl-accepting chemotaxis proteins, the most common genetic arrangement is for H-NOX to be upstream of a traditional two-component histidine kinase. H-NOX-associated histidine kinases (HaHKs) lack an intrinsic sensing domain and thus are predicted to participate in two-component signaling with the H-NOX protein acting as a sensory domain. H-NOX–HaHK thus participates in a modified two-component signaling system, or three-component signaling system. The first biochemical characterization of H-NOXregulated two-component signaling was shown in Shewanella oneidensis (Price et al., 2007). Purified SoH–NOX was demonstrated to inhibit the autophosphorylation activity of its associated kinase as either the oxidized protein $[ \mathrm { F e ( I I I ) { - } H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } ]$ or the ferrous protein bound to NO or CO. The ferrous-unligated protein has not been found to inhibit kinase activity. 

Studies with purified H-NOX and H-NOX-associated histidine kinase from Pseudoalteromonas atlantica, however, indicate that H-NOX inhibits its cognate kinase even in the ferrous form (Arora and Boon, 2012). What has been observed for both S. oneidensis and P. atlantica is that the H-NOX–NO complex exhibits a more potent inhibition of autokinase activity than either the ferrous-CO complex or the ferrous-unligated H-NOX. These results are suggestive of the selectivity of H-NOX as an NO sensor. 

The H-NOX concentrations used in these in vitro experiments are likely higher than physiologically relevant, but it is predicted that H-NOX is constitutively expressed in vivo and found in association with its partner kinase. In the event of NO binding, a conformational change is induced, leading to an inhibition in kinase activity and downstream processes. 

Phosphorylation networks in bacteria, as in higher organisms, are riddled with crosstalk. As a result, kinases and their cognate response regulators are not always found in the same operon, which makes them difficult to identify. Approximately one-third of operons encoding an H-NOX and a histidine kinase also encode a response regulator gene. Some of the response regulators found in H-NOX-containing operons have effector domains identified as HD-GYP or EAL cyclic-di-GMP phosphodiesterases, GGDEF diguanylate cyclases, or DNA-binding domains (Iyer et al., 2003). 

Our laboratory described the first identification and biochemical characterization of a cognate response regulator to an H-NOX-associated histidine kinase (H-NOX-associated response regulator (HaRR)) in P. atlantica (Arora and Boon, 2012). The response regulator, which is not located in the same operon as H-NOX, was identified using bioinformatics tools and is annotated as an HD-GYP-type cyclic-di-GMP phosphodiesterase. However, a multiple sequence alignment revealed degeneracy in the predicted active site residues, and the enzyme was found to lack phosphodiesterase activity. 

This PaHaRR protein does, however, exhibit autophosphatase activity, as is expected for a response regulator. In twocomponent systems, the duration of response regulator phosphorylation determines the duration of the stimulus response. As such, most response regulators have autophosphatase activity to control response time. In E. coli, the response regulator CheY, which is involved in chemotaxis, is seen to be phosphorylated for only a few seconds (Lukat et al., 1991; see Chapter 3.5). In contrast, SpoOF, the sporulation regulator from Bacillus subtilis, remains phosphorylated for up to 3 h (Zapf et al., 1998). In P. atlantica, the response duration for HaRR is on the order of minutes, which is of intermediate length compared with other characterized response regulators. 

Subsequently, identification of an identical response regulator in S. oneidensis, as well as two additional HaRRs, was reported (Plate and Marletta, 2012). These response regulators were identified by phosphotransfer profiling of all predicted response regulators in the organism. Along with the degenerate HD-GYP HaRR, SoHaHK is also able to participate in phosphotranser to a response regulator with an active EAL cyclic-di-GFP phosphodiesterase effector domain as well as a HaRR with a helix-turn-helix-type DNA-binding effector domain (Plate and Marletta, 2013). This is a perfect example of crosstalk in signaling pathways, with one kinase feeding into multiple response regulators with varying functions. The H-NOX two-component signaling system in S. oneidensis will be discussed in further detail in this chapter. 

## 3.3.6 NO–H-NOX-regulated two-component signaling involved in cyclic-di-GMP metabolism

In S. oneidensis, not only were the protein components of the two-component signaling pathway biochemically characterized, but also in vivo characterization of this H-NOX-associated twocomponent signaling pathway demonstrated that NO–H-NOX signaling functions in the biofilm life cycle of the organism (Figure 3.3.3) (Plate and Marletta, 2012). 

As mentioned previously, two of the three SoHaRRs are predicted to be involved in cyclic-di-GMP signaling (Plate and Marletta, 2012). In this system, as a function of NO–H-NOXregulated two-component signaling, the intracellular concentration of cyclic-di-GMP is inhibited in two ways. It has been demonstrated that the phosphorylated EAL HaRR is an active cyclic-di-GMP phosphodiesterase. Therefore, upon ligation of NO, H-NOX inhibits HaHK kinase activity, which should also result in dephosphorylation and inactivation of the EAL HaRR. Furthermore, the authors found that the un-phosphorylated HD-GYP HaRR also inhibits EAL activity, thereby ensuring inhibited cyclic-di-GMP phosphodiesterase activity in the presence of NO. Consistent with these biochemical observations, it has been observed that NO causes an increase in S. oneidensis biofilm formation. These data led the authors to hypothesize that biofilm formation may be a protective mechanism against NO, which at high concentrations can be damaging. The third response regulator involved in NO–H-NOX two-component signaling in S. oneidensis is a transcriptional repressor for all the genes in the NO–H-NOX signaling network (Plate and Marletta, 2013). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/7ece0795ead8a01b921333c6ed38f794e8b266b88fe92f04f75219e24d9e582e.jpg)



Figure 3.3.3 An NO–H-NOX two-component signaling pathway involved in cyclic-di-GMP signaling. In S. oneidensis, NO-bound H-NOX has been shown to inhibit the autokinase activity of an H-NOX-associated histidine kinase, thereby modulating the activity of three downstream response regulators: a helix-turn-helix-type transcriptional regulator, a degenerate HD-GYP phosphodiesterase, and an active EAL phosphodiesterase. This NO–H-NOX two-component signaling system is thought to regulate biofilm formation by modulating the intracellular cyclic-di-GMP (abbreviated CDG in this figure) concentration.


## 3.3.7 NO–H-NOX-regulated two-component signaling in Vibrio harveyi quorum sensing

Bacteria, which have traditionally been thought of as selfsufficient, unicellular organisms, are increasingly recognized as highly social organisms (Fuqua et al., 2001; Miller and Bassler, 2001; Ng and Bassler, 2009). Biofilm formation is one form of bacterial group behavior, but the key to understanding this group behavior of bacteria comes from understanding the ability of these organisms to communicate with each other, as well as their environment, by exchanging chemical signals. Quorum sensing, as the phenomenon is termed, regulates changes in global gene expression of entire bacterial communities, affecting behaviors such as virulence, biofilm formation, bioluminescence, and antibiotic resistance – all activities that are best served by large population sizes (see Section 21). 

Quorum sensing involves the production, secretion, and detection of small molecules known as autoinducers. Because the concentration of autoinducers in the environment should be proportionate to the number of bacteria synthesizing and secreting them, detection of autoinducers in the environment allows the cells to gauge cell density. Arrival at a critical population size or “quorum” triggers a signaling cascade regulating gene expression. 

V. harveyi and V. fischeri have served as model organisms for understanding quorum sensing (Ng and Bassler, 2009), because in response to high cell density, bioluminescence via luciferase expression is promoted. Using bioluminescence assays, researchers have been able to well-characterize three autoinducer-responsive histidine kinases (CqsS, LuxN, and LuxQ) that feed into master transcriptional regulators, such as LuxR, for phenomena like bioluminescence, biofilm formation, and virulence. 

In more detail, at low cell density, the autoinducer-sensing kinases all transfer phosphate to a histidine-containing phosphotransfer protein called LuxU, which in turn phosphorylates a response regulator called LuxO, which, when phosphorylated, represses LuxR expression by production of quorum regulatory RNAs (qrrs). Upon binding of autoinducers, kinase activity is inhibited, resulting in a net phosphatase activity and removal of phosphate from LuxO. In the absence of phosphorylated LuxO, qrrs are not produced and LuxR is expressed, allowing expression of the luciferase operon, which is observable as light production (Ng and Bassler, 2009). 

Interestingly, several Vibrio spp. bacteria have predicted hnoX genes in the same putative operon as genes that code for soluble histidine kinases that share a high sequence identity with the kinase domain of the well-characterized quorum-sensing kinase LuxQ. V. harveyi is one such organism, with a hnoX gene in the same predicted operon as a LuxQ-type kinase (termed H-NOX-associated quorum sensing kinase (hqsK)). Our laboratory has shown that nanomolar concentrations of NO increase the bioluminescence of V. harveyi, even at low population density (Henares et al., 2012). We have demonstrated that NO–H-NOX regulation of HqsK is responsible for this quorum-sensing phenotype (Figure 3.3.4). 

Phosphotransfer assays revealed that HqsK is an active kinase capable of exchanging phosphate with the quorum-sensing cascade through LuxU (Henares et al., 2012), just like CqsS, LuxN, and LuxQ. The binding of NO to H-NOX results in the inhibition of HqsK kinase activity, just as it does with traditional twocomponent signaling kinases like P. atlantica (Arora and Boon, 2012) and S. oneidensis (Price et al., 2007), described in this chapter. Unlike these canonical two-component signaling pathways, however, HqsK is a hybrid histidine kinase, containing an internal receiver domain; thus, the inhibition of HqsK activity by NO–H-NOX results in a net phosphatase activity, reversing phosphate flow in the signaling cascade, helping to dephosphorylate LuxU and LuxO, and leading to an increase in expression of the luciferase operon through LuxR (see Chapter 21.3). 

The fact that HqsK is able to exchange phosphate with LuxU, and is regulated by H-NOX, implicates this NO-responsive pathway as an additional arm in the quorum-sensing network of V. harveyi. In Vibrio cholerae and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, it has been seen that quorum sensing regulates biofilm formation and virulence (Ng and Bassler, 2009). In V. cholerae, in fact, quorum sensing is involved in opposite regulation of biofilm formation and bioluminescence through the regulation of intracellular cyclic-di-GMP levels. Indeed, in an additional study, we demonstrated that NO–H-NOX/HqsK signaling also regulates flagellar motion and biofilm formation in V. harveyi (Henares et al., 2013). 

## 3.3.8 NO–H-NOX-regulated two-component signaling in Vibrio fischeri

Another organism with an H-NOX–HqsK-type two-component signaling pathway is V. fischeri, a marine bacteria well-known for using quorum sensing and bioluminescence to establish its symbiotic relationship with Euprymna scolopes, the Hawaiian bobtail squid. Unlike V. harveyi, in V. fischeri, the primary quorum-sensing circuit is a LuxIR-type quorum-sensing pathway, in which the transcriptional regulator LuxR is itself also the autoinducer receptor (Ng and Bassler, 2009). However, several components that are characteristic of the V. harveyi quorumsensing circuit are also present in V. fischeri, including LuxN, LuxQ, and Lux. This V. harveyi–type quorum-sensing signaling cascade controls the transcriptional regulator LitR, which is similar to LuxR in V. harveyi. It has not yet been shown if NO– H-NOX/HqsK in V. fischeri regulates quorum-sensing behavior via LitR, but NO sensing through H-NOX has been shown to regulate the symbiotic colonization of E. scolopes by V. fischeri (Wang et al., 2010b). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/3c792cc587d44e1848bfbdcd04ebf56d70fe49c79aea69e88cddbe0581182bbd.jpg)



Figure 3.3.4 An NO–H-NOX two-component signaling pathway involved in quorum sensing. H-NOX has been shown to participate in the quorum-sensing circuit of V. harveyi by exchanging phosphate with LuxU, similar to other previously characterized quorum-sensing pathways (represented in grayscale). Dotted arrows represent phosphate flow and related events at low cell density, and solid arrows represent phosphate flow at high cell density (or upon NO binding to H-NOX). NO ligation to H-NOX inhibits HqsK, which ultimately leads to expression of the lux operon and luciferase production, resulting in bioluminescence.


Briefly explained, the symbiosis between the squid and V. fischeri works via colonization of the squid’s “light organ” by the bacteria (Nyholm and McFall-Ngai, 2004). The light organ provides a nutrient for rich bacterial growth. Thus, as a function of detection of cell density via quorum sensing, V. fischeri become bioluminescent. The squid is then able to take advantage of the produced light for camouflage to remain invisible to its nocturnal predators while hunting under moonlight. 

Host-generated NO has long been thought to play a role in this symbiosis; NO has been found in the ducts, appendages, and mucus linings of the squid through which the bacteria must pass en route to the light organ. Furthermore, colonization of the light organ by V. fischeri causes decreased NO production by the squid (Davidson et al. 2004). It has also been observed that NO upregulates Hmp transcription in the bacteria, which is a flavohemoglobin that binds NO (Wang et al., 2010b). 

An investigation into the role of H-NOX as an NO sensor in V. fischeri revealed that the hnoX deletion strain of V. fischeri is more effective than, and can outcompete the wild-type bacteria for, colonization of the squid light organ (Wang et al., 2010a). This was initially surprising because it was expected that the NO-rich conditions in the squid would be conducive to symbiosis, thus one would expect a sensor-deficient bacterial strain to be disabled in its ability to colonize. 

It is currently thought that NO–H-NOX may be involved in the tight regulation of iron acquisition and use by V. fischeri. Iron is an essential nutrient for bacteria, and one that is frequently limited. Thus, bacteria are programmed to scavenge the nutrient from their environment. However, high concentrations of iron are toxic, so NO–H-NOX may serve to prevent overaccumulation of iron by V. fischeri during colonization of the squid. This explains why the hnoX deletion strain has an initial growth advantage, in comparison to wild type, because the mutant bacteria can grow faster in the early stages of colonization due to greater access to iron. It was found that the wild-type strain exhibited a growth advantage over the hnoX mutant at time points longer than 24 h, however. This makes sense because it is likely that accumulation of too much iron is accompanied by a loss in fitness over time. 

## 3.3.9 Conclusions and perspectives

The specifics of NO–H-NOX-regulated two-component signaling are still being discovered. Nonetheless, it has become apparent that this is an important mechanism involved in the regulation of motility, biofilm formation, host colonization, and quorum sensing. Although there are currently many more questions than answers about NO-mediated two-component signaling, the source of NO and possible additional NO sensors are two issues that we will further discuss here.

## 3.3.9.1 Source of NO



Carlson HK, Vance RE, Marletta MA. 2010. H-NOX regulation of cdi-GMP metabolism and biofilm formation in Legionella pneumophila. Molecular Microbiology 77(4): 930–942. 





Schmidt I, Steenbakkers PJ, op den Camp HJ, Schmidt K, Jetten MS. 2004. Physiologic and proteomic evidence for a role of nitric oxide in biofilm formation by Nitrosomonas europaea and other ammonia oxidizers. Journal of Bacteriology 186(9): 2781–2788. 



One major unanswered question is that of the NO source. Why have these bacteria evolved complex signaling pathways to respond to NO? Is the source of NO environmental or endogenous? The role of H-NOX in V. fischeri suggests that the NO is host-generated in this symbiotic relationship (Wang et al., 2010a), but is this always the case? Symbionts for other H-NOXcontaining organisms are not known, but for an organism like V. harveyi it seems plausible that the bioluminescence serves a biological purpose rather than being simply a transcriptional byproduct. If the NO–H-NOX pathway in V. harveyi is strictly to be considered as involved in quorum sensing, the implication is that NO is behaving as an autoinducer produced by the bacteria themselves. The definition of quorum sensing is, however, expanding, and it is possible that NO is an interkingdom signaling molecule between bacteria and eukaryotes here rather than an endogenous one. Interestingly, V. harveyi has been detected as part of large algal blooms off the eastern coast of Africa, which may provide some clues into its ecological role. NO produced by NO synthase-containing Gram-positive bacteria in mixedspecies biofilm communities could be another possible source of NO as a form of interspecies communication (Gusarov et al., 2009). Alternatively, H-NOX-containing organisms are sometimes pathogens; thus, H-NOX could possibly serve as a defense mechanism against NO produced by immune response systems in the host. 



Carpenter AW, Schoenfisch MH. 2012. Nitric oxide release: part II. Therapeutic applications. Chemical Society Reviews 41(10): 3742– 3752. 





Spiro S. 2007. Regulators of bacterial responses to nitric oxide. FEMS Microbiology Reviews 31(2): 193–211. 



Endogenous NO produced by denitrification pathways have been observed in S. oneidensis and implicated as the NO source for H-NOX (Price et al., 2007). In fact, Shewanellaceae are wellknown for their ability to use a range of electron acceptors for anaerobic respiration, including nitrites and nitrates, thereby generating NO (Berks et al., 1995; Zumft, 1997). It has been suggested that H-NOX responds to NO as an endogenous product of anaerobic respiration as a feedback signal within anoxic biofilms to disperse to a free-swimming, planktonic state (Liu et al., 2012). 



Cock PJ, Whitworth DE. 2007. Evolution of prokaryotic twocomponent system signaling pathways: gene fusions and fissions. Molecular Biology and Evolution 24(11): 2355–2357. 





Stock AM, Robinson VL, Goudreau PN. 2000. Two-component signal transduction. Annual Review of Biochemistry 69: 183–215. 



There is no clear reason to assume that H-NOX responds to the same NO source or regulates the same behavior in all these organisms. Signaling proteins are often composed of modular domains, and it is possible that H-NOX is used as a NO signaling module in bacterial signaling circuits every time there is a need to respond to NO. Depending on the specific organism and ecosystem, H-NOX responsive signaling circuits could exist in a variety of flavors.

## 3.3.9.2 Multiple bacterial NO sensors



Denninger JW, Marletta MA. 1999. Guanylate cyclase and the ⋅NO/cGMP signaling pathway. Biochimica et Biophysica Acta Bioenergetics 1411(2–3): 334–350. 





Wang Y, Dufour YS, Carlson HK, Donohue TJ, Marletta MA, Ruby EG. 2010a. H-NOX-mediated nitric oxide sensing modulates symbiotic colonization by Vibrio fischeri. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA 107(18): 8375–8380. 



Interestingly, there are many bacteria that have been demonstrated to respond to nanomolar concentrations of NO that do not code for an H-NOX domain. For example, the cystic fibrosis–associated pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa is well documented to regulate biofilm development as a function of NO (Barraud et al. 2006), but does not encode hnoX. Therefore, an additional, uncharacterized NO sensor must exist. Indeed, we may ultimately learn that bacteria have multiple NO-regulated two-component signaling pathways.

# The two-component CheY system in the chemotaxis of Sinorhizobium meliloti

Martin Haslbeck 

Department Chemie, Technische Universitat M¨ unchen, Garching, Germany ¨ 

## 3.4.1 Motility and chemosensing

Motile bacteria orient and swim toward an optimal environment, propelled by helical flagella. The mechanisms of swimming and chemoreception as well as signal transduction have been studied intensively in Escherichia coli and Salmonella typhimurium (cf. Hazelbauer et al., 2008; Macnab, 1996; Sourjik and Wingreen, 2012; Stock and Surette, 1996; see Chapters 22.1 and 22.2). However, an increasing interest in nitrogen-fixing, non-enteric bacteria, which are attracted to the nutrients exuded from the roots of higher plants, revealed molecular mechanisms that differ from the enterobacterial paradigm (Armitage and Schmitt, 1997; Brencic and Winans, 2005; Scharf and Schmitt, 2002; Schmitt, 2002). Because 500 million years of evolution separate Enterobacteria from the members of the α subgroup of bacteria (Ochman and Wilson, 1987), including the nitrogen-fixing phyla Agrobacterium and Sinorhizobium, differences in their basic chemosensory pathways and in adaptations to their different environments are not surprising. S. meliloti currently serves as the best-studied prototype model of the chemotaxis system of α-Proteobacteria (Scharf and Schmitt, 2002; Wibberg et al., 2011). It is a Gramnegative bacterium of the rhizosphere, inducing nodule formation for nitrogen fixation in the rootlets of Medicago sativa. In the viscous environment of the soil, motility and detection of attracting root exudates from host plants require a specialized and complex pattern of chemosensing and motor control (Brencic and Winans, 2005; Scharf and Schmitt, 2002). In S. meliloti, most of the genes involved in these processes are chromosomally encoded in a single, major gene cluster referred to as the flagellar regulon, assisted by a second operon encoded on the symbiotic plasmid (Barnett et al., 2001; Meier et al., 2007). In contrast, the corresponding E. coli genes are spread over three different chromosomal regions. Gene expression in the flagellar regulon of S. meliloti is controlled hierarchically on three levels and involves transcription factors that differ from those of the enterobacterial system (Sourjik et al., 2000). Of special interest in this context is the existence of a growth-dependent transcriptional activator, which is autoregulatory in the intermediate level of the regulatory cascade (Rotter et al., 2006). 

Bacteria sense a change in the external concentration of an attractant or repellent with the help of dimeric membranespanning receptors, the methyl-accepting chemotaxis proteins (MCPs) (Mowbray and Sandgren, 1998). These MCPs localize in clusters to the cell pole and react to numerous attractants, including sugars, amino acids, flavonoids, and other stimuli, from the host plant by conformational changes (Gotz ¨ et al., 1982; Hazelbauer et al., 2008; Malek, 1989; Meier and Scharf, 2009; Sourjik and Berg, 2004). Deletion of any one of the receptor genes causes impairments in the chemotactic response toward most attractants, implying that chemoreceptor proteins in S. meliloti can sense more than one class of carbon source and work together as an ensemble of receptors (Meier et al., 2007; Meier and Scharf, 2009). The deletion of all MCPs causes a complete loss of the chemotactic response (Greck et al., 1995). Eight distinct MCPs, McpS–McpZ, serve as membrane-located transducers for attractants, and one of the receptors, McpY, differs from the others due to its cytoplasmic location. It possesses two tandem PAS domains, which are known to bind flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) (Taylor and Zhulin, 1999) and presumably help McpY to mediate aerokinesis (acceleration toward oxygen) (Zhulin et al., 1995) by sensing the redox state of the cell. Besides the eight MCPs, a further, soluble sensor, the internal chemotaxis protein (IcpA) (Greck et al., 1995; Meier et al., 2007; Sourjik et al., 1998), exists in S. meliloti. IcpA contains a conserved signaling domain, but neither a hydrophobic transmembrane domain nor a periplasmic receptor domain, which are classical features of MCPs. IcpA is a good candidate for sensing internal stimuli that reflect the metabolic state of a cell. 

## 3.4.2 Chemotaxis strategy and rotary speed variation of the flagellar motor

Due to their long phylogenetic distance (Ochman and Wilson, 1987) and the need to adapt to different biotopes, the flagella of enteric bacteria (γ-Proteobacteria) and S. meliloti differ significantly. S. meliloti is propelled by rigid, right-handed flagella, allowing the cell to swim efficiently in very viscous media, such as the surrounding soil (Gotz¨ et al., 1982). The flagella are assembled from four closely related flagellin subunits, FlaA– FlaD (Pleier and Schmitt, 1989; Sourjik et al., 1998), resulting in a complex fine structure dominated by three helical ribbons that lock the filament in the right-handed conformation (Schmitt et al., 1974; Trachtenberg et al., 1987). Hence, the motor of S. meliloti constantly turns clockwise (CW) and does not reverse its sense of rotation (Figure 3.4.1a). This is in contrast to the flagellar motors of enteric bacteria, such as E. coli, which are able to invert their rotation from clockwise to counterclockwise (Brown et al., 2011; Macnab, 1996; Stock et al., 2012). In recent decades, the structure of the self-assembling bacterial flagellar motor as well as the mechanisms in torque generation have been studied extensively for E. coli and S. typhimurium (cf. Brown et al., 2011; Stock et al., 2012). While the architecture varies in details between species, the core structure remains identical (Brown et al., 2011). 

However, the flagellar motors of S. meliloti can increase and decrease their rotary speed. This phenomenon of speed modulation, called chemokinesis, is based on a specialized rotor–stator interface (Figure 3.4.1b) (Attmannspacher et al., 2005; Schmitt, 2003). The decrease of the rotary speed of the 4–6 peritrichously inserted flagella is asynchronous. These differences in motor speed cause single flagella to leave the bundle or cause the bundle to fall apart completely, resulting in smooth or abrupt changes in the swimming direction, called caterpillar drive (Figure 3.4.1).

Figure 3.4.1 (a) The swimming pattern of S. meliloti. The biased random walk in a fading-out attractant gradient is driven by alternating between straight “runs” (highly frequent when attractant is present) and directional changes (highly frequent when the levels of attractant decrease). S. meliloti’s right-handed flagella always rotate clockwise (CW). The rotational speed increases during straight runs (bundle formation). When the rotational speed of individual flagella decreases in an asynchronous fashion, the bundle of flagella falls apart and the cell swims in a new direction (caterpillar drive). (b) Scheme illustrating the electrostatic contacts between FliG and MotA at the rotor–stator interface. In the presence of attractant (upper panel), the charged residues in the interface are in the optimal position, maximal torque generation is achieved, and the rotor runs at full speed. In the absence of attractant (lower panel), the interaction of the response regulator with the rotor leads to a conformational change in FliG. In the altered conformation, the positioning of FliG R294 and MotA E150 is not optimal due to the electrostatic repulsion (double-headed arrow) leading to lower torque generation and slower rotatory speed (Attmanspacher et al., 2005; Schmitt, 2003).

Figure 3.4.2 Scheme of signal transduction in S. meliloti from chemotaxis receptors (Mcp) to the flagellar motor. (a) In the absence of attractant, CheA auto-phosphorylates in an ATP-dependent manner and transfers the phosphoryl group to CheY2 and CheY1. CheY2-P slows down the motor speed. (b) In the presence of attractant, the interaction of CheS and CheA enhances the dephosphorylation of CheY1 (phosphate sink) and, thus, the back transfer of phosphoryl from CheY2-P to CheA, inactivating CheY2. MCP, methyl-accepting chemotaxis protein; Che, cytoplasmic chemotaxis proteins; A, histidine autokinase; S, adaptor protein enhancing CheA–CheY1 interaction; Y1 and Y2, response regulators; P, phosphoryl group; MotA and MotB, transmembrane proteins forming the energy-supplying proton (H+) channels; FliM, adaptor for CheY2-P; FliG, adaptor between rotor and stator involved in torque generation, structural changes upon CheY2-P interaction with the rotor modulate FliG conformation and result in a decrease in motor speed; CW, clockwise sense of flagellar filament rotation.


This speed variation of the flagellar motor is a special feature of α-Proteobacteria. The mutagenesis of conserved, charged amino acids in the rotor–stator interface between FliG (rotor) and MotA/B (stator) indicated a model where the motor speed is controlled by electrostatic forces (Figure 3.4.1b) (Attmannspacher et al., 2005). The interaction of the response regulator (CheY2-P) with FliM of the rotor (Figure 3.4.2) induces conformational changes in FliG, which seems to lead to a repositioning of the Arginin 294 of FliG in respect to Glutamate 150 of MotA, causing electrostatic repulsion of Aspartate 302 of FliG and Glutamate 150 of MotA (Figure 3.4.1b). This electrostatic repulsion seems to be the reason for the “slowdown” in rotary speed of the flagellar motor (Attmannspacher et al., 2005; Schmitt, 2003). 



Sinorhizobium meliloti pSymA megaplasmid. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 98(17): 9883–9888. 



While the basic assembly of the rotor–stator complexes as well as the flagella assembly cascade are similar and conserved in γ- and α-Proteobacteria (Brown et al., 2011; Eggenhofer et al., 2006; Macnab, 1996; Schmitt, 2003; Stock et al., 2012), S. meliloti encodes two specialized periplasmic motility proteins, MotC and MotE, in addition to the specialized rotor–stator interface (Figure 3.4.2) (Eggenhofer et al., 2004; Platzer et al., 1997). MotC interacts with the periplasmic domain of MotB and facilitates the proton flow through the MotA/B channel. The dynamics of interaction between MotB and MotC is necessary for the controlled proton flow and, thus, flagellar rotation (Platzer et al., 1997; Scharf and Schmitt, 2002). Recent observations especially on the motors of Rhodobacter sphaeroides and Bacillus subtilis, which also do not reverse their sense of rotation but switch between on and off states (“clutch” or “brake” mechanisms), show that protein dynamics in the motor complex seem to play a more prominent role in controlling the rotational behavior (cf. Brown et al., 2011). MotE is a dimeric chaperone, specifically responsible for the proper folding and stability of MotC (Figure 3.4.2), which gets rapidly degraded in the absence of MotE (Eggenhofer et al., 2004).

## 3.4.3 Signaling pathway



Brown MT, Delalez NJ, Armitage JP. 2011. Protein dynamics and mechanisms controlling the rotational behaviour of the bacterial flagellar motor. Current Opinion in Microbiology 14(6): 734–740. 



In response to attractants, signal transduction is mediated through a two-component regulatory pathway (see Section 3; cf. Hazelbauer et al., 2008; Macnab, 1996; Porter et al., 2011; Sourjik and Wingreen, 2012). The sensor, an adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-dependent histidine autokinase, activates a response regulator that acts as effector on the flagellar motor (Figure 3.4.2). In contrast to enteric bacteria, in S. meliloti two response regulators, CheY1 and CheY2, but no CheZ phosphatase, operate in the chemotactic signaling chain (Scharf and Schmitt, 2002; Schmitt, 2002; Sourjik and Schmitt, 1996). The absence of attractant or the presence of repellents enhances ATP-dependent auto-phosphorylation of the cognate histidine kinase CheA, which in turn rapidly transfers phosphoryl groups to the two-component CheY system. CheY2-P directs the slowdown of motor rotary speed (Figure 3.4.2a). Thus, this activated form of CheY2 is responsible for flagellar motor control and represents the chief regulator of motor function (Sourjik and Schmitt, 1996). 



Dogra G, Purschke FG, Wagner V, Haslbeck M, Kriehuber T, et al. 2012. Sinorhizobium meliloti CheA complexed with CheS exhibits enhanced binding to CheY1, resulting in accelerated CheY1 dephosphorylation. Journal of Bacteriology 194(5): 1075–1087. 





Eggenhofer E, Haslbeck M, Scharf B. 2004. MotE serves as a new chaperone specific for the periplasmic motility protein, MotC, in Sinorhizobium meliloti. Molecular Microbiology 52(3): 701–712. 



In the absence of any CheZ phosphatase, the activity of CheY2 has to be controlled by resetting the level of CheY2-P by an alternative phosphotransfer mechanism (Riepl et al., 2004; Scharf and Schmitt, 2002; Schmitt, 2002). The dissociation constants of CheA–CheY2 and CheA–CheY2-P are similar, and according to nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) studies, CheY2 and CheY2-P interact with the same site on the P2 domain of CheA in dependence of whether CheA is active or inactive (Figure 3.4.2) (Riepl et al., 2008). CheA is inactive in the presence of attractant, leading to the retro-transfer of the phosphoryl group of CheY2-P to CheA and then to CheY1, which acts as a phosphate sink (Figure 3.4.2b) (Schmitt, 2002; Sourjik and Schmitt, 1998). In a cell, CheY1 molecules are in 10- fold excess over CheA, and CheY1-P auto-dephosphorylates constantly (τ ∼ 10 s). Thus, CheY1 constantly tears phosphoryl groups out of the equilibrium and emulates the role of a CheZ phosphatase. This mechanism was first detected in S. meliloti and now appears to be ubiquitous among members of the α-subgroup of proteobacteria. In addition, S. meliloti encodes a dimeric protein CheS (Figure 3.4.2), which interacts with CheA. The CheA–S complex interacts ∼100-fold stronger with CheY1, and this enhanced interaction promotes CheY1 auto-dephosphorylation, resulting in an increased efficiency of the phosphate sink (Dogra et al., 2012). 



Eggenhofer E, Rachel R, Haslbeck M, Scharf B. 2006. MotD of Sinorhizobium meliloti and related α-proteobacteria is the flagellar-hooklength regulator and therefore reassigned as FliK. Journal of Bacteriology 188(6): 2144–2153. 



Taken together, the chemotaxis and motility cascade of α- Proteobacteria, as exemplified by S. meliloti, is highly specialized to the specific needs in the viscous surrounding of the soil. Characteristic and of special interest is the evolution of a twocomponent CheY system acting as phosphate sink and representing an alternative termination mechanism of the chemotactic signaling cascade.

## Hannah Schramke, Yang Wang, Ralf Heermann, and Kirsten Jung

Munich Center for integrated Protein Science (CiPSM) at the Department of Biology I, Microbiology,

## 3.5.1 Stimulus perception by histidine kinases

Bacteria live in environments where surrounding parameters like nutrient availability, osmolarity, pH, temperature, or cell density can change suddenly. Therefore, monitoring and adequate adaptation to these changing conditions are prerequisites to survive. For that reason, bacteria are equipped with specific signal transduction systems that mediate the response to varying environmental stimuli. The most widely distributed type of signal transduction system is the histidine kinase–response regulator (HK/RR) system, also known as the sensor kinase–response regulator system (see Chapter 3.1). The prototype of this system consists of a histidine kinase that detects the stimulus, and a response regulator (RR) that mediates the output response. Signalling is initiated when the HK autophosphorylates at a histidine upon stimulus perception. Subsequently, the phosphoryl group is transferred to an aspartate within the RR, resulting in modulation of its activity, and ultimately in the adaptation of the cell to the changed environment (reviewed in Stock et al., 2000). The number of HK/RR systems differs enormously between bacterial species. It is assumed that the overall number correlates with the variety of environmental cues the bacteria are exposed to. It ranges from zero in Mycoplasma genitalium, to over 30/32 (HK/RR) in Escherichia coli, 36/34 in Bacillus subtilis, 131/80 in Anabaena sp. strain PCC7120, and 132/119 in Myxococcus xanthus (Heermann and Jung, 2009). 

HK/RR systems have a modular domain organization (Parkinson and Kofoid, 1992; Swanson et al., 1994). They all share homology within the transmitter domains of the HKs and the receiver domains of the RRs. Transmitter and receiver domains contain the conserved H (histidine) and D (aspartate) boxes, respectively, and communicate via phosphorylation and dephosphorylation reactions (Figure 3.5.1). These modules are associated with various domains that function as input and output elements and are specific for each system. The input domain of a HK modulates the activity of the transmitter domain. Receiver domains activate or inhibit the corresponding output domains. Besides two-component systems with a single phosphotransfer step, phosphorelays exist that allow multiple phosphotransfer reactions. The HKs in those systems are so-called hybrid-HKs that contain a transmitter domain, which is fused to a receiver domain. The phosphoryl group is transferred from the H-box to the D-box within the respective HK. Then, the phosphoryl group goes to a histidine within a histidine-containing phosphotransfer domain (HPt), which either is located within the hybrid HK or forms a separate protein. The HPt domain then transfers the phosphoryl group to the receiver domain of the RR (for reviews, see Heermann and Jung, 2009; Jung et al., 2012). 

HKs are key players in bacterial signal transduction. They sense specific stimuli and transduce this information into an intracellular signal by initiating the phosphorylation cascade. Three general mechanisms for how HKs perceive stimuli are known (Figure 3.5.1) (Mascher et al., 2006). The majority of HKs sense extracellular stimuli. These HKs are membrane integrated by at least two transmembrane helices that frame the external sensing or input domain (Figure 3.5.1a). The corresponding transmitter domain is located in the cytoplasm. In these HKs, input and transmitter domains are located in two different cellular compartments, which make a signal transduction via the membrane indispensable. A second group of HKs sense the stimuli by the transmembrane domain alone or by a combination of the membrane helices and an N-terminal cytoplasmic domain (Figure 3.5.1b). The input domains of these HKs can contain up to 13 transmembrane helices. These HKs perceive stimuli that have their origins in the membrane interface or the cytoplasm. HKs that are either membrane associated or soluble realize a third mechanism of stimulus perception (Figure 3.5.1c). The stimulus sensed by this group is exclusively of intracellular nature. However, all groups of HKs share a basic mechanism of signal transduction, independent of how they perceive the stimulus. Upon stimulus perception, the HK is activated, which results in autophosphorylation at the

H-box with the γ-phosphoryl group originating from adenosine triphosphate (ATP). However, phosphorylation of one HK in Bacillus anthracis involved in induction of sporulation was found to be strictly dependent on guanosine triphosphate (GTP) (Scaramozzino et al., 2009). HKs are homodimers, and mostly autophosphorylation occurs in trans, implying that one monomer binds ATP and phosphorylates the conserved H-box of the other monomer (Filippou et al., 2008; Heermann et al., 1998). Furthermore, many HKs also function as phosphatases, meaning that they dephosphorylate the RR, and thereby switch off the signalling cascade (for a review, see Stock et al., 2000). 

All HKs share unique sequence motifs in their transmitter domains, designated as H, N, G1, F, and G2 boxes (Figure 3.5.1). The transmitter domain can be further dissected into two parts: the H-box containing the dimerization and histidine phosphotransfer domain (DHp), and the HK-type ATPase catalytic (HATPase c) domain, better known as the catalytic and ATP-binding (CA) domain (Dutta et al., 1999). 

Although the basic mechanism of HK/RR systems is quite well understood, several important issues are less clear, particularly the nature of the environmental stimulus sensed by the HKs. For a few examples, it is known that the activity of the HK can be attenuated by a so-called accessory protein that transmits a specific signal or that directly influences the enzymatic activities of the sensor (for a review, see Jung et al., 2012). However, the main activation mechanism of a HK is mediated by perception of a direct stimulus from the environment. Compared to the overall known number of different HKs, the corresponding stimuli have been experimentally verified in only a few cases. Generally, stimuli detected by HKs can be classified into chemical and physical parameters such as different ions, temperature, pH, oxygen pressure, osmolarity, autoinducers, the redox state of electron carriers, and the contact with host cells (for a review, see Calva and Oropeza, 2006). In many pathogens, HK/RR systems have been found to be important or even essential for virulence, which makes them interesting as potential specific targets for antimicrobial drugs (for a review, see Beier and Gross, 2006). However, it is obvious that the virulence-attenuated phenotype of many HK/RR mutants is caused by interference with the cells’ metabolic requirements rather than by changes in the production of specific virulence factors. The general understanding of how HKs work and how they are integrated into networks as well as the number of known stimuli that activate specific systems are constantly increasing. 

## 3.5.2 Chemical stimuli

For some transmembrane HKs, the chemical stimuli are already known (Table 3.5.1). The stimulus is perceived via periplasmic/extracellular or intracellular sensing domains that are characterized by a specific fold. The most common structures are PAS (Per-ARNT-Sim), GAF (cGMP (cyclic guanosine monophosphate), phosphodiesterases, adenylyl cyclase, and FhlA), CHASE (cyclase/HK-associated sensing extracellular), four-helix bundle (4HB), or nitrate and nitrite-sensing (NIT)

## 3.5.2.1 Organic compounds as stimuli

Sensing of nutrients is essential to adapt metabolic pathways according to available C-sources or to regulate chemotaxis. CitA and DcuS (Figure 3.5.2a) respond to external available tri- and dicarboxylates under anaerobic conditions. Structural and biochemical analysis revealed that the periplasmic domain of CitA from E. coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae is a high-affinity citrate receptor (Kaspar and Bott, 2002), while the periplasmic domain of DcuS has high affinity for C4-dicarboxylates (e.g., fumarate) and citrate (Kramer¨ et al., 2007). The structures of both domains are similar, composed of a PAS-like fold with a core structure consisting of four or five β-strands (Cheung and Hendrickson, 2008; Pappalardo et al., 2003; Reinelt et al., 2003). After ligand binding, the signal is transduced across the membrane resulting in autophosphorylation of CitA or DcuS, respectively. It has been shown that structural disorder within the cytoplasmic PAS $( \mathrm { P A S } _ { \mathrm { C } } )$ domain of DcuS is important to transduce the signal to the transmitter domain and to regulate kinase activity (Etzkorn et al., 2008). Furthermore, $\mathrm { P A S } _ { \mathrm { C } }$ is required for the interaction with the succinate transporter DctA, which acts as a co-sensor of DcuS (Monzel et al., 2013; Steinmetz et al., 2014). 

Recently, the nutrient-sensing two-component system FusK– FusR was identified in enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC). Sensing of fucose by the HK FusK was shown to regulate expression of virulence and metabolic genes and to be essential to colonize the mammalian intestine (Pacheco et al., 2012). 

In addition, E. coli contains a nutrient-sensing signalling network that is activated at the transition to stationary phase. This network is composed of the peptide–amino acid-responsive system YehU–YehT system, the pyruvate-responsive YpdA–YpdB system, and their target proteins YjiY and YhjX, two membraneintegrated transporters of yet unknown function (Behr et al., 2014). 

## 3.5.2.2 Inorganic compounds as stimuli

The PhoP/PhoQ two-component system is important for the adaptation to low $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ environments (Figure 3.5.2b). Furthermore, in enteric bacteria the system is known to regulate virulence and stress response, including intracellular survival, invasion, lipid A structure, resistance to antimicrobial peptides, and phagosome alteration (Gunn and Richards, 2007; Prost and Miller, 2008). The structure of the periplasmic sensing domain of E. coli PhoQ is similar to those of DcuS and CitA. Importantly, the PhoQ, DcuS, and CitA sensor folds are found to be distinct from the superficially similar PAS domain (Cheung et al., 2008). PhoQ binds divalent cations, particularly $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ , that form a metal bridge between the acidic surface of the sensing domain and the surface of the membrane, and consequently hold PhoQ in an inactive state (Cho et al., 2006). Low $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ concentrations, antimicrobial peptides, and acidic pH activate PhoQ, and these stimuli, found within phagosomes and intestinal tissues, may also serve as specific signatures of the host environment for these Gram-negative pathogens. In E. coli, PhoQ activity is additionally regulated by two small membrane proteins: B1500, which activates PhoQ by direct interaction and functions as a connector protein between the EvgS/EvgA and the PhoP/PhoQ HK/RR systems (see also Section 3.5.4) (Eguchi et al., 2007); and MgrB, which acts as feedback inhibitor and represses PhoQ activity (Lippa and Goulian, 2009). Besides direct ligand interaction, the redox state of the periplasm plays a crucial role in regulating PhoQ activity (Lippa and Goulian, 2012). Reducing conditions stimulate PhoQ activity, most likely by disruption of disulphide bonds in the periplasm (Lippa and Goulian, 2012). Moreover, recent studies indicate that the $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ transporter MgtA promotes transcription of over half of the PhoP target genes (Park and Groisman, 2014). As shown in this example, most HKs perceive multiple stimuli via ligand binding or protein–protein interaction, which results in formation of a complex network within the cell. 

$\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ is the most abundant cation in bacterial cells and is crucial for regulation of cell turgor, intracellular pH (see Section 16), and activation of several enzymes (Booth, 1985; Epstein, 2003; Suelter, 1970). The well-characterized HK/RR system KdpD/KdpE is activated under $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ limitation or salt stress (see Section 11; see also Section 3.5.4). The HK KdpD together with the RR KdpE regulate the expression of kdpFABC, encoding a high-affinity $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ uptake system in E. coli. The sensing domain of KdpD consists of a large (about 400 amino acids) N-terminal cytoplasmic domain, four transmembrane helices, and about 100 C-terminally amino acids at the cytoplasmic side (Figure 3.5.2c) (Zimmann et al., 1995). Since $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ plays a major role in maintaining turgor, it was first proposed that a decrease in turgor or some effect thereof activates the Kdp system (Laimins et al., 1981), a suggestion that could not be confirmed by further studies (Asha and Gowrishankar, 1993; Hamann et al., 2008; Sugiura et al., 1994). Instead, in vitro and in vivo studies indicate that KdpD senses changes in chemical intracellular parameters under hyperosmotic stress conditions. Indications for an effect of the ionic strength on KdpD activity are based on experiments with right-side-out membrane vesicles. An increase of the ionic strength in the lumen of the vesicles stimulates KdpD kinase activity (Jung et al., 2000). The loss of water is associated with an increase of the concentration of all dissolved molecules and consequently an increase of the ionic strength (Record et al., 1998). Thus, it is conceivable that KdpD detects alterations of the intracellular ionic strength. ATP, whose concentration is upregulated under hyperosmotic stress (Ohwada and Sagisaka, 1987), is regarded as another stimulus, because KdpD harbours a regulatory ATP-binding site within the input domain, which affects the ratio between kinase and phosphatase activity. $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ ions have an inhibitory effect on KdpD kinase activity (Jung et al., 2000). The effect of intracellular $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ on KdpD activation was corroborated by the observation that transcription of kdpFABC is also induced when cells are grown in the presence of Cs+, an inhibitor of K+ uptake systems (Jung et al., 2001b). A putative K+-binding site is suspected within the cytoplasmic extension of transmembrane helix IV (Rothenbucher ¨ et al., 2006; Zimmann et al., 2007) and seems to be important for the regulation of the phosphatase activity (Heermann et al., 2014). However, recent studies show that KdpD also senses changes of the extracellular K+ concentration (Laermann et al., 2013). This example shows that, despite extensive studies, the exact mechanism of stimulus perception and signal transduction within KdpD has not yet been resolved.

Figure 3.5.2 Domain organization and known stimuli of different HKs. (a) DcuS (E. coli), (b) PhoQ (E. coli), (c) KdpD (E. coli), (d) VirA (A. tumefaciens), (e) ArcB (E. coli), and (f) AgrC (S. aureus). Common domain folds are displayed in the same colour. Transmembrane helices are shown in dark blue; PAS and GAF signalling domains in red and dark purple, respectively; kinase domains subdivided in DHp (dark grey) and CA domain (light orange); receiver domains in light grey; and Hpt domains in dark orange. The periplasmic sensing domain of VirA (SensingP) is shown in white. Known stimuli are indicated and marked by black arrows at the position where they are supposed to act. TM, transmembrane helix.
