Adaptation to environments with different pH values requires sensing of the proton concentration. The VirA/VirG system of the Gram-negative plant pathogen Agrobacterium tumefaciens controls expression of virulence genes in response to acidic pH, monosaccharides, and phenolic compounds like acetosyringone (for a review, see Gelvin, 2006). Upon stimulus perception, VirA/VirG regulates the production of both the transferred oncogenic DNA and the DNA transfer machinery from the tumour-inducing Ti plasmid. The input domain of VirA consists of two transmembrane helices, a periplasmic domain, and a large cytoplasmic domain. VirA senses phenolic compounds produced by wounded plants in the cytoplasmic domain, which was identified as a GAF domain (Figure 3.5.2d) (Lin et al., 2014). Sugars that are also released by wounded plants act as strong enhancers of kinase activity. However, sugars are not directly sensed by VirA, but bind to the periplasmic sugar-binding protein ChvE, which then interacts with the periplasmic input domain of VirA. This periplasmic domain is also involved in pH sensing. This process is somehow coupled to sugar sensing, because deletion of chvE abolishes pH sensing (Gao and Lynn, 2005). Besides the kinase domain, the C-terminal cytoplasmic domain comprises a receiver domain, which was shown to have a positive regulatory effect on the kinase activity of VirA (Wise et al., 2010). 

Another pH-responsive system is the BarA/UvrY system, which regulates central carbon metabolism, motility, and biofilm formation by controlling the expression of noncoding RNAs, and therefore virulence of avian pathogenic E. coli (APEC) or insect pathogenic Photorhabdus luminescens (Herren et al., 2006; Krin et al., 2008). The HK BarA consists of two transmembrane helices, which flank a periplasmic sensor domain. BarA activity is inhibited at an external pH of 5.0 (Mondragon et al., 2006). Despite low pH, the BarA/UvrY system is also activated when glucose is present in the growth medium (Chavez et al., 2010). In this context, it might be that BarA senses aliphatic carboxylic acids like formate, acetate, propionate, and others, confirming its role in the regulation of carbon metabolism (Chavez et al., 2010). Furthermore, recent studies revealed that the RNA-binding protein CsrA is sufficient to properly activate BarA kinase activity (Camacho et al., 2014). 

The PmrB/PmrA system controls lipopolysaccharide modifications mediating resistance to the antibiotic polymyxin B in Salmonella enterica and was the first signal transduction system described to respond to extracellular iron (Gunn, 2008; Wosten et al., 2000; for a review, see Chen and Groisman, 2013). The periplasmic Fe3+-binding site is characterized by glutamate residues in the twice-repeated ExxE motif and on the serine residue at position 37 (Wosten et al., 2000). In addition, wild-type Salmonella grown at pH 5.8 was more resistant to polymyxin B than cells grown at pH 7.7. Substitution of a conserved histidine or either one of four conserved glutamic acid residues in the periplasmic domain of PmrB severely affected the mild acid-promoted transcription of PmrA-activated genes. Consequently, it is proposed that protonation of the periplasmic histidine and/or of the glutamic acid residues activates PmrB (Perez and Groisman, 2007). 

The Cpx system of E. coli represents another example for pH sensing. The system consists of the membrane-bound HK CpxA, the cognate RR CpxR, and the periplasmic protein CpxP, which somehow acts as a signal carrier for CpxA (see also Section 3.5.4 and Figure 3.5.3). CpxA generally senses different kinds of envelope stress and triggers the expression of periplasmic folding factors and proteases (Hunke et al., 2012; Raivio and Silhavy, 2001). Besides external pH, the system responds to altered membrane composition; overproduction of membrane lipoproteins; accumulation of misfolded proteins, such as the maltose-binding protein or pilus subunits; indole; and increased osmolarity (Danese and Silhavy, 1998; Fleischer et al., 2007; 

Hunke and Betton, 2003; Mileykovskaya and Dowhan, 1997; Snyder et al., 1995). The crystal structure of the CpxA periplasmic sensing domain of Vibrio parahaemolyticus revealed that it forms a globular PAS domain with a protruded C-terminal tail, which could be involved in ligand binding or CpxP interaction (Kwon et al., 2012). For Vibrio cholerae, it was shown recently that the Cpx response might be regulated by cell envelope stress caused by toxic compounds or iron depletion (Acosta et al., 2015; see Section 18). 

The NarX/NarL and NarQ/NarP systems regulate anaerobic respiratory gene expression in E. coli or S. enterica and respond to nitrate or nitrite, respectively. During anaerobic growth, these dual HK/RR systems control hierarchal use of alternative electron acceptors in the order of their electron potential. NarX and NarQ share a characteristic periplasmic input domain (NIT), for which two P-box sequences (18 amino acids) are characteristic, and that flank the two transmembrane helices. Out of these, 15 amino acids are identical in NarX and NarQ. It is suggested that two basic amino acids (His-45 and Lys-49) within the NarX P-box are responsible for discrimination between nitrate and nitrite (Williams and Stewart, 1997). In addition to the periplasmic P-boxes, both NarQ and NarX contain an extended cytoplasmic linker region that is important to transmit the signal (Appleman et al., 2003). 

## 3.5.2.3 Gaseous ligands as stimuli

The ArcB/ArcA system is important for regulation of numerous genes encoding enzymes of respiratory and fermentative metabolism in response to oxygen availability in E. coli. Under anaerobic conditions, ArcB is in its active state and phosphorylates the RR ArcA. ArcB is a hybrid HK that is anchored with two transmembrane helices connected by a small periplasmic loop in the cytoplasmic membrane. This HK has a cytoplasmic PAS domain within its input domain (Figure 3.5.2e) (Georgellis et al., 1998). It is suggested that ArcB senses oxygen availability indirectly since the lipophilic quinone analogues ubiquinone-0 (Q0) and menadione (MK3) inhibit the autophosphorylation activity (Georgellis et al., 2001). Furthermore, the quinone-dependent inhibition involves the formation of one or two intermolecular disulphide bonds between the PAS domains of two ArcB monomers. The completely reduced HK is kinase active, whereas the fully oxidized protein is kinase inactive. The disulphide bonds are believed to cause domain rearrangements that disturb the interaction of the transmitter domains within the dimer (Malpica et al., 2004). Furthermore, the fermentative metabolite D-lactate seems to be an effector that is additionally sensed by ArcB under anaerobiosis, resulting in enhanced kinase activity (Rodriguez et al., 2004). In Shewanella oneidensis, the Arc system consists of the hybrid HK ArcS, the phosphotransfer protein HptA, and the RR ArcA. ArcS has a different domain architecture compared to ArcB of E. coli (Lassak et al., 2013). Besides two cytoplasmic PAS domains, it also contains a periplasmic CaChe-sensing (calcium channels and chemoreceptor receptors) domain. Despite the different architecture, ArcS together with HptA can complement an 

E. coli arcB mutant in response to anaerobic conditions and vice versa, arguing for functional conservation of these two systems (Gralnick et al., 2005; Lassak et al., 2010; Shroff et al., 2010). 

The regulation of N2 fixation genes is of particular importance for the root-nodulating bacteria Bradyrhizobium japonicum and Sinorhizobium meliloti. The FixL/FixJ HK/RR system regulates the transcription of $\Nu _ { 2 }$ fixation genes (Gilles-Gonzalez et al., 1991). FixL also has a cytoplasmic PAS domain within its input domain that binds a ferrous haem molecule. At high oxygen concentrations, oxygen is bound to the ligand, resulting in inhibition of the kinase activity. In its deoxy state, FixL exhibits kinase activity, switching on the signalling cascade (Gilles-Gonzalez et al., 1991; Rodgers and Lukat-Rodgers, 2005). FixL activity is also modulated by binding of other gaseous ligands such as CO and NO, but to a far lesser extent (Tuckerman et al., 2002). These examples show that PAS domains in HKs fulfil various functions in stimulus perception. 

## 3.5.2.4 Antimicrobial peptides and autoinducers as stimuli

Bacteria communicate with each other via small diffusible molecules, a process that is referred to as quorum sensing (see Section 21). Some of these molecules are recognized by HKs. Gram-positive bacteria secrete peptides via dedicated ABC (ATP-binding cassette) export proteins. These peptides are recognized by HK/RR systems, such as ComP/ComA and ComD/ComE, regulating competence for DNA uptake in B. subtilis (Turgay et al., 1998) and Streptococcus pneumoniae (Suntharalingam and Cvitkovitch, 2005); or AgrC/AgrA in Staphylococcus aureus (Boles and Horswill, 2008) and FsrC/FsrA in Enterococcus faecalis (Nakayama et al., 2001), regulating virulence. The HK ComP of B. subtilis comprises six to eight membrane-spanning segments and two extracytoplasmic loops (Piazza et al., 1999) that sense the extracellular ComX pheromone. ComX is released at a constant rate per cell during growth (Bacon Schneider et al., 2002). ComX is produced as an inactive pre-form, activated after proteolytic cleavage by the protease ComQ (Piazza et al., 1999), and then released as an isoprenylated peptide (Okada et al., 2005). 

Biosynthesis of the virulence factor gelatinase in E. faecalis is another process that is dependent on cell density (see Section 21). In this case, a gelatinase biosynthesis-activating pheromone (GBAP) is secreted, an 11-amino-acid-long cyclic peptide containing a lactone structure, in which the α- carboxyl group of the C-terminal amino acid is linked to the hydroxyl group of the serine of the third residue. The precursor FsrD is processed by the cysteine protease FsrB to GBAP (Nakayama et al., 2006). GBAP binds to the periplasmic domain of the sensor kinase FsrC and activates signalling by FsrC/FsrA (Nishiguchi et al., 2009). Recent studies have revealed that GBAP binding to FsrC results in structural changes that affect particularly the region containing the aromatic amino acids Tyr and Trp (Patching et al., 2012). 

Virulence of S. aureus is regulated by a quorum-sensing system, in which autoinducer peptides (AIPs) are secreted and recognized by the HK AgrC (Figure 3.5.2f). The whole system consists of four proteins. AgrB is a transmembrane protein that appears to be involved in processing of the propeptide AgrD into the AIP pheromone, and its secretion and modification to form a thiolactone ring. The HK AgrC, which is anchored with six transmembrane segments in the membrane, binds the extracellular AIP and in turn modulates the activity of the RR AgrA. The sensor domain of AgrC is linked to the kinase domain via an α-helical structure, which is important for signal transmission. Binding of agonist or antagonist AIPs results in a twist movement of the helical structure in opposite directions that leads to activation or inhibition of AgrC kinase activity, respectively (Wang et al., 2014). Phosphorylated AgrA activates transcription of the RNAIII molecule, which is the regulatory effector of the system and is responsible for both positive and negative regulation of a variety of downstream targets, including genes encoding protein A, coagulase, enterotoxins, and haemolysins (Novick and Geisinger, 2008; Yarwood and Schlievert, 2003). 

A complex quorum sensing regulation is found in the free-living marine bioluminescent bacterium Vibrio harveyi. The three hybrid HKs – LuxN, LuxQ, and CgsS – sense the autoinducers HAI-1, AI-2, and CAI-1, respectively (Chen et al., 2002; Henke and Bassler, 2004; Higgins et al., 2007; Surette et al., 1999). These chemical signals are directly detected by LuxN and CqsS, while AI-2 is sensed by LuxQ after binding to the periplasmic protein LuxP (Neiditch et al., 2006; Swem et al., 2008). LuxN, the HAI-1 sensor, has nine transmembrane helices and belongs to the rare examples of membrane proteins with a periplasmic N-terminus (Jung et al., 2007). Biochemical characterization of the enzymatic activities of LuxN demonstrated that the presence of HAI-1 downregulates the kinase activity, while the phosphatase activity remains unaffected (Timmen et al., 2006). It has been shown that transmembrane helices 4, 5, 6, and 7 as well as the periplasmic loops 2 and 3 form the HAI-1 binding site (Swem et al., 2008). In detail, His-210 is important for recognition of the $\mathrm { C } _ { 3 }$ modification, and Leu-166 detects the chain length. Furthermore, a strong steady-state kinase activity prevents inhibition of the kinase activity by unspecific ligands (Ke et $a l .$ , 2015). The AI-2 sensor LuxQ is anchored with two transmembrane helices in the cytoplasmic membrane, which are connected by a large periplasmic loop containing two PAS domains. Co-crystallization of the periplasmic domain of LuxQ and LuxP revealed direct binding of these two proteins independent of AI-2 (Neiditch et al., 2005). However, binding of AI-2 to LuxP causes conformational changes in LuxQ (Neiditch et al., 2006). The autoinducer CAI-1 is recognized by the HK CqsS and is produced for intragenus communication (Ng et al., 2011). V. cholerae produces and detects C10-CAI-1 ((S)-3-hydroxytridecan-4-one), whereas CAI-1 of V. harveyi is characterized by the shorter tailed C8-CAI-1 (Ng et al., 2011). It was shown that Cys-170 in V. cholerae CqsS is important for recognition of the C10 chain (Ng et al., 2010). It is assumed that the closely related Photobacterium angustum uses CAI-1 signalling to adapt to stress conditions (Ke et al., 2014). The phosphorylation cascade is active when the extracellular autoinducer concentration is low (Freeman and Bassler, 1999). The phosphoryl group is transferred via phosphorelay, including the HPt protein LuxU, to the σ54-dependent transcriptional activator LuxO. Phosphorylated LuxO then activates transcription of four regulatory small RNAs (sRNAs) (Qrr1–4). Together with the RNA chaperone Hfq, these sRNAs destabilize the transcript of the master regulator LuxR (Pompeani et al., 2008; Tu and Bassler, 2007). Thus, LuxR controls the expression of genes of the quorum-sensing regulon, including genes required for bioluminescence, type III secretion, and production of siderophores and an exoprotease at high cell density (Waters and Bassler, 2005). The transcription factor AphA is the counterpart to LuxR at low cell density (Rutherford et al., 2011). It has been shown that AphA represses production of LuxR at low cell density, whereas LuxR represses AphA production at high cell density. This reciprocal regulation seems to be responsible for quorum sensing specific gene regulation (Rutherford et al., 2011). 

Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) uses epinephrine, norepinephrine, and AI-3 (quorum-sensing autoinducer-3) as chemical signals to regulate expression of virulence and flagella/ motility genes. These signals are sensed by the hybrid HK/RR system QseC/QseB. So far, QseC is the only known hybrid sensor kinase that responds to eukaryotic hormones, and thus mediates inter-kingdom signalling by functioning as a bacterial receptor (Clarke et al., 2006; Hughes and Sperandio, 2008). 

## 3.5.3 Physical stimuli

Sensing of physical stimuli is much more difficult compared to sensing of chemical stimuli. Nevertheless, some wellcharacterized examples of HKs exist which detect alterations in osmolarity, turgor, light, or temperature. These systems will be described exemplarily in this section. 

## 3.5.3.1 Osmolarity and turgor

In general, bacteria respond to hyperosmotic stress (see Section 11) in three overlapping phases: dehydration (loss of cell water) (phase I), adjustment of cytoplasmic solvent composition and rehydration (phase II), and cellular remodelling (phase III) (Wood et al., 2001). Since the water permeability of the cytoplasmic membrane is high, a higher osmolarity outside causes a rapid loss of cellular water (phase I). Consequently, the cellular turgor is reduced. In addition, high external osmolarity exerts other pleiotropic effects on the physiology of bacteria. For example, osmotically stressed E. coli cells are characterized by alterations in respiration, ATP and polyamine concentration, and cytoplasmic pH, and a downregulation of central metabolic pathways combined with a decreased transcription of genes encoding ribosomal proteins (Weber and Jung, 2002). Osmotically stressed B. subtilis cells exhibit alterations in the composition of the cytoplasmic membrane and the cell wall, the supercoiling of plasmid DNA, and defects in sporulation, iron uptake, chemotaxis, and motility (Steil et al., 2003; see also Section 11). 

Osmolarity is a physico-chemical parameter that cannot be deduced to a single molecule. Thus, cells might sense alterations in turgor, membrane strain, or shrinkage which affect the curvature of the membrane, external or internal osmolarity, external or internal ion concentration or ionic strength, changes of specific cytoplasmic or periplasmic solute concentrations, the transmembrane osmotic gradient, or macromolecular crowding (Morbach and Kramer, 2002; Sleator and Hill, 2002; Wood,¨ 1999; Wood et al., 2001). It has to be emphasized that all these changes are more or less related to the extremely fast (milliseconds) water efflux along the osmotic gradient, and therefore all the alterations described occur simultaneously, which makes it so difficult to discriminate the primary stimuli perceived by osmosensors. 

EnvZ/OmpR is one paradigm for an osmosensitive HK/RR system of E. coli that regulates the expression of ompC and ompF encoding two outer membrane porins depending on external osmolarity. EnvZ consists of a periplasmic input domain flanked by two transmembrane helices, similarly to HKs detecting chemical molecules at the extracellular side. However, truncation of the periplasmic domain does not affect on osmosensing, and a protein or ligand interacting with this domain has not been found (Egger and Inouye, 1997; Leonardo and Forst, 1996). An increase of the K+ concentration stimulates the kinase activity of EnvZ (Jung et al., 2001a). Since K+ accumulation is one of the first responses of E. coli to counteract an increased external osmolarity (phase II) (Epstein, 2003), it is suggested that EnvZ senses hyperosmotic stress by indirectly measuring alterations of the intracellular K+ concentration (Jung et al., 2001a). In addition, the intracellular four-helix bundle containing the phosphorylation site of EnvZ is stabilized at high osmolality (Wang et al., 2012), arguing that EnvZ senses alteration of the intracellular osmolarity. The question about the role of the transmembrane helices and the extended periplasmic domain in the input domain remains unsolved. 

The MtrB/MtrA HK/RR system is involved in an osmostress response of Corynebacterium glutamicum (Moker ¨ et al., 2007). The input domain of MtrB is composed of two transmembrane helices, a large periplasmic linker and a cytoplasmic HAMP domain (present in histidine kinases, adenylate cyclases, methyl-accepting proteins, and phosphatases). Membrane shrinkage has been ruled out as a stimulus for activation of MtrB. Instead, MtrB is activated upon the addition of various chemical compounds like sugars, amino acids, and polyethylene glycols on the same side as the cytoplasmic domains of the kinase are located. It is proposed that these compounds change the hydration state of the protein; shifting MtrB into the active state. Studies with truncated MtrB proteins lacking either the large periplasmic linker or the intracellular HAMP domain suggest that these domains are of minor importance for stimulus perception by MtrB. 

Although this book is about stimulus perception in bacteria, two interesting examples will be reported of how HKs respond to high osmolarity in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Two independent, but functionally redundant, osmosensing systems involving the hybrid HK Sln1 and the Sho1 branch stimulate the Hog1 MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase) cascade. Decreases of turgor, cell volume shrinkage, and removal of the cell wall have been found as stimuli for Sln1. Therefore, mechanical stimuli seem to activate the Sln branch (Reiser et al., 2003). The Sho1 branch that involves the osmosensors Hkr1 and Msb2 does not respond to changes in turgor. Recent data indicate a unique activation of the Msb2 osmosensor that is based on the interaction with the scaffold protein Bem1 and the actin cytoskeleton. It is suggested that the osmosensor Msb2 integrates signals from the external osmotic conditions with those from the internal cytoskeletal conditions (Tanaka et al., 2014). 

## 3.5.3.2 Light as stimulus

Light perception is one of the most essential features of many bacteria. During evolution, sophisticated photoreceptors have evolved. Especially phototrophic organisms, which depend on light as an energy source, have developed a complicated network of photoreceptors. Accordingly, cyanobacteria are capable to react to changing light conditions via phototactic responses (Choi et al., 1999) and regulate differentiation processes by special light qualities (Campbell et al., 1993). Light sensing also plays an important role in non-phototrophic bacteria to adapt to changing environmental conditions. Due to the capacity of UV light to generate reactive oxygen, negative phototaxis is a convenient mechanism to protect bacteria from photo-oxidative damage (Spudich and Bogomolni, 1984; Takahashi et al., 1990). 

In general, photoreceptors are chromoproteins consisting of an apo-protein moiety, which covalently or non-covalently assembles a chromophore as a prosthetic group for photoperception. The chromophore enables the holo-protein to undergo light-induced conformational changes that typically stimulate signalling cascades. Some chromoproteins have HK domains as regulatory domains, which will be described in more detail here. The differentiating bacterium Caulobacter crescentus contains the light-responding LovK/LovR system that is required for intercellular attachment and general stress response (Foreman et al., 2012; Purcell et al., 2007). The HK LovK is a soluble protein and has a so-called LOV (light–oxygen–voltage) domain, which is a flavin-binding blue-light photosensory domain. In response to visible light, LovK binds flavin as cofactor, undergoes a reversible photocycle, and displays increased autophosphorylation activity. Genes predicted to encode LOV-HKs are conserved across a broad range of bacterial taxa, from aquatic oligotrophs to plant and mammalian pathogens, such as Brucella melitensis, Brucella abortus, Erythrobacter litoralis, Xanthomonas spp., and Pseudomonas syringae. A function was found for some of them; for example, infection of macrophages by B. abortus was stimulated by light in the wild type, but was limited in photochemically inactive and null mutants, indicating that the flavin-containing HK functions as a photoreceptor regulating B. abortus virulence (Swartz et al., 2007). Similarly, a LOV-domain-containing hybrid HK is important for virulence in Xanthomonas spp. (Kraiselburd et al., 2012). 

Two full-length structures of the LOV HKs were resolved: EL346 from Erythrobacter litoralis HTCC2595 (Rivera-Cancel et al., 2014) and the engineered YF1, a hybrid of the LOV domain from B. subtilis YtvA and FixL from B. japonicum (Diensthuber et al., 2013). EL346 functions as a monomer, and YF1 is a dimer. Studies with EL346 indicated that light-induced conformational changes induce movements in the DHp domain affecting the DHp/CA interaction (Diensthuber et al., 2013). 

## 3.5.3.3 Temperature as stimulus

Many bacterial gene regulatory circuits are controlled by temperature, for example regulation of virulence. Thus, many examples for thermoregulation come from pathogenic organisms. Temperature-mediated regulation occurs at the level of transcription and translation. DNA supercoiling, changes in messenger RNA (mRNA) conformation (RNA thermometers), and protein conformation are well-known principles in thermosensing (Kortmann and Narberhaus, 2012; Schumann, 2009; see Section 13). There are also two HKs known to respond to temperature: CorS from P. syringae, and DesK from B. subtilis. 

The plant pathogenic bacterium P. syringae synthesizes high levels of the phytotoxin coronatine at the virulence-promoting temperature of 18 ◦C, but not at the optimal growth temperature of 28 ◦C. Temperature-dependent coronatine biosynthesis is regulated by the HK CorS and the RR CorR (Ullrich et al., 1995). The N-terminal input domain of CorS comprises six transmembrane helices, and CorS is believed to sense the fluidity and/or the fatty acid composition of the membrane via the transmembrane anchor. A temperature-dependent conformational change of CorS is proposed during which the sixth transmembrane helix leaves the membrane at $2 8 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ by flipping into the periplasm, so that the HPt domain is pulled into the membrane, avoiding phosphorylation (Ullrich et al., 1995). 

The membrane-integrated thermosensing HK DesK from B. subtilis becomes active when the temperature drops below $3 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ At this lower temperature, DesK and the RR DesR induce the Delta5-des gene coding for the Delta5-acyl lipid desaturase (Albanesi et al., 2004). The Delta5-acyl lipid desaturase catalyses introduction of double bonds into the lipids to restore membrane fluidity (Altabe et al., 2003). DesK has five transmembrane helices connected via a linker to the typical HK transmitter domain. Remarkably, the multispanning membrane domain of DesK could be simplified into a chimerical single membranespanning segment that is formed by the N-terminal part of the first helix and the C-terminal part of the fifth helix (Cybulski et al., 2010). This so-called minimal-sensor DesK was able to respond to changes in lipid fluidity like full-length DesK. Temperature variations lead to alterations in the thickness of the membrane, which is the cue sensed by DesK (Cybulski et al., 2010) (see Section 18). A region located at the N-terminal helix (Lys-10 to Asn-12), which is called the sunken buoy, is supposed to be buried in the hydrophobic region at lower temperature, when the membrane is thicker due to a more ordered packing of the lipids. This arrangement leads to a kinase-ON state. At higher temperatures, the lipids are more disordered, the membrane becomes thinner, and the “buoy” floats to the water– membrane interface, which leads to a phosphatase-ON state of DesK. The linker region transfers the information from the membrane-integrated part to the cytoplasmic catalytic domain (Inda et al., 2014). Thereby, this linker adopts two conformational states: state 1 forms a continuous helix from the membrane to the cytoplasm, and promotes the kinase state; state 2 is random coiled, bound to the phospholipid head groups at the water–membrane interface, and promotes the phosphatase state. Therefore, this linker that is equipped with a helix/random coil conformational duality can act like a transmission switch to adjust the DesK activities. 

## 3.5.4 Accessory proteins

Even though “two-component systems” consist of HK and RR as the core elements, many systems include additional components referred to as accessory proteins. These proteins are involved in stimulus perception (co-sensing proteins), fine-tuning (scaffolding proteins), cross-talk (connector proteins), or signal integration (allosteric effects), and play important roles in modulating the inputs and outputs of the signal transduction pathways. 

## 3.5.4.1 Membrane-bound co-sensors

UhpA/UhpB–UhpC in E. coli represents an ideal example for co-sensing. In this system, the cytoplasmic membrane– integrated receptor UhpC perceives the external molecule glucose 6-phosphate, transfers the signal to the membraneintegrated HK UhpB through UhpC–UhpB interaction, and stimulates phosphorylation of UhpB/UhpA (Figure 3.5.3a1). Phosphorylated RR UhpA induces expression of uhpT encoding the transport protein UhpT, which transports a broad range of phosphorylated sugars (Verhamme et al., 2002; Wright and Kadner, 2001). UhpC and UhpT are homologous (32% identity) secondary transporters, and they both belong to the major facilitator superfamily (Lalonde et al., 1999). It has been speculated that uhpC was generated by uhpT duplication and divergence. During evolution, UhpC kept the substrate-binding site but lost the transport capability. The input domain of the HK UhpB consists of eight putative transmembrane helices. It is supposed that UhpB interacts with the receptor UhpC via the transmembrane helices, resulting in UhpB–UhpC complex formation upon stimulus perception (Island and Kadner, 1993; Lalonde et al., 1999).

In B. subtilis, BceS/BceR is responsible for sensing the cell wall antibiotic bacitracin. In the presence of bacitracin, BceS/BceR induces transcription of the bceAB operon encoding a detoxification pump (Rietkotter¨ et al., 2008). Further studies suggested that BceS/BceR is dependent on BceAB for signal perception. A more accurate molecular mechanism was uncovered recently according to which bacitracin binds directly to BceB. Hence, depending on protein interaction with BceB, the HK BceS is able to sense bacitracin and alter its autophosphorylation activity to initiate the signal transduction process (Dintner et al., 2014). ATP binding and hydrolysis by BceAB and thus active transport is crucial for stimulus perception and kinase activation. A connection between ABC transporters and twocomponent systems, especially the ones conferring resistance against antimicrobial peptides, seems to be quite frequent in Firmicutes, and at least 70 examples are described for genes encoding HK/RR that are adjacent to those encoding ABC transporters (Dintner et al., 2011; Mascher et al., 2006). It is conceivable that the mechanism of co-sensing by these so-called trigger transporters is widely distributed (Tetsch and Jung, 2009). 

As the BceS/BceR system, the GraS/GraR system in S. aureus, which controls resistance against cationic antimicrobial peptides, depends on the transporter VraFG for stimulus perception. However, one more cytoplasmic accessory protein, GraX, is required for stimulating expression of the GraR regulated operon. It was proved that GraX interacts with GraS, GraR, and also the ATPase VraF (Falord et al., 2012). 

In Enterobacteriaceae, the outer membrane lipoprotein RcsF represents another example for co-sensing. It is part of the Rcs-FCDB phosphorelay, which mediates the response to cationic antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs) and envelope stress (Clarke, 2010; Farris et al., 2010). The two membrane-bound proteins RcsC and RcsD represent the HK and HPt protein, respectively. RcsB is the cognate RR, whereas RcsA is an accessory transcriptional activator. RcsC autophosphorylates and transfers the phosphoryl group to RcsD, which subsequently phosphorylates RcsB. Phosphorylated RcsB can either form a homodimer with another RcsB monomer or form a heterodimer with RcsA to regulate expression of the different operons within the Rcs regulon (Clarke, 2010; Wehland and Bernhard, 2000). Outer membrane stress causes an increase of RcsF concentration and accessibility to both RcsC and RcsD, which then results in Rcs phosphorelay activation (Farris et al., 2010; Rogov et al., 2011). RcsF might also interact with IgaA (YrfF), a membrane protein that inhibits the kinase activity of RcsC (Cano et al., 2002; Clarke, 2010). Furthermore, it has also been suggested that RcsF is a ligand-binding protein. RcsF can interact with the periplasmic maltose-binding protein and thereby be mislocalized to the cytoplasmic membrane to interact with RcsC (Umekawa et al., 2013). However, the exact role of RcsF for activation of the Rcs phosphorelay is still under intensive discussion. 

## 3.5.4.2 Periplasmic co-sensors

The co-sensor protein can also be a periplasmic protein which transduces the stimulus to the periplasmic input domain of the HK. One of the best characterized examples is CpxP, the periplasmic accessory protein of the CpxA/CpxR envelope stress response system (see also Section 3.5.1). The membrane-bound HK CpxA is stimulated by diverse conditions such as alkaline pH, altered membrane lipid composition, and osmotic stress. The periplasmic domain of CpxA is important for signalling, but the exact ligand is unknown (Dorel et al., 2006; Keller et al., 2011). The periplasmic accessory protein CpxP has been reported to downregulate autokinase activity of CpxA by physical interaction (Figure 3.5.3 a2). In vivo and in vitro studies provided direct evidence for the protein–protein interaction between CpxA and CpxP (Fleischer et al., 2007; Tschauner et al., 2014). 

Similarly, the sugar-binding protein ChvE in the periplasm of A. tumefaciens functions as co-sensor for the VirA/VirG system, which regulates the expression of virulence genes in response to phenolic compounds like acetosyringone (released by wounded plants) and acidic pH (see Section 3.5.1) (Gelvin, 2006). Upon interaction between ChvE and the periplasmic input domain of VirA, the sensing of sugars and environmental pH are coupled into the VirA/VirG signal pathway (Gao and Lynn, 2005). 

## 3.5.4.3 Cytosolic co-sensors

The cytosolic PII protein regulates activity of the cytosolic HK NtrB in response to the status of cellular nitrogen and energy in E. coli. The NtrB/NtrC system is responsible for the regulation of nitrogen assimilation. However, the HK NtrB cannot directly sense the nitrogen and energy status of the cell. Rather, the PII protein coupled with uridyltransferase/uridylyl-removing enzyme GlnD proved to be the real sensor. Cellular concentrations of α-ketoglutarate and glutamine affect the uridylyl status of PII. Uridylylated PII protein promotes the kinase activity of NtrB, while deuridylylated PII protein enhances its phosphatase activity (Buelow and Raivio, 2010; Schumacher et al., 2013; see Chapter 2.19). 

PhyR of C. crescentus is another example of a cytosolic co-sensor. PhyR is a conserved anti-anti-σ-factor in α- proteobacteria. It contains an N-terminal ECF σ-like domain, which can bind the anti-σ-factor of σT, NepR, and a C-terminal receiver domain that is phosphorylated by the HK PhyK (Herrou et al., 2010). Under general stress response conditions, like hyperosmolarity, carbon and nitrogen starvation, or desiccation, PhyK phosphorylates the RR PhyR and hence promotes binding of PhyR to NepR. Simultaneously, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ is released from NepR (Kaczmarczyk et al., 2014). 

Nitric oxide (NO) is produced by bacteria as an intermediate in the denitrification process from nitrate to nitrite (Rodionov et al., 2005). Due to its chemical reactivity and toxicity, a role as a signalling molecule was assumed to be unlikely. However, sensing of NO by haem-nitrite oxide oxygen binding (H-NOX) domains plays a crucial role in bacterial biofilm formation (see Chapter 3.3 and Section 22; for a review, see Plate and Marletta, 2012, 2013). The crystal structure of an H-NOX family member from Thermoanaerobacter tengcongensis revealed that H-NOX domains consist of an N-terminal helical and a C-terminal subdomain (Pellicena et al., 2004). The haem cofactor binds between the two subdomains via salt bridge formation to a highly conserved YxSxR motif (Schmidt et al., 2004). Many H-NOX genes are located in operons together with bacterial HKs (Plate and Marletta, 2013). It has been shown recently that the quorum-sensing signalling cascade of V. harveyi (see also Section 3.5.1) is also influenced by an H-NOX protein (Henares et al., 2012). In this case, the H-NOX protein interacts with the HK HqsK in the presence of NO and inhibits the kinase activity. Thus, the phosphorylation level of the phosphorelay protein LuxU and the transcriptional factor LuxO decreases, resulting in an increase of bioluminescence in the presence of NO. 

## 3.5.4.4 Scaffolding proteins

Scaffolding proteins are preferentially known in eukaryotes. These proteins assemble other proteins in diverse signalling pathways and thus influence signal transduction within the respective pathways. However, there exist also some examples of bacterial scaffolding proteins. The universal stress protein UspC is the first identified scaffolding protein influencing a bacterial HK/RR system, namely, the KdpD/KdpE system of E. coli (Figure 3.5.3b; see also Section 3.5.1). E. coli contains six Usp proteins. The copy numbers of four of them (UspA, UspC, UspD, and UspE) increase upon exposure of cells to starvation, moderate heat stress, oxidative stress, or osmotic stress (Gustavsson et al., 2002). It has been demonstrated that UspC, which accumulates within the cytosol under salt stress, interacts with KdpD at the Usp domain within the KdpD input domain and thus circumvents the inhibitory effect of $\mathrm { K } ^ { + }$ by stabilizing the KdpD/KdpE/DNA complex. This indicates that UspC fine-tunes the KdpD/KdpE signalling cascade under specific stress conditions (Heermann et al., 2009). 

The ApsS/ApsR system of S. aureus and S. epidermidis that detects antimicrobial peptides also recruits the scaffolding protein ApsX. The HK ApsS contains two transmembrane helices and a periplasmic loop with nine amino acids, which has been proven to be crucial for interaction with antimicrobial peptides (Li et al., 2007b; Otto, 2009). ApsX is a small cytoplasmic protein that is essential for the activation of the HK/RR system (Li et al., 2007a). Although the Aps system is present in a large number of Gram-positive pathogenic bacteria, homologues of ApsX are only found in staphylococcal species (Li et al., 2007b; Otto, 2009). It is likely that ApsX is a specific accessory protein for fine-tuning the ApsS/ApsR signal transduction pathway only in Staphylococcus species. However, the exact effect of ApsX on ApsS/ApsR signalling is yet unclear. 

## 3.5.4.5 Connector proteins

Some accessory proteins function as a connector between two signalling pathways (Figure 3.5.3c). The first characterized connector is an 85-amino-acid protein, PmrD, which mediates the cross-talk between the PmrB/PmrA and PhoQ/PhoP systems in S. enterica (Kox et al., 2000). PmrB/PmrA directly senses elevated levels of $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ and mild acidic pH, which makes the outer membrane permeable (Nagasawa et al., 1993; Yamamoto et al., 2005). The products of PmrA-activated genes modify lipopolysaccharides within the outer membrane and mediate resistance to the antibiotic polymyxin B and incremental $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ (see also Section 3.5.1) (Chen and Groisman, 2013; Wosten et al., 2000). The PhoQ/PhoP system responds to low environmental $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ (Garcia Vescovi et al., 1996), and expression of pmrD is under control of PhoQ/PhoP (Shin and Groisman, 2005; Shin et al., 2006). By binding to the N-terminal domain of the phosphorylated RR PmrA, PmrD protects it from dephosphorylation by the cognate HK PmrB and thereby indirectly promotes the transcription of genes that are regulated by PmrA. The PmrD-mediated connection enables S. enterica to be resistant to polymyxin B in response not only to the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ signal (which is sensed by the PmrB protein) but also to low $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ levels (which are sensed by PhoQ). 

Another example for a connector protein is B1500 in E. coli. B1500 is a membrane protein composed of 65 amino acids, and there is evidence that B1500 activates the PhoQ/PhoP system in E. coli via direct interaction with the HK PhoQ (Eguchi et al., 2007). B1500 confers acid resistance as well as multidrug resistance to E. coli, and its expression is under control of the EvgS/EvgA system (Eguchi et al., 2007; Utsumi et al., 1994). Hence, with B1500 as the connector, EvgS/EvgA also regulates genes controlled by PhoP. According to mathematical simulations, the connector-mediated regulatory pathway allows both signal amplification and persistence of expression that can hardly be realized by two independent transcriptionally regulated pathways (Kato et al., 2007). 

## 3.5.4.6 Allosteric regulators

As another example of an accessory protein, an RR can also carry out allosteric regulation of its cognate HK’s activities (Paul et al., 2008). In C. crescentus, the single-domain RR DivK is an essential factor which is involved in the regulation of division asymmetry and determination of the cell fate (Hecht et al., 1995). DivK is mainly phosphorylated by the HK DivJ and mainly dephosphorylated by the HK PleC. In addition, PleC also phosphorylates the RR PleD, which has diguanylate cyclase activity. Upon phosphorylation by PleC, PleD initiates a cyclic di-GMP-dependent morphogenetic programme. This process is promoted by DivK in a manner of switching PleC from a phosphatase into an autokinase state. Moreover, DivK also acts as an allosteric activator of the autokinase of DivJ, and thereby stimulates its own phosphorylation and polar localization (Figure 3.5.3d1). 

In addition to enhancing the kinase activity, accessory proteins can also alter the phosphatase activity of HKs (Figure 3.5.3d2). For example, SaeP and SaeQ were identified to regulate the phosphatase activity of the SaeS HK in the SaeS/SaeR system of S. aureus (Jeong et al., 2012). SaeS is stimulated by human neutrophil peptides and activates the production of major virulence factors. SaeS and SaeR are encoded in an operon with two genes encoding the lipoprotein SaeP and the cytoplasmic membrane protein SaeQ. SaeS alone hardly shows phosphatase activity to its cognate RR SaeR. However, when both SaeP and SaeQ are produced, they form a complex with SaeS, and subsequently the phosphatase activity of SaeS is activated. These two accessory proteins assist SaeS to accomplish the negative feedback regulation of the saePQRS operon.

The investigation of bacterial HK/RR systems is usually performed in monocultures and under lab conditions. However, these conditions do not reflect the natural environment where bacteria live. In nature, bacteria have to respond not only to a single stimulus but also to a wide range of simultaneous and fluctuating stimuli, and are forced to make “informed decisions.” For that reason, it is important to analyse how all HK/RR systems of a bacterium work and interact under natural multistress conditions in future.

HKs are versatile receptors for sensing diverse intracellular and extracellular stimuli, and their variable modular architecture makes HKs the perfect tools for the regulation of virulence factor production (for a review, see Beier and Gross, 2006). Besides the detailed knowledge about the phosphorylationbased signal transduction mechanism itself, surprisingly little is known about the molecular basis for its contribution to bacterial virulence in most pathogens. For most HKs that are involved in regulation of pathogenicity, the nature of infection-relevant signals as well as their regulatory networks are still unknown. Since HK/RR systems are promising targets for novel antimicrobial drugs, their molecular mechanism of sensing, the nature of their primary stimuli, as well as their auxiliary proteins have to be investigated in more detail in future.

## Sigma factors and stress responses

## C H A P T E R 4.1

# The extracytoplasmic function sigma factor EcfO protects Bacteroides fragilis against oxidative stress

Ivan C. Ndamukong, Samantha Palethorpe, Michael Betteken, and C. Jeffrey Smith 

Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Brody School of Medicine, East Carolina University, Greenville, North Carolina, USA 

## 4.1.1 Introduction

The Bacteroides are Gram-negative anaerobes that constitute a major component of the human intestinal microbiome. The human gut is a complex and constantly changing ecosystem in which hundreds of bacterial species must compete for limited resources and establish a niche in order to maintain their existence. In addition, Bacteroides fragilis is the most frequently isolated intestinal anaerobe found in clinical samples, where it is usually associated with intra-abdominal infections, abscess formation, and bacteremia. Thus, B. fragilis has the ability to flourish in two widely different environments, each with its own set of unique environmental and nutritional stresses. 

When B. fragilis cells translocate from their normal gut habitat, they must rapidly assess their new surroundings and adapt to the different environmental parameters. Protection against oxidative stress is critical as cells pass from the highly anaerobic colon to the more oxygenated tissues of the peritoneal cavity (Sund et al., 2008; see Section 10). Nutritional challenges also must be addressed. Typically in the colon, it is thought that competition for limited nutrients drives the development of the microbial community and that microbes must adapt to a constantly changing nutritional landscape. The passage of partially digested food helps create a nutrient gradient from the proximal to the distal colon. Sloughed-off cells and host secretions also contribute to the nutritional profile, but even these contributions change along the length of the colon. The glycosylation pattern of intestinal mucins varies from a more fucosylated secretion in the ileum to more sulfated, sialylated, and acetylated mucins in the distal colon (Robbe et al., 2003, 2004). There is little information on the nutritional sources used during infections of extra-intestinal sites, but it has recently been established that host glycoproteins provide an important energy source to which B. fragilis is particularly well adapted (Cao et al., 2014). 

The ability to detect changes in the environment and respond appropriately relies on a wide array of sensory surveillance systems that can monitor changes such as nutrient availability, pH, and redox state. Such systems include two-component sensor–regulator systems (TCSs) (see Section 3) and extracytoplasmic function (ECF) sigma factors (see Chapter 2.6). It is notable that the Bacteroides have one of the highest densities of these sensors coded in their genomes (Kiil et al., 2005). Characteristically, there are about 50 classic TCSs, 30 novel TCSfusion proteins, and 50 ECF sigma factors in the genomes of these species. We previously characterized one of these sensory systems, the EcfO–Reo sigma–antisigma factor system coded by BF638R 1336 and BF638R 1337, respectively (Ndamukong et al., 2013). EcfO–Reo has a role in protection against oxidative stress, but we do not yet know the mechanistic basis for this protection. EcfO is the first member of the ECF21 sigma factor family to be studied (see Chapter 2.6), and in this chapter we describe the conservation of this locus and other ECF21 sigma factors in the Bacteroidetes phylum. We also describe the genes in its regulon, their expression, and their potential function in responding to oxidative stress, extracytoplasmic stress, and extra-intestinal growth in an artificial abscess. 

## 4.1.2 EcfO and the ECF21 family of sigma factors

EcfO was first identified in an analysis of B. fragilis gene expression during oxidative stress (Sund et al., 2008; see Section 10). As described in this chapter, we reasoned that this regulatory factor might mediate a response that would mitigate the damage caused by oxidative stress; hence, it was chosen as a model for further study. Staron´ et al. (2009) described 43 distinct prokaryote ECF sigma factor families, many of which have never been characterized. EcfO is a member of the ECF21 family that is unique to the Bacteroidetes and has not been studied. A phylogenetic investigation shows that there are three subgroups of ECF21 in the Bacteroides, and every Bacteroides species has at least an EcfO homolog (Figure 4.1.1a). The subgroups include a closely related EcfO homolog (EcfO2) and a novel sigma factor– antisigma factor fusion protein with an Ecf21 signature. Most Bacteroides have both EcfO homologs, and several have all three, which is the case for B. fragilis. ECF21 sigma factors also are found frequently in the Flavobacteria and Cytophaga members of the Bacteroidetes, and these form phylogenetic lineages distinct from the Bacteroides.

For each protein shown, the species name and gene number are given.


The EcfO antisigma factor, Reo, is composed of several domains that likely form a signal transduction pathway that reaches from the cytoplasm to the outer membrane. Amino acids 1–48 are located in the cytoplasm and act to sequester EcfO prior to activation (Ndamukong et al., 2013). There is no evidence that a proteolytic event mediates activation. A transmembrane domain is present from residues 49–71 followed by a transmembrane beta barrel similar to outer membrane proteins like OmpA and PagP. This beta-barrel structure suggests integration into the outer membrane, where it might sense perturbations in the membrane. Another possibility is that some OmpA-like proteins can form channels for solutes to pass through, which may activate signal transduction as they pass through the channel. Reo homologs are conserved across all of the Bacteroides species. 

Each EcfO or EcfO2 has its cognate Reo, and even the sigma factor–antisigma factor fusion proteins such as BF638R 0227 have Reo-like C-terminal domains fused to the sigma factor domain. It is not surprising that phylogenetic analysis of the Reos shows the same three patterns of divergence as the sigma factors (Figure 4.1.1b). That is, each Reo has been conserved with its EcfO, suggesting there was a true gene duplication early in the Bacteroides lineage. Other members of the Bacteroidetes have Reo homologs associated with about half of their ECF21 sigma factors. 

## 4.1.3 The EcfO regulon

EcfO has a narrow regulon of nine genes, which includes the ecfO operon containing the ecfO and reo genes that are autoregulated (Table 4.1.1). EcfO has been demonstrated previously to be directly regulated by its antisigma factor Reo, which interacts with it at its N-terminus (Ndamukong et al., 2013). Chromatin affinity purification assays confirm that a binding site for EcfO exists at the promoters of the genes of its regulon. This regulon has a consensus recognition motif to which EcfO binds to initiate transcription of these genes in response to environmental stress. The regulon is responsive to a wide range of environmental stresses, including aerobic exposure and oxidative stress, membrane perturbation, entry into the stationary phase, and in vivo growth in an artificial abscess model (Table 4.1.1 and Figure 4.1.2a). The ecfO mutant strain was more susceptible to oxidative stress, whereas the reo mutant was more resistant to oxidative stress.

## 4.1.4 The NigD proteins in B. fragilis

Three genes encoding members of a novel superfamily of proteins, designated NigD, are part of the EcfO regulon. NigD proteins are found only in the Bacteroidetes phylum and the original NigD protein was first described in Prevotella nigrescens (pn-NigD), where its gene is located downstream of the gene encoding the bacteriocin NigC (Kaewsrichan et al., 2005; Teanpaisan et al., 2009). A family of five proteins with significant identity to pn-nigD are present in B. fragilis, and the three that are members of the EcfO regulon form a phylogenetic subgroup within the family (Figure 4.1.2b). The gene products with the greatest similarity to pn-NigC/D in B. fragilis are BF638R 0501 and 0502, with 50% and 22% identity, respectively, to their P. nigrescens homologs, but these are not controlled by EcfO. Originally, it was suggested that pn-NigD was a bacteriocin immunity protein due to its location in the operon, but this was never validated by experimental data. Perhaps the association of pn-nigD with the nigC locus suggests that this protein plays a role in secretion, membrane integrity, or maintenance of the local membrane environment. This idea is supported in part by data on the regulation of the EcfO regulon. Gene expression analyses show that EcfO-controlled nigD expression is induced in response to conditions that may induce membrane stress (see Section 18), such as oxidative stress (see Chapter 10), entrance into the stationary phase, and growth in vivo (Tables 4.1.1 and 4.1.2 and Figure 4.1.2a). In addition, we also have seen induction of the EcfO regulon in response to growth on a complex mixture of glycans isolated from porcine gastric mucin (Table 4.1.2). During growth with mucin glycans, B. fragilis induces the expression of about 25 polysaccharide utilization loci encoding unique outer membrane protein complexes (Cao et al., 2014). Perhaps the NigD proteins and other members of the regulon have a role in outer membrane stability in response to the insertion of so many new membrane complexes concurrently.

## 4.1.5 Characterization of the EcfO-regulated NigD proteins

In order to help identify a specific role for the NigD proteins, mutant strains with single, double, and triple mutations in the NigD genes BF638R 588, 743, and 1335 were constructed. The strains were tested under a variety of stress conditions, but even the effects on growth of the triple mutant were not especially noteworthy. There was a marginal defect in the ability of the double and triple mutants to resist free radical stress induced by menadione, but this was not as significant as we observed previously with the deletion of ecfO (Figure 4.1.3a) (Ndamukong et al., 2013). The absence of these proteins also does increase the stress level of the cells. This is evident from the observation that in the ecfO mutant and in the mutant of BF638R 1335, the basal anaerobic transcription levels of ahpC are very high compared to wild-type anaerobic cultures (data not shown). Complementation of these mutants brings the levels of ahpC back to near normal levels. 

Subcellular localization of the NigD proteins also may provide insight into their function. The proteins encoded by BF638R 0588 and 1335 were investigated as C-terminal histagged proteins expressed from the constitutive promoter on the plasmid pFD340. The plasmids were then transferred into the respective mutant strains, and the proteins were detected after subcellular fractionation by using a monoclonal antibody against the his-tag. The two proteins were both enriched in the membrane fraction (Figure 4.1.3b). We also wanted to determine if the proteins were surface exposed in the outer membrane. We carried out a proteinase K sensitivity assay using whole cells (Figure 4.1.3c), and the results showed that BF638R 1335 was exposed to the outside of the outer membrane, whereas BF638R 0588 was not exposed. We did not differentiate whether BF638R 0588 was present in the inner membrane or in the outer membrane but oriented toward the periplasm. This implies that these NigD proteins may not necessarily be redundant in function, but may be designed to act at different sites in the membrane.

Unexpectedly, we observed that BF638R 0588 and BF638R 1335 displayed a mass greater than predicted when electrophoresed on sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) gels. We hypothesized that there was a posttranslational modification, possibly due to glycosylation, and, consistent with this, there were two and four glycosylation recognition motives, respectively (D)(S/T)(A/I/LV/M/T), present in the amino acid sequences of BF638R 0558 and 1335, respectively (Coyne et al., 2013; Fletcher et al., 2009). To verify our hypothesis, we expressed the his-tagged NigD proteins in the background of the strain lacking the gmd–fcl–fkp glycosylation machinery. As expected, in the glycosylation-deficient strains, the his-tagged proteins had a decrease in molecular weight that was similar to their predicted unmodified molecular weights (Figure 4.1.3d). 

## 4.1.6 Radical SAM (rSAM) enzyme operon BF638R 4447 and 4448

The EcfO-regulated genes BF638R 4447–4478 are in an operon, with 4448 located upstream of 4447 and overlapping it by 98 base pairs. Chromatin affinity purification assays show that the promoter is located upstream of BF638R 4448, which encodes a lipoprotein that is commonly found in the Bacteroidetes lineage and is always associated with rSAM enzymes (Ndamukong et al., 2013). It has been postulated that these proteins play a role in rSAM enzyme localization and enzymatic functions, such as the rSAM-associated protein from Klebsiella pneumonia, PqqD, which has been shown to interact with PqqE in a critical function necessary for the biosynthesis of the cofactor PQQ (Wecksler et al., 2009). BF638R 4447–4448, along with other genes in the EcfO regulon, are induced in vivo in a rat abscess model 12–17-fold by day 4 and induced about eightfold during growth in defined minimal media containing mucin glycans as the carbon source (GEO GSE53883; Table 4.1.2) (Cao et al., 2014).

BF638R 4447 contains a highly conserved rSAM domain in its N-terminus. Two recent studies classified the superfamily of rSAM proteins containing over 2800 members with diverse functions in enzymatic catalysis (Frey et al., 2008; Sofia et al., 2001). They were identified by a conserved iron–sulfur cluster containing a signature motif, CXXXCXXC. The mechanism of rSAM enzymes has been extensively reviewed and has been found especially important in anaerobic physiology (Frey et al., 

2008; Marquet et al., 2007). The C-terminal of BF638R 4447 contains a SPASM domain first observed in SAM proteins in the subtilosin A, pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ), anaerobic sulfatase, and mycofactocin maturation rSAM families. The SPASM domain contains additional cysteine motifs that can coordinate additional [4Fe-4S] clusters. rSAM enzymes containing this domain tend to be involved in protein modification. Functionally distinct examples include anaerobic sulfatase maturation proteins, a quinohemoprotein amine dehydrogenase biogenesis protein, the Pep1357-cyclizing rSAM enzyme, and various bacteriocin biosynthesis proteins. This domain also is present in the MoaA, NifB, PqqE, coproporphyrinogen III oxidase, biotin synthase, and MiaB families (Haft, 2011; Haft and Basu, 2011). 

One class of the rSAM enzymes involved in posttranslational modification acts on anaerobic sulfatases. Sulfatases are inactive when first translated, and their active site contains a conserved cysteinyl or seryl residue that must undergo posttranslational modification to a $\mathrm { C _ { \alpha } \mathrm { - f o r m y l g l y c i n e ( F g l y ) } }$ residue for enzymatic functionality. Protein structural modeling of the BF638R 4447 amino acid sequence by the Phyre2 server and database (Kelley and Sternberg, 2009) predicts this molecule to be an anaerobic sulfatase-maturating enzyme (anSME) with 100% confidence, by using the model of the anSME of Clostridium perfringens (Goldman et al., 2013) and comparing a psi-blast multiple sequence alignment with 1000 protein sequences of the same rSAM family. Sulfatases are extensively found in the Bacteroides, but they are not well studied. One paper identified a single anSME, BT 0238, that was essential for the activity of 28 sulfatases in Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron (Benjdia et al., 2011). Mutation of this gene causes B. thetaiotaomicron to lose its sulfatase activity and its ability to grow on sulfated glycans. BT0238 shows homology to the gene BF638R 3016 found in B. fragilis (91.5% consensus positions and 85% identity positions). The next closest gene showing the strongest primary sequence and structural homology through the entire length of the protein is encoded by the gene BF638R 4447. It should be noted that, among the four rSAM proteins in B. fragilis that show significant sequence homology to BT 0238, only BF638R 4447 and 3016 show a conservation of both the N-terminal rSAM and the C-terminal SPASM domain (Figure 4.1.4a). A close look at the sequence alignment between BF638R 4447 and the C. perfringens anSME shows that the AdoMet cluster contains the three conserved cysteines and two additional cysteine residues at positions −4 and +4 from the active site motif CXXCXXXC. These could potentially participate in complete coordination and occupation of the [4Fe-4S] cluster. We also observe that only the first and third cysteines that coordinate cluster I of auxiliary cluster binding sites are conserved. This makes the SPASM domain of this protein potentially available as a substrate ligation site since the [4Fe-4S] cluster would not be fully coordinated (Figure 4.1.4c). 

As mentioned in this chapter, when B. fragilis is grown in defined medium containing mucin glycans that are rich in sulfated glycans, the EcfO regulon is induced when compared to anaerobic cultures grown in defined media containing glucose (Table 4.1.2) (Cao et al., 2014). The regulon is among the top 19±7% of genes induced in the abscess and within the top 9±4% of genes induced by mucin by a factor greater than two fold. This induction together with their structural homology to the anSME open many questions as to their role in modifying sulfatases, because the homolog of BT 0238 (BF638R 3016) also is conserved in B. fragilis but is not induced in mucin glycan media. Similar to B. thetaiotaomicron, which has 28 genes encoding sulfatases, B. fragilis has 15 sulfatases with a conserved active site that can be potentially modified by the anSME. 



Ndamukong IC, Gee J, Smith CJ. 2013. The extracytoplasmic function sigma factor EcfO protects Bacteroides fragilis against oxidative stress. Journal of Bacteriolog y 195: 145–155. 



BF638R4447 can be tested for sulfatase-modifying activity by co-expressing it with a bona fide sulfatase and measuring enzymatic activity. Its localization compared to BF638R 3016 would have to be addressed to determine if their localization is essential for their differential function. The role that the accessory lipoprotein coded by BF638R 4448 plays in the function of BF638R 4447 also needs to be investigated. The fact that such a protein-modifying enzyme is controlled by an ECF sigma factor helps us understand the different layers of control this bacteria requires to turn on genes that respond to different environmental and substrate conditions to meet its specific needs.

## C H A P T E R 4.2

# Regulation of energy metabolism by the extracytoplasmic function (ECF) ?? factors of Arcobacter butzleri

Irati Martinez-Malaxetxebarria1,2, Rudy Muts1, Linda van Dijk1, Craig T. Parker3, William G. Miller3, Steven Huynh3, Wim Gaastra1, Jos P.M. van Putten1, Aurora Fernandez-Astorga2, and Marc M.S.M Wosten¨ 1,∗ 



1Department of Infectious Diseases and Immunology, Utrecht University, Utrecht, The Netherlands 





2Department of Immunology, Microbiology and Parasitology, Faculty of Pharmacy, University of the Basque Country (UPV-EHU), Vitoria-Gasteiz, Spain 





3Produce Safety and Microbiology Research Unit, Agricultural Research Service, US Department of Agriculture, Albany, California, USA 



## 4.2.1 Introduction

Arcobacter spp. are Gram-negative, small, motile, and spiralshaped bacteria belonging to the Campylobacteraceae family. Arcobacter is currently composed of 18 species (Levican et al., 2012; Levican and Figueras, 2013). Within this genus, A. butzleri, A. cryaerophilus, and A. skirrowii are associated with animal and human diseases, such as reproductive disorders, mastitis, and diarrhoea in animals (Anderson et al.,1993; Higgins et al.,1999; Neill et al.,1979; On et al.,2002), and enteritis and occasionally bacteraemia in humans (Lerner et al., 1994; Prouzet-Mauleon et al., 2006; Samie et al., 2007; Wybo et al., 2004). Arcobacter spp. were classified in 2002 as emerging pathogens by the International Commission on Microbiological Specifications for Foods (ICMSF, 2002). The main reservoirs for Arcobacter spp. are water environments, especially sewage and coastal waters (Moreno et al., 2003; Musmanno et al., 1997; Rice et al., 1999). 

The human clinical isolate A. butzleri RM4018 was the first strain of the genus being completely sequenced (Miller et al., 2007). Genome analysis revealed that this bacterium is coding for a large number of signal transduction systems; apart from a large number of two-component systems, it codes for seven σ/anti-σ factor pairs belonging to the ECF family (see Chapter 2.6) of σ factors, suggesting that A. butzleri is able to respond to many different environmental signals. Currently, two other Arcobacter spp. genomes are available: those of A. nitrofigilis (Pati et al., 2010) and A. cibarius (Adam et al., 2014a). Although A. butzleri is probably not the only ECF σ factor containing 

Arcobacter spp. (Adam et al., 2014b,c; Toh et al., 2011), the plant-associated nitrogen-fixing A. nitrofrigilis and the animalassociated A. cibarius do not seem to possess ECF σ factors (Adam et al., 2014a; Pati et al., 2010). 

ECF σ factors have been identified in both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, and they are fundamental for bacterial adaptation to different environments and for survival under different stress conditions (Helmann, 2002; Llamas et al., 2009). Their role in cellular physiology is highly variable and includes adaptation to membrane-affecting compounds; extreme temperatures and pH; light; high pressure; carbon, nitrogen, and iron starvation; oxidative and osmotic stress; and the regulation of virulence in pathogenic organisms (Helmann, 2002; Shaw et al., 2008; see Chapter 2.6 and Section 4). Despite their diverse effects, ECF σ factors share common features. In most cases, ECF σ factors are co-transcribed with their cognate anti-σ factor. The anti-σ factor, which often spans the inner membrane, sequesters and inactivates the cognate σ factor at the inner face of the cytoplasmic membrane. Upon a specific external stimulus, the ECF anti-σ factor is inactivated by protein degradation and the σ factor is released from the membrane, where it associates with RNA polymerase and mediates transcriptional activation of its target genes (Raivio and Silhavy, 2001). The ECF anti-σ factor can also be released from the ECF σ factor by a phosphorylated response regulator NepR; this partner-switching mechanism has recently been discovered in alphaproteobacteria (Campagne et al., 2012). Some ECF σ/anti-σ factors form, together with an outer membrane TonB-dependent receptor, a trans-envelope signal transduction pathway (Visca et al., 2002). These TonB-dependent receptors are involved in the uptake of specific molecules, but they also sense and transmit, via the anti-σ factor, extracellular signals that lead to the activation of a specific ECF σ factor. 

In A. butzleri RM4018, the seven ECF σ factor pairs are genetically unlinked, but for each pair, the σ factor gene is positioned adjacent to and in the same orientation as the putative cognate anti-σ factor gene. The amino acid identity between any two of the seven ECF σ factors varies between 30 and 49%, suggesting that each ECF pair plays a different role in the biology of strain RM4018 and responds perhaps to a different suite of external signals. 

In the present study, we investigated the role of the A. butzleri RM4018 ECF σ factors. We developed the genetic tools to manipulate A. butzleri and determined the regulons of most ECF σ factors using a combination of microarray-based transcriptome analysis and functional assays. 

## 4.2.2 Materials and methods

Bacterial strains, plasmids, and growth conditions: Bacterial strains and plasmids used in this work are listed in Table 4.2.1 A. butzleri strains were routinely grown at $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in brain heart infusion (BHI) broth (Oxoid) or on Mueller Hinton (MH) agar (Oxoid) supplemented with 5% sheep blood (Biotrading). E. coli strains were routinely grown at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in lysogeny broth (LB) or on LB agar plates (Biotrading) supplemented with ampicillin (100 μg/ml) or kanamycin (50 μg/ml) when needed. 

Construction of A. butzleri ECF σ factor and ECF anti-σ factor mutants: The genes encoding the seven ECF σ factors and their cognate anti-σ factors were amplified using the primer pairs AB0986F/AB0987R, AB1044F/AB1044R, AB1437F2/AB1437R2, AB1460F/AB1460R, AB1576F/1576R, AB2151F/AB2151R, and AB2300F/2300R (Table 4.2.2); the proofreading enzyme Pfu (Promega); and A. butzleri RM4018 chromosomal DNA as template. The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) products were tailed with a $5 ^ { \prime } { \mathrm { - A } }$ nucleotide using Taq polymerase (Invitrogen) and ligated into the pGEM-T Easy vector (Promega) to obtain pGEMab0983-0984, pGEMab1040- 1041, pGEMab1429-1430, pGEMab1452-1453, pGEMab1567- 1568, pGEMab2164-2165, and pGEMab2315-2316 (Table 4.2.1). Inverse PCR was performed on the σ/anti-σ plasmids to delete a large part of both the σ and anti-σ factor (σ/anti-σ knockout plasmids) or of only the anti-σ factor encoding genes (anti-σ knockout plasmids). Unique BamHI restriction sites were introduced at the same time. The plasmid pGEMΔab1429-1430 was obtained by digesting plasmid pGEMΔab1429 with BamHI and $B c l [$ . The knockout constructs were created by digestion of the inverse PCR products with BamHI and ligation to a 1.4 kb BamHI fragment containing a kanamycin resistance gene (aph(3′ )-III) from pMW2 (Wosten, 1997). The ECF¨ σ factor genes were inactivated by marker exchange mutagenesis. The knockout plasmids were introduced into A. butzleri RM4018 by electrotransformation (Martinez-Malaxetxebarria et al., 2012). 

Homologous recombination resulting in double-crossover events was verified by PCR. 

Phenotype characterization: Growth curves were generated by diluting pre-cultures grown overnight in BHI to a starting optical density $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 5 5 0 } )$ of 0.05 in 30 ml of BHI. The 30 ml cultures were grown in conical flasks under aerobic conditions, 150 rpm at $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . Bacterial growth and cell density were monitored by measuring the absorbance at 550 nm at different time intervals. The exponential growth rate was calculated from four separated growth experiments. Several stress conditions that limited the growth of the wild-type Arcobacter strain were tested. To measure the influence of extreme temperatures, the starting cultures were incubated at $4 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ or $6 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 15 min prior to their incubation at $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . To study the effect of the pH on the growth of the strains, the pH of the BHI was adjusted to pH 5 or 9. Osmotic stress was tested by adding 0.35 M NaCl to the BHI. In additional experiments, other stress-inducing chemicals were added to the BHI to concentrations that limited the growth of the wild-type Arcobacter strain. These chemicals included ethanol (5%); sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) (1%); the iron chelator 2,2-dipyridyl (300 μM); the oxidative stress-inducing chemicals $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (0.04%) and diamide (2 mM); and antimicrobial compounds such as penicillin G and polymyxin B (25 μg/ml). Motility assays were performed by stabbing the strains with a pipette tip into a semisolid medium (thioglycolate medium containing 0.4% agar; Difco), followed by incubations under aerobic conditions at 30 ◦C or 37 ◦C for 48 h. 

RNA isolation: Overnight grown cultures of A. butzleri were diluted to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 5 5 0 }$ of 0.1 in BHI and incubated at $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ on a shaking platform set at 150 rpm. RNA was isolated from 5 ml of mid-logarithmic phase cultures $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 5 5 0 }$ of approximately 0.5) using the $\mathrm { \bar { R } N A - B e e ^ { \mathrm { \bar { T } M } } }$ kit (Tel-Test, Inc.), following the manufacturer’s specifications. 

Microarray hybridization and analysis: For expression profiling, an indirect comparison of gene expression levels was performed (Lucchini et al., 2005; Yang and Speed, 2002). In this microarray experimental design, each labeled complementary DNA (cDNA) was combined with labeled genomic DNA from A. butzleri RM4018. Mixtures were hybridized to a previously designed and manufactured A. butzleri DNA array (Miller et al., 2007). Labeling of RNA and DNA, a hybridization procedure, and microarray data analysis were performed as previously described (Wosten¨ et al., 2006). Details of the microarray have been deposited in the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) repository (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/) under platform accession number GPL14948. The microarray dataset has been deposited in the NCBI GEO repository (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/) under accession number GSE34089. 

Real-time reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR): Primers used in this assay were designed using the Primer Express software (Applied Biosystems) and are listed in Table 4.2.2. Prior to amplification, RNA samples were treated with ribonuclease (RNase)-free DNase I (Invitrogen). RT-PCR was performed on
