Nitrate–nitrite assay: The nitrate reductase activity was determined by measuring the production of nitrite from nitrate as previously described (Sellars et al., 2002). Briefly, strains were grown overnight (16 h) under aerobic conditions in BHI broth containing 20 mM of sodium nitrate. Nitrite accumulation in the supernatant was detected by mixing 50 μl of the culture supernatants with 850 μl of 1% (w/v) sulphanilamide dissolved in 1 M of HCl and 100 μl of 0.02% (w/v) naphthylethylenediamine solution. After 15 min, the formation of p-sulfobenzeneazo α-naphthylamine was measured at 540 nm. The amount of nitrite present in 50 μl culture supernatant was estimated using a nitrite standard curve. The nitrite production was adjusted to the total bacterial proteins present in the culture as estimated by using the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) protein assay kit. To determine the nitrate concentration in Arcobacter culture supernatants, the supernatants were 10 times diluted in BHI. The diluted-culture supernatants were incubated with sulphanilamide and naphthylethylenediamine, as described for the nitrite detection. Next, a trace amount of zinc dust was added to the mixture. The zinc dust reduces nitrate to nitrite, and a red color develops due to the formation of p-sulfobenzene-azo α- naphthylamine. After 2 min, the zinc has settled on the bottom, and 900 μl of the supernatant was transferred to a new tube and the absorbance of the red color was measured at 540 nm. The amount of nitrate present in 50 μl culture supernatant was estimated using a nitrate standard curve that was also treated with zinc dust. Reactions were measured four times and repeated with two independent cultures. 

Sox enzyme activity assay: Overnight cultures in BHI were washed once with Arcobacter Minimal 1 (AM1) medium. The bacteria were subsequently diluted in sodium sulfite–, phenol red–amended AM1 medium to an $\mathrm { O D } _ { 5 5 0 }$ of 0.05 and allowed to grow in completely filled capped 5 cm glass vials. The strains, which were able to oxidize sulfur, caused a drop in the pH that was visible as a color change from red to yellow. After 6 h of growth at $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ absorbance at 564 nm was measured, and the results obtained for the wild-type strain were set at 100%. 

Citrate uptake assay: The ability of the strains to utilize citrate was determined using Simmons citrate agar (Oxoid). Strains grown overnight on MH agar supplemented with 5% sheep blood were streaked onto Simmons Citrate Agar supplemented with 0.01% sodium pyruvate. Cells were incubated at $3 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ under aerobic conditions for 48 h. The strains that were able to use the citrate as a carbon source increased the pH of the medium, resulting in a color change of the medium from green to blue. 

Statistical analyses: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to identify if any of the mutations significantly changed the growth rate of the Arcobacter strains. Statistical analyses were performed using the SPSS 19.0 statistical package program (SPSS Inc.). 

## 4.2.3 Results

## 4.2.3.1 Mutagenesis of the ECF ?? factor and anti-?? factor encoding genes

For each ECF σ/anti-σ pair, mutational inactivation of the anti-σ factor results in constitutive induction of the σ response, whereas mutational inactivation of the σ factor results in the downregulation of ECF-dependent transcription (Alba and Gross, 2004; Raivio and Silhavy, 2001). This allowed us to study the function of the ECFs in A. butzleri strain RM4018 without knowing the specific signal(s) that activate them. In order to address the role of the seven ECF σ factors in A. butzleri RM4018, we inactivated either both the σ and the anti-σ factors, or the anti-σ factor alone. After modifying the Arcobacter mutagenesis protocol described by Ho et al. (2008), we were able to replace the ECF σ/anti-σ factor genes AB0986/0987 $( \sigma ^ { 1 } , \mathsf { A } \sigma ^ { 1 } )$ , AB1044/1045 $( \sigma ^ { 2 } , \mathrm { A } \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ , AB1460/1461 $( \sigma ^ { 4 } , \mathrm { A } \sigma ^ { 4 } ) , A B I 5 7 6 / 1 5 7 7 ( \mathrm { A } \sigma ^ { 5 } , \sigma ^ { 5 } )$ , and $A B 2 3 0 0 / 2 3 0 1 \left( { \mathrm { A } } { \sigma } ^ { 7 } , { \sigma } ^ { 7 } \right)$ with the Kmr cassette. We also obtained single mutants in the anti-σ factor genes $\mathrm { A } \sigma ^ { 1 } , \mathrm { A } \sigma ^ { 2 } , \mathrm { A } \sigma ^ { 4 } , \mathrm { A } \sigma ^ { 5 }$ , and $\mathrm { A } \sigma ^ { 7 }$ . All mutants contained the Kmr cassette in the same orientation as the ECF genes. As no suitable Arcobacter shuttle plasmids exist and no other antibiotic cassettes could be used, we were unable to perform complementation studies. 

## 4.2.3.2 Phenotype characterization

Comparison of the various mutants with the parent strain RM4018 revealed differences neither in bacterial shape or colony formation on sheep blood plates nor in growth rate in BHI medium as statistically estimated by ANOVA $F = 1 7 7 7 \ ( p >$ 0.05) (Figure 4.2.1a,b). A common role of ECF σ factors is to protect bacteria against external stress (Helmann, 2002). Exposure of the A. butzleri mutant strains to extreme temperatures $( \mathrm { e . g . , 4 ^ { \circ } C }$ or $6 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ) _ { : }$ , pH 5 or 9, or subinhibitory concentrations of stress-inducing chemicals (e.g., ethanol, SDS, the metal ion chelators EDTA and 2,2-dipyridyl, the oxidative stress-inducing chemicals $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and diamide, or the antimicrobial compounds penicillin G and polymyxin B) did not yield significant growth or morphology differences (data not shown). Similarly, the motility of the mutants on semisolid medium was unchanged compared to the wild type. These results indicated that the functions of the Arcobacter ECF σ factors might be different from those in other bacterial species. 

## 4.2.3.3 Identification of ECF ?? factor–regulated genes

To identify the genes regulated by the RM4018 ECF σ factors, RNA was isolated from wild-type and mutant strains grown to mid-logarithmic phase and subjected to microarray-based transcriptome analysis. To obtain maximal ECF σ factor–dependent transcript differences, transcripts of each σ/Aσ mutant and its cognate Aσ mutant were compared. Genes showing more than a fourfold change in transcript levels were considered as ECF σ- dependent. Based on this criterion, the ECF σ factors σ1, $\sigma ^ { 2 } , \sigma ^ { 4 }$ , $\sigma ^ { 5 } ;$ , and $\sigma ^ { 7 }$ were found to regulate 3, 65, 14, 42, and 72 genes, respectively (Martinez-Malaxetxebarria et al., 2012). None of the ECF σ factors appeared to regulate its own transcription. Interestingly, more than 30 genes were regulated by two or more ECF σ factors (Table 4.2.3). In agreement with the phenotypic characterization, the identified ECF σ-dependent genes indicate that the ECF σ factors of A. butzleri regulate genes other than ECF σ factors in other bacterial species.

## 4.2.3.7 Genes regulated by AB2301 (ECF $\bullet ^ { 7 } )$

The transcriptome analysis revealed that $\sigma ^ { 7 }$ activated 37 genes and repressed another 35 (Martinez-Malaxetxebarria et $a l . ,$ , 2012). Almost all annotated genes repressed by $\sigma ^ { 7 }$ were activated by $\sigma ^ { 2 } .$ . The genes encoding the putative TctABC transport proteins (AB0103–0105) were the most upregulated genes by $\sigma ^ { 7 }$ , whereas the sox operon and AB0494–AB0495, encoding an acetate kinase and a phosphate acetyltransferase, were the most downregulated. Although it did not affect the transcription of its linked TonB-dependent receptor gene (AB2299), $\sigma ^ { 7 }$ activated two other TonB-dependent receptor genes AB0705 and AB1870. 

The A. butzleri ECF σ factors regulate parts of the electron transport chain: Unlike the tonB genes, which also appear to be regulated by ECF σ factors in other bacterial species, we found that a large number of genes regulated by A. butzleri ECF σ factors are involved in the electron transport chain. To verify that the ECF σ factors indeed influence the electron transport chain, we first performed real-time RT-PCR on the ECF-dependent tonB, nap, sox, and tct genes. We could confirm that the tonB genes AB0988, AB1462, and AB1573 are indeed upregulated by ECF $\sigma ^ { 1 }$ , $\sigma ^ { 4 }$ , and $\sigma ^ { 5 }$ , respectively (Figure $4 . 2 . 2 \mathrm { a } , \mathrm { c } , \mathrm { d } )$ . ECF $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ activated the nap and sox genes (Figure 4.2.2b), of which the latter were repressed by $\sigma ^ { 7 }$ (Figure 4.2.2e). The real-time RT-PCR results also confirmed that the tct genes are downregulated by ECF $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ and upregulated by $\sigma ^ { 5 }$ and $\bar { \sigma } ^ { 7 }$ (Figure 4.2.2b,d,e). 

To prove that the differences in nap, sox, and tct transcripts result in phenotypic differences, we determined the nitrate reductase activity, the ability to oxidize sulfate, and the utilization of citrate in ECF mutants compared to the wild type. As expected, none of the strains except A. butzleri Aσ2::Km produced nitrite from the supplied nitrate in the presence of oxygen (Figure 4.2.3a). The constitutive expression of $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ in the case of the $\mathrm { A } \sigma ^ { 2 }$ ::Km mutant led to nitrite production regardless of the presence of oxygen, indicating that ECF $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ upregulates the Nap-type nitrate reductase. To investigate whether the altered transcription levels of the sox genes resulted in a change in Sox enzyme activity, all the strains were grown for 6 h in AM1 medium supplemented with sulfite and the pH indicator phenol red. The mutants $\Delta \mathrm { A } \sigma 2$ and $\Delta \sigma { } ^ { } / \mathrm { / A } \sigma { } ^ { } 7$ further induced the change in medium pH observed during growth of the parental strain, indicating that these mutants have an increased ability to oxidize reduced sulfur compounds (Figure 4.2.3b). These results confirmed that ECF $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 7 }$ regulate the Sox sulfur oxidation proteins in an opposite way. Finally, we investigated whether these strains are able to utilize citrate, which causes an increase in the pH and a color change of the medium when these bacteria are grown on Simmons agar. In agreement with microarray and real-time RT PCR results, all strains except the mutants $\Delta \mathrm { A } \sigma 2$ and $\Delta \sigma { } 7 / \mathrm { A } \sigma { } 7$ caused a color change of the media, indicating that the ΔAσ2 and Δσ7/Aσ7 mutants could not metabolize citrate (Figure 4.2.3c).

## 4.2.4 Discussion

Although Arcobacter has been classified as an emerging pathogen (ICMSF, 2002), knowledge on this organism is still limited. The genome sequence of A. butzleri strain RM4018 (Miller et al., 2007) revealed that, unlike other characterized members of the epsilon proteobacteria, this strain possesses seven putative extracytoplasmic function (ECF) σ factors. These σ factors are often involved in the regulation of virulence or stress-related genes in other bacteria (see Chapter 2.6). In the present study, we developed genetic tools to manipulate A. butzleri and used these tools to investigate the function of the putative RM4018 ECF σ factors. A. butzleri is resistant to many different antibiotics (Atabay and Aydin, 2001; Houf et al., 2004; Miller et al., 2007); therefore, it was difficult to find a suitable antibiotic cassette to inactivate the ECF σ factor–encoding genes. Only a kanamycin resistance gene from Campylobacter coli (Labigne-Roussel et al., 1987) appeared to be functional in strain RM4018. By electroporation, we were able to generate 10 different mutants, inactivate five of the seven ECF σ factors, and identify the corresponding regulons. Despite repeated attempts, we were unable to mutate the ECF σ factors AB1430 (σ3) and AB2165 (σ6), which may indicate that these factors are essential for bacterial growth under the conditions employed. 

ECF σ factors are involved in a wide range of environmental responses in many bacterial species (Shaw et al., 2008; see Chapter 2.6). They are mainly divided into stress response ECF σ factors and iron starvation ECF σ factors (Braun et al., 2003). Our results indicate that the ECF σ factors of the strain RM4018 are involved in neither iron starvation nor the stress response. Furthermore, we found no evidence of positive regulation of their own transcription, as often found for other ECF σ factors (Alba and Gross, 2004). Except for the tonB genes, the RM4018 ECF σ factors regulate completely different sets of genes. This seemingly atypical gene regulation in Arcobacter has also been noted for the regulation of the flagellar genes as Arcobacter lacks the σ factors FliA and RpoN, which in many bacterial species regulate flagellar biosynthesis (Miller et al., 2007). Therefore, in contrast to other eubacteria, many conserved genes in A. butzleri appear to be regulated by a σ factor belonging to a different σ factor class; therefore, knowledge on transcription regulation of conserved genes described in other bacterial species cannot be simply extrapolated to A. butzleri. 

In A. butzleri RM4018, five out the seven ECF σ/anti-σ factor pairs are flanked by genes encoding putative TonB-receptor proteins. In other species, the ECF σ/anti-σ factors form, together with an outer membrane TonB-dependent receptor, a cellsurface-signaling (CSS) system (Visca et al., 2002). Transcriptome analyses showed that $\sigma ^ { 1 } , \sigma ^ { 4 }$ , and $\sigma ^ { 5 }$ regulate the expression of the TonB-dependent receptors encoded by the same loci, suggesting the putative presence of three potential transenvelope signal transduction systems in A. butzleri RM4018. Most of the described CSS systems are involved in iron signaling and transport (Koebnik, 2005). However, other functions have been described, including for the Ralstonia solanacearum Prha–PrhIR system, which senses the presence of a plant cell wall structure and initiates a regulatory cascade that induces the hypersensitive response and the transcription of pathogenicity genes (Brito et al., 2002). The role of the three putative CSS systems in A. butzleri RM4018 remains to be elucidated, as the growth of mutants in these systems is not affected by iron limitation. 

Transcriptome analysis, as well as functional assays, showed that A. butzleri ECF σ factors also regulate a number of genes involved in the binding and transport of specific compounds, energy metabolism, and sulfur oxidation. We showed that Arcobacter does not reduce nitrate under aerobic conditions (Figure 4.2.3a), although it does under anaerobic conditions (data not shown). The ECF $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ is involved in this environmental adaptation as the $\mathrm { A } \sigma ^ { 2 }$ ::Km mutant produces nitrite under aerobic conditions. This may indicate that oxygen stress has an effect on ECF $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ activity. Several genes must be indirectly regulated by the ECF σ factors as they were upregulated in the ECF σ mutants. Interestingly, and also seen in Bacillus subtilis (Luo et al., 2010), a number of these genes are regulated by more than one ECF σ factor, which indicates that they may be needed under different growth conditions. For example, $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 7 }$ regulate the dctPQM and sox genes in an opposite way. The DctPQM proteins form a tripartite adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-independent periplasmic transporter, which catalyzes the uptake of $\mathrm { { \dot { C } } _ { 4 } }$ -dicarboxylates like malate, fumarate, and succinate in many aerobic bacteria (Janausch et al., 2002). The Sox proteins that are not found in other members of the Campylobacteraceae are involved in the oxidation of reduced sulfur compounds in sulfur, photo-, and chemo-lithotrophic bacteria (Ghosh and Dam, 2009). Similarly, we showed that $\sigma ^ { 5 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 7 }$ activate, while $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ caused a downregulation of, the expression of the tctABC genes encoding a tricarboxylic transport system. Despite this, only $\sigma ^ { 7 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ appeared to have a significant effect on citrate utilization. In many bacterial species, a two-component signal transduction system activated by citrate is responsible for the activation of the tctABC genes (Brocker et al., 2009). In A. butzleri, the putative TctABC system may also depend on the two-component system (AB0105–0106) located directly downstream of the putative tctABC genes. The expression of AB0105–0106 was not dramatically affected by $\sigma ^ { 5 } .$ , and this may explain why citrate utilization was distinct between Δσ5/Aσ5 and Δσ7/Aσ7. Altogether, the genes regulated by the different A. butzleri ECF σ factors indicate that the ECF σ factors form a complex network of regulons that have a major role in regulating bacterial metabolism. 



International Commission on Microbiological Specifications for Foods (ICMSF). 2002. Microorganisms in foods 7 – microbiological testing in food safety management. New York: Kluwer/Plenum, p. 175. 



In conclusion, we have shown in this initial study that the ECF σ factors of A. butzleri control the transcription of a complex network of regulons that contain genes that are not commonly regulated by the ECF σ factors family of proteins. These genes are mainly involved in energy metabolism. In contrast to other eubacteria, many conserved genes in A. butzleri appear to be regulated by a σ factor belonging to a different σ factor class.

## C H A P T E R 4.3

# Extracytoplasmic function sigma factors and stress responses in Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis

Thiago L.P. Castro1, Nubia Seyffert1,2, Anne C. Pinto1, Artur Silva2, Vasco Azevedo1, and Luis G.C. Pacheco3 



1Biological Sciences Institute, Department of General Biology, Federal University of Minas Gerais, Pampulha, Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil 





2Institute of Biological Sciences, Federal University of Para, Bel´ em, Guam´ a, Bel´ em, Par´ a, Brazil´ 





3Health Sciences Institute, Federal University of Bahia, Salvador, Bahia, Brazil 



## 4.3.1 Introduction

Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis is a Gram-positive bacterium belonging to the CMNR group, which encompasses genera of great medical and veterinary importance: Corynebacterium, Mycobacterium, Nocardia, and Rhodococcus. C. pseudotuberculosis can cause different diseases in wildlife animals and also in animals of economic interest, like goats, sheep, horses and cows. (Baird and Fontaine, 2007). In small ruminants, it causes a chronic and worldwide disease called caseous lymphadenitis (CLA) (Dorella et al., 2006). 

The main clinical manifestation of CLA is the development of encapsulated abscesses in the superficial lymph nodes. An internal form of the disease may occur, in which abscesses arise in visceral organs such as the lung, liver, kidney and spleen (Baird and Fontaine, 2007; Williamson, 2001). 

Facultative intracellular pathogens like C. pseudotuberculosis are able to resist different stress conditions during the course of infection (Bashyam and Hasnain, 2004; Rohde et al., 2007). When it is captured by phagocytes, C. pseudotuberculosis is capable of surviving inside phagolysosomes, where it replicates continually until cell lysis occurs, allowing bacteria to infect new host cells (McKean et al., 2007; Rohde et al., 2007; Tashjian and Campbell, 1983). 

Among the elements that protect C. pseudotuberculosis against the antimicrobial activity promoted by the host cells are: (I) the corynomycolic acids on the bacterial cell wall and (II) the and agents that effectively detoxify reactive nitrogen and oxygen species (Bogdan et al., 1997). Bacterial persistence inside phagolysosomes is also dependent on the adaptation to low hydrogenionic potential (pH) levels and neutralization of proteolytic enzymes produced by the host. 

Bacteria released from lysed phagocytic cells can reach several organs and colonize the lymph nodes. It has been shown that this dissemination is enhanced by the sphingomyelinase activity conferred by the exotoxin phospholipase D (Dorella et al., 2006). In the lymph nodes, the lesion begins with the formation of epithelioid cells which isolate the bacteria, what culminate in the caseous necrosis that characterizes CLA. The caseous material is surrounded by epithelial cells, lymphocytes, and a layer of fibrous connective tissue. As the lesion progresses, the cellular and fibrotic coat repeatedly suffers necrosis, allowing the granuloma to expand in a way that it resembles the layers of an onion (Dorella et al., 2006). 

From a microbiological perspective, it is likely that C. pseudotuberculosis modulates its gene expression in order to promote important physiological changes that may benefit the course of infection. In this regard, studies based on genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics and immunomics have been performed for C. pseudotuberculosis to elucidate the molecular basis of its establishment inside the host (Pacheco et al., 2011; Santos et al., 2012; Seyffert et al., 2014; Soares et al., 2013). 

## 4.3.2 Sigma factors in pathogenic bacteria

An important step for gene regulation in bacteria is the transcription initiation, which is driven by the RNA polymerase. An active RNA polymerase comprises a core – formed by the subunits α2, β, β′ and ω – and a variable subunit called sigma (σ) factor, which binds transiently to the core and provides this enzyme the ability to recognize specific gene promoters (Helmann, 2002; Paget and Helmann, 2003; Sachdeva et al., 2010; see Chapter 2.4). Thus, each variety of sigma factor acts as a global regulator that ensures the expression of up to hundreds of genes that constitute one a regulon (Mooney et al., 2005). 

Bacteria possess at least one main sigma factor (factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { A } } )$ which activates housekeeping genes and cannot be silenced. Alternative sigma factors are often present though, and they play different roles that contribute to cell homeostasis in a number of adverse situations. In some cases, the genes comprising an alternative regulon present a primary function, such as the ones involved in sporulation in Bacillus subtilis. In other cases, one regulon comprises genes that exert physiologically correlated functions, as the ones that are controlled by factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ in Listeria monocytogenes. These are important for general stress response, in addition to cellular maintenance in the stationary phase of growth (Helmann, 2002; Kazmierczak et al., 2005). 

Among the alternative regulators, the extracytoplasmic function (ECF) sigma factors stand out for their involvement with processes related to the cell membrane and wall, which interact directly with the host in pathogenic bacteria (Kazmierczak et al., 2005; Potvin et al., 2008; see Chapter 2.6; Section 4). For example, the ECF sigma factors regulate several mechanisms that may interfere with the synthesis of exopolysaccharides, the influx and efflux of inorganic compounds (e.g., iron), and the secretion of proteases. Extracellular processes like these compose the repertoire used for infection and evasion of the host’s immune system (Bashyam and Hasnain, 2004; Helmann, 2002; Jordan et al., 2008). 

Bioinformatic analysis based on the genome sequence revealed the presence of eight different sigma factors in C. pseudotuberculosis, among which the factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { A } }$ is presumably essential for cell viability and the factors $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { C } } , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { D } } , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } } , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } } , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { K } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } }$ are alternative factors. Homologues for these sigma factors have been studied in the closely related species Corynebacterium $g$ lutamicum (see Chapter 4.3) and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Table 4.3.1). However, little is known about their functions in C. pseudotuberculosis. 

## 4.3.3 Transcriptome analysis in C. pseudotuberculosis

Studying the transcriptome (set of gene transcripts in an organism) is important for better understanding the roles that different components (e.g., sigma factors) play in the cell, assisting the research on bacterial pathogens. In this context, the recent improvement in DNA-sequencing technologies – often referred to as next-generation DNA sequencing (NGS) – have fostered significant advances in the genomic era, providing in an unprecedented way a large amount of high-quality data. These data are useful not only for genome-oriented studies, but also for global gene activity evaluation. 

By taking advantage of RNAseq capabilities, it was possible to depict the gene expression profiles of C. pseudotuberculosis exposed to conditions in vitro that resemble the harsh environment found inside macrophage cells: elevated acidity, high osmolarity, and temperature increase (Pinto et al., 2014). When compared to bacteria cultured at the standard condition – liquid brain heart infusion broth (BHI) under $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and 140 rpm agitation – the bacteria submitted to stress were promptly able to modulate the activity of several sigma factors in a significant way, according to data generated by the NGS platform SOLiDTM 3 Plus (Table 4.3.2). 

Among the alternative sigma factors predicted in C. pseudotuberculosis, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ is likely to be the only one whose functions are not directly related to extracytoplasmic events. In many bacterial species, this sigma factor is involved in the general stress response, providing the cell with additional elements for homeostasis maintenance in tough situations. In this regard, it would be reasonable to expect the activation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ in $C .$ pseudotuberculosis under different stress conditions. However, this gene regulator was significantly activated only under acidic stress, a condition in which most of the ECF sigma factors also present upregulation (Table 4.3.2; see Section 14). It is interesting to note that in M. tuberculosis, the sigB gene can be activated by ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ , which can also activate sigE and sigM (Manganelli et al., 2002; Song et al., 2008). As sigH shows to be more strongly activated under acidic stress in comparison to heat shock and high osmolarity, and sigE and sigM are also upregulated in this condition, it is possible to suggest that a similar co-regulation profile takes place in C. pseudotuberculosis.

Another sigma factor gene activated under acidic stress is the sigC, whose transcription level was almost twice the value found under the control condition (Table 4.3.2). In spite of the fact that its role is not yet elucidated in C. pseudotuberculosis, the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { C } }$ is known to be important for virulence in M. tuberculosis. It has been shown that the lack of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { C } }$ does not affect the proliferation and persistence of this bacterium in the mouse lung tissue, but the progression of damages and the death of experimentally infected mice are clearly delayed (Sun et al., 2004). Since the protective effect of a live attenuated vaccine may be increased by the use of persistent bacilli, the authors suggest the use of a ΔsigC mutant M. tuberculosis strain for immunization against tuberculosis. 

The expression of the sigD gene in C. pseudotuberculosis was induced only under osmotic stress and heat shock condition (Table 4.3.2; see Sections 13 and 16). A study revealed that the inactivation of sigD in M. tuberculosis strain interferes with the regulation of a set of genes involved in ribosomal protein synthesis during the stationary-growth phase (Calamita et al., 2005). Moreover, the ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { D } }$ -deficient M. tuberculosis is less virulent than the wild type, causing reduced mortality in mice (Calamita et al., 2005; Raman et al., 2004). To date, one single study suggested that the ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { D } }$ may be involved in the C. pseudotuberculosis virulence, based on the fact that the activity of the gene encoding this factor is significantly induced when the bacterium is cultured in foetal bovine serum – which contains various host factors – in comparison to BHI-based cultures (Carvalho et al., 2014). 

Under acidic conditions, the gene encoding the factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ in C. pseudotuberculosis was expressed at a level 2.5-fold higher than the one found in the control (Table 4.3.2). It has been shown that the mutation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ in M. tuberculosis, Vibrio cholera and Haemophilus influenza results in strains with lowered virulence and persistence within the host, during experimental infection (Craig et al., 2002; Kovacikova and Skorupski, 2002; Manganelli et al., 2004). Furthermore, the inactivation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ increases the susceptibility of M. tuberculosis to environmental stresses and impairs the bacterial replication inside macrophages infected in vitro (Manganelli et al., 2001). 

In turn, sigH was significantly induced in C. pseudotuberculosis exposed to the three stress conditions tested (Table 4.3.2). As discussed, ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ is capable of recognizing promoters upstream the genes sigB, sigE, and sigM in M. tuberculosis. The σH is likely to play a central role in stress response in C. pseudotuberculosis as well. Interestingly, a ΔsigH mutant M. tuberculosis strain presented higher susceptibility than the wild type to the action of different oxidative agents and heat shock in vitro, suggesting an important role in detoxification for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ when in adverse environments (Patek and Ne´ ˇsvera, 2011). Still, although the ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ -deficient strain is capable of replicating and persisting within macrophage cells like the wild type, it is likely that this sigma factor plays an important role in M. tuberculosis virulence (Manganelli et al., 2002). The $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ also responds to the heat shock and oxidative stress in the non-pathogenic C. glutamicum. This fact suggests that the functions performed by this regulator are required for full virulence in C. pseudotuberculosis. 

Located in a pathogenicity island in the genome of C. pseudotuberculosis, the gene sigK was significantly activated under the heat shock condition (Table 4.3.2). Similarly to the sigM, the sigK gene was not represented by a great number of transcripts when compared to the genes encoding other sigma factors. This could indicate that the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { K } }$ participates more effectively on a later stage of growth that was not assessed in this work. It is likely that the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { K } }$ regulates genes which are associated with virulence. These are the genes which are contribute to the bacterial survival in hostile environments (Kazmierczak et al., 2005). 

Finally, the sigM gene was significantly activated following exposure of C. pseudotuberculosis to the high osmolarity (see Section 11) and acidic conditions. In M. tuberculosis, it was observed an increase in the expression of sigM during the stationary phase of growth and after exposure to the heat shock (Agarwal et al., 2007). 

## 4.3.4 Study of the sigma factor $\sigma ^ { \ E }$ through directed mutagenesis

Several previous studies have sought to evaluate the roles played by different ECF sigma factors in corynebacteria and mycobacteria, through construction and analysis of mutant strains lacking specific sigma factor–encoding genes (Patek and Ne´ ˇsvera, 2011; Sachdeva et al., 2010). The gene coding for the ECF sigma factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ has been one of the most extensively studied in these bacteria, and it has already been shown to participate in regulation of cell envelope–stress responses (Ando et al., 2003; Manganelli et al., 2001; Pacheco et al., 2012; Park et al., 2008; see Section 18) and to contribute to intracellular growth (Casonato et al., 2014; Fontan´ et al., 2008; Manganelli et al., 2001) and virulence (Ando et al., 2003; Manganelli et al., 2004; Pacheco et al., 2012). Besides, this gene has been found to be part of a small set of genes specifically upregulated in response to nitrosative stress in mycobacteria (Fontan´ et al., 2008; Ohno et al., 2003; Schnappinger et al., 2003; Voskuil et al., 2003, 2011; see Section 17). Recently, a $\Delta s i g E$ mutant strain of M. tuberculosis, lacking the sigma factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ , has been proposed as a live attenuated vaccine against tuberculosis since it induces a higher protection level when compared to vaccination with Mycobacterium bovis BCG (Hernandez et al., 2010). 

A ΔsigE strain of $C .$ pseudotuberculosis has also been constructed through insertion of a kanamycin resistance cassette by homologous recombination at the sigE locus (Pacheco et al., 2012). The mutant strain obtained was more sensitive to cell surface, acidic, and nitrosative stresses. Interestingly, a specific role for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ in resistance to the latter stress condition has not yet been demonstrated for other bacteria (Pacheco et al., 2012). 

The involvement of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ in resistance to cell surface stress conditions, generated by sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) or lysozyme treatment, is an attribute shared by other Actinobacteria (Table 4.3.3; see Section 18). Similarly to what has been shown for C. pseudotuberculosis, a ΔsigE strain of C. glutamicum was more susceptible to cell surface stressors, whereas osmotic and oxidative stress conditions did not affect growth of this bacterium. Additionally, sigE mutation rendered C. glutamicum more sensitive to heat shock, as had been previously reported for M. tuberculosis (Manganelli et al., 2001; Park et al., 2008). Noteworthy is that different ECF sigma factors may perform concerted (or even redundant) roles in the responses to different stressing agents (Mascher et al., 2007; see Chapter 2.6). As an example, transcription from the sigE gene of M. tuberculosis is regulated by another ECF sigma factor, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ , under heat shock conditions (Mehra and Kaushal, 2009; Raman et al., 2001). As shown in C. pseudotuberculosis, sigE expression seems to be upregulated in response to acidic pH, but not in response to heat shock or osmotic stress (Pinto et al., 2014). Corroborating this, growth of the ΔsigE strain of C. pseudotuberculosis was significantly impaired in acidified culture medium, whereas resistance of this strain to salt and thermal stresses was not affected (Pacheco et al., 2012).

aGene ontology (GO) biological process annotation. 


The studies with the C. pseudotuberculosis strain lacking sigma factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ suggested two novel roles for this transcriptional regulator in actinobacterial responses to environmental stresses: it has been demonstrated that this protein (i) is required for resistance to nitric oxide (NO) stress and combined NO–peroxide stress (see Sections 10, 17), and (ii) contributes to regulation of the bacterial exoproteome under stress conditions (Pacheco et al., 2012). 

Previous studies with M. tuberculosis have already reported that the sigE gene is transcriptionally activated under NO stress in vitro and during intracellular growth (Fontan´ et al., 2008; Ohno et $a l . _ { \cdot }$ , 2003; Schnappinger et $a l .$ , 2003; Voskuil et al., 2011). The NO-specific transcriptional response in this bacterium partially overlaps the dormancy regulon and involves the genes encoding the ECF sigma factors $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ and ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ (Ohno et al., 2003; Schnappinger et al., 2003; Voskuil et al., 2003). It became clear in the studies with the ΔsigE strain of C. pseudotuberculosis that this sigma factor is indeed implicated in full resistance to nitrosative stress. Growth of this strain was significantly impaired by treatment with biologically relevant concentrations of NO, generated in vitro by the NO donor DETA/NO (diethylenetriamine NONOate). The sigE requirement for resistance to NO has also been demonstrated in vivo, as the ΔsigE strain shows lowered persistence in wild-type mice following experimental infection, whereas its persistence is much longer in nitric oxide synthase (iNOS)-knockout mice, which fail to produce an efficient intracellular NO response during infection (Pacheco et al., 2012). Inside the host cell, nitrosative stress is exacerbated through a combination of NO with reactive oxygen species, for example in the formation of the considerably more reactive antimicrobial agent peroxynitrite (ONOO−) (Ehrt and Schnappinger, 2009). C. pseudotuberculosis lacking $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ was much more sensitive to the combined action of NO and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ when compared to growth under NO stress only. This fact supports the idea that this protein participates in resistance to combined NO–peroxide stress during intracellular infection (Pacheco et al., 2012). 

The well-documented participation of the sigma factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ in processes related to the cell envelope led to the hypothesis that deletion of the sigE gene could alter regulation of the bacterial exoproteome (i.e., the entire set of proteins found in the extracellular milieu), both under normal physiological conditions and particularly under environmental stresses. This possibility is reinforced by the fact that, in M. tuberculosis, the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ protein upregulates several genes that code for secreted proteins or that are directly involved in protein secretion pathways (Fontan´ et al., 2009; Peterson et al., 2015). In fact, marked differences were observed between the set of proteins exported by the ΔsigE strain of C. pseudotuberculosis in comparison to the exoproteome of the wild-type strain, following treatment with biologically relevant concentrations of NO. Among the set of proteins specifically exported under NO stress, it was possible to detect a functional signature of exoproteins involved mostly in metal ion acquisition and redox homeostasis (Table 4.3.3). Nevertheless, the dependence on the sigma factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ for regulation of exportation of these proteins remains to be demonstrated (Pacheco et al., 2012).

# The complex roles and regulation of stress response ?? factors in Streptomyces coelicolor

Jan Kormanec, Beatrica Sevcikova, Renata Novakova, Dagmar Homerova, Bronislava Rezuchova, and Erik Mingyar 

Institute of Molecular Biology, Slovak Academy of Sciences, Bratislava, Slovak Republic 

## 4.4.1 Introduction

Sigma (σ) factors are essential regulatory subunits of RNA polymerase conferring promoter specificity to RNA polymerase catalytic core enzyme. They enable recognition of specific promoters, thus directing expression of a specific set of genes (so-called regulon of the corresponding σ factor; see Chapters 2.4, 2.15 and Section 4). E. coli and B. subtilis contain seven and 18 different σ factors, respectively. This variety of σ factors ensures control of basal gene expression, as well as global regulation of gene expression in response to various environmental or developmental signals. Two unrelated families of σ factors, $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ and $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ , have been identified. The dominant $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ family comprises several groups: essential primary σ factors directing expression of most housekeeping genes; non-essential homologues of primary σ factors, some of which have roles in the stationary phase; a collection of alternative σ factors; and distantly related extracytoplasmic function (ECF) σ factors (Gruber and Gross, 2003; see Chapter 2.6). However, homologues of the other type of σ factor, $\sigma ^ { 5 4 }$ , are not found in streptomycetes, so they are not considered in this chapter. 

Alternative σ factors, with which this chapter is mainly concerned, include several further subgroups: flagellar σ factors such as E. coli $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F l i A } }$ , heat shock σ factors such as E. coli $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ , general stress response σ factors represented by B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } { } _ { ; }$ , and sporulation σ factors such as B. subtilis ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { { F } } } , { \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { { G } } } , { \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { { E } } } ;$ , and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { K } }$ . Alternative σ factors are regulated at the transcriptional, translational, and posttranslational levels. One common mechanism of their regulation is a reversible interaction with their specific negative regulators, anti-σ factors, which sequester them from their interaction with core RNA polymerase (Gruber and Gross, 2003; Helmann, 1999; see Chapter 2.6). 

In their natural habitats, bacteria are exposed to various stresses. These stresses elicit production of a common group of proteins, so-called general stress response proteins, having non-specific, essential, protective functions under stress, and also stress-specific proteins, each having a specific protective function against a single stimulus. The response to these stress conditions is mediated in many bacteria in part by alternative σ factors, which govern expression of genes encoding the stress response proteins (Price, 2002). The general stress response has been most studied in two model organisms, Gram-negative Escherichia coli, which is developmentally simple, and Grampositive Bacillus subtilis, which is developmentally complex, being able to undergo endospore formation as the most extreme response to nutritional stress. Similar stress response genes are activated in both organisms, but in $E .$ coli the general stress response is governed by σ factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { S } } ,$ , which is related to primary σ factors, while in B. subtilis and other related Gram-positive bacteria, it is mainly governed by alternative σ factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } { } _ { ; }$ , which is an example of a group of σ factors found only in Gram-positive bacteria. The activity of B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ is controlled by an anti-σ factor RsbW, an anti-anti-σ factor RsbV, and two PP2C phosphatases, RsbP and RsbU (Hecker et al., 2007, Hengge-Aronis, 2002; Price, 2002). Further members of the sporulation σ factors $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } } , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { G } } , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ , and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { K } } )$ are involved in sporulation (see below), but there is little interplay between the stress response and sporulation σ factor systems. 

In striking contrast to B. subtilis and E. coli, there are independent responses to different stress stimuli in Streptomyces. In addition, responses to several stimuli are associated with different stages in the organism’s multicellular developmental programme (Vohradsky et al., 2000). This chapter is mainly concerned with this interplay. 

## 4.4.2 Regulation of the Bacillus subtilis general stress response ?? factor $\sigma ^ { \ B }$ by partner switching

The general stress response σ factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ of B. subtilis is the best characterized example of this group of σ factors in Grampositive bacteria. The sigB gene encoding $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ is located in an operon together with other genes (rsb) encoding regulators of its activity. In unstressed cells, basal-level expression of the operon is directed by the $\mathrm { P _ { A } }$ promoter, which is recognized by the primary σ factor. On exposure to stress conditions, the operon is auto-catalytically activated by means of the $\mathrm { P _ { B } }$ promoter, which is recognized by RNA polymerase containing $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ (Figure 4.4.1a). Activity of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ is controlled mainly on the posttranslational level by a partner-switching mechanism involving the RsbW anti-σ and the RsbV anti-anti-σ, along with interplay of various protein kinases and phosphatases (Figure 4.4.1b). This regulation integrates signals from two different stresses: energy stress (such as carbon, phosphorus, and oxygen starvation), and environmental stress (such as acid, ethanol, heat, or salt stresses). In unstressed cells, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ is sequestered by the anti-σ factor RsbW, which contains a serine protein kinase HATPase c domain specific for its antagonist anti-anti-σ factor RsbV. The phosphorylated RsbV-P cannot interact with RsbW anti-σ factor. After stress activation, one of two PP2C phosphatases (RsbU in the case of environmental stress, and RsbP during energy stress) is activated and dephosphorylates anti-anti-σ factor RsbV-P. The dephosphorylated RsbV then can interact with RsbW, thus leaving $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ free to interact with core RNA polymerase. The resulting RNA polymerase holoenzyme form directs expression of about 200 general stress response genes.

(b) Scheme of the regulation of B. subtilis σB by a phosphorylation partner-switching mechanism under stress conditions (Eymann et al., 2011; Hecker et al., 2007; Marles-Wright et al., 2008; Price, 2002). The lines ending with an arrow or a perpendicular line indicate positive or negative regulation, respectively. See text for further details.


How are the two phosphatases for RsbV-P activated? In the energy stress signal transduction pathways, phosphatase RsbP requires the activator RsbQ. The induction of the RsbP–RsbQ phosphatase activity coincides with a drop of cellular adenosine triphosphate (ATP) level, although the molecular mechanism is unknown. Signalling through the environmental pathway involves a large 1.8 MDa complex, called the stressosome, that contains multiple copies of the paralogous co-antagonists RsbRA, RsbRB, RsbRC, RsbRD, and the RsbS antagonist, which together bind the RsbT kinase. Activation of the stressosome by different stresses, which is mediated by the different phosphorylation patterns of the RsbR paralogues, leads to RsbT kinase activation and the phosphorylation of RsbS. This results in the release of the RsbT activator from the complex. It can then activate the RsbU phosphatase. Feedback control to ensure reversibility of the process after overcoming the effects of stress conditions is mediated by the RsbX phosphatase, which dephosphorylates RsbS-P (Eymann et al., 2011; Hecker et al., 2007; Marles-Wright et al., 2008; Price, 2002). 

In B. subtilis, another pathway responding to growth-limiting conditions leads irreversibly to sporulation. This developmental process is governed by crisscross regulation of several different σ factors in alternate compartments (the mother cell and the forespore compartments). Synthesis and activation of each σ factor at the proper time and location are morphologically coupled by a complex regulatory network. The key regulatory protein initiating this process, σ factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } } { } _ { ; }$ , is initially inactive after expression. Its activation involves a similar partner-switching mechanism as for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } { } _ { ; }$ , via anti-σ factor SpoIIAB and its antagonist anti-anti-σ factor SpoIIAA. Initially, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ is held inactive by SpoIIAB, and SpoIIAA is inactive because of its specific phosphorylation by SpoIIAB. However, completion of the septum delineating the forespore compartment activates a sporulation septum-located phosphatase SpoIIE, which dephosphorylates SpoIIAA in the forespore compartment. SpoIIAA then binds SpoIIAB, leaving $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ free to interact with RNA polymerase. Thus, in B. subtilis, these two different response systems (general stress response and sporulation) provide the cell with considerable flexibility, and depending upon inputs it can decide to continue into reversible stress response (governed mainly by $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } )$ or irreversible sporulation (governed by $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ and also by other sporulation-specific σ factors and regulatory proteins) (Price, 2002). 

## 4.4.3 Streptomyces coelicolor: a complex organism with exceptionally numerous ?? factors

S. coelicolor is the model species of a genus of Gram-positive soil-dwelling filamentous bacteria with a life cycle somewhat resembling that of eukaryotic fungi. On solid media, spores germinate to produce hyphae that grow by tip extension. Hyphae branch to form a vegetative substrate mycelium. Sporadic vegetative septa separate compartments with many chromosomes. In response to a variety of signals, special reproductive aerial hyphae emerge from the mycelium, similarly growing by tip extension. After their growth ceases, they undergo septation into unigenomic prespore compartments which finally mature into chains of ovoid spores that permit survival and dispersal. Genetic analysis of differentiation has defined two classes of developmental mutants; bld mutants that are unable to form aerial mycelia, and whi mutants that form aerial mycelium but are unable to complete the life cycle (Flardh and Buttner,¨ 2009). This morphological differentiation coincides with socalled physiological differentiation – the production of various special metabolites, including the majority of known antibiotics and other bioactive products (Figure 4.4.2). 

All streptomycetes contain a very large linear chromosome, and the 8.7 Mb genome of S. coelicolor (GenBank Acc. No. AL645882, containing 7846 annotated ORFs, SCO0001– SCO7846) contains as many as 65 genes for σ factors (Bentley et al., 2002). They include four homologues of principal σ factors $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { H r d A , B , C , D } } )$ , a homologue of flagellar σ factors (σWhiG), nine close homologues of B. subtilis general stress response σ factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } ,$ , and 51 ECF σ factors (Figure 4.4.3; see Chapter 2.6). 

Of the four homologues of principal σ factors, σHrdB (SCO5820) the functional principal σ factor is essential for recognition of housekeeping genes. The function of an additional three homologues, σHrdA(SCO2465), σHrdC(SCO0895), and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H r d D } } ( \mathrm { S C O } 3 2 0 2 )$ , is currently unknown, since deletion of their genes (hrdA, hrdC, and hrdD) had no phenotypic effect upon growth and differentiation, even in a triple deletion mutant (Buttner et al., 1990; Buttner and Lewis, 1992). Some suggestion about their function in different developmental stages may arise from expression studies of their orthologues in S. aureofaciens CCM 3239, where the principal σ factor gene hrdB was transcribed in all developmental stages, hrdD was active only in the vegetative substrate mycelium, and hrdA only during morphological differentiation (Kormanec and Farkasovsky, 1993). Recently, transcriptomic studies in S. coelicolor revealed

the highest expression of hrdD during spore germination, thus indicating a possible role in this process (Strakova et al., 2013). 

A homologue of flagellar σ factors, σWhiG (SCO5621), is essential for aerial mycelium septation, as a whiG mutant of S. coelicolor produced only long aerial hyphae without any sign of septation to the prespore compartments (Chater et al., 1989). Unlike its homologues in other bacteria, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W h i G } }$ has no role in motility and chemotaxis, processes that are absent from streptomycetes. 

To date, only a few of the many ECF σ factors have been characterized in S. coelicolor. ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ (SCO3356) has a role in cell wall homeostasis (Paget et al., 1999). Its functional homologues responding to cell envelope stresses in various bacteria (see Section 18) are regulated by their cognate membranebound anti-σ factors through their controlled proteolysis after stress signals (Rowley et al., 2006). In contrast, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ in S. coelicolor is not regulated by an anti-σ factor, but its gene, $s i g E ,$ is regulated by the CseB–CseC two-component signal transduction system (see Section 3) induced by cell wall-damaging compounds (Hong et al., 2002). Likewise, the expression of the $s i g Q$ gene for the ECF σ factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { Q } }$ (SCO4908) is controlled by a two-component signal transduction system, AfsQ1– AfsQ2. This σ factor, together with AfsQ1–AfsQ2, is conditionally required for both secondary metabolism and differentiation (Shu et al., 2009). One of the best studied ECF σ factors in S. coelicolor, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { R } }$ (SCO5216), has a role in thiol-oxidative stress response. Its activity is regulated by its cognate anti-σ factor RsrA, which senses the reduced state of the cell and is inactivated after oxidative stress, thus releasing ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { R } }$ . In addition to the control of its regulon, ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { R } }$ appears to inhibit development under oxidative stress (Paget et al., 1998, 2001). Interestingly, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { R } }$ directs expression of the housekeeping principal σ factor ${ \mathfrak { C } } ^ { { \mathrm { H r d B } } }$ through a second promoter, hrdBp2, induced after thiol-oxidative stress (Kim et al., 2012). Two further ECF σ factor, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B l d N } }$ (SCO3323) and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ (SCO2954), have a different role in morphological differentiation. σBldN is required for aerial mycelium formation, and is developmentally regulated. In addition, σBldN is translated as a pro-protein which undergoes proteolytic maturation during differentiation (Bibb and Buttner, 2003; Bibb et al., 2000). Although $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { U } }$ is not normally required for development, its uncontrolled activity by disruption of the gene encoding its cognate anti-σ factor blocks aerial mycelium formation (Gehring et al., 2001). Another ECF σ factor, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { L i t S } }$ (SCO0194), is required for lightinduced production of carotenoids (Takano et al., 2005). Finally, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ (SCO3892) negatively regulates morphological differentiation and secondary metabolism, at least in part by inhibiting the transcription of an operon for ClpP protease, which is itself the main agent of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ degradation. ClpP-mediated degradation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ is prevented by binding of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ to its cognate anti-σ factor RstA. However, during differentiation RstA is degraded, leaving $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { T } }$ vulnerable to degradation (Mao et al., 2013). 

The last group of S. coelicolor σ factors comprises nine close homologues of B. subtilis general stress response σ factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ . Interestingly, sequence comparison with B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ revealed that they all are highly conserved in two regions, 2.4.and 4.2, that are important for promoter recognition in the -10 and -35 promoter regions, indicating that they all recognize very similar promoter sequences (Figure 4.4.4). 

Characterization of these nine σB homologues $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } } , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { G } } , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ , $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { I } } , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { K } } , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { L } } , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } }$ , and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { N } } )$ revealed their roles mainly in the control of morphological differentiation or the osmotic stress response (see Section 11). Interestingly, two of them, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ and ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ , regulate both processes (Cho et al., 2001; Kelemen et al., 2001; Kormanec et al., 2000; Sevcikova et al., 2001; Viollier et al., 2003a), indicating a connection between stress responses and differentiation. Moreover, the regulation of these $\mathbf { \bar { \sigma } } ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues in $S .$ coelicolor seems to be more complex than that of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ in B. subtilis, since this strain contains genes for as many as 45 homologues of the B. subtilis anti-σ factor RsbW, 17 homologues of the anti-anti-σ factor RsbV, and 44 homologues of RsbU–RsbP phosphatases (Mittenhuber, 2002). The remainder of this chapter summarizes the current knowledge about the role and regulation of these nine $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues in S. coelicolor. 

## 4.4.4 Role of $\sigma ^ { \mathsf { F } }$ and ${ \mathfrak { \sigma } } ^ { \mathbb { N } }$ in morphological differentiation in two different compartments of S. coelicolor

The first characterized B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologue in S. coelicolor was $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ (SCO4035) (note that several of the S. coelicolor σ factors share names with σ factors of B. subtilis, but none of these synonymous σ factors are orthologous – we have tried to make clear which organism’s σ factors are being discussed from the context). Phenotypic characterization of a sigF mutant of S. coelicolor revealed the role of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ in the control of the late stages of morphological differentiation, in spore maturation and pigmentation. The mutant produced smaller spores with thinner walls that were sensitive to detergent and defective in grey-brown spore colour (Potuckova et al., 1995). A similar phenotype was found for a $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ mutant of S. aureofaciens CCM 3239 (Rezuchova et al., 1997). In contrast to the operon organization of B. subtilis sigB (Figure 4.4.1a), S. coelicolor sigF is monocistronic, and no homologues of anti-σ factor and anti-anti-σ factor genes are located in its vicinity (Figure 4.4.5). The expression of sigF is directed by a single developmentallyregulated promoter, sigFp. Its transcription is induced during sporulation and spatially restricted to the prespore compartment. The activity of sigFp is dependent upon six early whi genes (whiA, B, G, H, I, and J) required for sporulation septum formation. They all encode regulatory proteins, including sporulation-specific σ factor σWhiG. However, this dependence is likely indirect, as no similarity to the σWhiG consensus sequence has been found in the sigFp promoter (Kelemen et al., 1996; Sun et al., 1999). Currently, we have no further clues about the details of regulation of this spatially and temporally-regulated $s i g F p$ promoter. 

The first characterized target of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ was the whiEVIII gene (SCO5321) in the whiE biosynthetic cluster for the grey spore pigment, explaining the defect of sigF mutants in spore pigmentation (Kelemen et al., 1998). Another target of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ is a developmentally-regulated promoter directing expression of sspA (SCO7434) encoding a sporulation-specific secreted lipoprotein that plays a role in sporulation septum formation and spore maturation. The activity of sspAp was detected only in spore chains, and SspA was localized in the spore wall. The sspAp promoter is also a direct target of BldD, a cyclic di-GMP-sensing DNA-binding protein essential for morphological differentiation and antibiotic production that represses transcription of many developmental genes in vegetative substrate mycelium (Figure 4.4.5) (den Hengst et al., 2010; Tzanis et al., 2014). 

Although sigF is not located in an operon with anti-σ factor and anti-anti-σ factor genes, one of the 45 homologues of the B. subtilis RsbW anti-σ factor, RsfA (SCO4677), has been found to specifically interact with $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ . RsfA seems to negatively regulate antibiotic production and morphological differentiation, both of which are enhanced in an rsfA mutant. These results indicate that RsfA may be an antagonist regulator of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ . In addition, two of the 17 homologues of the B. subtilis RsbV anti-anti-σ factor, SCO0781 and SCO0869, interact with RsfA in a yeast twohybrid system. Thus, a complex regulatory system regulates $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ activity (Kim et al., 2008). Interestingly, rsfA is also under negative control by the master negative regulator BldD (den Hengst et al., 2010).

Immediately downstream of sigF there is another gene, sigN (SCO4034), encoding a $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologue (Figure 4.4.5). Mutational analysis of sigN revealed its conditional role in development. Its transcription is driven by two developmentallyregulated promoters, sigNp1 and sigNp2, which are upregulated during aerial mycelium formation. The activity of the sigNp1 promoter is specifically confined to aerial hyphae, and is dependent upon sigN, thus indicating autoregulation of sigN expression. In spite of their close proximity, mutual transcriptional analysis indicated that there is no interdependence between sigN and $s i g F$ expression. 

Another direct target of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { N } }$ is the developmentally regulated nepA gene (SCO4002), encoding a small extracellular protein NepA, and a nepA mutant has a developmental phenotype similar to that of a sigN mutant. Transcription of the σN-dependent nepAp promoter is spatially confined to a new developmental compartment, the so-called subapical stem, which defines an interface between the aerial and substrate hyphae. These results indicated the role of $\cdot _ { \sigma ^ { \mathrm { N } } }$ in this new compartment (Dalton et al., 2007). Therefore, in contrast to the role of B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ in general stress response, these two $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues have different functions in regulating morphological differentiation at two distinct developmental stages (Figure 4.4.5). 

## 4.4.5 Role of the S. coelicolor ${ \mathfrak {sigma } } ^ { \Bag }$ in osmotic and oxidative stress response as well as differentiation

SCO0600 encodes another homologue of B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } { } _ { ; }$ , confusingly also called $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ . It has a dual function in osmotic stress response (see Section 11) and morphological differentiation. A sigB mutant is sensitive to hyperosmolarity and impaired in aerial mycelium formation, conferring a Bld phenotype (Cho et al., 2001). In contrast to previous cases, the sigB gene is part of an operon preceded by the rsbA (SCO0599) and rsbB (SCO0598) genes, encoding homologues of an anti-σ factor RsbW and anti-anti-σ factor RsbV of B. subtilis, respectively. The operon is transcribed from two separate promoters (Figure 4.4.6), an osmotic stress-inducible sigBp1 and a constitutive sigBp2. The sigBp1 promoter is a direct target for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ , thus indicating its autoregulation. Interestingly, in contrast to B. subtilis RsbW (160 amino acids), RsbA is much longer (307 amino acids). Its C-terminal domain (amino acids 121– 309) is similar to RsbW and contains all critical residues of the serine protein kinase HATPase c domain. However, its N-terminal domain (amino acids 1–120) shows no similarity to any protein in the database. Both full-length RsbA and its C-terminal domain (RsbA-CTD) bind $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ and prevent its activity to direct transcription of the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ -dependent $s i g B p I$ promoter. Moreover, the phenotype of an rsbA mutant (precocious aerial mycelium formation and elevated transcription of the sigBp1 promoter) was opposite to the phenotype of the sigB mutant, consistent with the role of RsbA as a $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } .$ - specific anti-σ factor. In spite of similarity to anti-anti-σ factors, RsbB lacks a conserved phosphorylatable serine residue, is not phosphorylated by RsbA or RsbA-CTD, and does not antagonize RsbA activity. However, one of the 17 homologues of the B. subtilis RsbV anti-anti-σ factor, RsbV (SCO7325), antagonizes the inhibitory function of RsbA on $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ -dependent transcription and is phosphorylated by RsbA-CTD in vitro. Interestingly, the N-terminal domain of RsbA prevents this phosphorylation. It is suggested that this blockage is released in vivo through interaction with some other factor(s). The rsbV gene is part of a putative rsb $, V - r s b R - r s b S - r s b T - r s b U I - r s b U$ operon which is directed by the osmotic stress-inducible $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } .$ - dependent rsb $V p$ promoter. These results suggest the regulation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ with the anti-σ factor RsbA and the anti-anti-σ factor RsbV by a partner-switching mechanism similar to that of B. subtilis. The induction in S. coelicolor of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ -dependent genes by osmotic stress results from modulation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ activity by both RsbA and RsbV regulators (Cho et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2004) 

The activity of S. coelicolor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ is further modulated by another regulator, OsaC (SCO5747), a large protein containing an N-terminal RsbW-like kinase HATPase c domain, sensory Pas and Gaf domains, and a C-terminal RsbU-like phosphatase domain. OsaC is essential for osmoadaptation at high osmolarity, and the osaC mutant is unable to form aerial mycelium in high osmotic media. It is required to return expression of $s i g B$ and consequently the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ regulon to its basal level after overcoming osmotic stress. This activity involves its N-terminal anti-σ factor kinase HATPase c domain which interacts with $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ after subsidence of osmotic stress (Fernandez-Martinez et al., 2009). 

Transcriptomic analysis of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ -dependent genes in S. coelicolor revealed that $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ is a master regulator governing osmotic and oxidative stress response (see Section 10) as well as morphological differentiation via a network of other σ factors. More than 280 osmotic stress-induced genes were found to be prominently regulated by $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } .$ . Among them, there are those participating in osmoregulation, biosynthesis, and transport systems for osmoprotectants (e.g., glycine, betaine, proline, and glutamate). In addition, many genes for anti-oxidative functions (like catalases, thioredoxin, DpsA, cysteine, and mycothiol biosynthesis) were also found under the control of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } .$ . In addition, three other σ factor genes (hrdD, sigL, and sigM) were osmotic stress-induced in a $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ -dependent manner. Two of them encode other $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues, ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { L } }$ (SCO7278) and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } }$ (SCO7314). Their mutual transcriptional and proteomic analysis revealed their dependence in a hierarchical order $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } \xrightarrow { \cdot } \sigma ^ { \mathrm { L } } \xrightarrow { } \sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } }$ . Moreover, phenotypes of their mutants suggested their sequential action in morphological differentiation. $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ has a role in aerial mycelium formation as described above, ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { L } }$ is involved sporulation of aerial hyphae, and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } }$ in efficient sporulation (Lee et al., 2005). Interestingly, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } }$ has been found to specifically interact with an anti-σ factor homologue RsmA (SCO7313), the gene of which is located immediately upstream of sigM. The interaction between $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } }$ and RsmM depends on the presence of an iron–sulphur [2Fe-2S] cluster in RsmA. The loss of this cluster in RsmA, in response to an as yet unknown signal, leads to the activation of ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { { \bar { \mathrm { M } } } }$ by releasing this inhibitory interaction with RsmA. This unusual mechanism is different to the phosphorylating partner-switching mechanism of activation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { { B } } }$ in B. subtilis and S. coelicolor (Gaskell et al., 2007). The scheme describing the regulation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ , taking into account all these results, is described in Figure 4.4.6 

## 4.4.6 Connection between stress response and differentiation mediated by $\sigma ^ { \mathsf { H } }$

Another B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologue, ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ (SCO5243), has been suggested to have a dual role in S. coelicolor, in regulation of the osmotic stress response (see Section 11) and morphological differentiation. Its gene, sigH, is a part of an operon

Bent arrows indicate the positions and direction of promoters. Red-coloured lines ending with an arrow indicate activation, whereas blue-coloured ones ending with a perpendicular line indicate repression. ushY (SCO5245), ushX (SCO5244), sigH (Figure 4.4.7). The ushX gene encodes a protein similar to anti-σ factor RsbW, although lacking important residues of the serine protein kinase HATPase c domain. However, the protein product encoded by the more upstream ushY gene exhibits no sequence similarity to any of the B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ regulatory Rsb proteins. The expression of the operon is directed by four promoters expressed differentially during development and in response to several stress conditions. The constitutive sigHp1 promoter insures a basal level of the whole operon in all developmental stages and also irrespective of any stress conditions. The other, sigHp2, is induced preferentially upon osmotic stress. The sigHp3 promoter is induced by heat shock, and is also developmentally regulated, being induced in the later stages of development. Its activity is confined to the prespore compartment. This developmental regulation may be because it is directly negatively regulated by the developmental transcription factor BldD. Conversely, the sigHp4 promoter is active mainly in the vegetative substrate mycelium (Kormanec et al., 2000; Kelemen et al., 2001). The sigH operon is autoregulated in that the osmotic stress-induced sigHp2 promoter is directly dependent upon $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ (Sevcikova et al., 2001). Moreover, UshX has been shown to be a specific anti-σ factor for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ , inhibiting sigHp2 transcription (Sevcikova and Kormanec, 2002). In addition to the complex transcriptional regulation,
