$\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ undergoes intriguing posttranslational regulation. The sigH gene is translated to three translational products, $\sigma ^ { { \mathrm { H } } 5 2 } , \sigma ^ { { \mathrm { H } } 5 1 }$ , σH51, and ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } 3 7 }$ , which can all initiate transcription after association with RNA polymerase core enzyme. The large forms, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } 5 2 / 5 1 }$ , are present mainly in the exponential phases of growth in liquid media or in early stages of development on solid media. Their level dramatically decreases in the stationary phase or in the later stages of development, and the shorter form, σH37, increases. In addition, these large forms are posttranslationally processed to truncated $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } 3 8 }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } 3 4 }$ forms during the stationary phase or in the later stages of development. Hence, elimination of the large $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } 5 1 / 5 2 }$ and accumulation of the short $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } 3 4 / 3 7 / 3 8 }$ forms are developmentally regulated and indicate a role of the truncated forms in the morphological differentiation (Viollier et al., 2003b). 

The activity of ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ is also regulated by an anti-anti-σ factor homologue BldG (SCO3549). UshX has been found to interact with BldG, and abolition of the osmotic induction of the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ -dependent sigHp2 promoter in the bldG mutant indicates a role of BldG in activation of ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ by a partner-switching mechanism similar to that of B. subtilis. The mechanism of ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ activation in S. coelicolor is as follows (Figure 4.4.7). Under unstressed conditions, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ is sequestered by UshX. After a signal related to an osmotic stress, BldG is activated by dephosphorylation by an unknown RsbU–RsbP-like PP2C phosphatase. This dephosphorylated BldG interacts with UshX to relieve ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ , which in turn can associate with core RNA polymerase to transcribe the genes of its regulon, including the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ -dependent sigHp2 promoter that autoregulates the sigH operon (Sevcikova et al., 2010). This type of regulation seems to be conserved in streptomycetes, as a similar mechanism of ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ activation by BldG has also been reported in Streptomyces griseus (Takano et al., 2011). Interestingly, dephosphorylated BldG also interacts with the anti-σ factor ApgA (SCO3548), probably activating some other homologue of B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ , making this regulation even more complex (Parashar et al., 2009; Sevcikova et al., 2010). 

In B. subtilis, the anti-σ factor RsbW acts also as a specific protein kinase through its serine protein kinase HATPase c domain to phosphorylate the anti-anti-σ factor RsbV. Such phosphorylated RsbV-P then cannot interact with RsbW anti-σ factor to activate $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ (Hecker et al., 2007; Price, 2002). BldG is also phosphorylated in vivo, and the level of its phosphorylated form is highest during late vegetative growth and aerial mycelium formation, and subsequently decreases during sporulation of aerial hyphae. Moreover, this phosphorylation is critical for the development of S. coelicolor A3(2) (Bignell et al., 2003). Neither ApgA nor UshX contains the catalytic residues of the HATPase c kinase domain, so they are unable to phosphorylate BldG. Instead, the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ -specific anti-σ factor RsfA has been shown to interact with BldG and specifically phosphorylate its conserved phosphorylatable serine residue. Therefore, in addition to its role as negative regulator of sporulation-specific σ factor σF, it also negatively regulates the activity of $\mathbf { \partial } _ { \mathbf { O } } \mathrm { H }$ through phosphorylation of BldG (Mingyar et al., 2014). Consistent with the time of activation of both these σ factors, BldG is dephosphorylated during sporulation of aerial hyphae (Bignell et al., 2003). These activities of BldG presumably account for the developmental deficiency of bldG mutants (Bignell et al., 2000). 

The implied role of ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ in stress response and also in differentiation has been confirmed by the phenotypic analysis of a sigH mutant. The mutation affected at least two different processes: the growth at high osmotic conditions and septation of aerial hyphae into spores, thus conferring a Whi phenotype (Sevcikova et al., 2001). The sigH deletion mutant was later reported to have no obvious phenotype, although a different genetic background was used. However, double deletion of both ushX (prsH) and sigH affected aerial mycelium formation (Viollier et al., 2003a). 

This dual role of ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ in osmotic stress response and morphological differentiation is underlined by functional characterization of genes that belong to its regulon. Expression of the gltB, gltD operon (SCO2026, SCO2025), encoding subunits of glutamate synthase, is directed by three promoters, of which one, gltBp2, is directly dependent upon ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { H } } .$ . Glutamate synthase corresponds to a branch of the ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ regulon involved in osmotic stress response, as glutamate has an osmoprotective function (Kormanec and Sevcikova, 2002a). The morphological differentiation branch of the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ regulon is represented by three sporulation-specific genes. One, ssgB (SCO1541), is directed by a single developmentally-regulated ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ -dependent ssgBp promoter. It encodes a key regulator of aerial mycelium septation which is involved in the direct recruitment of FtsZ rings to the positions of sporulation septa in aerial hyphae (Kormanec and Sevcikova, 2002b; Sevcikova and Kormanec, 2003; Willemse et al., 2011). A second member of the regulon, sigJ (SCO1276), encodes an ECF σ factor. Expression of sigJ is directed by a single developmentally-regulated $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ -dependent sigJp promoter that is active in the late stages of differentiation. Although a S. coelicolor A3(2) sigJ mutant has no obvious phenotype, the expression of sigJ indicates its role in the later stages of development. This dependence represents a new cascade of σ factors in regulation of differentiation in streptomycetes (Mazurakova et al., 2006). The last characterized member of the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ regulon is represented by the dpsA gene (SCO0596), encoding a nucleoid-associated protein DpsA. DpsA plays a dual role in S. coelicolor A3(2), in stress response and contributing to nucleoid condensation during sporulation. Its single dpsAp promoter is osmotic stress- and heat shock-induced. The osmotic stress induction is dependent upon both $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ and ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ , while the heat shock induction depends only upon ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ . The expression of dpsA is also developmentally controlled, being upregulated during sporulation and confined to the aerial hyphae. This upregulation is dependent upon $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ , and not upon $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } .$ . In addition, its expression during development is directly dependent upon sporulation-specific transcription factor WhiB (Facey et al., 2011). The activation of the genes of the ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ regulon is consistent with the model (Figure 4.4.7), where $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ activation occurs after osmotic stress and during the late stages of differentiation, when it accumulates and also undergoes posttranslational processing. 

## 4.4.7 Regulation of S. coelicolor ??I by a partner-switching mechanism

Although the sigB-homologous genes in S. coelicolor are only occasionally adjacent to their cognate anti-σ factors and anti-anti-σ factors, in the case of another $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologue, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { I } }$ (SCO3068), two genes, prsI (SCO3066) and arsI (SCO3067), encoding homologues of anti-σ and anti-anti-σ factors, respectively, are located divergently next to the sigI gene (Figure 4.4.8). ArsI contains a sulphate transporter/anti-σ factor antagonist domain (STAS) of anti-anti σ factors including a conserved phosphorylatable serine residue, and PrsI contains a RsbW-like HATPase c protein kinase domain that suggests its role in phosphorylation of its cognate pair protein. Transcription of sigI is governed by a single osmotic stress-induced sigIp promoter. It is not dependent upon $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { I } } .$ Therefore, in contrast to sigH and sigB, sigI expression is not autoregulated. Expression of arsI is directed by a single constitutive promoter arsIp, and prsI is transcribed from two tandem promoters, a constitutive prsIp2 and an osmotic stress-induced prsIp1. Likewise, none of these promoters was dependent upon $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { I } }$ (Figure 4.4.8). The presence of the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } .$ -like consensus sequence upstream of both osmotic stressinduced sigIp and $p r s I p I$ promoters suggests that they may be recognized by some other $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologue. However, their expression is not significantly dependent upon two other osmotic stress response σ factors, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ and ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ . They may be recognized by other $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues, as all these σ factors are highly similar in the regions 2.4 and 4.2 that are responsible for interaction with cognate promoters (Figure 4.5.4). Therefore, there may be partial overlap in the recognition of these promoters by these similar σ factors. This complex transcription of the sigI, prsI, and arsI genes suggests an involvement of $\cdot _ { \sigma ^ { \mathrm { I } } }$ in the osmotic stress. However, deletion of sigI did not affect growth, even at high osmolarity. As several $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { { \bar { B } } } }$ homologues are osmotic stress-induced, it is likely that the absence of sigI may be compensated by some other homologue. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/d1617a2a-6f92-4fd7-9abc-16b20df4c261/8c2b79f64f8ee301c54517e9e0c60c20d2bbd27055064b0e404ff2bdf471d6f4.jpg)



Figure 4.4.8 Model of regulation of S. coelicolor σ factor σI . The genes are indicated by thick arrows of the same colour as encoded proteins (ovals). Bent arrows indicate the positions and direction of promoters. Red-coloured lines ending with an arrow indicate activation, whereas blue-coloured ones ending with a perpendicular line indicate repression. See text for further details.


PrsI has been found to specifically interact with ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { I } } ,$ thus indicating that it is a $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { I } } \cdot$ -specific anti-σ factor. Likewise, PrsI specifically interacts with and phosphorylates the anti-anti-σ factor homologue ArsI. However, the PrsI–ArsI complex has been formed only with a dephosphorylated form of ArsI. Thus, PrsI serves as a specific kinase for ArsI and negatively regulates its activity. These data indicate that $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { I } }$ activation occurs by a partner-switching mechanism similar to B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ (Figure 4.4.8) (Homerova et al., 2012). 

## 4.4.8 Role of $\sigma ^ { \kappa }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathsf { G } }$

The last two $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues characterized in S. coelicolor are $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { K } }$ (SCO6520) and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { G } }$ (SCO7341). No homologues of anti-σ factor and anti-anti-σ factor genes are located in the vicinity of their genes. Phenotypic analysis of a $s i g K$ deletion mutant indicated a negative role of ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { K } }$ in morphological differentiation and secondary metabolism (Figure 4.4.2), since the deletion of $s i g K$ results in precocious aerial mycelium formation and sporulation, as well as increased production of antibiotics (actinorhodin and undecylprodigiosin). Transcription of sigK from its single $s i g K p$ promoter gradually increased in substrate mycelium before development into the aerial mycelium, when it is partially dependent upon $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { K } } ,$ , then remains constant during later developmental stages. This transcription pattern seems to be in contrast with its role as a negative regulator of differentiation. However, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { K } }$ is regulated at the posttranslational level. It is relatively abundant in the early vegetative substrate mycelium phase, then it decreases rapidly in the late stages of substrate mycelium and during the formation of aerial mycelium, and it is absent in the late stages of development during sporulation of aerial mycelium. This pattern of posttranslational $\bar { \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { K } }$ regulation is consistent with its inhibitory role on differentiation, which is relieved by its degradation during the later stages of development (Mao et al., 2009). 

No specific role could be assigned for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { G } }$ . Disruption of its gene, $s i g G ,$ , has no obvious effect on growth, morphology, differentiation, and production of antibiotics, even under different stress conditions. Expression of sigG was undetectable during all developmental stages and after several stress conditions (osmotic stress, heat shock, cold shock, oxidative stress, acid stress, and ethanol stress). However, two promoters were identified using a heterologous E. coli two-plasmid system as dependent upon $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { G } }$ , and they both were transcribed in vitro after association of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { G } }$ with S. coelicolor core RNA polymerase. However, as for sigG, expression of these two promoters could not be detected in S. coelicolor (Kormanec et al., 1999; Sevcikova et al., 2005). 

## 4.4.9 Interconnection of S. coelicolor $\sigma ^ { \ B }$ homologues and concluding remarks

As mentioned above, all these S. coelicolor homologues of B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ are highly similar in the regions 2.4 and 4.2 that are responsible for interaction with cognate promoters (Figure 4.4.4). Therefore, they all might recognize very similar promoters. It is likely that regulons of these σ factors partially overlap, unless there is some regulatory mechanism assigning a particular promoter just for a specific σ factor. 

Actually, many $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } .$ - and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ -dependent promoters are only partially dependent upon the particular σ factor (Kormanec and Sevcikova, 2002b; Lee et al., 2005), thus indicating the recognition of the promoters by an additional $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologue. As mentioned in Section 4.4 $^ { . 6 , }$ the best characterized example of such overlapping is the osmotic stress-induced $d p s A p$ promoter, directing expression of a gene for the DpsA protein with a dual role in stress response and differentiation, which is clearly dependent upon both $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ (Facey et al., 2011). Likewise, the B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } .$ -dependent Pctc promoter, which is identical to the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ consensus sequence in the -35 and -10 promoter regions, is induced by osmotic stress in S. coelicolor $\mathrm { A } 3 ( 2 )$ and is recognized in the in vitro transcription assay by RNA polymerase containing three $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues, ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { B } } , { \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ , and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { I } }$ (Viollier et al., 2003a). Moreover, when used in a heterologous E. coli two-plasmid system (Novakova et al., 1998), the Pctc promoter was active with all nine $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues of S. coelicolor A3(2) (J. Kormanec, unpublished results). These data are in agreement with the fact that the consensus sequence of the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ -dependent promoters in S. coelicolor A3(2) (GNNTN– $\mathrm { N _ { 1 4 - 1 6 }  – G G G T A C / T } )$ is highly similar to the B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ consensus $( \mathrm { G T T A A - N _ { 1 2 - 1 4 } - G G G T A T } )$ (Lee et al., 2004). However, some $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues are rather specific in the recognition of their target promoters, like the ${ \mathfrak { C } } ^ { \bar { \mathrm { F } } }$ -dependent $s s p A p$ promoter (Tzanis et al., 2014). Moreover, the activity of some ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues is restricted to specific cell types during development, such as the prespore compartment for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ (Sun et al., 1999) and the subapical stem of the aerial hyphae for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { N } }$ (Dalton et al., 2007). Therefore, some other mechanisms should exist to ensure this specificity. One of them could be additional roles of transcriptional activators for the induction of these promoters, as previously found for the WhiB regulator in the developmental induction of the ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { H } } .$ - and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } .$ -dependent dpsAp promoter (Facey et al., 2011). It is also reasonable to assume that some specificity in the promoters, most likely in the -35 and -10 promoter regions, should exist among these σ factors. However, up to now no specific bases in these regions have been assigned to the specific $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues. Comparison of the -10 region for the ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ - dependent promoters revealed the sequence GGGCAT in the -10 region that is partially different to the consensus sequence of the ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { { \bar { \mathrm { B } } } _ { \cdot } }$ -dependent promoters, GGGTAC/G (Facey et al., 2011). However, no direct evidence has confirmed this suggestion. Thus, this investigation will be a challenge for further studies. 

Another case of the regulatory interconnection arises from a multitude of homologues of anti-σ factors (45) and anti-anti-σ factors (17) in S. coelicolor (Mittenhuber, 2002), suggesting that some anti-σ factors may interact with more than one σ factor or anti-anti-σ factor. Indeed, a pleiotropic anti-anti-σ factor BldG has been found to specifically interact with at least three anti-σ factors (ApgA, UshX, and ${ \mathrm { R s f A } } )$ , and this interaction is involved in activation of at least two differentiation-specific σ factors, ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { F } }$ (Mingyar et al., 2014; Parashar et al., 2009; Sevcikova et al., 2010). In addition, RsfA also specifically interacts with two other proposed anti-anti-σ factors, SCO0781 and SCO0869 (Kim et al., 2008), although they are not specifically phosphorylated by this protein kinase. On the other hand, SCO0869 is phosphorylated by PrsI, a σI -specific anti-σ factor, which additionally phosphorylates the anti-anti-σ factor ArsI. Moreover, in addition to RsfA, another anti-σ factor is present in S. coelicolor that phosphorylates BldG (Mingyar et al., 2014). 

In B. subtilis, the critical signal to activate $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ is transduced through the activation of the RsbU and RsbP PP2C phosphatases (Hecker et al., 2007; Price, 2002). However, S. coelicolor contains at least 44 RsbU–RsbP homologues. Moreover, their domain analysis revealed that, in addition to a PP2C phosphatase domain, they contain a large variety of other domains involved in signal transduction pathways (Mittenhuber, 2002). This indicates a complex interplay of various signals to activate particular anti-anti-σ factors. However, none of these RsbU– RsbP homologues has been investigated to control σ factor activation yet. Based on these data, it is clear that the cascades of the activation of these nine $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues in S. coelicolor are rather complex and partially interconnected. Further comprehensive work will be needed to reveal the complete picture of this interesting and complex activation. Such experiments are in progress also in our laboratory. 

Investigation of the nine $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues also revealed that many of them are involved in the osmotic stress response (see Section 11), and there is an interconnection between this response and differentiation. Based on the current results, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ acts as a master regulator of the osmotic stress response, governing expression of two other osmotic stress-induced $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues, ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { L } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } }$ (Lee et al., 2005). However, microarray analysis during osmotic stress revealed different osmotic stressinduced kinetics for the osmotically-induced $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } .$ -homologous genes in this order: sigI, sigB, sigK, sigM, sigH, and sigL (Karoonuthaisiri et al., 2005). Based on our preliminary results, osmotic stress-induced genes with early kinetics are dependent upon $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ and those with late kinetics are dependent upon ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ , in the correlation with this kinetics (J. Kormanec, unpublished results). Therefore, the osmotic stress response in S. coelicolor is a rather complex process involving multiple $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ -homologues. Their regulatory proteins and regulation, even regulons, might be interconnected, thus ensuring the integration of multiple signals leading to the activation of a specific gene set. 

At least two $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ homologues, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ and ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ , have dual roles in osmotic stress response and differentiation. Why should this be? As soil bacteria, in addition to nutrient limitation and other physical stress stimuli, such as low and high temperatures, and oxidative, acid, and alkaline stresses, streptomycetes are often exposed to desiccation in their natural habitat. To deal with this, the osmotic stress response maintains intracellular turgor within physiological acceptable levels. This may explain why multiple σ factors have evolved to control this osmotic stress response. Also, internal turgor has been suggested to be important in two different stages during differentiation, first at the time of initiation of aerial mycelium formation, and in the second stage during aerial mycelium septation (Bruton et al., 1995). Thus, the osmotic state seems to be an important physical element for differentiation in Streptomyces. Based on their mutant phenotypes, σB might be involved in this first stage and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ in the second stage. 

It is evident that the process of the stress response in S. coelicolor is different from that of unicellular bacteria like E. coli and B. subtilis, and owing to its connection with development it is rather complicated. Further experiments are still needed to decipher this complex regulatory network.

# Proteolytic activation of extra cytoplasmic function (ECF) ?? factors

Jessica L. Hastie and Craig D. Ellermeier 

Department of Microbiology, University of Iowa, Iowa City, Iowa, USA 

## 4.5.1 Introduction

Signal transduction across the membrane is critical for bacterial adaptation to environmental changes, and one mechanism of signaling utilizes extra cytoplasmic function (ECF) σ factors. ECF σ factors alter gene expression by interacting with RNA polymerase to promote transcription of specific genes in response to environmental signals (Helmann, 2002; Lonetto et al., 1994; Staron´ et al., 2009). Most ECF σ factors are encoded in an operon with a gene encoding an anti-σ factor, which inhibits the ECF σ factor from interacting with RNA polymerase, and thus transcription of target genes (Brown and Hughes, 1995; Staron´ et al., 2009). In the presence of the inducing signal, the ECF σ factor is released from the anti-σ factor to interact with RNA polymerase and transcribe genes in response to the initiating signal (Brown and Hughes, 1995; Staron´ et al., 2009; see Chapter 2.6 and Section 4). 

ECF σ factors encompass the largest group of alternative σ factors and are part of the $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ family of σ factors (Staron´ et al., 2009). However, compared to other σ70 family σ factors, the ECF σ factors are structurally compact (Staron´ et al., 2009). The primary σ factors, including $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ in Escherichia coli, are considered the “housekeeping” σ factors. The primary σ factors are composed of four domains, have high promoter melting capabilities, and are more flexible in promoter recognition allowing transcription of genes encoding a wide range of cellular processes (Campagne et al., 2014). Conversely, ECF σ factors only contain two of the four domains found in the primary σ factors; domains 2 and 4 (Lonetto et al., 1994; Staron´ et al., 2009). In addition to interacting with RNA polymerase, these domains are necessary for recognizing the -10 and -35 regions of bacterial promoters. Domain 4 recognizes the -35 region and is responsible for initial promoter recognition (Lane and Darst, 2006; see Chapter 2.6). Domain 2 was recently shown to provide promoter specificity using a protein pocket in subdomain 2.3 to target the flipping out of one base, rather than two, during promoter melting (Campagne et al., 2014; Darst et al., 2014). As a result, promoter melting becomes less efficient, but promoter specificity for unique promoters increases. This specificity is thought to allow an organism encoding multiple ECF σ factors the ability to distinguish closely related promoter sequences (Darst et al., 2014). 

The number of ECF σ factors within an organism can vary greatly. Thorsten Mascher’s group characterized ECF σ factors into groups based on comparative genomic analysis of ECF σ factor/anti-σ factor pairing, gene organization, and domain architecture resulting in 43 major groups from analysis of 369 genomes (Staron´ et al., 2009; for an update see Chapter 2.6). There are many mechanisms of activation depending on the structure of the σ factor/anti-σ factor pair. In Chapter 2.6, Thorsten Mascher highlights the range of known mechanisms including proteolytic cascade, partner switching, phosphorylation, conformation change, or protein–protein interactions. Here, we present the current knowledge of those anti-σ factors degraded by a stepwise proteolytic cascade known as regulated intramembrane proteolysis (RIP). Additionally, we provide insight into how some anti-σ factors have secondary roles in addition to sequestering the ECF σ factor from RNA polymerase. 

## 4.5.2 Regulated intramembrane proteolysis

Proteolytic cleavage is a common mechanism used to regulate many bacterial processes including enzyme activation, protein clearance, and cell-to-cell signaling. RIP specifically degrades membrane proteins by the sequential action of multiple proteases (Brown et al., 2000). In the presence of the inducing signal, a site-1 protease cleaves the extracellular domain of a membrane-bound protein. Following site-1 protease cleavage, the truncated membrane protein is cleaved by a site-2 protease within the transmembrane region of the protein. The remainder of the cleaved protein is then active, or in some cases further degradation by cytosolic proteases is required to release a transcription factor. RIP is a process that is conserved from bacteria to humans (Brown et al., 2000). The general mechanism appears rather simple: two cleavage events to remove a membrane protein (Figure 4.5.1). However, the types of proteases involved in RIP vary widely depending on the organism, and some RIP systems require additional accessory proteins that influence the regulation of these cleavage events. The best studied ECF σ factors regulated by RIP are found in groups ECF01– 04, which have high sequence similarity, and are known collectively as the RpoE-like ECF σ factors (Staron´ et al., 2009; see Chapter 2.6). 


Figure 4.5.1 General mechanism of RIP in ECF σ factor activation. In the absence of a stress signal, the σ factor is prevented from interacting with RNA polymerase by a transmembrane anti-σ. (a) This inhibition is released upon exposure to an inducing signal that causes site-1 protease (S1P) cleavage to occur. (b) Site-2 protease (S2P) cleavage immediately follows. (c) Finally, cytoplasmic proteases degrade the remainder of the anti-σ to release the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E C F } }$ to activate genes in response to the signal.

## 4.5.3 ECF ?? factor activation by RIP

Most of the work on RIP-regulated ECF σ factors has focused on $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ from E. coli (ECF02) $\quad \mathrm { o r } \ \sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ from Bacillus subtilis (ECF01). Group ECF01 is diverse and found in nine different phyla, while ECF σ factors in group ECF02 have high sequence similarity and are primarily found in proteobacteria (Staron´ et al., 2009). Generally, these ECF σ factors are activated by a form of cell envelope stress, and the anti-σ factors have a single-pass transmembrane region and an N-terminal anti-σ domain (ASD) (Staron´ et $a l .$ , 2009). While we have a detailed understanding of ${ \mathfrak { c } } ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ activation in E. coli, recent evidence suggests that ECF σ factors from other organisms may utilize variations in the method of RIP to control activation of ECF σ factors. Here, we compare the mechanisms of RIP regulation known for ECF σ factors. 

## 4.5.3.1 E. coli ??E

$\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ is essential in E. coli and is required for outer membrane biogenesis (De Las Penas˜ et $a l .$ , 1997b; Hiratsu et al., 1995). Activation of this system is controlled by the accumulation of misfolded outer membrane β-barrel proteins in the periplasm due to either improper expression of the genes encoding these proteins or damage to the outer membrane (De Las Penas˜ et al., 1997b; Missiakas et al., 1997). $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ activity is inhibited by the anti-σ factor RseA, a single-pass transmembrane protein that sequesters $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ in the absence of outer membrane stress (De Las Penas˜ et al., 1997a). Additionally, two factors encoded by $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ also modulate $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ activity: RseB and RseC (De Las Penas˜ et al., 1997a). RseB is a periplasmic protein that negatively regulates $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ activity through RseA (Ahuja et al., 2009; De Las Penas˜ et al., 1997a). RseC is an inner membrane protein that activates $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ activity by an unknown mechanism (De Las Penas et al., 1997a; Missiakas et al., 1997). 

$\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ is activated by the destruction of RseA. This process is initiated by the site-1 protease DegS, a member of the HtrA– DegP family of serine proteases (Ades et al., 1999; Wilken et al., 2004). In the absence of stress, the activity of DegS is inhibited by the DegS PDZ domain (Walsh et al., 2003). PDZ domains are small domains (∼80–90 amino acids) that often bind to the C-termini of other proteins (Fanning and Anderson, 1996). The PDZ domain of DegS binds to the unique C-termini of unfolded outer membrane proteins relieving the inhibition of DegS activity and allowing for cleavage of RseA at site-1, which eventually leads to σE activation (Grigorova et al., 2004). This model is supported by the observation that removal of the PDZ domain results in constitutive cleavage of RseA and activation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ (Walsh et al., 2003). 

Following site-1 cleavage by DegS, the site-2 protease RseP further processes RseA by cleaving RseA within the transmembrane helix (Alba et al., 2002; Kanehara et al., 2002). RseP is a site-2 intramembrane protease that contains two PDZ domains, RseP-PDZ-N and RseP-PDZ-C (Inaba et al., 2008). Post RseP cleavage, the remaining cytosolic portion of RseA is degraded by the cellular proteases ClpXP, ClpAP, Lon, FstH, and HslUV (Chaba et al., 2007). Upon release from RseA, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ binds to RNA polymerase and transcribes a wide range of genes involved in protein folding and lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis in addition to transcribing the genes of the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ operon including rpoE $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } } )$ , rseA, rseB, and rseC (Dartigalongue et al., 2001). 

The periplasmic protein RseB inhibits $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ activity by directly binding RseA (Ahuja et al., 2009; Cezairliyan and Sauer, 2007; Collinet et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2010). It is thought that RseB protects RseA from DegS cleavage by masking the DegS cleavage site (Grigorova, 2004; Kim et al., 2010). Recent evidence suggests that RseB is released from RseA upon binding to lipopolysaccharide (LPS), thus allowing DegS cleavage (Lima et al., 2013). Thus, DegS and RseB serve as independent mechanisms to tie $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ activation to outer membrane damage. 

$\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ orthologs are found primarily in γ-proteobacteria including Salmonella, Pseudomonas, Vibrio, and Yersinia (Alba and Gross, 2004; Rhodius et al., 2006). In fact, many of the genes involved in regulating $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ activity (rpoE, rseA, rseB, rseC, rseP, and degS) are functionally conserved in these organisms. Although slightly different environmental conditions lead to activation of these $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ homologs, it is thought that these conditions result in the accumulation of one or more outer membrane proteins, which serve as the trigger leading to σ factor activation, similar to what occurs in E. coli (Rowley et al., 2006). See Chapter 4.7 for further details comparing $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ regulation in E. coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. 

## 4.5.3.2 B. subtilis ${ \mathfrak { \sigma } } ^ { \boldsymbol { w } }$

Of the seven ECF σ factors in B. subtilis, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ is the best studied in terms of the mechanism of activation. Various cell envelope stressors (including heat, alkaline stress, and cell wall active antibiotics) activate ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { w } }$ resulting in transcription of 89 genes (Cao et al., 2002; Helmann, 2006; Wiegert et al., 2001; Zweers et al., 2012). However, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ activation is best achieved by antimicrobial peptides produced by other bacteria, and is required for resistance to many of these antimicrobial peptides (Butcher and Helmann, 2006; Ellermeier and Losick, 2006). $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ is encoded immediately upstream of the gene encoding the anti-σ factor RsiW, and in the absence of cell envelope stress, RsiW sequesters $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ to the membrane (Yoshimura et al., 2004). In the presence of cell envelope stress, RsiW is cleaved by the site-1 protease PrsW, a metallo-protease with similarity to a CAAX prenyl endopeptidase in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Ellermeier and Losick 2006; Heinrich et al., 2009). Unlike $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ in E. coli, cleavage by the site-1 protease is not sufficient for cleavage by a site-2 protease. Prior to site-2 cleavage, RsiW is trimmed by an unknown protease (Heinrich et al., 2009). After RsiW trimming occurs, the site-2 protease RasP (a homolog of RseP in E. coli) cleaves RsiW within the transmembrane domain helix (Schobel et al., 2004). The remaining cytoplasmic portion of RsiW is degraded by ClpXP or ClpCP (Zellmeier et al., 2006). B. subtilis encodes a second negative regulator of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ activity, YsdB, and a mutation in ysdB causes a slight increase in $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ activity (Ellermeier and Losick, 2006; Turner and Helmann, 2000). YsdB is a transmembranebound protein, but unlike RseB it is not known how YsdB inhibits $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ activation. 

## 4.5.3.3 B. subtilis $\bullet ^ { \boldsymbol { v } }$

Another ECF σ factor in B. subtilis, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } } ;$ , is also controlled by RIP. $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ is a member of the group ECF30, which is primarily found in Firmicutes, and only 50% of the members are co-transcribed with an anti-σ factor (Staron´ et al., 2009). However, similar to $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ , activity of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ is inhibited by a single-pass transmembrane anti-σ protein (RsiV), which prevents $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ from interacting with RNA polymerase (Hastie et al., 2013). Although both $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ are controlled by RIP, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ regulation is different in several key aspects. 

First, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ is activated by a wide range of cell envelope stressors, but $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ is activated only by lysozyme, which cleaves the β 1-4 linkage between N-acetyl-D-glucosamine and N-acetyl-D-muramic acid (Alderton and Ward, 1945; Callewaert and Michiels, 2010; Guariglia-Oropeza and Helmann, 2011; Ho et al., 2011). Interestingly, only C-type lysozymes activate $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ , while other muramidases are unable to activate $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ (Guariglia-Oropeza and Helmann, 2011; Hastie et al., 2014). 

Second, the site-1 protease responsible for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ activation appears to be redundant. Determination of the site-1 protease cleavage site revealed that the cleavage site followed an AXA motif, suggestive of signal peptidase cleavage (Hastie et al., 2014). Mutation of the signal peptidase recognition AXA motif to AXW abolishes site-1 cleavage of RsiV, suggesting a signal peptidase is involved (Hastie et al., 2014). B. subtilis has five chromosomally encoded signal peptidases (Tjalsma et al., 1997; van Roosmalen et al., 2001). Since signal peptidases in B. subtilis have overlapping substrates (Bolhuis et al., 1996), multiple signal peptidases likely have a role in RsiV degradation. SipS was sufficient to induce cleavage of RsiV at site-1 in vitro only in the presence of lysozyme (Hastie et al., 2014). Since peptidoglycan is not present in the in vitro reactions, it suggests that the muramidase activity of lysozyme is not necessary for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ activation. Furthermore, a catalytically inactive version of lysozyme still activates $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ (Hastie et al., 2014). 

A third difference from $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ activation is that the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ anti-σ factor is responsible for sensing the inducing signal lysozyme. RsiV contains a relatively large extracellular domain that is predicted to form a β-grasp domain. The extracellular domain of RsiV directly interacts with lysozyme at a $\mathrm { K _ { d } }$ of ${ \sim } 7 0$ nM (Hastie et al., 2014). This observation combined with the observation that lysozyme is required for SipS to induce site-1 cleavage in vitro suggest that the anti-σ factor RsiV directly senses lysozyme. However, the molecular changes that occur when lysozyme binds RsiV that allow cleavage by signal peptidase are not known. 

Upon removal of the extracellular domain by signal peptidase, the site-2 protease RasP cleaves RsiV within the membrane. In the absence of rasP, a truncated version of RsiV accumulates at the site-1 protease processing site (Hastie et al., 2013). The cytoplasmic remainder of RsiV is presumably degraded by cytoplasmic proteases similar to RsiW. Upon release from RsiV, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ interacts with RNA polymerase to transcribe genes required for lysozyme resistance. This includes oatA, which encodes a peptidoglycan O-acetylase that adds an acetyl group to peptidoglycan, which prevents further lysozyme damage (Guariglia-Oropeza and Helmann, 2011; Ho et al., 2011). Other cell envelope– modifying genes (abh, ywaC, bcrC, dltABCDE, pbpX, and yqjL) are induced to a lesser degree by $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ (Guariglia-Oropeza and Helmann, 2011). These genes are also regulated by $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ , $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { X } } { } _ { ; }$ , and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } }$ , suggesting the low-level activation by $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ may be due to overlap in promoter recognition (Guariglia-Oropeza and Helmann, 2011; Luo and Helmann, 2009). The high level of induction of the sigVrsiVoatA operon compared to other targets may be due to the specific response required for lysozyme resistance, thus resulting in a relatively small $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ regulon. 

$\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ has been studied in two other Gram-positive organisms that are nosocomial pathogens, and highly resistant to lysozyme: Clostridium $d i f \hbar$ cile and Enterococcus faecalis (Ho et $a l . ,$ , 2014; Le Jeune et $a l .$ , 2010). The lysozyme resistance provided by $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ activation is thought to protect against the host innate immune response. A csfV mutant is attenuated in the hamster C. difficile infection model, and bacterial burden from a sigV mutant is reduced in a mouse E. faecalis model (Ho et al., 2014; Le Jeune et al., 2010). Regulation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ in these organisms appears to follow the same trend as in B. subtilis. Lysozyme binds the purified RsiV extracellular domain of both C. difficile and E. faecalis (Hastie et al., 2014). Additionally, both organisms have multiple signal peptidases and contain RasP homologs. In E. faecalis, it has been shown that an eep mutant, which encodes a site-2 protease homolog, prevents $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ activation (Varahan et al., 2013). Although these homologs appear to follow the same mechanism as in B. subtilis, it is not known if other factors are involved. E. faecalis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ can reportedly be activated by heat and ethanol stress, although not to the same degree as is seen in the presence of lysozyme (Benachour et al., 2005). As RsiV is responsible for sensing the inducing signal lysozyme by direct binding, it is unclear how RsiV would also sense heat and ethanol stress, or if an alternative mechanism is involved. 

## 4.5.3.4 Pseudomonas putida IutY

In Gram-negative bacteria, the outer membrane is an additional barrier to the extracellular environment. Thus, to sense the extracellular surface, some ECF σ factors in Gram-negative bacteria also require an outer membrane receptor, which is responsible for sensing the inducing signal. The combination of ECF σ factor, anti-σ factor, and outer membrane receptor is known as cell-surface signaling (CSS) cascades (Braun et al., 2006; Llamas et al., 2014). The P. putida iron utilization and transport (Iut) ECF σ factor is a CSS system and is controlled by RIP (Bastiaansen et al., 2014). 

Iut responds to the siderophore aerobactin under conditions of iron deficiency (Bastiaansen et al., 2014). This system is unusual in that the σ and anti-σ are a hybrid protein IutY. Like other anti-σ factors that are part of CSS cascades, IutY contains a FecR domain in the C-terminal region of the anti-σ factor. FecR domains are highly conserved regions that resemble leucine zipper motifs and are suggested to aid in interaction with the outer membrane receptor (Braun et al., 2003). Activation of this system involves a specific outer membrane receptor IutA, which binds to aerobactin (Bastiaansen et al., 2014). Screening a transposon library of P. putida revealed the periplasmic protease Prc (Tsp or Ctp) to be required for site-1 cleavage and MucP (RseP) to be required for site-2 cleavage (Bastiaansen et al., 2014). It is hypothesized that interaction of IutA with IutY initiates site-1 cleavage; however, like RsiV and lysozyme, it is unclear how the binding initiates site-1 cleavage (Bastiaansen et al., 2014; Llamas et al., 2014). Upon RIP-mediated site-1 and site-2 cleavage, the cytoplasmic portion of this hybrid anti-σ/σ directly interacts with RNA polymerase to transcribe genes involved in aerobactin uptake (Bastiaansen et al., 2014). 

## 4.5.3.5 Other CSS systems in Pseudomonas

P. aeruginosa also encodes CSS systems that respond to pyoverdine (Pvd), ferrioxamine (Fox), and ferrichrome (Fiu), and it is suggested they use a RIP mechanism to control σ factor activation. These systems show decreased activation in a ΔrseP mutant (Bastiaansen et al., 2014; Draper et al., 2011). Additionally, a Δprc mutant reduces but does not abolish activity to the same extent as a $\Delta r s e P$ mutant in the Fox and Fiu systems, suggesting a role for Prc and possibly another protease in activating these systems (Bastiaansen et al., 2014). Unlike the Iut CSS system, it appears the cleavage events required by these systems can occur independent of the presence of signal (Bastiaansen et al., 2014; Draper et al., 2011). Further investigation is necessary to determine the exact mechanism and role of RIP in these systems. 

## 4.5.4 Proposed ECF ?? factors regulated by RIP

There are several anti-σ factors proposed to be regulated by RIP, based on their ability to be degraded by either a known site-1 protease or site-2 protease, and the presence of a transmembrane-bound anti-σ factor. In B. subtilis, six of the seven ECF σ factors have transmembrane-bound anti-σ factors (Yoshimura, 2004). It is likely that others in addition to $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ will be regulated by RIP, although this has not been directly tested. 

## 4.5.4.1 C. difficile $\pmb { \sigma } ^ { \mathsf { T } }$

C. difficile has three ECF σ factors, each with a transmembrane anti-σ factor; CsfV(σV)–RsiV, CsfU–RsiU, and CsfT–RsiT (Ho and Ellermeier, 2011). Only the inducing signal for CsfV is known (lysozyme), and, as mentioned, it is predicted that this system is regulated by a similar mechanism as $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ in B. subtilis. The inducing signals for the other two systems, CsfU and CsfT, are not known. RsiU is a multipass transmembrane protein, while RsiT is a signal pass transmembrane protein (Ho and Ellermeier, 2011). C. difficile contains a homolog of the site-1 protease PrsW from B. subtilis, which is 34% identical and 58% similar (Ho and Ellermeier, 2011). PrsW is co-expressed with RsiU or RsiT in B. subtilis and causes RsiT, but not RsiU, to be degraded (Ho and Ellermeier, 2011). These data suggest that RsiT is regulated by RIP through a mechanism involving PrsW (Ho and Ellermeier, 2011). C. difficile has a homolog of the site-2 protease RasP; however, the role of this site-2 protease has not been investigated. 

## 4.5.4.2 Mycobacterium tuberculosis $\bullet ^ { \mathsf { K } } , \bullet ^ { \mathsf { L } } , \bullet ^ { \mathsf { D } }$ , and ${ \pmb { \sigma } } ^ { \pmb { \mu } }$

Four of the 10 ECF σ factors in M. tuberculosis are regulated by the site-2 protease Rip1 (Sklar et al., 2010). Anti-σ factors RskA $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { K } } )$ , RslA (σL), RsdA $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { D } } )$ , and RsmA $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } } )$ are all cleaved by Rip1 (Schneider et al., 2014; Sklar et al., 2010). However, the site-1 proteases involved in these proteolytic cascades are not known. Three orthologs of DegS – Rv3668c, PepA, and Rv1043c – have been tested as possible site-1 protease candidates; however, mutations of these proteases do not block activation of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { K } }$ , σL, or $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } }$ (Sklar et al., 2010). It may be that the site-1 protease required for activation of these ECF σ factors is not homologous to DegS or multiple proteases may be able to perform site-1 cleavage. 

## 4.5.5 Other roles for site-2 proteases

All known site-2 proteases in bacteria belong to the same family of zinc metalloproteases, and often have multiple substrates and roles within the cell. In addition to cleaving RsiW and RsiV in B. subtilis, RasP also cleaves the cell division protein FtsL (Wadenpohl and Bramkamp, 2010). Likewise, Mycobacterium tuberculosis Rip1 (Rv2869c) cleaves the divisomal transpeptidase PBP3 (FtsI) under conditions of oxidative stress (Mukherjee et al., 2009). 

Vibrio cholerae has a homolog of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ that is also regulated by DegS and the site-2 protease YaeL (a homolog of RseP). Additionally, YaeL also helps regulate another transcription factor, TcpP, which is stabilized by the membrane protein TcpH (Matson and DiRita, 2005). In contrast to ECF σ factors that are activated upon release from the membrane, TcpP stabilization at the membrane by TcpH activates toxT gene expression, which is important for virulence (Matson and DiRita, 2005). Thus, YaeL acts to decrease transcription of toxT, by degrading TcpP in a DegS-independent mechanism (Matson and DiRita, 2005). 

In eukaryotes, signal peptide peptidases have a preference for membrane proteins with a type II orientation (NH , cytosolic; COOH, extracellular) (Chou and Elrod, 1999). Anti-σ factors that have been cleaved at site-1 often resemble processed signal peptides. Thus, it may not be surprising to find that in addition to their role in ECF σ factor activation, site-2 proteases are also involved in clearing processed signal peptides from the membrane (Saito et al., 2011). This suggests that site-2 proteases can function in an analogous manner to signal peptide peptidases from eukaryotes. 

## 4.5.6 Diversity of site-1 proteases

Site-2 proteases are often identified based on homology; however, site-1 proteases are more challenging to identify due to either their specificity or redundancy in the case of $\sigma ^ { \dot { \mathrm { v } } }$ . In the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ system, DegS uses the PDZ domain to interact with the Nterminal regions of unfolded outer membrane proteins (Walsh et al., 2003). It is not known what molecular events allow PrsW to cleave RsiW in the presence of cell envelope stress (Heinrich et al., 2009). However, the isolation of mutations in prsW, which render $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } }$ activation constitutive, suggest that PrsW may indeed be the sensor for cell envelope stress (Ellermeier and Losick, 2006). In the case of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ activation, site-1 cleavage is thought to be mediated by RsiV binding the inducing signal lysozyme (Hastie et al., 2014). Thus, in the three best studied cases of RIP-mediated ECF σ factor activation in bacteria, the general process is conserved, but the mechanisms governing this are quite diverse. 

## 4.5.7 Transmembrane anti-?? factors as sensors

The B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { V } }$ anti-σ factor, RsiV, is the first example of a RIP-regulated anti-σ factor that directly binds and senses the inducing signal to initiate anti-σ factor destruction in a Grampositive organism. The anti-σ/σ factor IutY from P. putida appears to use a similar mechanism, although the interaction is indirect as part of a CSS system. IutY interacts with IutA, the aerobactin receptor, to initiate RIP, although the exact mechanism is not known (Bastiaansen et al., 2014). 

There are other examples of membrane-bound anti-σ factors involved in direct protein–protein interactions in groups ECF05–10. Groups ECF05–09 are generally CSS systems involved in iron acquisition similar to the FecI system from E. coli (for a detailed review on this ECF σ factor, see Brooks and Buchanan, 2008). Proteolysis may have a function in some of these systems (P. aeruginosa Pvd, Fox, and Fiu, mentioned in this chapter), but the exact role is not clear. Additionally, based on putative sensing domains of the anti-σ factors from Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron in group ECF10, it is hypothesized that these ECF σ factors may be responsible for responding to polysaccharides present in the environment of the intestinal tract (Karlsson et al., 2011; Mascher, 2013; Xu et al., 2004). 

Another anti-σ factor from Clostridium thermocellum is known to have a role in sensing polysaccharides. C. thermocellum, a Gram-positive anaerobic bacterium, is known for its ability to hydrolyze cellulose through an enzymatic complex known as the cellulosome (Kahel-Raifer et al., 2010). Extracellular carbohydrates affect the composition of the cellulosome by regulating which enzymes and structural components are present, thus ensuring the correct factors are present to break down available carbohydrates (Nataf et al., 2010). Six putative operons encoding alterative σ factors and anti-σ factors were identified that have homology to the B. subtilis $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { I } } -$ –RsgI pair, and are involved in regulating the genes that encode the cellulosome (Kahel-Raifer et al., 2010). All six σI -like σ factors are upregulated in the presence of cellulose and xylan (Nataf et al., 2010). Additionally, the RsgI-like anti-σ factors have larger extracellular domains compared to B. subtilis RsgI. Based on these large domains, these anti-σ factors were predicted to have a role in sensing polysaccharides. These extracellular domains contain putative carbohydrate binding (CBM3 and CBM42), sugar binding (PA14), and glycoside hydrolase family 10 (GH10) domains (Nataf et al., 2010). Three of the anti-σ factors with CBM3 carbohydrate-binding domains have been crystalized and assessed for their ability to bind crystalline and amorphous cellulose, xylan, xyloglucan, and galactan from a variety of plant sources (Yaniv et al., 2014). It was found that differences in structure accounted for preferential binding to different carbohydrate sources, suggesting a method of differentially regulating genes (Yaniv et al., 2014). However, it is currently unknown how the RsgI-like anti-σ factors’ interaction with carbohydrates facilitates activation of the σ factor. 

## 4.5.8 Conclusions

With the advances in genomics sequencing, the identification of ECF σ/anti-σ pairs has greatly expanded. However, the challenge remains of identifying the inducing signal(s), regulated genes, and mechanism of activation. Activation by RIP is a common mechanism for controlling gene expression, and new systems are exposing variations in the initiation of RIP. Although there are many examples in which the site-1 protease controls activation $( \mathrm { e . g . , } \sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } } \mathrm { a n d } \sigma ^ { \mathrm { W } } )$ , it is also clear that in some cases the anti-σ factor is able to control when activation occurs by directly interacting with the environmental signal $( \mathrm { e . g . , \mathfrak { o } ^ { V } }$ and IutY). Interestingly, these systems are not part of the RpoE-like family of ECF σ factors. It is likely that other ECF σ factors regulated by RIP will also display adaptations involved in sensing the inducing signal by either the site-1 protease, the anti-σ factor, or another adaptor molecule.

# The ECF family sigma factor $\sigma ^ { \mathsf { H } }$ in Corynebacterium glutamicum controls the thiol-oxidative stress response

Tobias Busche and Jorn Kalinowski¨ 

Microbial Genomics and Biotechnology, Center for Biotechnology (CeBiTec), Bielefeld University, Bielefeld, Germany 

## 4.6.1 Introduction

Corynebacterium glutamicum is a Gram-positive soil bacterium that belongs to the order Actinomycetales, which also includes genera like Mycobacterium and Streptomyces. C. glutamicum is an industrial microorganism that is used for the large-scale production of various amino acids (e.g. glutamate and lysine). It has also been shown to produce vitamins (Huser ¨ et al., 2005), organic acids (Wieschalka et al., 2012), higher alcohols (Blombach and Eikmanns, 2011), diamines (Kind et $a l .$ , 2010), and polylactic acid (Song et al., 2012). The data provided by the complete C. glutamicum genome sequence (Ikeda et al., 2003; Kalinowski et al., 2003) enabled genome-wide analyses and the application of comparative genomics to assign functions to uncharacterized genes. Furthermore, the availability of genetic engineering methods, its easy cultivation, and its “generally recognized as $\operatorname { s a f e } ^ { \mathrm { \infty } }$ status have helped to make it a model organism for systems biology investigations in the Corynebacterineae, comprising important pathogens such as Corynebacterium diphtheriae and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Wendisch et al., 2006). 

The C. glutamicum genome codes for seven different sigma subunits of RNA polymerase, all of them of the $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ type. These sigma factors fall into three groups according to the classification by Gruber and Gross (2003): the primary sigma factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { A } }$ (Group 1), the primary-like sigma factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ (Group 2), and alternative factors $\bar { \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { C } } , \mathfrak { o } ^ { \mathrm { D } } , \bar { \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { E } } , \mathfrak { o } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ , and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } }$ , which are all members of Group 4, also called extracytoplasmic function (ECF) sigma factors (see Chapter 2.6). ECF sigma factors are a central signaling mechanism in bacteria, outnumbered only by the already wellknown modes of 1CS and 2CS signaling, and they represent the third pillar of bacterial signal transduction (Staron´ et al., 2009). 

A comprehensive comparative genomic analysis of the ECF sigma factor protein family identified more than 40 distinct major groups of ECF sigma factors. The five ECF sigma factors of C. glutamicum belong to five different subgroups and are part of the M. tuberculosis ECF sigma factor set, which consists of 10 ECF sigma factors, and of Streptomyces coelicolor, which has 51 ECF sigma factors (Staron´ et al., 2009; Ulrich and Zhulin, 2010). The C. glutamicum sigma factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { C } }$ belongs to group $\mathrm { E C F } 3 6 , \sigma ^ { \mathrm { D } }$ to group ECF40, and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } }$ to group ECF27. The members of these groups are exclusively found in Actinobacteria. $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { C } }$ and ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { D } }$ are characterized in M. tuberculosis, and both were found associated with pathogenicity (Calamita et al., 2005; Karls et al., 2006). Of the ${ \sigma } ^ { \overset { \mathrm { ~ \tiny ~ ~ } } { \mathrm { ~ \tiny ~ 1 ~ } } }$ group, only the function of C. glutamicum $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { M } }$ was analyzed in detail, showing that it regulates genes involved in the oxidative stress and the heat stress response (Nakunst et al., 2007; see Chapter 2.6). 

The ECF sigma factor ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ belongs to the group ECF12 $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { R } } .$ like proteins), and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ to the group ECF14. The proteins of the subgroups ECF11 to ECF15 are not closely related, but all have cytoplasmic antisigma factor proteins to control their respective activities. The antisigma factors corresponding to $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ are encoded by the rshA and cseE genes, respectively (Busche et al., 2012; Park et al., 2008). A common feature of ECF sigma factor genes is that they are mostly co-expressed with genes encoding their cognate antisigma factor (Staron´ et al., 2009; see Chapter 2.6). 

All antisigma factors of the RshA–RsrA group have a ZAS domain (zinc-binding antisigma domain), and all analyzed members have a function in sensing redox balance and are involved in the stress response to an imbalance of the redox state causing oxidative stress (Staron´ et al., 2009; see Section 10). The sigma factor–antisigma factor pairs $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { R } } { \mathrm { - R s r A } }$ in S. coelicolor and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } } .$ –RshA in M. tuberculosis (both of them orthologs of $C .$ glutamicum ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } } { \mathrm { - R s h A ) } }$ regulate main parts of the thioloxidative stress response. The $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { R } } .$ –RsrA pair is found to control the response to disulfide stress by the reversible oxidation and inactivation of the antisigma factor, inducing transcription of genes encoding thioredoxins, mycothiol metabolism, proteases, and others that constitute the disulfide stress response in S. coelicolor (Paget et al., 1998, 2001; Park and Roe, 2008). In addition, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { R } }$ acts in an auto-inducing manner via a ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { R } }$ -responsive promoter upstream of the sigR–rsrA operon. The same holds for $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } } { \mathrm { - R s h A } }$ in M. tuberculosis, which controls among others the cellular redox systems, such as thioredoxin genes trxA, trxB1, and trxC, and the gene encoding thioredoxin reductase trxB2 (Raman et al., 2001). Since heat stress is intrinsically tied to oxidative stress, these genes are also involved in heat stress response (see Section 13). 

In the first part of this chapter, we will review and discuss the transcriptional organization of the C. glutamicum sigH–rshA operon and its regulation under a thiol-oxidative stress response, compared with orthologous genes (sigR–rsrA in S. coelicolor and sigH–rshA in M. tuberculosis). The second part will deal with the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ regulon and how it was expanded by different studies in the last decade. In the third part, we introduce the massively parallel sequencing of complementary DNA (cDNA), known as RNA-seq, as a novel tool for the comprehensive and detailed analysis of bacterial sigma factor networks at the examples of the sigH–rshA operon and $\mathsf { a c } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ target gene in C. glutamicum. 

## 4.6.2 Transcriptional organization of genes encoding $\sigma ^ { \mathsf { H } }$ and its corresponding antisigma factor RshA

As introduced in Section 4.6.1, a common feature of ECF sigma factor genes is that they are co-transcribed with genes encoding their cognate antisigma factor (see Chapter 2.6). The same arrangement of the sigH (cg0876) and rshA (cg0877) genes was found in the genomes of C. glutamicum ATCC 13032 (Kalinowski et al., 2003), C. glutamicum strain R (Toyoda et $a l .$ , 2015), and C. jeikeium (Tauch et al., 2005). In the C. glutamicum genomes, the translational stop codon of sigH is only separated by two nucleotides from the translation initiation codon of rshA, indicating an operon-like structure (Busche et al., 2012). 

In C. glutamicum, four promoters upstream of sigH–rshA, all of them housekeeping promoters recognized by $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { A } }$ , transcribe the whole operon (Figure 4.6.1). This was shown by Northern analyses (Busche et al., 2012) and recently validated by RNA-seq (Pfeifer-Sancar et al., 2013). The most upstream of them $( \mathrm { P s i g H _ { A 4 } } )$ is likely to be controlled by the SOS response regulator LexA (see Section 7) (Jochmann et al., 2009). The reason for having multiple promoters might ensure fine-tuning, either by the action of additional transcription factors like LexA or by the different affinities of these promoters to ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { A } }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ , the non-essential sigma factor of C. glutamicum that also targets housekeeping promoters (Larisch et al., 2007). Experimental observations are in line with this assumption. It was shown by real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and transcriptional reporter fusions to a chloramphenicol acetyltransferase gene (P-sigH::cat) that the activity of the sigH promoter was elevated in the stationary phase and after oxidative stress (Kim et al., 2005a; Toyoda et al., 2015). 

The gene rshA is separately transcribed by a $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ -dependent internal promoter located in the sigH protein coding region upstream of rshA, which was shown by Northern blot and primer extension analyses (Busche et al., 2012). To analyze the promoter region of the rshA gene, a DNA fragment (301 base pairs (bp) upstream of rshA) was transcriptionally fused to the promoterless reporter gene cat. These measurements confirmed that rshA is also transcribed from the separate $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ -dependent Prsh $A _ { \mathrm { H } }$ promoter but at a very low level in the absence of stress, a condition at which $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ is inhibited by RshA. 

Additionally, Toyoda et al. (2015) still detected about half of the PrshA activity in a sigH mutant of C. glutamicum strain R. An additional induction of the promoter activity in the deletion mutant of rshA after heat shock to the level of the stressed wild type was reported as well. These authors speculate that the remaining rshA promoter activity and the heat induction imply involvement of a sigma factor other than ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ . Due to an RNAseq analysis of the C. glutamicum transcriptome in which we identified more than 2000 transcriptional starting points (TSPs) (Pfeifer-Sancar et al., 2013), we were able to reexamine the upstream region of rshA. Indeed, an additional TSP was identified upstream of the ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ -dependent promoter $\mathrm { P } r s h A _ { \mathrm { H } }$ . The corresponding promoter (TCAGCC – 20 nt – TATTAT) shows high similarity to the consensus sequence of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { A } } / \sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ -dependent promoters in C. glutamicum. 

The promoter was not detected in the study of Busche et al. (2012), probably because it was too weak to be noticeable by Northern analysis under standard growth conditions. During creation of the sigH mutant, this promoter was occasionally removed by the deletion within the sigH coding region. 

Combined with the facts that the $s i g B$ gene is transcribed via $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ and that $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ recognizes promoters that appear to be very similar if not indistinguishable from ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { A } }$ -dependent promoters (reviewed in Patek and Nesvera, 2011), there is potential that ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ controls the transcription of rshA additionally and indirectly by the use of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ , coupling the specific stress response with a more global physiological status of the cell. This would explain the additional upregulation of Prsh $\mathrm { A _ { A } }$ after heat shock, dependent on the ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ -dependent primary-like sigma factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ . The sigma factor $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ could have a higher affinity to Prsh $\mathrm { A _ { A } }$ than ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { A } }$ . Transcription of rshA from the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ -dependent promoter Prsh $A _ { \mathrm { H } }$ and from the putative indirectly ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ -dependent and additionally regulated $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { A } } / \sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ -dependent promoter $\mathrm { P } r s h A _ { \mathrm { A } }$ may lead to an excess of RshA protein over $\bar { \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ under stress conditions. This excess was probably evolved to guarantee a very fast and efficient shutdown of ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ -dependent transcriptional activation as soon as stress conditions end, and the high amount of RshA is reduced to its active form by the action of thioredoxins and mycothiol systems whose synthesis is induced by the action of ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ (Busche et al., 2012). Thus, ${ \sigma } ^ { \mathrm { H } }$ in $C .$ glutamicum and other corynebacteria is negatively regulated by the antisigma factor at the protein level, as is known for most actinomycetes (Kim et al., 2012), and additionally regulated by a positive feedforward or amplification loop of rshA at the transcriptional level, amplifying the regulation potential of RshA (Busche et al., 2012).
